0.title: Releasing the libraries
0.content: How an agent publishes the HCERT libraries (STT-NFR-002) once the owner has supplied credentials. Nothing is published yet. No GitHub workflow publishes and no workflow holds a credential: CI runs only the dry runs below, in the check, kotlin and rust jobs of .github/workflows/requirements-kg.yml. An agent runs the commands here, from a clean checkout of the release tag, and stops at the first failure.

1.title: What is published
1.content: One version for all of them, from VERSION (STT-NFR-001), with an entry in CHANGELOG.md that cites each smart-trust changes.md entry it implements. | Registry | Coordinates | Built by | . | Maven Central | io.github.litlfred:hcert-api, io.github.litlfred:hcert-core (Kotlin Multiplatform: the root module, plus -jvm and -js) | gradle -p tools/hcert-kotlin publishDryRun | . | crates.io | litlfred-hcert (library name hcert) | cargo package in tools/hcert-rust | . | npm | @litlfred/hcert-kotlin-js (Kotlin/JS ES module) | tools/release-packaging/assemble-npm.mjs | . | npm | @litlfred/hcert-component (the Rust WebAssembly component, transpiled with jco) | tools/hcert-rust/build-component.sh, then assemble-npm.mjs | . The coordinates follow the repository’s GitHub org (the owner’s decision of 2026-10-23). Their single source is "repository": "<org>/<name>" in smart-trust-tools.json: the Maven group is io.github.<org> (a namespace the org can verify on the Sonatype Central Portal through GitHub), the npm scope is @<org>, and the crate is <org>-hcert, because crates.io has no namespaces (the Rust library itself stays hcert). The Gradle build and tools/release-packaging/coordinates.mjs derive them; check-version.mjs fails if Cargo.toml, a POM or a package.json disagrees. Moving the repository to another org (say, WorldHealthOrganization) means changing that one field, renaming the crate in Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock as the check asks, and verifying the new namespaces below. The Kotlin package root stays who.smart.trust. Android uses the -jvm jar as it is; there is no AAR until an androidTarget() exists.

2.title: Once, before the first release
2.content: . | Licence. Apache-2.0 (the owner’s decision of 2026-10-23; OI-14). LICENSE is the official text from apache.org (sha256 cfc7749b…3d30); the crate ships its copy tools/hcert-rust/LICENSE (the check requires it to be identical), assemble-npm.mjs copies it into each npm package, and every jar carries it as META-INF/LICENSE. | Maven Central. Sign in to https://central.sonatype.com with the litlfred GitHub account; the io.github.litlfred namespace is verified by that. Generate a user token (View Account → Generate User Token): it is a name and a password, CENTRAL_TOKEN_USER and CENTRAL_TOKEN_PASS below. | Signing key. Central requires an OpenPGP signature on every file. Generate a key for releases, then publish its public half: gpg --quick-gen-key "Carl Leitner (smart-trust-tools releases)" ed25519 sign 2y gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format long # note the key id, KEYID below gpg --keyserver keys.openpgp.org --send-keys KEYID gpg --keyserver keyserver.ubuntu.com --send-keys KEYID . The key stays on the owner’s machine (or a hardware token). No key, token or passphrase is ever committed or given to a workflow. | crates.io. Sign in with GitHub at https://crates.io, verify an e-mail address, and create an API token scoped to publish-new and publish-update for the crate litlfred-hcert (CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN). | npm. The packages are scoped to the npm user litlfred. Create a granular access token with read and write on @litlfred/* (NPM_TOKEN), with two-factor authentication on the account. | .

3.title: Pre-release checks
3.content: From the repository root, on main, with a clean tree: . git status --porcelain # must print nothing git log -1 --format=%H origin/main # must equal HEAD; CI green on it cat VERSION # the version to release, no pre-release suffix . | Set the version, if it changes, in the three places that hold it, then let Cargo update its own entry in the lock (no other crate moves): echo 0.1.0 > VERSION sed -i 's/^version = ".*"/version = "0.1.0"/' tools/hcert-rust/Cargo.toml # the [package] version, the only line it matches (cd tools/hcert-rust && cargo update --workspace --offline) . | In CHANGELOG.md, replace — unreleased in the version’s heading with the date (## [0.1.0] — 2026-11-02), make sure every wire-format or subclaim-default change cites its smart-trust changes.md entry, and point the link at the tag ([0.1.0]: https://github.com/litlfred/smart-trust-tools/releases/tag/v0.1.0). A wire-format or subclaim-default change needs a major or minor bump. | Run the checks CI runs, and the dry runs: node tools/release-packaging/check-version.mjs bun run check:req-nodes python3 tools/test-plan/make_test_plan.py --check python3 tools/wit2kotlin/wit2kotlin.py --check gradle -p tools/hcert-kotlin --no-daemon compileKotlinJvm compileKotlinJs :hcert-core:jvmTest :hcert-core:jvmTestCoverageCheck :hcert-core:compileProductionLibraryKotlinJs (cd tools/hcert-rust && cargo test --locked && cargo test --locked --features qr --test api) . | Commit (Release 0.1.0), push to main of litlfred/smart-trust-tools, wait for CI to pass on that commit, then tag it with a signed tag and push the tag: git tag -s v0.1.0 -m "smart-trust-tools 0.1.0" git push origin v0.1.0 . | . Every artefact is then built from a fresh clone of the tag, never from a working copy: . git clone --branch v0.1.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/smart-trust-tools.git /tmp/stt-release cd /tmp/stt-release bun run cat mount:lock && bun install # the mounted layers, for check:req-nodes . toolchain/node_tools.sh # jco, from the lockfile, no install scripts .

4.title: Maven Central (Central Portal bundle upload)
4.content: . | Publish into the build-local repository and check the result. Every archive is reproducible (no timestamps, fixed order), so building the tag twice from a fresh clone gives the same jars, klibs, sources jars and POMs. The Kotlin Gradle plugin (2.0.21) writes the org.gradle.libraryelements attribute into hcert-api’s .module files or not depending on which tasks the build runs, so run exactly this command: gradle -p tools/hcert-kotlin --no-daemon publishDryRun node tools/release-packaging/check-version.mjs tools/hcert-kotlin/build/maven-dry-run . publishDryRun lists, for each of hcert-api, hcert-api-jvm, hcert-api-js, hcert-core, hcert-core-jvm and hcert-core-js: the .pom, the .module (Gradle metadata), the main artefact (.jar, or .klib for -js), -sources.jar, -javadoc.jar (the module README; the KDoc is in the sources) and, for the root modules, -kotlin-tooling-metadata.json. Gradle writes .md5, .sha1, .sha256 and .sha512 beside each. | Sign every artefact (not the checksums, not maven-metadata.xml): repo=tools/hcert-kotlin/build/maven-dry-run find "$repo" -name 'maven-metadata.xml*' -delete find "$repo" -type f ! -name '*.md5' ! -name '*.sha1' ! -name '*.sha256' ! -name '*.sha512' \ -exec gpg --local-user KEYID --armor --detach-sign {} \; find "$repo" -name '*.asc' -exec gpg --verify {} \; . | Bundle the repository layout and upload it, as a deployment the owner releases by hand (USER_MANAGED): (cd "$repo" && zip -qrX ../central-bundle-0.1.0.zip io) token=$(printf '%s:%s' "$CENTRAL_TOKEN_USER" "$CENTRAL_TOKEN_PASS" | base64 -w0) curl --fail --request POST \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $token" \ --form bundle=@tools/hcert-kotlin/build/central-bundle-0.1.0.zip \ "https://central.sonatype.com/api/v1/publisher/upload?name=smart-trust-hcert-0.1.0&publishingType=USER_MANAGED" # prints the deployment id curl --fail --request POST --header "Authorization: Bearer $token" \ "https://central.sonatype.com/api/v1/publisher/status?id=DEPLOYMENT_ID" . Wait for "deploymentState": "VALIDATED"; on FAILED, the response lists each problem. Then release it, which cannot be undone: . curl --fail --request POST --header "Authorization: Bearer $token" \ "https://central.sonatype.com/api/v1/publisher/deployment/DEPLOYMENT_ID" . (or Publish on the deployment at https://central.sonatype.com/publishing/deployments). | .

5.title: crates.io
5.content: cd tools/hcert-rust cargo package --locked --list # exactly: Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, README.md, DEPENDENCIES.md, LICENSE, src/*.rs cargo package --locked # builds the .crate on its own, from target/package/litlfred-hcert-0.1.0 cargo publish --locked --dry-run CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN=... cargo publish --locked . The tests are not in the crate: they read the shared vectors at ../../vectors, so they run from the repository. The component feature reads the WIT contract at ../../api/wit and so builds only from the repository too; the component is published to npm instead. A crates.io version cannot be replaced, only yanked (cargo yank --version 0.1.0).

6.title: npm
6.content: tools/hcert-rust/build-component.sh /tmp/stt-component gradle -p tools/hcert-kotlin --no-daemon :hcert-core:compileProductionLibraryKotlinJs node tools/release-packaging/assemble-npm.mjs --out /tmp/stt-npm \ --component /tmp/stt-component \ --kotlin-js tools/hcert-kotlin/hcert-core/build/compileSync/js/main/productionLibrary/kotlin node tools/release-packaging/check-version.mjs /tmp/stt-npm node tools/conformance-ts/run.mjs rust /tmp/stt-npm/hcert-component # the shipped files pass the suite node tools/conformance-ts/run.mjs kotlin /tmp/stt-npm/hcert-kotlin-js for p in hcert-component hcert-kotlin-js; do (cd /tmp/stt-npm/$p && npm pack --ignore-scripts --pack-destination /tmp/stt-npm) done sha256sum /tmp/stt-npm/*.tgz # record in the release notes . Then publish the tarballs that were checked, not the directories (scoped packages are private unless --access public): . printf '//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=%s\n' "$NPM_TOKEN" > /tmp/stt-npmrc npm publish /tmp/stt-npm/litlfred-hcert-component-0.1.0.tgz --access public --ignore-scripts --userconfig /tmp/stt-npmrc --otp=CODE npm publish /tmp/stt-npm/litlfred-hcert-kotlin-js-0.1.0.tgz --access public --ignore-scripts --userconfig /tmp/stt-npmrc --otp=CODE rm /tmp/stt-npmrc . An npm version cannot be republished once used, even after npm unpublish.

8.title: Actor and role administration
8.content: Process_ActorRoleAdministration · strict · 6 step(s) . Changing who can do what: adding an actor, opening or closing a role to one, granting or revoking a permission — and auditing the graph afterwards, because the declaration and the graph are two things that can disagree. You are in this process when the substrate every other diagram’s lanes bind to is what is changing. That is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit: a role added without an audit is a lane binding that resolves today and may not tomorrow, and nothing else in the corpus would notice. Retirement, never deletion. An actor id is referenced from commits, sidecars and other declarations, so removing one makes an old record unreadable while retiring one leaves it legible and says the actor has stopped. i i i i i i

10.title: Lanes — who acts
10.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Administrator | administrator | All four administration verbs — add, assign, grant, retire — converge at Gateway_Changed onto the same CallActivity_CodeChangeReview, so no kind of substrate edit gets a lighter review path than another; and Gateway_AuditClean’s ‘no’ branch (A13) loops back to this lane rather than ending the process, because whether a major finding holds the change is this lane’s policy call, not something Task_RunKgAudit decides for it. | . | Graph audit (system) | build-pipeline | Runs only after CallActivity_CodeChangeReview has already completed its own review, because the breakage this lane exists to catch — a join across role, lane, actor and skill — is invisible to a code reviewer reading the diff in isolation; ordinary code review clears the edit, and only this lane’s whole-graph pass can tell whether it silently broke something three diagrams away. | .

11.title: Steps
11.content: Every one of the 6 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Add an actor, and declare its kindTask_AddActor | Administrator | role-model | Human, agentic or mechanical. A userTask because the agentic/mechanical line is JUDGEMENT — role-model.md says so — and reading it wrong disqualifies the actor from every judgement task it exists to perform, silently. | . | Open or close a role to an actorTask_AssignRoles | Administrator | role-model | The join every other diagram depends on. An empty roles is a DETERMINED empty — it says the actor takes on none — and is not the same as an absent one, which asserts nothing. | . | Grant or revoke a permissionTask_GrantOrRevoke | Administrator | role-model | A permission travels with the PARTICIPANT and cross-cuts every lane, so unlike a role it cannot be scoped by the diagram it is used in. Granting one is a standing decision, which is why this lane is person-only and why the log capture on this process is on. | . | Retire an actor — never delete oneTask_RetireActor | Administrator | deletion-requires-confirmationrole-model | An actor id is referenced from roles, diagrams, beans and commits, so removing the file leaves every one of those unable to tell retirement from accident. Same rule, and the same reason, as a scrapped bean. | . | Branch, gates, PR and reviewCallActivity_CodeChangeReview | Administrator | continual-progress | Called rather than restated. The mechanics of getting an edit reviewed and merged are not specific to the role graph, and a second description of them is a second thing free to disagree with the first. Where cat-harness.sdlc is switched on, this step is the opt-in process code-change-review (Process_CodeChangeReview, sdlc/processes/code-change-review.bpmn); it is not called from here, because a layer without that sub-graph does not have it (owner card Q-OPTIN-CALLS A, 2026-11-12). | . | Audit the graphTask_RunKgAudit | Graph audit (system) | role-model | AFTER the change, not before. Every criterion here is a join — role to lane, actor to role, activity to skill — so what an administrative edit breaks is not in the file it edited. 14.title: Adjudication — judgement, when the mechanism ran out of facts
14.content: Skill adjudication: Settle a review that reached no mechanical or consensus agreement. What makes a disagreement adjudicable, the shape its implementations share, why the adjudication LEADS the criterion while the checker’s entry is kept beneath it, and the dispensation that records the reason — scoped to a version, never precedent. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Human Translation Workflow, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Translation round trip (untainted), Translation Workflow, Narrative review, Review task, Voice overlay review, Adjudication, CRDM close-out, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Criterion adjudication, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, A harness’s default rendering, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Wireframe design review, Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review, Getting started, Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Review and publish a folio, Make a decided public comment change, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Skill id: adjudication · Package: sdlc-core .

15.title: What it is
15.content: Adjudication is a judgement of the feedback of one or more feedback providers, when a review reached no mechanical or consensus agreement. It carries the same dispensation process: the reason for the choice, as per contextual requirements. These activities are adjudications: . | where | the decision, in its own words | . | translation-workflow · Task_Adjudicate | “The round trip establishes that two readings differ. Which one is right is a human call.” | . | ingest-l1-completeness-gate · Task_FlagDrift | “A machine can detect that two readings differ. Which one is right is a human call.” | . | refresh-materialized · Task_Adjudicate | “A human or agentic decision, never a merge rule. Which side wins depends on why the local edit was made, and a process that picked automatically would be choosing without the one fact that decides it.” | . | review-narrative · Task_AdjudicateVoice | “Three outcomes, all legitimate: the register is wrong for this genre; the criterion does not belong in this genre; or the block is a stated exception and a reviewer entry records why.” | . | voice-review · Task_Adjudicate | “The same three outcomes … fix the prose; scope it on the voice; or the rule applies and this block is an exception.” | . | src/routes/relevance.ts | “writing human_adjudicated alongside — never overwriting — the agent’s assessed_by. Both survive.” | . | schemas/library/bib-verification.ts | a discriminated Verifier union, agent-only vs human-adjudicated, “and *also carry human_adjudicated if a human has subsequently”* ruled | . Each restated the same rule because nothing generalised it; this skill is that generalisation.

16.title: The judgement and its outcomes are separate processes
16.content: Callers ask different questions: whether a drift is real, whether a passage is acceptable, whether two entries agree, which side wins a conflict, whether a finding stands. Only the QA-criterion question has a criterion to scope or a dispensation to grant, and a callActivity runs the whole subprocess, so the outcomes cannot live in the shared process. The branches live with the caller, not in an enum passed to it, because the codes select different tasks: a caller’s local-wins would point at A_ScopeCriterion. So the split is at the judgement: . | what | where it lives | why there | . | entry condition, untainted dispatch, person-or-agent restriction | adjudication.bpmn | it must not vary, and restating it per caller is how it drifts | . | the three QA-criterion outcomes, A_RecordEntry, the dispensation | criterion-adjudication.bpmn | it depends on what was asked | . | a requirements document’s sign-off: approve amend reject defer cancel (code list adjudication-requirement-set), A_RecordSignoff, GW_SignoffRecorded | crdm-signoff.bpmn (BA_Signoff), crdm-close.bpmn (BA_Confirm); spec-kit’s adjudicated status by the same codes | the answer moves a requirement SET’s stage | . The requirement-set caller records before it branches. Every answer goes to A_RecordSignoff, which appends a requirement-signoff attestation (the attestations graph, test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set>.attestations.json): who — kind, id, actor, the QA reviewer’s identity fields — when, about what (the set or one member), the outcome, the stage it moves the set to, the reason and the permalink to the issue comment. GW_SignoffRecorded then reads the record BACK through decisions/requirement-signoff-recorded.dmn, with facts check:requirements --signoff-facts <reqset:slug> computes from the store, so a sign-off nobody recorded loops back rather than proceeding. What that means when you call it . A_Adjudicate declares <cat-harness.processes:adjudication defers="caller"/> — it IS an adjudication and the permitted answers are yours. Declared rather than left as a missing codes, so a marker lost by accident and a deferral on purpose do not parse the same. | Asking the QA-criterion question? Call Process_CriterionAdjudication and declare <cat-harness.processes:adjudication accepts="stands scope dispensation"/>. The engine compares your list with what that process actually offers. | Asking something else? Call Process_Adjudication and declare <cat-harness.processes:adjudication codes="…"/> on your own call activity, with your own gateway coding the same set. The engine refuses a mismatch between the two, and refuses a partly-coded gateway, which reads as complete. | Declaring nothing is legal and reported by check:workflow-refs. Some callers are in that state on purpose: what each should ask is open, and guessing would make an undecided thing look checked. | . Whatever you ask, A_RecordEntry’s rule follows the outcome: a judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a checker that was never run. It is relaxable="false" wherever it lands, which is with the caller that records, because the entry written depends on what was adjudicated.

17.title: Two senses of the word, and only one is this
17.content: The corpus also uses adjudicated as an adjective meaning settled: evidence-retrieval calls published DAKs “already-adjudicated guidance”, and ingest-extract-structure says extracted candidates are “never adjudicated verdicts”. Both are correct English and neither is this process. Grepping for the word finds them; only the activity list above is the process.

18.title: What makes a disagreement ADJUDICABLE
18.content: Not “somebody is unhappy”. schemas/sdlc/block-qa.ts already declares the three reviewer kinds — script, agent, human — and allows multiple entries per criterion, which makes the entry condition computable rather than declared: . | state | what it is | . | mechanical agreement | the script entry passes | . | consensus | entries of different kinds agree on one criterion | . | adjudicable | entries for ONE criterion disagree | . So you are in adjudication when the sidecar holds two entries for the same criterion that do not agree. Anything else is a review, a complaint, or a bug report, and each of those has somewhere else to go. A missing entry is not a disagreement. One reviewer and no checker is a review; one checker and no reviewer is a gate. Adjudication needs both sides present, which is why it cannot be entered by an actor simply declaring it — and why adjudication.bpmn’s first gateway leaves the process rather than guessing.

19.title: The adjudicator is dispatched, not briefed
19.content: This skill does not restate the parties — untainted-verification owns them, and the split matters more here than anywhere else, because the adjudicator is the party best placed to ruin the measurement: . adjudicator | is given adjudicator_sees and the checker’s output — never the artefact itself | produces pass / warn / fail, each drift named . An adjudicator shown the artefact can talk itself into any reading of the finding, and that failure raises no error: it produces a verdict that measured nothing. UntaintedDispatch declares the context per criterion and untaintedPartitionDefects reports overlap when both parties can read the same file. Read that skill before you dispatch one.

20.title: The adjudication LEADS; the checker’s entry is KEPT
20.content: voice-review.bpmn, and this is the rule the whole skill turns on: . “The adjudication LEADS the criterion and the script entry is kept beneath it: a disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.” . Do not resolve the disagreement away. Both entries stay in the sidecar, the human’s on top under the sweep’s “most-recent matching-hash entry wins” rule. A sidecar showing only the winning answer has lost the fact that a checker read it differently — which is exactly what somebody re-running the check next month needs to know. The same rule holds outside the diagrams: /api/relevance/adjudicate writes human_adjudicated alongside assessed_by, and bib-verification.ts carries the same pair on a discriminated union. Neither shares code with the diagrams, which is evidence that it is the right rule rather than a local convention. This is also the answer to “adjudication if code and narrative disagree”: record the disagreement, lead with the judgement, keep the other entry.

21.title: The dispensation is a VERSION, never a precedent
21.content: The outcome carries its reason. That mechanism already exists and is schema-backed — block-qa/v1’s multi-reviewer primitive, documented at length in q-usage-watcher (the science layer): . | a kind: "human" entry with result: "pass" overrides the script’s fail for the same criterion; | only while its field_hash matches the current source files; | notes carries the reason — “reason for choice as per contextual requirements”. | . That hash gate is the design, not a limitation. A dispensation is scoped to the version it was granted against: change the block and it lapses, and must be re-granted. So a dispensation never becomes precedent, and there is nothing to overturn later — the source moving overturns it. A dispensation with no notes is not a dispensation. It is an override somebody applied to get to green, and nobody can review it afterwards. So A_Dispensation is marked relaxable="false" in criterion-adjudication.bpmn, with A_RecordEntry. The judgement is free and the record is not, because a judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a checker that was never run.

22.title: Who adjudicates — a skill that spreads, an entitlement that does not
22.content: | object | what it is | . | feedback-provider (role) | offers a finding — a checker, a review agent, a reader, an SME. Plural by design: one or more feedback providers. | . | adjudicator (role) | settles it, with a reason. Inherits reviewer. | . | adjudication (permission) | may WRITE the settling entry. | . Knowing the discipline and being entitled to apply it are different, and the repository already separates them. permissions.json: “a permission CROSS-CUTS roles”. Adjudication happens in four lanes bound to four different roles (narrative-reviewer, translation-adjudicator, reviewer, user), so: . | the skill is carried by every role whose lane holds an adjudicate activity, because each of them has to be able to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint; | the permission adjudication is held by the actor, alongside review-comments (record a finding) and approval-authority (accept a change). It is neither: settling a disagreement between two findings is not reporting one and not accepting the change. | . A reviewer reports; an adjudicator settles. That is why review-task.bpmn keeps accept-or-send-back in one lane: a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. translation-adjudicator is a specialisation of adjudicator.

23.title: Where it sits against its neighbours
23.content: | store | holds | skill | . | todos/feedback/ | a person’s feedback ON content — the intake | todo-review | . | test/attestations/block-qa/ | the adjudicated (non-script) reviewer entries per criterion — the record, on main | the qa-* family; schema qa-attestations/v1 | . | test/results/block-qa/ | the derived report, which keeps a projection composed from the store; its record is on the qa-reports branch | the qa-* family | . | beans/ | the work plan | todo-manager (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) | . Adjudication consumes an intake and writes a record. It is not a rival to either, and todo-review’s own disambiguation block — which separates itself from todo-manager and is silent about verdicts — is the seam it fits into.

24.title: What this does NOT cover
24.content: The narrative-asserts-code axis. Whether prose asserts what an artefact actually does is a different question, currently answered only for Lean (proof-narrative-lean-equiv). code-node-review asks whether a NODE is correct — that it declares what it is, that its references resolve — not whether the prose matches. 27.title: Adjudication
27.content: Process_Adjudication · advisory · 3 step(s) . A criterion’s reviewer entries disagree and no mechanism can settle them: this is the judgement that does, and the record it must leave. You are in this process when a sidecar holds two entries for ONE criterion that do not agree — a script failing what a reviewer passed, an agent and a person reading the same block differently. That is the entry condition and it is computable, which is why the first gateway leaves rather than guessing: one reviewer and no checker is a review, one checker and no reviewer is a gate, and neither is adjudicable. Nobody enters this process by declaring that they have entered it. Three things the diagram holds that prose kept losing. The adjudicator is DISPATCHED rather than briefed — given the findings and the checker’s output and, deliberately, never the artefact, because an adjudicator shown the artefact can talk itself into any reading of the finding and that failure raises no error. The adjudication LEADS the criterion and the checker’s entry is KEPT beneath it, because a disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information and a sidecar showing only the winner has lost it. And the dispensation is scoped to the version it was granted against by its field_hash, so it lapses when the source moves and never becomes precedent. This process ENDS at the judgement. What the answer means, and what is done about it, belongs to whoever asked — criterion-adjudication.bpmn is the QA-criterion specialisation, where the finding stands, the criterion is scoped, or a dispensation is granted with its reason. Until 2026-09-23 those three lived here and every caller ran them: six diagrams called this process and only two asked a question they answer. Bean bvuk. What stays shared is what must not vary: the entry condition nobody may declare their way past, the untainted dispatch, and the restriction to a person or an agent. What a legitimate outcome IS does vary, and it now varies where it is asked. i i i

34.title: Steps (one per process activity)
34.content: . | Origin and licence. Record the authors, venue, identifier, and the licence the source itself states. | No stated licence means reference only: the library entry holds headings, page ranges and a summary in our own words. | A source with no origin is a house process. Write a skill instead of a methodology. | . | Ingest (Process_Ingestion, library-ingestion) — the basic flow: the source is accepted, its metadata goes into the KG, and it is catalogued in library/. Reading a document into sections is a content-type refinement above this layer, and it keeps the rules that applied here: choose the rung mechanically, and never accept an inferred chapter tree. | Related work (Process_RelatedWork, related-work-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)). Search work items (beans list --json, beans query) and the repository’s issues and open PRs for work the method touches. | Categorize each hit: overlaps, coordinate; affected by; out of scope; or unrelated. Give each a one-line summary. | Judgement decides the categories. Present them with context, options and a recommendation (interaction-modality §4.1), and ask whether and how to coordinate. Do not act before the answer. | This is the same step CRDM runs when a requirement starts or changes in chat. | . | Render the method faithfully: what the source says, section by section, then a table of what is adopted and what is refused, each with its reason. | Extensions beyond the source are marked as ours. | Reported results are not imported as facts. | . | Place it by ownership (methodology-adoption §4), and declare the directory. | Integrate by calling, not copying. 37.title: Subagent memory — what a durable entry may claim
37.content: Skill agent-memory: Durable memory for a subagent — the three entry labels and what each promises, why entries are authored as graph nodes rather than in the generated file, the injection budget that silently truncates, and archiving as the third state between “reaches everybody” and “deleted”. Named by: Remote-mount a dependency . A subagent declaring project memory gets its own directory; the first 200 lines (or 25 KB) of that directory’s MEMORY.md are injected into its system prompt at start, and it reads and writes the directory as it works. Maintaining it is part of the work. A session that establishes a durable fact in an agent’s area adds it in the same change; a session that re-measures a number updates the entry with the fresh value and date, because a memory file that only accretes becomes the thing it exists to prevent. This curated memory is not a memory record, and a work item is. The entries here are read during a process and never written by one. A memory record is what a process keeps as it runs (memory-record-core in cat-harness-tools schemas/kg/memory-record.ts, owner ruling Q17 of 2026-11-03), and a work item is a memory record with more structure: a status, a type, a priority, a parent and what it blocks. Both are worked with the same memory Tools (memory_note, memory_checkpoint, memory_recall); see todo-manager (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan).

38.title: Every entry carries exactly one of three labels
38.content: | label | what it promises | . | STABLE | a path, a command, a rule. Trustworthy as written. | . | TRAP | a specific way the task goes wrong, with the evidence that established it. | . | BASELINE | a measured number, stored with the command that produced it and the date, and never quoted as a current answer. | . A TRAP is what stops a failure the project has paid for once being paid for twice. An entry that merely restates a rule is STABLE — a TRAP needs the incident. A baseline with no measurement is refused by the schema. A table of how to measure is a STABLE fact, not a measurement. A watcher whose subject is a live signal holds no baselines at all: every one goes stale by design.

39.title: Entries are authored as nodes; the file is generated
39.content: Edit the node; CI assembles. The assembled file under .claude/ is a projection that CI writes and commits, never an agent (harness-projections). Run the assembler locally in its check form to see what it would change. One entry per file, each declaring its own $schema, a label, a summary, and the agents it reaches — one entry can reach several agents, so a fact two agents need is not written into two files. The assembly check gates it, so an entry edited and never assembled fails the build. The generated file is written only between its markers, as the README sync is, so each file’s hand-written session log stays intact. A file with no markers is reported as not opted in, left alone, and never counted as up to date.

40.title: Vendor target mapping — one memory source, generated per target
40.content: Every declared memory directory is the single source of truth; the assembler projects it into each active vendor target, and --check gates both drift and per-target budgets: . | target | path | scope | budget | . | Claude Code per-agent | .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md (+ detail/<slug>.md) | nodes referencing <agent> or agent-less | 200 lines | . | Antigravity per-agent skill | .agents/skills/<agent>-memory/SKILL.md (+ detail/<slug>.md) | nodes referencing <agent> or agent-less | 24,000 bytes | . | Antigravity workspace rule | .agents/rules/agent-memory.md | all agents, grouped under ## <agent> | 24,000 bytes | . | Repo-wide AGENTS.md | AGENTS.md (<!-- cat-harness:agent-memory:begin/end -->) | live agent-less nodes (tags.references has no kind: "agent") | 32,768 bytes (32 KiB) | . | Gemini CLI per-agent | .gemini/agents/<agent>.md | the Claude agent’s prompt + nodes referencing <agent> or agent-less | 32,768 bytes | . | OpenAI Codex per-agent | .codex/agents/<agent>.toml (developer_instructions) | same | 32,768 bytes | . | Cursor per-agent | .cursor/agents/<agent>.md | same | 32,768 bytes | . | GitHub Copilot per-agent | .github/agents/<agent>.agent.md | same | 30,000 characters (vendor limit) | . Agent-less nodes feed the repo-wide AGENTS.md section when AGENTS.md opts in with memory markers (missing and no-markers remain distinct third states). Only Claude has per-agent memory; the other hosts get a whole definition. Gemini CLI, Codex, Cursor and Copilot read per-agent definition files whose body is the prompt. So each .claude/agents/<agent>.md is projected into one file per host: its prompt, then its memory nodes inline, because imports are not portable. Tools map only where the host documents an equivalent. Cursor also reads .claude/agents/, but .cursor/ wins on a name clash, so Cursor gets its own file (the Claude copy carries no memory). An agent with memory but no definition gets no file and is reported no-definition. The formats and their sources are in the header of cat-harness-tools/scripts/agent-memory-vendors.ts. Byte-budgeted targets drop whole nodes lowest-priority first, never mid-entry. When a target exceeds its byte budget, the assembler drops baseline before trap and trap before stable (oldest createdAt first), names every dropped node per target, and fails --check until entries are split into detail/ or archived.

41.title: The budget truncates silently, so it is checked two ways
41.content: Keep the injected file under the line budget. The harness drops the overflow without saying so. A truncated entry still looks complete to the agent reading it, so the check covers both an entry whose heading falls past the budget and a region whose end does. An entry too long to fit declares its evidence as detail, split at a body marker and written beside the injected file — and pruned when the entry stops declaring one, so a stale detail file cannot outlive the claim it supported.

42.title: Archiving is the third state, and the check order is load-bearing
42.content: Retiring an agent archives its memory; it does not delete it. An archived entry is a node of the graph that reaches no agent’s prompt — the state between untagged, so reaches everybody and gone. Deleting an entry throws away work somebody else paid for; same discipline as a scrapped work item. Archived must be checked BEFORE the untagged rule. An archived entry has no agent tag once its agent is gone, so checking it second hands it to every agent. Do not re-home an entry into an agent that does not own the subject. Budget is not the constraint — a detail split makes room; forcing a fact into an unrelated lane is. Archive it, record why, and say what would justify un-archiving it.

43.title: Scoping: by agent, with role tags
43.content: Memory is knowledge, and knowledge belongs to the lane, so entries are tagged with a role. Generation still goes through the agent axis, so tagging a lane is additive and changes no generated byte; keep the two axes separate. A CI watcher is a mechanical role, so a system lane is its correct home; a guard that exercises judgement is not, because judgement is what a system lane excludes. Every live entry carries a lane tag, so an untagged entry added now goes to every agent.

44.title: A memory entry never outranks a skill
44.content: The agents defer to skills/ as the source of truth. Memory summarises; the skill governs. Where the two disagree, the skill wins and the memory entry is wrong — fix it.

45.title: The layer’s two declared assets are maintained here too
45.content: README.md and AGENTS.md are declared assets with a declared purpose, and their upkeep belongs to this skill. | role | purpose | layer | delivery | . | instance-readme | what the layer is, for a reader | context | read as a file | . | agent-instructions | what a cold agent does here, in order | context | read as a file | . | agent memory | durable facts an agent must have without asking | context | injected | . This table is DECLARED, not described. All three columns are ASSET_ROLES in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts — one record of objects per ROLE, never per asset, because per-asset copies of a role’s purpose drift apart. layer and delivery are required on AssetRoleDef, so a new role decides them at the keyboard rather than at CI. The layer column makes a process step that writes one of these a defect. processMayWriteAsset(role) answers it through the same layerIsWritable rule the graph typologies use, so assets and directories cannot disagree about what context permits. For a role this layer does not govern it returns undefined — the third state, never to be read as permission. The delivery column is mechanical. Memory is spliced into a prompt, so it pays a budget — MEMORY.md’s first 200 lines, with the overflow dropped silently. A file is opened, so nothing truncates it. So AGENTS.md may be long and a memory entry may not, and a fact that must arrive unasked is a memory entry. asset-roles.test.ts asserts it: the longest declared AGENTS.md in the checkout runs past the 200-line budget, which is legal only because its delivery is file. AGENTS.md augments the README; it never restates it. The README answers what is this; AGENTS.md answers what do I do, in what order. A session that establishes a durable fact about a layer updates the one whose question it answers — and if it answers neither, it is a memory entry. bun run cat check:subgraph-coverage reports any layer missing either asset; both are required of every layer, because one with a README and no AGENTS.md is mute to an agent, and the reverse leaves a reader with nothing saying what the layer is. bun run cat check:asset-roles keeps the declaration single: it reports a required role ASSET_ROLES does not govern, a role a running process would be allowed to write, or an asset restating purpose, layer or delivery on itself. That last check reads the RAW declaration, because KgAssetSchema is a non-strict z.object and drops an unknown key when parsing.

47.title: Agent permissions — asked for, explained, granted by a person, recorded
47.content: Skill agent-permissions: Securing what a coding agent may do without asking, from the person who can grant it: the secure-agent-permissions sub-process, run at session start and on demand when an action is denied. Vendor-neutral: the coding agent is a Tool (Claude Code is one; Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot and Codex are others), and each Tool’s own config format belongs to its adapter, not here. Covers the permissions the harness’s processes need, least privilege, how each one is explained before it is granted, how a grant is recorded, and the rules that no grant relaxes: never self-granted, generated projections are CI’s, and merging to main is never a standing permission. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . processes/process/secure-agent-permissions.bpmn (Process_SecureAgentPermissions) is the process. It is called from session-state-machine.bpmn (Call_SecurePermissions, after the session record opens), so it is part of starting work in a layer. It also runs on demand when an agent hits a denied action. A denial is a reason to ask. It is never a reason for the agent to edit its own configuration. A run that finds every needed permission granted and recorded ends at End_Current without asking anything.

48.title: Three layers, three questions, and this skill answers the third
48.content: | layer | question | where it lives | . | role | what does the performer of this lane need to KNOW? | skills on the role (role-model) | . | actor permission | what may this participant DO in the harness, in any lane? | skills/permissions/permissions.json actions, granted by ODRL rules under policies/ | . | agent Tool permission | what may this coding agent do on this machine without stopping to ask? | the Tool’s own config, written through its adapter; the grant recorded as below | . The third layer enforces the second at the agent host. Editing hooks or settings exercises admin-settings; writing content exercises content-authoring. An agent Tool permission never widens what the actor’s ODRL grants allow. It only decides whether the host stops to ask.

49.title: The permissions the processes need
49.content: Grant only what the layer’s processes actually call, and the narrowest form that does the job. | permission | what it allows | why a process needs it | notes | . | run the gates | run the repository’s test, typecheck and cat check scripts | every gate a PR must pass before merge-to-main | read-only checks first; a writer (regen) is a separate grant | . | push a feature branch | git push to a non-default branch | continual-progress: commit early, push, open the PR at the first commit | never the default branch; never --force, only --force-with-lease | . | open and update a PR | create a PR, comment, label it | continual-progress, issue-working, merge-queue handover | never merge | . | edit agent hooks and settings | change the Tool’s hand-edited config | only when a hook or setting is itself the defect | per change, never standing: the exact diff, the reason, then the owner’s yes (harness-projections) | . | write generated projections | regenerate the Tool’s projections of the graph | none: CI regenerates them on the PR head | not granted to an agent at all (harness-projections) | . | merge to main | — | — | never a Tool permission. Every merge is its own owner-authorised run of merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). No allow-rule for a merge command is ever written. | .

50.title: Explaining one before it is granted
50.content: Task_Explain follows interaction-modality §4.1: context, options, recommendation, question. The test is whether the owner can answer without opening anything. For each permission: . | What it allows, concretely: the command or file pattern, and what the agent will then do without stopping. | Why a process here needs it: name the process and the step. | Options, narrowest first: the exact pattern, a wider one, or no grant (and what then keeps asking). | The exact config change, as a diff in the Tool’s own format, produced by its adapter. | The recommendation: least privilege, unless there is a measured reason for more. | .

51.title: Recording a grant (not relaxable)
51.content: Before the config is written, one record per permission, granted or refused: . agent-permission: by: <the person's login> on: <ISO-8601 date-time> tool: <Tool id, e.g. the coding agent's Tool node> permission: <a row of the table above> scope: session:<id> | instance | until:<ISO-8601> answer: granted | narrowed | refused diff: <sha256 of the config diff shown> evidence: "<the person's words, verbatim>" (<session link or comment permalink>) . Post it on the PR that carries the config change, and in its commit message. A refusal is recorded too, so the next session does not ask the same question blind. A config rule with no grant on the record is reported as unrecorded (Task_ReadGrants). It is not treated as granted, because a rule nobody can account for cannot be told from one an agent wrote for itself.

52.title: Rules no grant relaxes
52.content: . | Never self-granted. The grant is a person’s (Task_OwnerGrants is fulfilled by a person only). The config write is done by the person, or by the agent writing exactly the diff the person consented to. If you are composing the consent, you are the grantor, and you may not be (the confirmation-waiver rule, applied to the agent host). | Generated projections are CI’s. No permission lets an agent write them (harness-projections). | Hand-edited agent config changes per change, with consent. A standing grant to edit settings does not exist. Each edit is its own diff, reason and yes. | Merging to main is never granted here. See merge-to-main. | A broad instruction is not a grant. “Fix all issues until green”, “get the session start working” and “stop the prompts” authorise investigation. They do not authorise widening what the agent may do. Bring the diff back. | .

53.title: Per-Tool specifics belong to the Tool, not here
53.content: Where a Tool keeps its permissions, how a rule is spelled, and which of its files are generated are properties of that Tool, and belong on its Tool node or adapter (bpmn-processes §”A Tool’s OWN procedure is the Tool’s subprocess, not the skill’s prose”). For example, Claude Code keeps permission allow-rules in .claude/settings*.json.

54.title: What this does not do yet
54.content: . | No coding-agent Tool nodes or adapters exist in cat-harness. Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot and Codex have no Tool node here. claude is declared only as an actor (scenarios/actors/claude.json). Until adapters exist, Task_IdentifyTools reports “no adapter” and leaves the config write to the person. | GW_Gap is a judgement. Computing it needs the needed set (from the processes this layer runs) and the granted set (from the config, through an adapter). No tool produces both yet. | The permission rows are not yet ODRL actions. They map onto existing actions (admin-settings, content-authoring) in the table above, but are not declared in permissions.json; declaring them belongs with the adapters that read them. | .

56.title: ArchiMate models — every view, element and relationship a node
56.content: Skill archimate-models: ArchiMate models as knowledge-graph content: how a layer declares the Archi models it holds, what the archimate subgraph gives every model, view, element and relationship (an IRI, a thin page, and every view drawn as SVG from the model’s own diagram, and its metamodel derived and checked), how to version the models, how to wire them into a folio’s staging build and navbar, how to count and lower the crossed lines in a view before committing it, why every view carries a plain-language key, why names are the source’s own terms linked to their SKOS concepts, and why no Java, no Archi CLI and no Archi HTML report is ever part of the pipeline. Read before adding, authoring, publishing or rendering an .archimate file, before citing an ArchiMate element from prose, and before reaching for Archi’s own tooling in CI. Named by: Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it . Skill id: archimate-models · Package: ui-core · Subgraph: cat-harness/archimate/ · Tools: archimate-check, archimate-metamodel, archimate-blocks, archimate-pages, archimate-crossings, archimate-detangle, archimate-actors · Process: archimate-publish (processes/ui/archimate-publish.bpmn) .

57.title: The rule
57.content: An ArchiMate model is content, and every view, element and relationship in it is a node. The model is authored in Archi and committed where it is held. Everything a reader sees is made from it on each build, by the archimate subgraph, in TypeScript, with no tool installed: . | node | IRI (under the graph’s path) | page |   | . | model | <m>.jsonld | <m>/ | views; elements by layer | . | view | <m>/views/<id>.jsonld | <m>/views/<slug>/ | the drawing, <m>/views/<id>.svg | . | element | <m>/elements/<id>.jsonld | <m>/elements/<slug>/ | documentation, properties, relationships, views it is in | . | relationship | <m>/relationships/<id>.jsonld | <m>/relationships/<id>/ | its ends, the views it is drawn in | . Ids are Archi’s own (id-<32 hex>). An element therefore keeps its IRI across a model’s versions wherever Archi kept its id — the property the RA mapper’s mappings already depend on. Never rewrite one; the reader refuses an id that is not filename-safe rather than minting one nobody chose.

58.title: Readable page paths: slugs, worked out each build
58.content: The IRI stays the id; only the page is at a slug. A view’s or element’s page is at <m>/views/1-central-health-workforce-registry/, while its node keeps <m>/views/<id>.jsonld. Cite the IRI when a link must last: the page path is for reading. Relationships keep id paths, since almost none are named. Slugs are worked out from the names on every build (cat-harness-tools/archimate/schemas/slugs.ts). Nothing is committed and nothing redirects, so: . | a rename moves the page, and the old path is gone (a clean break; there are no <m>/views/<id>/ page paths); | on a clash the object first in the model keeps the plain slug and a later one gets -<first hex of its id>; | an author can choose a slug in Archi with a slug property (lower-case words joined by -); a malformed one, or two objects choosing the same one, is refused rather than rewritten; | an object with no readable name keeps its id as its path. | . Do not put slugs in the IRIs: the mapper keys on the ids, and a rename would move an IRI.

59.title: The metamodel is derived, never drawn
59.content: Do not draw a metamodel view. Which element types a model uses, and which relationships it draws between them, is computed from the model by the Tool archimate-metamodel (cat-harness-tools/archimate/schemas/metamodel.ts): . | every element type, with how many elements it has; | every pattern (source type, relationship, target type), with its count and the ids of the relationships that follow it; | for each pattern, whether ArchiMate allows it, from Appendix B of ArchiMate 3.2 as Archi holds it (archimate/schemas/archimate-relationships.json, MIT, written only by scripts/import-archi-relationships.ts; to adopt a newer table, re-run it on a newer Archi checkout); | the placeholder elements: an element named after its own type (“Goal”, “Application Component (MS)”). They are how a metamodel gets drawn by hand inside a model, so they and their relationships are listed and kept out of the patterns. A Grouping or Junction left with its default name is not one. | . archimate-pages draws the same result on each model’s Metamodel in use page (<m>/metamodel/), linked from the model page and the rail: a class diagram laid out from DOT by Graphviz in WebAssembly (@hpcc-js/wasm-graphviz, no binary, no JVM), with the same diagram as DOT, Mermaid and JSON beside it (<m>/metamodel.dot|.mmd|.json|.svg), and tables of the types and patterns, each pattern linking its relationships. archimate-metamodel --check fails when a relationship follows a pattern ArchiMate does not allow. Placeholders are reported, never fatal: a model is its authors’, so removing a hand-drawn metamodel view is their call. Cite the derived page instead of the view in the meantime. The steps run in this order, all in the pipeline lane of process archimate-publish: archimate-check, then archimate-metamodel --check, then archimate-pages. A refused relationship goes back to the model’s author.

60.title: Actors come first; the model points at them
60.content: The SMART Guidelines order is fixed: a DAK’s L2 generic personas become the IG’s L3 FHIR ActorDefinitions, and the architecture realizes them (DPI-H RA §4.3.2). So the ActorDefinitions are written in the IG, from the DAK personas, and the model only points at them. A model author tags the box that realizes an actor in Archi with the property fhir-actor, whose value is the actor’s canonical URL (fhir-actor = http://smart.who.int/ra/ActorDefinition/FacilityRegistry), the same way an element carries skosConcept. | Never generate an ActorDefinition, or any FSH, from the model. When the model has a box with no actor, the actor is missing from the IG: add it there, from the persona, then tag the box. | Never decide which box realizes which actor from names. That is the model authors’ call, made in Archi. A box may realize several actors (one tag each), and an actor may be realized by several boxes. | A #system actor goes on an application or technology element (an ApplicationComponent, an ApplicationInterface, a Node). A #person actor goes on a BusinessActor or BusinessRole. Any other kind of element cannot realize an actor. | Check the tags with the Tool archimate-actors: bun run cat archimate:actors --instance . --model <id>. It fails on a value that is not a canonical URL, a tag that names no ActorDefinition of the IG, an element kind that cannot be an actor, and a type mismatch. It warns about each ActorDefinition that no element realizes. With --strict that warning becomes a failure. --json gives element → actors and actor → elements, for the pages’ back-links. | . Data objects follow the same rule. A data object points at an existing logical model with logical-model = <canonical>. Write the logical model in the IG first. Never derive a logical model from the model’s boxes. The data object’s class diagram will be generated from that logical model once the IG holds one, so tag the data object now and do not draw the diagram.

61.title: A document’s tables and figures are drawn, not typed
61.content: A table or figure in the document that restates the model is generated from data by the Tool archimate-blocks, and --check keeps it from drifting. | Relationship rules and types live once, as an archimate-relationship-rules/v1 file in the archimate directory (cat-harness-tools/archimate/schemas/rules.ts). The document’s rules table and relationship-types table are drawn from it (config tables), with the caption and footnotes left as the editors wrote them. | The rules are in charge, not the model. For a rules table that names a model, the Tool reports rules the model never uses, relationships no rule covers, rules ArchiMate’s own table refuses, and relationship types the rules use but the document never explains. The editors decide, link by link, whether to fix the model or add a rule; nothing is rewritten from the model. | A figure that is a view names an svg in its figures entry. The Tool writes the view there with the same renderer as the view’s page, and the block shows that SVG instead of a picture. Check the drawing against the published figure first: element names in the model must match the document’s. | .

62.title: Untangle every view you touch
62.content: A change to a view never adds tangles, and every view you touch leaves with no more than it came with. A tangle is a line crossing another line, or a line running through a box that is not one of its ends and does not hold one. Groups (bands) are not boxes here; a line may cross a band. Every time you add, move or re-route anything in a view: . | Count before. bun run cat archimate:crossings --model <file> --view <id or page slug> lists each tangle by the boxes it joins. | Make the change. | Let the tool lower it. bun run cat archimate:detangle --model <file> --view <id or page slug> reports what it would do: re-route lines (straight, an L, or a Z through a free lane between rows) and swap same-size boxes in the same row or column. It keeps a change only if the count goes down. Add --apply to write it, or --routes-only when the boxes’ places carry meaning (an order, a flow). | Look at the drawing (gen-archimate-pages.ts --out, or the view’s SVG) before and after. The count is a gate, not taste: undo a swap that breaks a reading order, and fix by hand what the tool cannot (it never adds, resizes or regroups boxes). | Count after, and say both numbers in the PR: “view X: 10 crossings, 13 through a box → 1, 2”. More tangles after than before is a finding to fix before review, not a note. | . Ways to untangle by hand, in the order to try them: . | Put a box beside the boxes it is joined to: a line’s ends in neighbouring rows, not across the view. | Order a row like the row it connects to (the order of the boxes above), so lines between the two rows run parallel. | Route a long line along the gap between rows or bands, with right-angle bendpoints, rather than diagonally across boxes. | Nest instead of drawing a line where the notation allows it (composition, aggregation, assignment, realization): a box drawn inside another already says how they relate, and the renderer draws no line for it. | When nothing else works, a view shows too much: split it. | .

63.title: Every view carries a key for readers who do not know ArchiMate
63.content: Readers of a view are mostly not architects. Every rendered view carries a plain-language key below it, saying what each colour, shape, line and end used ON THAT VIEW means, in words a reader without ArchiMate understands (“Realization: makes real, or achieves”), not the specification’s terms alone. render-view.ts draws it by default, keyed only to what the view uses. Do not turn it off for a published view, and do not export a view without it. When the renderer gains a new mark, the key gains its line in the same change.

64.title: Names are the source’s own terms, linked to their concept
64.content: An element or view named from a source uses the source’s own term, and links to that term’s SKOS concept. Not our paraphrase, shortening or merger of two terms. When a model depicts a module of a handbook, the box is named as the handbook names it, and the element carries the concept’s IRI (a property, e.g. concept = the skos:Concept IRI in the source’s glossary scheme) so its page links to the definition. | No concept for the term yet: add it to the source’s glossary scheme first, from the source’s own words, then name the element. | The source’s term is too long for a box: keep the full term as the name and let the renderer wrap it; a short form goes in skos:altLabel, never in place of the name. | Our term and the source’s disagree: that is a content decision (term-disagreement), not something to settle by renaming in Archi. | .

65.title: The model is never a source of the glossary
65.content: An authored model depicts concepts; it never defines them. Meaning lives in the SKOS glossary, read from the source documents. So: . | Never write a term, label, definition, focus or relationship into a glossary from a model someone authored in Archi. An element with no term is a term to add from the source’s own words, not from the box. | The glossary may drive the model (archimate-from-glossary, a content layer’s Tool): names, documentation and relationships flow from the terms into the model, and Archi keeps the layout. | The term pages’ “depicted by” links read skosConcept on each build and write nothing into the glossary, so they are allowed. | The one exception is an ingested model, received from elsewhere and held as a source under the layer’s library/. It may seed the glossary once (archimate-from-glossary --seed --from library/…), like any other ingested source. The Tool refuses --seed on any model outside library/. | .

66.title: No Java, no Archi CLI, no Archi report — ever
66.content: The Archi command line (com.archimatetool.commandline.app) renders an HTML report and view images, and it is not part of any pipeline here: . | it needs a JVM, a virtual display (xvfb) and a ~200 MB download on every run — too heavy for CI, and impossible in a web client, which is where an agent or a reader working in the browser is; | its views are raster images nobody can link into, and its pages are not nodes: nothing it writes has an IRI in the graph. | . render-view.ts draws the same views from the same coordinates — the bounds Archi stores for every box (made absolute, since Archi nests a child’s bounds in its parent’s) and the relative bendpoints it stores for every line — into SVG in ArchiMate’s notation, every box a link to its element. The reader handles Archi’s native XML and its zipped archive with node:zlib. If a view ever needs something the renderer does not draw, extend the renderer; do not bring Archi back into a workflow. The same reasoning applies to any other Java-only ArchiMate tooling (jArchi scripts, coArchi). Authors use Archi on their own machines; the pipeline never does.

67.title: What a layer declares
67.content: . | A directory of graph typology archimate in its <instance>.json, with a coverage.visualiser naming <dir>/index.html so the navbar carries a tile to it (harness-tiles). served: true only if the pages are written into the graph rather than a site build. | cat-archimate.config.json, at the layer root or inside that directory: { "$schema": "cat-archimate-config/v1", "directory": "<id>", "models": [{ "id", "file", "title"?, "description"? }] }. | cat-harness in its needs, directly or through its closure. | . Order matters when a platform is pinned. A declaration naming the archimate typology throws in every platform reader that does not know the kind yet (cat-harness.ts: unknown graph typology). Move the layer’s pin of cat-harness to a commit carrying this subgraph first, then declare.

68.title: Versions — one folder per SemVer version
68.content: A model is named for the version of the thing it describes. In a WHO IG repository that is the version: in sushi-config.yaml: archimate/0.2.0/, with earlier drafts as SemVer pre-releases (0.2.0-draft.1, …). The model id in the config is that version, so …/archimate/0.2.0/elements/<id>.jsonld is both versioned and stable. Never name a folder v2, prev1 or current: a label that says nothing about what it is a version of invites two identical models under two names.

69.title: In a folio’s build
69.content: bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/archimate/scripts/check-archimate.ts --instance . bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/archimate/scripts/gen-archimate-pages.ts --instance . --out _site . Run both in the staging build, after the document site is built and before the navbar pass, so the pages are railed like every other page. --out is the normal mode: a few models yield thousands of pages, which belong in a build, not a commit. gen-archimate-pages.ts without --out writes into the graph and --check gates it, as the openapi subgraph does, for a layer small enough to commit its pages.

70.title: Citing the model from prose
70.content: Link the element’s or the view’s page, never a copy of a picture. A view’s SVG links relative to its own address, so it can also be embedded in a document as a figure (<m>/views/<id>.svg) and stay current with the model. Where the document and the model disagree — a figure in the text that is not a view in the model — that is a finding for the model’s authors, not something to paper over with an exported image.

71.title: What is not read yet
71.content: The Open Group exchange format; custom images and fonts on a diagram (each box names its type in its corner instead of Archi’s icons — the icons are the tool’s artwork, not the notation’s); sketch and canvas views; ingesting a model from another repository. Each is an extension of schemas/archimate.ts or render-view.ts, in TypeScript.

72.title: Do not
72.content: . | Draw a metamodel, or any class diagram of the model’s types, by hand: cite the derived “Metamodel in use” page. | Run Archi, a JVM or xvfb in a workflow to render a model. | Commit exported view images beside a model; they go stale on the next edit. | Name model folders by anything but the version they describe. | Declare the archimate typology in a layer whose platform pin predates it. | Commit a change to a view without counting its tangles before and after. | Publish a view without its key, or name an element from a source in words the source does not use. | .
