80.title: Artefact reachability — load is not evaluability, and a test is not a caller
80.content: Skill artefact-reachability: Which declared executable artefacts can be reached — decision tables, BPMN diagrams, self-declared entry points. Read before trusting that a .dmn works because it loads, before concluding a script has a caller, and before building any reachability report: load is not evaluability, a test is not a caller, and where a grep fails in both directions the subject has to be narrowed rather than the signals. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . A declared executable artefact that nothing can reach is indistinguishable, from outside, from a decision nobody takes. That sentence is the whole skill. Run bun run cat audit:reachability before saying a decision table works, before saying a script has a caller, and before building any reachability report of your own. audit:reachability:check is a step in code-quality-gates.yml, so gates.ts derives it and bun run cat gates runs it. --strict is not wired: the self-declared entry points nothing runs are a backlog, and failOnNew is what makes a new one fail meanwhile. A check: alias never arrives ahead of its workflow step — gates.ts’s unrunScripts ratchet refuses one that no workflow runs — because an unwired gate must never read as a passing one.

81.title: Loading a table is not evaluating it
81.content: A table can load, carry a clean kg-qa verdict, and still be unevaluable by any caller: kg-audit’s decision-outcomes-used calls loadDecisionTable and possibleOutcomes, and neither parses a unary test, so a cell such as not("green") (which unaryTest throws on) passes. Likewise a script can be declared, documented and tested while nothing runs it. That is audit-coverage’s thesis in a new place: coverage is a relation between an instrument and the question it was built for. A loadability check measures loadability; evaluability is a different question.

82.title: Load is not evaluability — ask the EVALUATOR, never a grep
82.content: unreadableExpressions in src/workflow/decision-table.ts asks the question by running the evaluator over a probe, atom by atom. It lives beside the grammar rather than in the gate, and that placement is the rule: . A checker that restates a grammar is a second spelling of it, free to disagree with the first. Green on a table the engine refuses, or red on one it accepts — and nothing says which is wrong. Three things the walk had to get right, each of them a way to miss a finding: . | A comma-separated test cannot be handed to unaryTest whole. It is parts.some(…), so the first atom that matches ends the walk. 0, [1..5] reports clean if you ask once and 0 is the probe. | The probe is the number 0, the one value that reaches every branch without a type complaint. Under that probe a DecisionError is not “wrong fact type” — it is a rule that can never evaluate for any fact, such as > "a" — so it is reported rather than swallowed. | Output cells count. evaluate calls literal on every output column and possibleOutcomes reads only the first, so an unreadable literal in a second output column is invisible to every existing reader. | . Keep unaryTest throwing. Its own comment says why — “so an expression this evaluator does not implement can never be mistaken for a rule that simply did not match”. That property is what makes an unevaluable table findable; an evaluator that returned false for what it cannot read would make a table route confidently and wrongly. An unevaluable table is a hard failure, not a finding. It fails --check, which runs on every push. That is a deliberate divergence from audit-coverage, where --check fails on staleness alone: there, every finding is an unmet ambition; here, a table nothing can evaluate is a broken artefact.

83.title: A diagram is reachable when the ENGINE’s resolver reaches it
83.content: Same discipline, one layer out. The denominator is every .bpmn that any layer declares; the numerator is processFiles — the list workflow_list prints and workflow_start resolves against. processFiles keys by file stem and keeps the first claimant (if (!seen.has(stem))). So a dependency’s diagram whose stem collides with the root’s is dropped from the list, and workflow_start cannot reach it by stem or by bpmn:process id, because the id fallback searches the same list. Nothing measured that. A reachability guard over a corpus that is reachable today locks in a property the repository has rather than demanding work. A calledElement naming a process no file defines is NOT a finding. The loader’s own comment settles it: a folio may legitimately call out to a process it does not host, and the call stays opaque by design. Reporting it would turn a modelling decision into a permanent red. What this does NOT re-answer . | question | whose it is | . | does every activity’s <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> resolve? | check:workflow-refs (hard on a dangling ref), and kg-audit’s skill-* criteria | . | is any gateway pointing at this decision at all? | kg-audit’s decision-outcomes-used | . | which audits reach which KIND of node? | audit-coverage | . | can a node of this kind be TYPED? | check:kind-validators | . A third reader of one relation is a third answer free to disagree with the other two. The reference counts are recorded in the sidecar and never graded, so the measurement is visible without a second verdict being minted.

84.title: When a grep fails both ways, narrow the SUBJECT — not the signals
84.content: Two approaches fail. Asking the broad question (is any module reached by nothing?) returns hundreds of findings, mostly corpora discovered by directory walk — content blocks, schema modules a registry names, the tests bun test globs — which no inference can tell from a module nobody can run, and a gate with hundreds of findings is switched off within a week. Narrowing the signals (require an invocation verb beside the mention) still leaves dozens, mostly schema modules a declaration points at. What works is narrowing the subject. A module with a #! shebang or an import.meta.main guard has said it is runnable. That is a declaration inside the file, which is what directory-conventions insists a contract must be — extension is a coincidence; a declaration inside the file is the contract — and “does anything run this?” then has one right answer. The corpus is counted on each run and the sidecar holds the number; a count in prose is the next thing to go stale. audit-coverage says prefer a declaration where inference fails in both directions. This adds the move you make when there is no declaration to prefer: find the declaration the corpus already carries, and make that the subject. A mention is not a caller, and that distinction decides everything . Crediting every textual mention credits a script whose only callers are <bpmn:documentation> prose (and the generated glossary JSON that carries that prose onward). A grep over mentions clears the very defect this tool exists to catch. So a mention counts only on a line that also carries an invocation: a runtime, a spawn, or this repo’s own in-process tool dispatch. It is coversIn’s rule again — a parser over text has to tell a use from a mention — and here the use has a verb beside it. Two things that follow: . | Read the dot-prefixed callers explicitly. gitFiles excludes every dot-prefixed segment, so .github/workflows/ and .claude/commands/ — where most invocation actually lives — are invisible to a corpus walk. Reading only code-quality-gates.yml reported minify-site.ts and staging-rotate.ts as run by nothing; feature-staging.yml runs both. | Exclude your own sidecar. Its findings QUOTE the paths it reports, so reading it credits every module named in a finding with being reached, and the report clears itself one run later, permanently. Derive the path from the constants that write the file, so a relocation cannot leave the exclusion pointing elsewhere. audit-coverage states the general rule: a measurement must not be a term in itself. | . Two unrun states, and one number for both would hide the worse one . | state | what it means | . | invoked | something runs it | . | declared | nothing runs it, and it SAYS how it is reached — @entrypoint | . | entry-point-orphan | nothing runs it and nothing but a test imports it: it exists only as a claim | . | entry-point-latent | nothing runs it, and it IS a live library: a dead CLI branch on a reached module | . The last two are different pieces of work, and merging them would bury a module nobody can run inside a list of unused --help branches. Same reasoning as audit-coverage’s typed-only: a state exists to keep two findings from collapsing into one. A test is not a caller. A test proves a module works; it does not make it reachable. @entrypoint — say how you ARE reached . * @entrypoint script:merge:steward * @entrypoint none — written for the merge-steward tile, not built yet * @entrypoint spawned by scripts/foo.sh . Exactly one space, the star, one space — a continuation or an indented example is a mention, for coversIn’s reason, and this skill’s own code block above is one. A script:<name> claim is verified against package.json, because a declaration that can be checked should be; the free-text forms are recorded as your assertion and not graded. Under-claiming is recoverable — the count says so out loud. Over-claiming looks like reachability, which is the defect.

85.title: Three rules for building any reachability report
85.content: Commit the relation, print the census . The sidecar holds which decisions are evaluable, which diagrams the resolver reaches, which entry points are run, and the gateways pointing at each decision. It does not hold module totals: a census moves on any commit that adds a file, and a gate stale by default is one people learn to regenerate without reading. Judge against a baseline; never compare a committed copy . The records live on the qa-reports branch, so <instance>/test/results/ is a working copy and not a record. A writer writes it, qa:publish pushes the tree once per CI run, and a gate reads the baseline through judgeQaResult — --against <ref> for the branch, and a baseline that cannot be asked is unknown: reported, never a pass, never a failure. Compose the path with qaResultPath(root, stem) and nothing else: no caller spells QA_RESULTS_DIR itself, so moving the working copy is one line. failOnNew is how a soft finding bites. It asks directly whether a new orphan shows up in a diff. The standing orphans are inherited and do not fail; the next one fails on the commit that introduces it. Do not use staleness of a committed sidecar as a proxy for a backlog: the records are not on main, so there is nothing committed to be stale. failOn is for broken artefacts, and this is the one divergence . audit:coverage fails --check only on what is new, because every finding it has is an unmet ambition. Here the hard families are broken artefacts — a table nothing can evaluate, a diagram the resolver cannot reach, two diagrams answering to one name — so they go in failOn and fail whether or not a baseline calls them new. A defect is not less of one for having been there yesterday. --strict promotes entry-point-orphan to the same footing for the day the backlog closes. A sweep prints its own denominator, and a checker does not write . generalise-the-fix §1.2a: a report over zero diagrams passes every assertion in it. This refuses with EXAMINED NOTHING rather than reporting clean. And --check does not write. A checker that repairs the staleness it reports cannot be falsified — red once, green on the rerun, the file still stale in the repository.

99.title: Asset extraction — the index goes in, the contents do not
99.content: Skill asset-extraction: Reading a container — a zip, a PDF, a saved web page — into the knowledge graph. What goes in by default (metadata), what does not (contents), the three timestamps that sit near each other and mean different things, and why a producer string is evidence. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links . A container arrives in uploads/: a zip of a saved web page, a PDF, a tarball. Something inside it is wanted. What enters the knowledge graph is the INDEX — what is in there, how big, what type, when it says it was written — and not the files. Contents are extracted only when a person explicitly asks. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-assets.ts <container> bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-assets.ts <container> --extract <path> --because "<why>" . The first writes a folio-extraction/v1 record beside the container. The second additionally writes one named entry, and refuses without a reason.

100.title: Why metadata is the default
100.content: A container’s index is cheap and complete: a zip’s central directory carries every entry’s size, name and timestamp without decompressing a byte. That is enough to answer what is in here, how big is it, and is any of it what I want — which is every question asked before somebody decides to take a file. Extracting by default costs the opposite: a working tree full of files nobody chose, each of which now looks committed-on-purpose to the next reader, and none of which carries a reason. --because is required, and it is the point of the flag. An entry written to disk with no stated reason cannot be told from one nobody authorised. The schema refuses it (ExtractedAsset.superRefine), so this is not a habit that depends on remembering.

101.title: The three timestamps, and the one that gets confused
101.content: |   | says | . | dc.date.issued | when the PUBLISHER published the work | . | materializedAt | when WE brought the bytes local | . | capturedAt | when a TOOL produced this file out of something else | . An extraction timestamp is never a publication date. For example, a WHO IRIS capture: . zip entries 2026-09-20 07:42 (all 11 of them) page PDF CreationDate D:20260920074221 info PDF CreationDate D:20260920074925 . The style guide those files contain was published in 2020. Every timestamp in the capture is 2026, and every one of them is the moment somebody pressed save. Folding the two would date a 2020 publication to 2026 and lose the only evidence the artefact is second-hand. isSingleCapture() computes the distinction rather than asserting it: when every entry shares one minute, ONE ACT wrote the container and no entry’s date says anything about that asset’s own history. When they differ, the container preserved real dates and they can be read as such.

102.title: A producer string is evidence, and is recorded verbatim
102.content: Both captured PDFs carry Producer: Skia/PDF m152. That is Chrome’s print-to-PDF — so neither file is WHO’s own PDF, both are printed web pages, and nothing else in a file listing, a byte count or a checksum shows it. Recorded as written, never normalised to “Chrome”: the version is part of the evidence, and a normaliser is a place for the fact to get smaller. This is the mechanical half of a judgement the IRIS intake already records by hand — the page PDF is filed with role none, because “we looked and it is not what it appears to be” is a different fact from “nobody looked”.

103.title: What is NOT dropped silently
103.content: A zip written on macOS carries a __MACOSX/ shadow per entry. Skipping them quietly makes the asset count disagree with the container’s own, and a reader reconciling the two finds nothing to explain the gap. They go in omitted[] with a pattern, a reason and a count.

104.title: Derived renderings — the artefact we MADE, out of bytes we hold
104.content: A cover thumbnail, an OCR text layer, a page raster, a converted figure: none of these came from the source. They were produced here, from something the source supplied, and the catalogue records an artefact, not where it came from — so a derived file with a plausible name and a materialized state is indistinguishable from one the publisher shipped. DSpace makes this concrete. It generates a THUMBNAIL bundle of its own, so “a THUMBNAIL bitstream on an IRIS item” reads, to anything downstream, as IRIS’s thumbnail. The three WHO IRIS covers in this repository are not those: iris.who.int is egress-blocked here, nothing upstream was fetched, and each is page 1 of a PDF already held, rasterised by cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-cover.py. Three rules, in the order they bite: . | of names what it was DERIVED FROM, not what it is ABOUT. The Handle identifies the item; putting it on a cover we rendered asserts IRIS supplied the image. local:cat-harness/uploads/<file>.pdf#page=1 says the true thing and resolves to the true thing. | The declaration is authored, and the tool refuses without it. the content core’s scripts/gen-covers.ts will not write bytes for a THUMBNAIL whose materialization.note does not declare the derivation. Generating that sentence would make the check circular — a tool cannot attest to its own output. | purpose: working, never archival. A rendering is regenerable from bytes already held and answers no source-loss question; MaterializationSchema already refuses a working copy that claims to discharge sourceLoss, and this is the case that rule was written for. | . Take the determined division, not the clever one. pdf-cover.py renders page 1 and calls it the cover, for the same reason pdf-pages.py sections by page: page 1 is a determined answer and “the cover” is not. Covers differ in shape (portrait, landscape, a scanned title page), and a heuristic has no way to say when it is unsure. Record the geometry. Bitstream.pixelWidth/pixelHeight exist so a listing reserves the box before the bytes arrive. Absent is unmeasured, not square. Check the claim where the check can actually run. A gate that re-renders a derived artefact needs the backend that produced it, and the CI job that runs this repository’s gates installs ruff and nothing else (stated on ingest-stdlib’s Tool node). Do not install a backend in the gate job, and do not degrade to could-not-determine — that would report unknown on every CI run, which is a check nobody can read. Split the claim instead. Of the five things a node asserts about a derived image, four need no decoder at all: . | claim | needs the backend? | . | the bytes exist | no | . | their sha256 is the declared one | no | . | their length is the declared one | no | . | their pixel dimensions are the declared ones | no — a PNG’s IHDR puts width and height at bytes 16..24, big-endian | . | these bytes are what that source renders to | yes | . So the gate keeps its teeth everywhere and gains the last row where the backend happens to be present — and it says in its own output which of the two it ran, because “3 covers verified” would read identically either way and the two are different assurances.

105.title: Where the record lives
105.content: Beside the container, in uploads/. uploads/ is a state graph — a queue that ingestion drains — so an extraction record is not L1 corpus and does not read as one. What a THEME or a LIBRARY entry cites is the extracted file’s localPath, which exists only once somebody asked for it.

108.title: Audit coverage — measured, with denominators
108.content: Skill audit-coverage: Which audits reach which KIND of node, measured rather than inferred. Read before concluding that a corpus is unaudited, before writing a criterion for one, and before building any coverage report — the gate half must be declared, an undeclared declarer is counted, and the stored record holds the relation rather than the census. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . A sidecar count is a fine measurement of sidecars and says nothing about gates. That sentence is the whole skill. Run bun run cat audit:coverage before saying a corpus is unaudited, before writing a criterion for a kind, and before building any coverage report of your own.

109.title: A zero sidecar count is not “unaudited”
109.content: kg-qa sidecars measure kg-audit’s criteria exactly, and KG_SUBJECT_KINDS has no bean — so zero sidecars over the work item store is the right answer to “how many criteria reach this kind” and no answer at all to “is this kind audited”: the check:bean-* gates, check:ready-to-close, check:stale-paths and check:harness-dirs audit work items. This is covered-is-not-reachable one level out: coverage is a relation between an instrument and the question it was built for, and the signal in reach is rarely the signal you need. It is not a second answer to check:kind-validators. That asks whether a kind can be typed — does it have a validator that loads. This asks who judges it. A kind can be perfectly typed and audited by nothing, and a validator sweep reports it as covered.

110.title: The gate half is DECLARED, never inferred
110.content: A gate names the kinds it covers in its own module docblock: . * @covers bean-defs, beans * @covers none — .github/workflows/ is not a declared graph typology * @covers computed — it sweeps whichever kinds declare `nodeSchemas` . The tempting alternative is to infer it: grep each gate’s source for a kind’s name or its declared directory. It fails in both directions at once. A gate that mentions beans/defs/ in passing scores as auditing work items; a gate that resolves its directory through directoriesForGraph names no path and scores as auditing nothing. Both answers wrong, neither looking wrong: could-not-determine rendered as clean (directory-conventions). Five states, because three real gates cannot use a static list . | state | what it means | . | declared | names its kinds | . | none | has decided it audits no declared graph — check:workflows reads .github/workflows/ | . | computed | derives its set at run time — check:kind-validators sweeps whatever declares nodeSchemas, so a literal would go stale silently | . | no-script | bun test, eslint, tsc — nothing here to annotate | . | undeclared | has not said | . none and undeclared are different facts and collapsing them would leave a gate that genuinely audits no graph with silence as its only honest answer. computed exists because writing today’s answer as a literal is the snapshot BASE_GRAPH_TYPOLOGIES’ own doc refuses for counts in prose. An undeclared gate is counted and printed, never zero, and every “unaudited” verdict is stated as an upper bound while any remain. That is check:kind-validators’ state 2, for its reasons. All gates declare, so audit:coverage:require-all is wired in CI and the findings are verdicts rather than bounds. The flag is what keeps it closed: a new gate arriving undeclared turns them back into an upper bound, silently, unless something fails. The output still states the caveat whenever the count is non-zero, because the day it reopens is the day a reader needs to be told. When you cannot tell, do not annotate — and then go and read it . A fabricated @covers credits a kind with coverage nobody checked. Under-claiming is recoverable — the count says so out loud. Over-claiming looks like coverage. To resolve an undeclared gate, read its scan set, not its title: check:retired-front-matter is computed, because its set is kgRoots(instance) plus the undeclared .claude/skills/ convention; and check:agents-claims covers code, not docs, because it grades the symbols a prose claim names while AGENTS.md itself is a node of no declared graph.

111.title: Four states per kind, and a single zero cannot tell them apart
111.content: | state | what it means | the case that earns the name | . | no-directory | no layer declares one of this kind | bean-defs, declared inside beans/beans.json, reached through its parent — and carrying gates | . | empty | a directory exists and holds nothing | a determined empty | . | typed-only | a declared validator TYPES its nodes; nothing judges them | none here | . | unaudited | files, and nothing at all — not even a validator | none here | . bean-defs is why the first state is not a gap: it has coverage and no directory of its own. A report that printed 0 for its directory count and left the reader to infer would have manufactured a finding. So every row prints all four counts and names its state rather than leaving it to be read off a zero. typed-only is a finding, and that is the whole reason it exists . A kind whose validator check:kind-validators parses its nodes against looks unreached, because that gate declares @covers computed, which this report counts as neither coverage nor gap. Do not call it covered. --strict fails on typed-only as its own family, because typing is not judging — a kind can parse perfectly against its schema while nothing has an opinion about what it says. What the state buys is telling two different pieces of work apart: a schema parses these nodes and no criterion reads them is not nothing whatsoever reaches this kind. check:harness-state carries one family per kind, and --strict is green and wired in CI. The state stays, because the next kind to arrive will pass through it — and the flag is what stops it resting there. A validator must reach the nodes that are produced . | A kind’s schema must point at the module that holds its shape, not the one that holds its path. A pointer to where a fact is not written is worse than none: a reader who follows it concludes the shape is undeclared on purpose. | Every writer stamps $schema. Consumers route a node by its tag and skip a file that has none, so a writer that omits it leaves only hand-written files validated. A validator over the nodes nobody produces is not coverage. | An untyped node read by a shell script degrades rather than fails: a jq failure branch prints a line nobody acts on. That is why interaction and issue-marks declare validators. | .

112.title: Three rules for building any coverage report
112.content: A measurement must not be a term in itself . If the report’s own sidecar lives in a graph it counts, writing it changes the next run’s answer, and the gate is satisfied only by running the writer twice. Exclude your own output, derive the path from the constants that write it so a relocation cannot leave the exclusion pointing elsewhere, and test that one run converges. Store the RELATION, print the census . The record is stored on the qa-reports branch keyed by commit. Do not record files and sidecars in it: a writer in one graph would turn another graph’s coverage gate red, and a file count that moves whenever anybody adds a page makes the gate stale by default — one people learn to regenerate without reading. What belongs in the sidecar is what defines coverage: declared directories, criteria reaching the kind, gates declaring it, the state. Those move when coverage moves, which is when a reviewer needs the diff. One bit of the census — hasFiles — is all the states need. Recording a count would make the report depend on the signal it exists to replace. A docblock that documents a tag necessarily contains the tag . coversIn read audit-coverage.ts’ own worked examples of @covers as declarations, crediting the coverage report with auditing the work item store. Any parser over docblocks has to tell a use from a mention, and indentation is the distinction JSDoc already provides: ^ \* @covers , exactly one space either side of the star.

113.title: What --check fails on, and what it does not
113.content: --check computes and judges, and writes nothing. It fails on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — a kind that lost its audit, a gate that stopped declaring, in the commit under review — and not on its own sidecar being stale: derived QA results live on the qa-reports branch, so nothing committed is left to be stale. The baseline is read with --against <ref> (a qa-reports ref such as main). A baseline that is not there is UNKNOWN — printed, never a pass, never a failure, because an unwritten baseline is not this change’s defect. A checker that mutates its own subject cannot be falsified (red once, green on the rerun, the file still stale), which is the one property generalise-the-fix (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) Move 3 asks a guard to have. A kind whose directory is declared but absent from the checkout reads unknown, not empty: an absent answer is never printed as a determined zero. A directory that declares storage reads stored instead: its files are on the branch, fetch them with bun run qa:fetch. The findings are reported and do not fail. --strict fails on an unaudited kind and --require-all on an undeclared gate, for the day each gap is meant to close. A gate that refused every push until somebody wrote criteria for interaction/ is a gate that gets switched off within a week.

123.title: Block actions: [edit] and [feedback] on every block
123.content: Skill block-actions: Every block of a rendered document links back to where it can be changed: [edit] opens the block’s Markdown source in GitHub’s editor, and [feedback] opens a GitHub issue about that block, from the folio’s own issue form when it has one, listing the change-sets that already discuss the block. Use when a reader, reviewer or agent needs to propose a change to one block, when setting up a folio’s feedback issue form, or when a document site’s links point nowhere. Named by: Public comment on a review draft . A reader who finds something wrong in a block is one click from proposing the fix or saying what is wrong, and the click lands on the block, not on the repository. The links are per block, because a block is what a comment, a change-set and an edit are about. The code is folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts; the Tool is block-actions; the document build (build-document-site.ts) draws the links on every labelled block, and the public-comment overlay adds the issues that already discuss the block.

124.title: What each link does
124.content: | link | opens | what the person does next | . | ✎ edit | the block’s source (folio/<doc>/<chapter>/<root>.md, or its .ts if it has no .md) in GitHub’s editor, on main | edits and proposes the change; GitHub makes the branch and the pull request, which is reviewed like any content change (content-change-review.bpmn) | . | 📣 feedback | a new issue about the block | describes the problem; the issue is intake, and a public-comment folio triages it like any other comment (public-comment skill) | . | discussed in #n | the issue of each change-set the block’s comments are in | joins the existing discussion instead of opening a duplicate | .

125.title: Every issue is coded with its content
125.content: [feedback] codes the issue with the slug of the document it came from: the title reads Feedback [dpi-h-ra]: <section> — <block> and the body opens with **Content:** \dpi-h-ra``. A folio with several documents, or a repository that takes issues about more than one thing, can then sort feedback by what it is about without opening it. The code is in the title rather than only a label because GitHub silently drops a prefilled label when the reporter has no triage rights, and most public reviewers do not.

126.title: The issue form is the folio’s, and optional
126.content: With no form, [feedback] opens a blank issue whose body already says which block, which section, the source link and the block’s address on the site. It works on day one. A folio that wants structured feedback adds a GitHub issue form at .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/block-feedback.yml (start from the shared templates/issue-forms/block-feedback.yml, whose answers the drafting review sheet imports: skill review-sheet-script) (another name with --issue-template). The link then names the form and prefills only the fields the form declares, matched by id: . | field id | filled with | . | block | the block’s label (its anchor) | . | section | the heading the block is under | . | source | the block’s source path in the repository | . | page | the page it renders on | . | url | the block’s address on the published site (needs --site-url) | . | content | the document’s slug, the code the issue is triaged by | . A form may declare any subset, and fields it does not declare are not sent. Add the questions you want answered (what is wrong, a suggested wording, the reviewer’s organisation) as further fields; they are left for the person.

127.title: Where the repository comes from
127.content: GITHUB_REPOSITORY in CI, else the checkout’s origin when it is on GitHub, else --github <owner/repo>. No repository, no links: a page with no links is honest, a page with broken ones is not. --no-block-actions turns them off for a build that should have none.

128.title: Two forms of the same links
128.content: . | Full (blockActionsHtml): every href written into the page. Used on a one-page document and on index.hydrated.html, so the links work without JavaScript. | Compact (compactActionsHtml + compactActionsScript): the block’s facts as data attributes, and the hrefs built in the browser when a pointer or focus reaches them. Used on a lazy page’s shell, where a prefilled URL per block would bloat the page. The browser builder, BLOCK_URLS_JS, is held equal to editUrl and feedbackUrl by block-actions.test.ts; change both together or the test fails. | . The recipe lives in the harness, cat-harness-tools/src/core/edit-links.ts, so every layer can use it; this package re-exports it. It is published once as assets/js/edit-links.js (held equal to the code by a test). On a page, mark a link data-fa-link="edit|source|feedback" and either give its host the facts (data-src, optional data-repo, data-line, data-block, data-sec) or leave a GitHub blob/edit href, which the runtime reads the facts from. Generators that write Markdown use markdownEditLink. Three places keep their own link on purpose: the public-comment dashboard’s Discuss (it opens a change-set discussion, not feedback on a block), the bootstrap site’s Improve this page (bootstrap-tools may import nothing outside itself), and an IG page’s per-section ✎ / 📣 (SOURCE_LINKS_JS in build-ig-site.ts): a section’s heading can live in an included file, and its issue is titled after the section with the page apart. The IG page’s own Edit this page link does use the recipe. Any page that shows edit or feedback links uses these, not a URL of its own: one recipe, so a change to the issue form or the branch reaches every page at once.

129.title: In the library: edit opens the folio, never the source
129.content: A library entry is a frozen source: the version published for public comment stays in library/ exactly as circulated, and the changes the review asks for are made in folio/. So the library’s Document view (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts, drawn by the platform viewer and by build-library-site.ts on a folio’s site) shows: . | link | on | opens | . | source | the document, each section | the library’s own file on GitHub, read-only | . | 📣 feedback | the document, each section | an issue coded with the entry: Feedback [<entry>]: <section> | . | ✎ edit | each section, and its contents row | the FIRST folio block of the folio section MATERIALISED from it | . A section is matched to the folio by its number, else its title, through the folio-review-anchors/v1 file whose library names the entry. A section the folio has no counterpart for (a PDF’s front matter) gets no ✎ edit, because a guessed link would open the wrong block. The platform’s own library has no materialisation, so it shows source and feedback only. bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/build-library-site.ts --repo <folio> --out _site publishes a folio’s library at <out>/folio-assistant-core/<library dir>/<entry>/, the same <base>/<handler>/<kind>/<subject> route every viewer follows.

130.title: Using it as an agent
130.content: # one block's links, to hand a reader bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts --repo <folio> --block prose:1-1-4-a8e0b3 # every block's, as JSON bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/block-actions.ts --repo <folio> . When someone in a chat says “this paragraph is wrong”, give them the block’s feedback link, not the repository’s issue page, and the edit link if they can propose the wording themselves.

133.title: Relationship first, visualisation later
133.content: Skill board-diagram-interchange: A board is a DIAGRAM OF a folio, not a container of one. The OMG split between the semantic model and its layout, why the arrow runs one way, and what a note may never carry. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Treat a board like the OMG specifications treat BPMN layout: relationship first, visualisation later. BPMN separates the semantic model — bpmn:process, its tasks and its flows — from Diagram Interchange: BPMNDiagram, BPMNShape, BPMNEdge, which say where each of those was drawn. They are two documents about one subject, and the layout one points at the semantic one, never the other way. A folio board is the same shape: . semantic model notes, anchors, content nodes what is true diagram interchange board-positions.json where it was drawn .

134.title: What follows
134.content: A folio is complete with no board. Deleting every board loses layout and no content. That is the test to apply when you are unsure whether something belongs on the board or in the folio: if losing it would lose a fact, it is not layout. A note carries no x, no y, no board, no position — for the same reason a BPMN task carries no coordinates: layout lives on top of notes, not as data within them. One note may sit on several boards, at different places, without the note arbitrating between them. A coordinate on the note could not express that; a layer above it does so for free. An orphan is swept from the LAYER, which is the easy direction: one file, one pass, and nothing edited out of a note a person owns.

135.title: The arrow, and how it is kept
135.content: folio ──▶ board ──▶ position ──▶ note allowed note ──▶ position / board / folio REFUSED . This is a property a future edit can break silently, so it is checked rather than described. schemas/board-positions.test.ts asserts two things against the SOURCE: . | no field named x, y, board or position appears in todo.ts, carried-note.ts, landing-sticky.ts or note-anchor.ts; | board-positions.ts imports zod and nothing else — it names notes by id, and an id needs no type from the layer below. | . The first guards the failure that actually happens: somebody adding coordinates to a note “for convenience”, which makes a content node carry state and gives one note two answers on two boards.

136.title: Two graph typologies, because they are two things
136.content: | kind | holds | what it is | . | boards | content | what a board is and what it shows | . | board-positions | state | where each note was drawn | . content-context-and-state-graphs refuses a content node that carries state, which is the same rule one level up. And check:graph-typology-work asks a sharper question of the second: it is state, written by a running process every time somebody moves a note — but state that records a position in a PROCESS is work, and state that records a position on a CANVAS is not. Both kinds declare recordsWork: false.

137.title: A board declares what it SHOWS, and absent means everything
137.content: schemas/ui/board.ts: an optional filter over pages and kinds, OR within an axis and AND across them. Absent is the default and it means the whole folio — a query rather than a stored list, because a list of content nodes needs something to notice that a listed node was renamed and that a new one was never added, and a query has nothing to fall behind. Every harness above the floor has a board filled with all contents, which is the absent filter — so the minimal board and the total board are the same document.

138.title: Mergeability is the reason for the shape, and its limit is stated
138.content: Positions are the most concurrently-edited state a folio has: two sessions moving two notes is the ordinary case. So the document is sorted and indented, one note per line-block, and the sort is idempotent — a writer that reshuffled on save would conflict with every other save. It is a partial fix. Two notes that sort adjacent still conflict, because the inserted lines overlap. This removes the guaranteed conflict, not every conflict, and it should not be trusted further than that.

139.content: Not the rendering. How a board draws, when a card becomes its avatar and what an open window does are board-windows. Not the tiles. Which boards and viewers a reader can reach is harness-tiles.

153.title: Board: relocate content to the trashcan
153.content: Process_BoardRelocate · strict · 5 step(s) . Moving open content to the trashcan from the board, with the reader’s confirmation in front of the move and not behind it. You are in this process when the fishbone is used on open content. The confirmation gateway has a real “nothing moved” end state, because a destructive action whose refusal is not drawn is a destructive action somebody performs by accident. The order of the two writes is the content of the diagram. The CONTENT relocates, and only then are its positions dropped and orphans swept — the folio carries what is true, the layout layer carries where it was drawn, and the arrow never runs the other way. Sweeping first would leave the board authoritative over the folio for the length of one step. i i i i i

158.doc: Board: relocate content to the trashcan
158.title: Board: relocate content to the trashcan
158.content: Generated from folio-assistant-core/processes/ui/board-relocate.bpmn by gen-processes-viz.ts — do not edit here. All processes · folio-assistant-core processes .

159.title: Start in the avatar, open into a window
159.content: Skill board-windows: Everything starts as its avatar; opening projects a window onto the board. The two mechanisms that must not be conflated, z-order, and the fixed chrome a content kind fills in. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Everything starts as its avatar, and [x] closes a window back to it. Opening projects a window onto the board; selecting any part of a window raises it. Each content kind controls its own avatar and rendering, and opens into a full-screen panel with fixed controls such as [x], [linksrc] or [edit].

160.title: TWO mechanisms, and conflating them is the defect
160.content: |   | trigger | who | . | semantic zoom | the card’s rendered width crosses a declared threshold | automatic | . | open / close | [x], or opening a card | a person | . An open window is not a zoom state: it is projected onto the board rather than being the card grown large, so it survives zooming out. Only [x] closes it. Collapsing the two gives a board where a card can close itself with no action taken, and where [x] and a zoom-out are indistinguishable. Semantic zoom is the GLASS’s, not the board’s . Every board slot — a landing sticky and a todo sticky alike — is one component: the same closed square tile (--fa-sticky-tile-size) with the theme’s faded art, and the same compact icon row underneath it. A slot is its closed tile at every width, so semantic zoom does not run on the board. It decides what a card shows on the folio glass, where a card is resized freely. Do not add a width observer to the board grid: it would be a zoom with nothing to change, and the next agent would read it as the card’s state.

161.title: One sticky, one icon row, in one order
161.content: Under every sticky, on every panel: view, edit, pin, send to fsh-guts, as icon buttons. An icon-only control carries aria-label (what a screen reader announces) AND title (the same words on hover); they are not interchangeable. No control sits inside the card body. The open window’s bar uses the same icons for the same acts. A link the sticky cannot serve is absent, never dead.

162.title: Pin is a toggle onto the FOLIO glass
162.content: There is one store answering “what is on my glass”: the folio. A second store holding a page-level copy of the card gets no glass tools, no folio geometry and no shelve, and has to be special-cased by the glass filter and count. | Pin makes the sticky a folio asset — todo/<id> (the key the glass’s own Todos panel pulls a todo out under, so the two ways onto the glass agree) or landing/<slot> — with shown: true, drawn by the glass’s own card path and placed by placeOnGlass. A landing sticky’s theme, picture URL and text travel in the entry as data, never as stored markup. | Unpin is shelveFromGlass — the middle of the three states below. The entry stays; the same pin puts it back, where the reader left it. | The pressed state is the store’s answer (folioStateOf(key) === "glass"), never the button’s memory. The glass’s own × shelves too, and the row’s pin follows it. | .

163.title: Send to fsh-guts asks first
163.content: A control a reader has to ask about has not said what it does, so discard is named for where it goes (Send to fsh-guts, the trashcan that is kept) and opens a confirmation that names the sticky, says it is restorable and per-browser, and says where it is restored from — the fish in the navbar’s icon row. Focus starts on Cancel; Cancel and Escape do nothing but close it. A dialog whose dismissal performs the act did not ask. The window bar’s send is the same act and takes the same confirmation. The inverse is Restore in fsh-guts.

164.title: The threshold is declared, inherited, and traceable
164.content: schemas/kg/semantic-zoom.ts (instance data: semantic-zoom.json): a folio default (belowPx) with a per-kind override (byKind) — the repository’s inheritance rule (inherit everything, override anything; a variant states only what it CHANGES). So: . | the folio always has a number, and every kind resolves to one; | a kind that states nothing is complete, not invalid — requiredness is checked after resolution, never on the declaration; | an override carries a required because, and the resolver returns the source alongside the value, so a reviewer can tell a deliberate override from a folio default that does not fit. | . The boundary is stated once. Strictly below the number, so the declared width is the last one that still shows words. A boundary written one way in a comment and the other way in the renderer makes a card flicker.

165.title: Z-order: selecting any part raises
165.content: Windows stack, and selecting any part of one raises it — not a title bar, any part, because a reader who clicks into a window’s content has already said which one they mean. Z-order is session-only. The DI layer carries no z: a committed stacking order would make every raise a file write and every two sessions a conflict, on the most concurrently-edited state a folio has. If that proves wrong, z is one optional field in the positions document.

166.title: The chrome is fixed; the kind fills it in
166.content: A content kind declares which controls it offers, and the platform fixes the frame: . | [x] is always present and always in the same place, so a reader learns the frame once; | a declared control that names nothing known is a finding, not a missing button; | a control the environment cannot perform is hidden, and the reason reported — a dead [edit] 404s for exactly the reader who cannot edit, which reads as “this page is broken” rather than “you cannot do this”. | .

167.title: Closing must have a reachable inverse
167.content: An action whose inverse is not reachable is not a toggle. On an overlay, close may set hidden, because the launcher tile re-opens it. On a board that IS page content, hidden removes a section of the page, so the inline board collapses to a control in its own position, and focus follows it — left alone, focus lands on <body> and the keyboard position is gone. A control two clicks deep inside a collapsed launcher does not count as reachable. A default of “hidden” is allowed only with the inverse on screen. The glass’s tile strip starts slid away; its “Show tiles (N)” tab stays in view, in the strip’s own position, and the same tab hides the tiles again. See harness-tiles §”The glass strip”.

168.title: The floor, which is not negotiable
168.content: This layer’s declared interaction profile is low-dexterity. Every board action is keyboard-operable; drag is an accelerator and never the only way in. Targets are at least the tile size. And the board is ALWAYS collapsible to a linear, tile-based listing — a board that cannot be read linearly cannot be read by a screen reader, printed, or translated. The listing is the ARTEFACT and the board is the overlay . The board is an extra laid over a simple tile-based listing. So the floor must be correct with no JavaScript at all, not merely when the board is toggled off: notes built only by docs-ui.js from a fetch of assets/todos/index.json give a reader with JavaScript off no note, no count, and no hint that notes exist. Three checks follow: . Document order, never the board’s order. The board may stack by BPMN subprocess depth; the floor does not, because document order is what a screen reader and a printout depend on, and a floor that reordered would be a second answer to “what comes next”. Collapsed, never removed. When the board mounts it moves the listing into a disclosure so the page does not show the same notes twice. It does not delete it, hide it from assistive technology, or display: none it: a listing the board removed would have no way back while the board is open. Assert against the SERVED HTML. A test that reads the DOM passes because the board built that DOM. The assertion is on bytes the server sent — a browser context with javaScriptEnabled: false over the same renderer the generator writes with.

169.title: The folio belongs to the HARNESS, not to the library
169.content: A content library is something a reader browses — a replica, a published layer, any folio published as a site. A folio is the reader’s own surface: their notes, the assets they have materialised, the documents they created or linked. So the folio visualisation is cat-harness’s, available by convention on any harness, and a library never implements its own. A library may have its own landing page and its own harness; neither is licence to build a second folio. Consistency is the requirement: a reader moving between libraries must find the same folio, because the point of carrying a folio is that it does not change underneath them. A note or a todo MAY reference nodes in another KG library. The folio is not scoped to the library it is pulled down over, so a renderer must not assume local resolution.

170.title: A tile, or an avatar?
170.content: A tile is what the HARNESS declares, an avatar is what the FOLIO holds, and a theme is how either one looks rather than a third kind. The test is in harness-tiles §”A tile, or an avatar?”, and only there, because one rule with two homes is free to drift.

171.title: An asset has THREE states, not two
171.content: Pulling the folio down gives a glass — a surface over whatever is being browsed, carrying sticky notes and the avatars of materialised assets, including materialised KG like cat-bootstrap or cat-harness themselves. | state | where the asset is | how it got there | . | in the library | not the reader’s at all | the default | . | in the folio, not displayed | materialised into the folio’s own reproduce directories — library/ for the bytes, uploads/ for a source — off the glass | the reader closed it, “back in library” | . | on the glass | displayed in the pulled-down folio | the reader pulled it out of the library | . “In the folio” is not folio/. The folio is the reader’s REPOSITORY, of which library/ and uploads/ are declared parts — both carry dependents: "reproduce". folio/ is a different graph typology: renderable authored content. corpus-grep searches library/ only, so a node materialised anywhere else reads as ABSENT to every consumer. Closing returns an asset to the middle state and NEVER to the first. Only its display goes. Putting it back on the glass is a separate act performed from the library, not from the glass it just left. A two-state model would make closing a sticky and un-materialising an asset the same gesture, and a reader tidying their glass would silently discard work; the middle state is what makes closing cheap enough to do freely. When you implement close, check that the library offers the way back — not that the glass does. Close says where the way back is, at the moment of closing. The glass’s [x] opens a confirm that names the layer’s library and links it; Escape and Cancel leave the card where it is, and only the confirm shelves it — after which the glass says, with the same link, where the asset went. Naming the library matters because a reader holding assets from several libraries would otherwise have to remember which one each came from. The place is the card’s own, so there are three. A library card goes back to its layer’s library, a todo to the Todos board, and a landing sticky pinned to the glass to the page it was pinned from; calling a sticky “your Todos” would send the reader to a list it was never on. One function answers “where does this card go back to”, and the confirm, the status after it and the [x] button’s own label all read it, so the three cannot disagree. The confirm is the page’s one confirm dialog, shared with sending a sticky to fsh-guts, so focus-on-Cancel and Escape-cancels are stated once. Opening a library card goes to the asset’s visualizer when its index entry declares one, else to its entry page; resizing is a corner drag, with +/− in move mode and the move bar’s buttons as the non-drag path.

172.title: Two settings panels, two names, each points to the other
172.content: The glass has its own settings (theme, avatars, opacity, blur), and the page has its own under ▦ Actions (scheme, reading preferences, the Discarded fish, Declared kinds). They are named “Glass settings” and “Page settings”, so a screen reader does not read two controls identically, and each panel opens with a link to the other, as its first control, because a reader who opens the wrong panel needs a pointer to the right one. Site chrome and board state are unrelated settings but they are neighbouring places, and a reader moves between places. | The names are declared once (SETTINGS_NAMES in docs-ui.js), because each panel’s link prints the OTHER panel’s name; a panel renamed in one place only would leave the other panel’s link naming something that no longer exists. | The link must OPEN its target, not toggle it, and not open it underneath. The glass’s openPanel closes a panel that is already open, and the open glass covers the sidebar where Page settings lives. So the glass-to-page link shuts the glass first, and the page-to-glass link shuts the launcher first. In both cases focus lands on the target panel’s heading. | No link to nothing. A page with a glass and no sidebar has no launcher. Each panel registers an opener, and the link is drawn only when its target registered one. | . The same holds for any future pair of panels that share a word: name each one for what it acts on, and point each one at the other. scripts/tests/settings-labels-distinct.test.ts checks the source; test/settings-crosslinks.e2e.ts checks the rendered page at 1280×800 and 390×844, by mouse and keyboard.

173.title: Lazy window content fetch and render safety
173.content: Rendering the board with N cards makes 0 per-card detail fetches up front: each board slot (todoSlot / renderBoardTiles) renders only its summary tile/avatar. When a card carries a per-card detail or artifact URL (detailHref, bodyHref, artifactHref, or a non-inlined jsonldHref), opening its window (openCard / createLazyWindowLoader.openWindow) fetches that card’s content lazily on open, caches the result by card id (so re-opening uses the cached result and never pre-fetches the other N - 1 cards), and renders any body or tool/skill output through the declared renderToolOutput (RENDER_AS: text, url, markdown, json) and safeHref boundary (schemas/ui/render-output.ts, site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js). A refused URL scheme (such as javascript:) is never fetched and is shown as escaped text.

176.title: Reading a knowledge graph before you have anything
176.content: Skill bootstrap-kg-navigation: Read and navigate a knowledge graph with nothing installed — no MCP server, no tools, no harness. Named bootstrap- so it cannot be confused with a navigation Skill of a Harness that is installed. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . This skill assumes a text editor and nothing else. No MCP server, no skill-fetching tool, no work-plan store, no build. If those exist they are not yours to rely on yet — see AGENTS.md.

177.title: A graph is files that declare what they are
177.content: Three facts carry the whole model, and every one of them is checkable by reading: . | A layer declares the directories it scans, in its declaration at its root. Each entry is an id, a path, and the kinds of graph found there. | A directory is a place to look, not a type. One may hold more than one part of a graph, so the directory does not say what its files are — the files do, in their own front matter or $schema. | Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. An override matches on an entry’s id, never its path. Matching on path turns one relocated graph into two, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | . Two more words you will meet in a declaration. A field this skill does not describe is an Extension: a Harness added it, and you ignore it. A Harness’s own kind of declaration, which requires everything bootstrap’s does and adds Extensions, is a Subkind of bootstrap’s: read it as bootstrap’s, and it still means what it says. Versions and addresses. A declaration may state its version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and an iriBase. Every identifier it mints, and every page meant for a person, is then <iriBase>v<major>/…: the address carries the major alone, so only a breaking release moves it. The exact release you read is fixed by the pin that brought this repository to you, not by the address. Bootstrap’s own are in its declaration; read them there rather than trusting a copy.

178.title: Do this, in order
178.content: . | Read the repository’s declaration. If there is none, this repository is not a layer yet, and that is the case bootstrap exists for. | Find the entry whose graphTypologies name the kind you want. In bootstrap they are named for what they hold: skills, processes, scenarios (the Roles), schemas and models. The entry’s path is relative to the declaration. | Read the files in that directory. A markdown file declaring name: and description: in front matter is a skill — its body is the instruction you were looking for. A file declaring $schema: is stating that it is something else, and is not a skill however it is named. | Follow a reference by id, not by path. A node that names another names it by id; resolve it through the declaration rather than guessing a filename. | .

179.title: What “I could not determine” means here
179.content: An absent declaration and an unreadable one are different: . | what you found | what it means | what to do | . | no declaration | not a layer yet | this is bootstrap’s case — continue | . | a declaration that will not parse | a layer asserting something broken | stop and say so; do not fall back | . | a declared directory that is not there | the declaration is wrong | stop and say so — scanning nothing and reporting a clean run is the defect | . | no declaration for a kind you want | this layer has none of it | that is an answer, not a failure | .

180.title: What this skill is NOT
180.content: It does not describe what a Harness above bootstrap holds, such as its content or its checks: those belong to the Harness you have not loaded yet. If you need one of them to finish bootstrap, the boundary is in the wrong place — say so rather than importing the definition.

Skill id: bpmn-authoring · Package: workflow · Named by l2-dak-authoring.bpmn (Business processes · BPMN 2.0, Business analyst lane) and crdm-requirements.bpmn (Phase 2: Map current workflow (BPA), Agent lane). Author BPMN 2.0 business process diagrams — both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn.

183.title: Inputs and outputs
183.content: schemas/skills/bpmn-authoring/: . | in — processName (required), sourceWorkflow, existingBpmn, participants | out — bpmnFile, diagramFile, taskCount, gatewayCount, participantCount | . graphviz is a declared capability with degradation: skip — layout help degrades, authoring does not stop.

184.title: Diagram Interchange is not optional
184.content: A .bpmn with no DI section — no explicit x/y on its shapes — parses and renders blank, although the XML looks complete. bun run cat render:bpmn renders every diagram to docs/assets/img/workflows/ with bpmn-js in headless Chromium; bun run cat render:bpmn:check fails when an SVG is stale. Run the renderer and look at the SVG before you call a diagram done.

185.title: Readable at 100%: check it before and after (author check)
185.content: Every diagram you write or touch must, when you are done: . | fit 1400 × 900 in diagram units, so its 16px text reads at about 14px in a 1200px band without zooming; every task a fixed 120 × 120 square: boxes never grow to fit their names, and a name that does not fit is shortened (TASK_SIZE in the tools layer); | have no label on another label, on a flow (its own included), on a box or across a lane line: a gateway’s question above the diamond, its answers beside their flows, every label inside one lane; | have right-angled flows and every name inside its box, pool and lane names inside their strips; | have no crossing flows, and the lane order that keeps flows between lanes shortest: each lane sits next to the lanes it exchanges flows with, so no flow crosses a lane it does not stop in. A lane that talks to only one other lane, such as an owner who only approves the merge steward’s card, goes on the outside, next to that lane (owner, 2026-11-07: “swap owner lane down to reduce arrows across non interacting actor lanes”). | . bun run cat bpmn:detangle <file> reports all of it, and --write fixes what it can (lane order, right angles, box and lane sizes, label places). Run it before and after, and put both counts in the PR. Zero findings on every diagram you touch, or it does not merge (owner, 2026-11-02, after 63 of 80 harness diagrams were found with findings: “improve bpmn authoring process/skills so doesnt happen again”). A report nobody has to act on is how they piled up. Run bpmn:detangle <file> --check last; a finding you leave needs a reason in the PR, and only diagram-too-wide / lane-order may be left that way. Then look at the render: the check cannot yet see a box drawn across a lane line or outside its own lane, two flows drawn on top of each other, or a flow that wanders through a lane it does not stop in. Those are found only by looking. The same findings are in render:bpmn’s warnings and the process’s QA report, so a reviewer sees what the author left. The procedure, and why the budget is 1400 × 900, is bpmn-detangle.

186.title: In this repository, a diagram is executable
186.content: processes/**/*.bpmn are not pictures. workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete run them, and workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. That has consequences for how you author: . | Every activity carries <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="…"/> naming the skill that implements it, and <cat-harness.processes:bean store="beans/"/> where it touches the work plan. bun run cat check:workflow-refs fails on a ref that resolves to nothing, and bun run cat kg:audit additionally fails when the named skill exists but no package can serve it. | Every lane names a role. Declare the role once as a top-level <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> (before the collaboration and the process), and set partitionElementRef="<role id>" on the lane; the id is the role’s in scenarios/roles.json, verbatim. Lane names are free text; an explicit ref is the join that does not depend on spelling. <bootstrap.processes:role ref> is the deprecated form. A diagram using any bootstrap.processes: element declares the namespace as the first child of <bpmn:definitions>: <bpmn:import namespace="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns/" location="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns.jsonld" importType="http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld"/>. | A store is not a lane. Lanes are for people and agents, the roles that act. A place where things are kept, such as the work plan (work items), a corpus, a session record, an activity log or a published bucket, is a <bpmn:dataStoreReference>. The tasks that read or write it point at it with data associations, and each task sits in the lane of whoever does it. A “Work plan — beans” lane holding “Open the bean” says the store does the work, when the agent does. | The process’s own bpmn:documentation opens with what it is for. Its first sentence is the diagram’s row on the publication-workflow page. kg-export carries it on the Process node as summary (the whole text as description), the page reads it from the published named-subgraph JSON-LD (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) rather than from anything written by hand, and check:process-index fails when a declared diagram’s node has none. So that sentence says what the process does or answers — not who asked for it, which work item or issue it came from, or where the work got to. Those belong later in the documentation, or in the work item. | A gateway may be computed rather than chosen — see dmn-authoring. | Policy is declared on the process. <cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement="strict"/> means workflow_gate refuses a step that is not enabled; absent policy means strict. Steps marked relaxable="false" may never be relaxed by any package. | .

187.title: Readable diagrams: what the research supports
187.content: These rules are what holds up from the BPMN comprehension research, checked mechanically. kg:audit reports each rule below per process (src/workflow/diagram-quality.ts in the tools layer). The sources, and how strong each rule’s evidence is, are in the process-model-quality methodology. | Separate routing from work. A task never has two outgoing flows: put an exclusive or parallel gateway after it, or a reader must guess fork vs choice (activity-implicit-split, major). A loop-back INTO a task is fine. A gateway either joins or splits, not both (gateway-mixed). A question is a gateway, never a task: a box named “Should it leave now?” or “Separate this graph?” is a decision drawn as work. If someone must judge first, draw that as a task (“Judge whether it should leave”) or a call to Process_AskThePerson, then the question on the gateway after it. | Keep it small. Split by phase into call activities past 20 flow nodes (process-size). That 20 is house style. The only threshold with evidence is 7PMG’s 50 (process-decompose, major), and it predicts modelling errors such as deadlocks, not reading speed. | One start event per process level (process-single-start). Several named end events are fine, and the work item CLOSE pattern needs them. | A decision is a question, its branches are the answers (decision-label-question). | Label activities verb-object: imperative verb, then its object (Review the draft, not Draft review) (activity-label-verb-first). The evidence is one study of how ambiguous labels felt (29 students), so this is reported, never gated. | A name says the step, nothing else. No trailing [skill] slug: the skill is in <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>, and the page links it from there. No step numbers (“1 ·”, “Phase 2:”, “P1.1”): the flows already give the order, and a number in front breaks verb-first. A number that cites a section of a source document goes in the task’s documentation. A list of numbered steps is a sign the diagram copies a document’s outline; group the steps into phases instead. | . Split by phase: how . A diagram can be right in every step and still unreadable on its page. When process-size fires, or a diagram has a start event per lane, split it like this: . | The top-level process shows the phases. Each phase is a <bpmn:callActivity calledElement="…"> to its own process. Keep at the top only what moves the work between phases: who hands off to whom, and the decisions that send it back (rejected → revise). A loop that crosses phases is drawn at the top; a loop inside a phase stays in that phase. | A phase lives in its own file, <parent>-<phase>.bpmn, next to the parent, with its own process id (Process_<Parent><Phase>) and a first documentation sentence that says what the phase does. It becomes the phase’s row on the publication-workflow page like any other diagram’s. | A phase that ends two ways ends in two named end events, and the caller’s gateway right after the call reads which one it reached, as GW_BeanYours reads Process_BeanOpen’s. | Keep the node ids when you move nodes into a phase. A test, a schema or a skill that points at Task_X then changes only its file and process, not its id. | Open and close the work item at the top, once. A process that is only ever called runs on its caller’s work item, so a phase calls neither Process_BeanOpen nor Process_BeanClose (check:bean-calls). “Once” holds for the top as well: a process with several outcomes routes them all into one Process_BeanClose call, which decides itself whether the work item is completed, scrapped or blocked, and only then branches to its named end events. One close per outcome repeats the same box and makes the diagram wide. | A caller’s adjudication accepts looks one level down. If the judgement moves into a phase, put accepts on the call to that phase, and take it off any caller further up. | Name a call activity for the phase, verb-object like any activity (“Review the change”), not for its file. | . A phase that only one parent calls is still worth its own file: the point is the page a reader opens, not reuse. Untangle every diagram you touch . The same discipline as ArchiMate views (archimate-models §”Untangle every view you touch”), and the same geometry: a change never adds a tangle. Run bun run cat kg:audit before and after, and compare edge-crossing, edge-through-node and edge-rectilinear for the diagram, and check that no shape has a flow in and a flow out on the same point and that each lane’s rows sit at k/(n+1) of its height (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”). Say both counts in the PR. Route loop-backs in the channel below the lane (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”), then look at the rendered SVG. What the evidence does NOT support . Do not import these from style guides or model output; each was checked: . | Mandatory left-to-right flow. Figl & Strembeck 2015 (44 people) found no significant difference in accuracy or time across four directions. Lay out left-to-right for consistency, not because it reads faster. | A word cap on labels, a gateway fan-out cap of 4, and a fixed colour palette. No study behind them. Colouring matching split and join gateways made novices more accurate and experts faster, not more accurate (Reijers et al. 2011). | OR-gateways need no rule: the process model refuses inclusive gateways at load. | .

188.title: If it has actors, activities and a control flow, it is BPMN
188.content: Not a Mermaid fence. Mermaid stays for the things that are not processes — component maps, lattices, navigation graphs. The audit of which is which is on the publication workflow page, which the content core authors.

189.title: Why this skill is in a platform package
189.content: It covers both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn, and platform processes such as crdm-requirements.bpmn name it, so it cannot live in a content-type package: a platform process depending on a content-type package crosses the boundary the platform-boundary-guard subagent keeps. Its DAK material stays here rather than in a second skill, because a generic skill naming a domain worked example is ordinary, and two skills that must be read together to author one diagram are not.

190.title: When a layer above transforms it
190.content: A layer built on this one may transform an authored business process into another artefact — FHIR Shorthand, for instance — and then the BPMN is a source artefact rather than documentation of one. Author it knowing it will be transformed: names and ids you choose here appear in what is generated. That layer’s own tooling skill has the mechanics; this one names no layer above it.
