306.title: Content Graph — Editorial Organisation Skill
306.content: Skill content-graph: Editorial graph analysis skill — builds a content graph from uses[], interprets, proofs, and examples relationships; builds a chapter/section topology graph; and applies heuristics to identify forward references, cross-section/cross-chapter coupling, and sections that are too sparse or too dense. Produces actionable reorganisation suggestions and can implement approved moves. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch .

307.title: Two relations — read this first
307.content: A block participates in two different dependency relations, and this skill is about the first one: . | Relation | Source | Answers | Maintained by | . | editorial | uses[] | “what must a reader have read to follow this?” | agent / human — it is authored content | . | formal | the content type’s formal reference → its dependency graph | “what does this block’s formal layer actually invoke?” | machine-derived, never hand-written | . They diverge in both directions, legitimately: a formal layer invokes helpers nobody needs to read about; a claim is motivated by an example it never formally cites. Never populate uses[] from a formal graph — it destroys the editorial signal every heuristic below is computed from. The layer that ships a formal content type defines its formal dependency graph and links down to this skill. The reorganisation heuristics in this skill (forward references, coupling, section balance) are editorial-only by design: reading order is a question about readers, so mixing formal edges in would make the answers wrong, not richer. Impact questions (“what breaks if this changes?”) want the union of both. Build it with pipeline/content-graph.ts, whose accessors default to the union and take an optional EdgeKind filter: . bun run pipeline/content-graph.ts content/<paper> . Auditing whether uses[] is well used is a separate skill: uses-editorial-review (plus the mechanical uses QA axis).

308.title: Overview
308.content: This skill analyses the full content graph of the project at two levels: . | Block graph — Every content block is a node. Edges represent editorial relationships: uses[] (reader-prerequisite), interprets (remark → statement), proofs[] (proof → statement), examples[] (example → statement). The block graph captures the argument structure as presented to a reader. | Chapter/section graph — Chapters and sections are nodes. A directed edge from section S₁ to section S₂ exists whenever a block in S₁ uses a block in S₂. The section graph captures the pedagogical reading order. | . These two graphs are used together to apply heuristics and generate ranked reorganisation suggestions.

309.title: When to Use This Skill
309.content: . | “content graph” / “content organisation” | “cross-chapter arrows” / “cross-section dependencies” | “forward references” / “minimise forward refs” | “sections too small” / “sections too large” / “section balance” | “disentangle content” / “reorganise chapters” | “analyse content connections” | “show me the block graph” / “show me the chapter graph” | “what blocks should move?” / “suggest reorganisation” | .

310.title: Prerequisites
310.content: . | Python 3 and graphviz (installed automatically if missing) | Content block .ts files in content/<paper>/ | Chapter manifests with sections → blocks structure | .

311.title: Heuristics
311.content: The skill applies the following heuristics, each producing a severity- ranked finding: . H1 — Forward references (severity: HIGH) . A forward reference occurs when block A uses block B, but B appears later in the document than A. These cause readers to encounter concepts before they are defined. A block’s position is its (chapter_number, section_index, block_index) tuple in document order. forward_ref: A (pos P_A) uses B (pos P_B) where P_B > P_A . Ideal: 0 forward references. Acceptable: ≤ 5 (genuine architectural cycles). Flag for action: > 5. H2 — Cross-chapter coupling (severity: MEDIUM) . A cross-chapter edge occurs when block A in chapter C₁ uses block B in chapter C₂ (C₁ ≠ C₂). Count cross-chapter edges per chapter pair (C₁ → C₂): . | Edges going forward (C₁.number < C₂.number): blocks in early chapters depend on later chapters’ content → may be a problem (forward reference by chapter). | Edges going backward (C₁.number > C₂.number): normal; later chapters build on earlier ones → fine. | . Flag: chapters with more than 10 cross-chapter forward edges. H3 — Cross-section coupling (severity: MEDIUM) . Same as H2 but at section granularity within a single chapter. Report any section pair where ≥ 3 blocks reference each other across section boundaries. Ratio metric: cross_section_edges / total_edges_in_chapter. | Ratio < 0.20: well-structured | 0.20–0.40: moderate coupling | 0.40: high coupling — restructuring likely needed . | . H4 — Section too sparse (severity: LOW) . Sections with fewer than 3 content blocks (excluding intro prose) risk fragmenting the narrative. They are candidates for merging with an adjacent section. Threshold: < 3 non-prose blocks. Exception: Intro/overview sections (first block is prose). H5 — Section too dense (severity: LOW) . Sections with more than 18 content blocks are hard to navigate. Threshold: > 18 blocks. Suggestion: Split along natural dependency boundaries within the section. H6 — Isolated blocks (severity: LOW) . A block with no uses[] edges (other than prose/intro) and no block in uses[] of other blocks is isolated. It may belong to a different section or chapter, or may be dead content. H7 — Remark / example ratio (severity: INFO) . Sections where remark + example blocks outnumber the content type’s claim-bearing blocks (for a paper folio, definition + theorem + lemma + proposition + corollary + conjecture) by more than 2:1 may have too much interpretation and too little substance — or vice versa.

312.title: Placement Principles for New/Changed Content
312.content: The heuristics above detect problems post-hoc. The placement principles below are proactive: agents must follow them when creating new blocks or significantly changing existing ones. PR1 — Topical home chapter . Every block belongs in the chapter whose topic it primarily addresses. Build a topic map for the project (chapter directory → primary topic scope) and use it to decide. If a block spans two chapters’ topics, split it (see PR5). PR2 — Forward-reference avoidance . A new block should appear after all blocks it uses[]. Run content-graph-analysis.py after placement and verify zero new forward references. PR3 — Section density bounds . When adding blocks to a section, check the count stays within 3–18 blocks. If adding would exceed 18, split the section first (H5). If a removal would drop a section below 3, consider merging (H4). PR4 — Cross-chapter dependency direction . New blocks should depend backward (on earlier chapters), not forward. If a new block in Ch 3 needs to use something from Ch 7, either: . | Move the dependency to Ch 3 first, or | Place the new block in Ch 7 instead. | . PR5 — Topic-coherent blocks . Before accepting a new block, verify it addresses a single topic. If the .md content contains material belonging to multiple chapters, split it into separate blocks placed in their respective chapters. Defer to block-density R1 for the full audit. PR6 — Table extraction on creation . If a new block’s .md contains a table with > 5 data rows, extract it immediately to a table block (kind: "table", label: tbl:<name>-data). Reference it from the parent block via uses[]. Do not wait for a later audit. See block-density R3 for details. PR7 — Reorganisation map update . After any block move, section split/merge, or directory rename, update docs/reorganization-map.md with the change. This is mandatory — it is the downstream debugging reference for tracing broken labels and imports.

313.title: Placement Checklist (for agents)
313.content: When adding a new block or significantly changing an existing block: . | □ Identify the primary topic → select home chapter (PR1) | □ Check uses[] deps appear earlier in document order (PR2) | □ Check target section has 3–18 blocks after insertion (PR3) | □ Verify no new forward cross-chapter edges (PR4) | □ Verify block is single-topic; split if not (PR5) | □ Extract tables > 5 rows to table blocks (PR6) | □ Update docs/reorganization-map.md if anything moved (PR7) | □ Run python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py to confirm | .

314.title: Workflow
314.content: Step 1 — Parse the content tree . Read the paper manifest to enumerate chapters. For each chapter, read its manifest to enumerate sections and their block lists. Assign each block a document position (chapter_number, section_index, block_index). For each block .ts file, extract: . | label, kind, uses[], interprets, proofs[], examples[] | . Step 2 — Build the block graph . Build an adjacency map: . edges[(from_label, to_label)] = edge_type # "uses"|"interprets"|"proof"|"example" . Index every block’s document position: . position[label] = (chapter_no, section_idx, block_idx) . Step 3 — Build the chapter/section graph . For each chapter pair (C₁, C₂) count directed edges from blocks in C₁ to blocks in C₂: . chapter_edges[(c1_num, c2_num)] += 1 . For each section pair within the same chapter, count cross-section edges: . section_edges[(s1_label, s2_label)] += 1 . Step 4 — Apply heuristics . Run each heuristic (H1–H7) and collect findings. Each finding has: . | severity: HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW / INFO | heuristic: H1–H7 | description: human-readable explanation | blocks: list of involved block labels | suggestion: proposed action | . Step 5 — Generate visualisations . Two DOT/SVG outputs (via Graphviz): . 5a. Chapter/section graph (/tmp/content_chapter_graph.svg) . | Nodes: chapters (large boxes) containing sections (small boxes) | Edges: weighted directed arrows between sections | Color: red = forward cross-chapter edges, orange = high cross-section coupling, gray = normal backward dependencies | . 5b. Block graph heat-map (/tmp/content_block_heatmap.svg) . This is the DEPENDENCY heat map, for a paper’s structure. For “where should a reviewer of this edit look first”, the heat map is the review page’s section-by-metric table, and the review-heatmap skill says what each of its columns means. | Nodes: blocks (grouped by chapter/section in clusters) | Edges: forward references only (red), cross-chapter edges (orange) | Isolated blocks highlighted in yellow | . Step 6 — Report findings . Print a ranked report (HIGH → LOW → INFO): . ## Content Graph Analysis: <paper> ### Summary - Total blocks: N | Chapters: N | Sections: N - Total block edges: N (uses/interprets/proof/example) - Cross-chapter edges: N | Cross-section edges: N - Forward references: N ### HIGH — Forward References (H1) - block A (ch1/sec2) uses block B (ch3/sec5) ← B defined later Suggestion: move B earlier, or add stub to ch1 ### MEDIUM — Cross-Chapter Coupling (H2) - Ch4 → Ch1: 14 forward edges ← Ch4 blocks depend on Ch1 Top offending blocks: ... ### LOW — Sparse Sections (H4) - sec:my-section (Ch3): 2 non-prose blocks Suggestion: merge with adjacent sec:other-section ### LOW — Dense Sections (H5) - sec:my-dense-section (Ch4): 20 blocks Suggestion: split into two sections along a dependency boundary . Step 7 — Interactive suggestions . After the report, offer the user a numbered menu of actions they can approve: . What would you like to do? [1] Move block X from sec:A to sec:B [2] Split sec:large-section into two sections [3] Add a new section "Preliminaries" in Ch3 to absorb forward refs [4] Merge sec:sparse-1 and sec:sparse-2 [5] Show detailed block graph for chapter N [6] Re-run analysis after changes [0] Done . For each approved action, make the minimal changes to the .ts manifest files. Step 8 — Implement approved moves . For a block move (action [1]): . | Remove the block name from blocks[] in its current section. | Add the block name to blocks[] in the target section at the correct position (after its uses[] dependencies). | Re-run the analysis to confirm improvement. | . For a section split (action [2]): . | Ask the user to name the two new sections and choose a split point. | Rewrite the chapter manifest with two section({...}) entries. | Move blocks to the correct new section. | . For a section merge (action [4]): . | Combine the two blocks[] arrays in document order. | Remove the merged-away section from the chapter manifest. | . Always show a before/after energy comparison: . Before: energy=142, backward_edges=12, sparse_sections=3 After: energy=87, backward_edges=4, sparse_sections=1 .

315.title: Python implementation
315.content: The core algorithm is a standalone Python script: . pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py . Usage: . # Full heuristic report cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py # Write report to /tmp/content-graph-report.md cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --md # Generate concrete, implementable reorganisation proposals cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --proposals # → output also written to /tmp/content-graph-proposals.md # Specific chapter only cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --chapter <chapter-dir> # Generate visualisations cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --visualise # Export graph as JSON (for MCP consumption) cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --json > /tmp/content-graph.json . Proposal kinds (–proposals output) . | Kind | Description | Trigger | . | split | Split a dense section (> 18 blocks) along natural comment boundaries | H5 | . | merge | Merge two adjacent sparse sections (< 3 non-prose blocks each) | H4 | . | move | Move a block that is forward-referenced by ≥ 3 earlier blocks | H1 | . | reverse | Fix an interprets/example block that appears before its target | H1 | . Each proposal includes: . | A unique ID (P1, P2, …) for stable reference | Exact chapter manifest path and section labels to edit | Concrete blocks[] array changes to make | Expected forward-reference reduction | . Chapter naming convention . Directory names are descriptive slugs with NO chapter numbers: . | introduction/, <topic-a>/, <topic-b>/, etc. | The paper manifest chapters[] array defines the chapter order | Chapter numbers are auto-derived: numbered chapters get sequential 1, 2, 3… | Chapters with tabLabel set (e.g. "I", "G") are unnumbered (\chapter*{}) | To reorder chapters: just reorder lines in the paper manifest — no renames needed | . Key functions: . | parse_paper(root) → {chapters, sections, blocks, positions} | build_block_graph(blocks) → {nodes, edges} | build_section_graph(blocks, positions) → {chapter_edges, section_edges} | apply_heuristics(graph, positions) → [Finding] | generate_proposals(...) → [Proposal] (split/merge/move/reverse) | generate_dot_chapter(graph) → SVG path | generate_dot_blocks(graph) → SVG path | report(findings) → formatted text | .

316.title: Integration with other skills
316.content: | After this skill | Use next | . | Block moves approved | the content type’s block validation skill — verify schema integrity | . | Forward refs identified | chapter-complexity-review — block-level reorder within chapter | . | Cross-chapter coupling found | the content type’s critical-path analysis skill — trace logical dependency chain | . | Sparse sections found | editor — add missing content blocks | . | Dense sections found | block-density / the content type’s block review skill — audit individual blocks for splitting | . | Proposals generated | Approve with user, then implement via manifest edits + re-run | . | New content proposed | Run placement checklist (PR1–PR7) before accepting | . | Block too long / multi-topic | block-density — single-topic coherence audit | . | Large table found in block | block-density R3 — extract to table block | . | Feature branch ready to merge | /prepare-merge (slash command) — upstream check + placement + density + one-voice | .

317.content: | File | Purpose | . | /tmp/content_chapter_graph.svg | Section-level topology | . | /tmp/content_block_heatmap.svg | Block-level dependency heat-map | . | /tmp/content-graph.json | Machine-readable graph export | . | /tmp/content-graph-report.md | Full analysis report | . | /tmp/content-graph-proposals.md | Concrete reorganisation proposals | .

318.title: Drawing it
318.content: bun run cat content:graph:uml --root <content dir> --out <dir> [--status <status file>] (Tool content-graph-uml) draws this graph under the graph-rendering rules: . | chapters as packages; | uses[] and interprets solid, the content type’s formal edges dashed purple (supplied by the content type’s formal-graph builder); | status fills from the content type’s status file; | one diagram per chapter, with blocks in other chapters as dashed stubs; | portrait and landscape views, and a --check that needs no Java. | . It builds on buildContentGraph, so it draws exactly the graph the QA checks read. content-graph-analysis.py --visualise re-parses the sources instead and has no staleness check.

353.title: Running CI, not just assuming it
353.content: A local build runs on a warm cache, your toolchain and your flags; CI runs cold on its own. A local green is evidence about your machine, not about the branch. Push, then dispatch the workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <workflow>.yml --ref <branch>, or the actions_run_trigger MCP tool), wait for it, and record run URL + conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. If dispatch is refused for lack of actions: write, say so in the PR and give the command a maintainer should run. Also check when CI last ran (actions_list → list_workflow_runs): a workflow nothing dispatches can sit red on main while the content it checks stops building.

354.title: A green build only covers what the target reaches
354.content: Before reading “build green” as a claim about the corpus, check what the build target actually compiles. Build systems often default to narrow roots: the target compiles its root plus whatever that root imports, not every source in the directory. Where sources are found and what is built are separate settings. The check is cheap in any build system — count build artifacts against sources. A ratio far from 1 means the green is scoped, and any corpus-wide number read off that build — open-obligation counts, coverage, warning totals — is an undercount by construction. Say what the build covered, not just that it passed.

358.title: Where the results go — not into a commit
358.content: A test run’s results are derived: re-running the plan over the same tree and data reproduces them. They are kept where every derived QA result is kept — the orphan qa-reports branch, keyed by the commit they were computed on (main/<sha>/, pr/<n>/<sha>/), written by bun run cat qa:publish (the CI job qa-publish) and read back with bun run qa:fetch. Do not regenerate a results file in order to commit it. Two things a test run produces are not derived, and they stay on main: . | A reviewer’s judgement of a case — an SME or QC reviewer’s verdict, an agent’s adjudication — goes to test/attestations/ (qa-attestations/v1), because no re-run can reproduce it. | A certification — an accountable decision taken on a plan’s rollup — also stays on main, beside the attestations, and is then signed through qa-report-signing (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). | . “Regression comparison” against a previous version is a comparison against its stored results: --against <ref> on a gate, or qa:fetch --ref for a report. A previous version with no stored entry is UNKNOWN — say so; never read it as “no regressions”.

366.title: /continual-progress — trackable, always-PR’d, continually-committed work
366.content: Skill continual-progress: Make in-flight work trackable by others in real time — open a PR from the first commit, push small coherent increments continuously (never hoard uncommitted work), keep a live status checklist in the PR body, and post brief intent on the PR + any overlapping sibling PRs. Use on any multi-step or long-running task, especially when siblings/agents or the author may need to follow, cherry-pick, or take over mid-flight. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Sibling agents and the author can only coordinate with work they can see. This skill makes every in-flight task trackable in real time: the PR is open from the first commit, progress lands as a stream of small pushed commits, and the PR body carries a live status checklist. It is the visibility complement to /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) (which triages across PRs); this one governs how your own PR stays legible while you work.

367.title: The four invariants
367.content: . | Always have an open PR (from commit #1). Branch, make the first (even stub) commit, push, open the PR — before further work. The PR is the durable, visible artifact; the chat session is ephemeral. Never accumulate work on a local branch with no PR. Never ask permission to open one — branch, commit, push and PR are all pre-authorised. | Commit + push small, coherent increments — continuously. Each logically distinct change is its own commit (a single fix, a single module, a single unit of work). Push after each commit (or every 2–3 if moving fast). A watcher should be able to git log your branch and see a legible, bisectable trail — not one giant drop. Target: no more than ~20–30 min of work between pushes on a long task. | Keep a live status checklist in the PR body. Maintain a - [ ] / - [x] checklist of the task’s sub-parts in the PR description (or a pinned top comment), updated as each increment lands. A sibling or the author should be able to read the PR body and know exactly what is done / in-flight / remaining — without reading the diff or asking in chat. | Post brief intent — on your PR and overlapping siblings. One short intent line on PR-open (“doing X on <files>; will touch <scope>”); a one-line comment on any sibling whose scope overlaps (“starting <theme> on <files>; flag conflicts”). Don’t stream comments — update the checklist (invariant 3) for routine progress; comment only for genuine coordination (overlap, a blocker, a handoff-relevant finding). Defer to /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) for the full cross-PR triage protocol. New work posts its intent only after the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work” has been run and recorded in the workplan work item. | . Bean edits are pushed to the state branch, not the PR . Work item and workflow-instance edits (beans/defs/*.md, beans/workflows/*.json) do not belong in the PR’s commit set. The code PR contains code, test, and documentation changes destined for main. Work-plan progress, work item claims, status updates, and notes are written directly to the work-plan store through its configured Tool (work-plan-store (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan); on a git state branch, bun run cat state:push per work-plan-store-git-branch). The PR description references the work item via Closes-bean: <id> (or in the status checklist), but commits on the PR branch must not bundle work item file edits. This avoids merge conflicts on work item files and prevents work-plan edits from triggering code CI workflows.

368.title: The fifth invariant, and the one agents get wrong
368.content: . | Do not hold a green change proposal back waiting for someone to look at it. This is the rule that gets inverted in the name of care, and inverting it is not caution — it is a blocked reviewer. | . An agent that has built something it cannot fully verify — a rendered page, a diagram, a UI — must not leave it open and ask the human to confirm from a preview first: . A human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it, and a preview pasted into chat is a strictly worse proxy than the deployed thing. Holding the merge does not transfer the verification to them — it withholds the only form in which they could do it, and asks them to adjudicate from a screenshot. Link the PAGE, never the site root . When you ask somebody to look at a rendered artefact, link the artefact. Not the site it is on, not the preview’s front door — the exact URL of the thing you changed. Linking the root makes the reader reconstruct a route the agent already knew, and every extra click is a cost passed to a reader who may type with difficulty. It also hides a real failure: an agent that links the root has not checked that its page is reachable at all. So: . | One link per thing to look at. Two changed pages is two links, each labelled with what to look for on it — not one root and a sentence of navigation. | Deep-link past the index. If the change is on /docs/<iris-replica>/kg-to-portal.html, that is the URL, not /docs/<iris-replica>/. | Take it from the preview’s page list, never from memory or a source path: a branch slug is exactly the kind of string that is almost right. The rule, and where the list comes from, is feedback-deep-links. | The root is the right link for precisely one thing — a change to the landing page itself. | . This is the same rule as the invariant above, one step further on. A human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it; they also cannot assess it from a link to somewhere near it. What to do with the thing you could not verify . Say it in the body, and merge anyway. ## Not verified is a real section and an honest one; an unmerged proposal is not a substitute for it. Reversibility is what makes this safe — a docs or content change is one revert away, and the cost of reverting is far below the cost of a human blocked on a decision they have no artefact for. A pipe discards the exit code — so a piped run cannot verify anything . cmd | tail makes $? the status of tail. Every claim that a command PASSED must come from a run without a pipe, or from ${PIPESTATUS[0]}. This is mechanical rather than a matter of care, because care does not prevent it. A command whose output sounds like a failure, run through a pipe, reads as a silent pass, and one whose output sounds like a pass hides a failure; a silent pass is what this repository treats as worse than a loud failure. So: when the question is “did this pass”, run it bare. When you want both the output and the verdict, run it twice or capture the status first. Reading a verdict off prose you piped is the same error as quoting a count from prose. A template is not a page — verify the BUILD, not the source of it . The invariant above says a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. This is its twin, and it is the one an agent breaks: . An agent cannot assess a rendered artefact from the template that generates it. A correct template and a correct page are different claims, and only the second is what a reader loads. Every source gate can pass over a defect that exists only in the build’s output. For example, a Liquid -%} that strips the space between two attributes makes Kramdown stop treating a block as HTML and escape it into visible text, while unit tests, lint, type checks, gates, e2e and accessibility suites all read valid sources and pass. So the rule is mechanical, not a matter of diligence: . | When the artefact is a built page, the evidence is the built page. Build the site and read the output. Reading the template proves the template. | A screenshot of a scratch render is not a screenshot of the build. If the real build cannot run locally (here the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway — a pass-through _layouts/default.html is enough to see what Kramdown did. Stub the part that cannot run; never substitute the part under test. | State which one you looked at. “Rendered and checked” is ambiguous between the two, and the ambiguity is where this hid. | . check:escaped-markup, run in docs-site.yml against the assembled _site/, covers the escaped-markup case, because the assembled site is the only place the answer exists. It does not retire the rule: the next defect of this shape will be in whatever the build does that no source gate can see. The exceptions, and none of them is “I am unsure” . | Never merge red. A failing or unrun required check is a real blocker. | Never merge over an unresolved review thread you have not answered. | Where the repository requires explicit merge permission, that wins, and nothing here relaxes it by a word. Some folios require an explicit “merge it” from the author for every merge to the default branch. There the rule reads: get it green, get it mergeable, say once that it is ready, then stop — do not re-ask on a timer, and do not let “not merged yet” become a reason to stop pushing. | . Green means handed to the Merge Steward — an agent never merges to main here . The merge policy for folio-assistant. It is the “explicit merge permission” case above, made into a hand-off rather than a question: . | Never merge to main yourself — not with gh pr merge, not with the MCP merge tool, not after a green run, not under a standing “merge it” from earlier in the session. | When CI is green on EVERY job (the run list, not the PR page — see prepare-merge §”NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN”; on a draft, the fast tier), and when the queue allows (§”Pace the ready marking” below): mark the PR Ready for review, add the label ready-to-merge, and comment ready: <head sha> — the full sha of the head that went green, so a push after it is visibly not what was declared ready. | Ask the merge manager to merge, in six lines (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). First check that a merge manager is active and live: the latest merge manager: <session id> announcement, and that session answered within the stall window. Send it the PR URL and full head SHA, your session URL, 1-3 sentences on what changed, the rendered preview URL for that head (or no preview: <reason>), what to look for in the preview, and full tier green as judged. It posts them in its chat and asks the owner by card. An approval the owner gives in your own session does not authorise a merge. With no live merge manager, follow merge-manager-watcher (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”The sibling’s side: find the merge manager first”: measure whether one is needed, then either manage your own PRs or elect one with your siblings. If your request is not acknowledged within the stall window, the merge manager has stalled: re-elect without it. The format is in §”The merge request: six lines” there. | The Merge Steward session (“Separation”) merges. It brings main in, runs regen, re-checks and merges. That is its lane, not yours. | If it reports red, it is yours again: fix, push, wait for green on every job, then re-label and comment ready: <new head sha>. | . Wherever a merge does happen, it is the merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) sub-process: evidence on the head, the owner’s authorisation for that merge, recorded, then the merge. So “merge anyway” in §”What to do with the thing you could not verify” reads here as mark it ready anyway, and “merge it as soon as it is green” in the fix-forward section below reads as hand it over as soon as it is green. The point of both is unchanged: a green PR is not held back. Pace the ready marking — the runner pool is shared . The Actions runner pool is shared across the owner’s repositories. A draft PR runs only the fast tier, and marking it ready starts the full tier, about 10 jobs. So the number of PRs marked ready at once is what fills the queue: . | Open every PR as a draft. | Mark it ready only when its own change is done and its fast checks pass. | Check the queue first: gh api "repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/runs?status=queued" --jq .total_count. If it is more than about 2 queued runs per runner (5 runners on 2026-10-24, so more than about 10), hold the marking and check again later. | At most 3 ready, CI-pending PRs per agent per repository. Hand one over or let it finish before you mark another. | A fix that unblocks other work may jump the line: a link in the repin chain, or a fix for a red main. | . Holding a PR as a draft for pacing is not holding back a green PR: the fast tier is green, and the hand-off above waits for the full tier. The merge manager enforces this rule (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Cancel CI”). When the runners are saturated, it closes superseded PRs, cancels stale queued runs that never started, and asks the owners of the lowest-priority PRs to return them to draft: merge-manager-watcher (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Runner relief”. A new gate is proven downstream before it lands . A PR that adds a gate or check:* script to a lower layer passes on its own main, says how downstream layers run it, and shows a dry run over a fresh folio-assistant mount. Otherwise the next re-pin inherits the breakage (prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream”). One pusher per PR branch . Only the session that owns a PR pushes to its branch (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Anyone else sends the owner the change, on the PR’s thread or by message. Every push restarts the full CI run: on 2026-11-07, three sessions pushed to folio-assistant#2985 within 10 minutes, and each push restarted it. Stack instead of waiting . Do not wait for a dependency to merge before starting work that needs it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “they dont need to wait for a merge to start working on a feature branch needing a dependent feature branch. They can stack”). The process is the first row of merge-request.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). | In the same repository: branch from the dependency PR’s branch, and open a draft PR whose base is that branch. Pull later changes of the dependency in with merge commits. Never rebase or force-push another session’s branch. | Across layers: develop against the dependency’s branch laid over a fresh mount. A draft may pin the dependency PR’s full head SHA (never a branch) so that CI sees it (remote-mount §”Stacking across layers”). | A re-pin is its own PR. Put the pins, and nothing else, in one PR, and stack the work that needs them on it. A fix the re-pin needs lands in its owning layer first (owner ruling, 2026-11-07; remote-mount §”Re-pinning”). | Say so: write stacked on <repo>#<n> in the PR body, and list the order in the merge request. | When the base lands: retarget the PR onto main, merge main in (across layers: re-pin to the dependency’s merge commit on main), then mark it ready by the queue rule. Never merge the stacked PR into its base branch, and never mark it ready while it pins an unmerged commit. | . Two green PRs can merge into a red main, and the answer is to fix forward . A PR is tested against the main it last merged, not the main it lands on. Two PRs that are each green can still combine into a failure that neither branch contained, and no regen on either branch can see it. The policy is to fix forward, not to add a merge queue or an “up to date” requirement. So: . | Watch main’s CI after every merge of yours, not only your PR’s — whoever pressed the button. “My PR was green” does not mean main is green. | A red main whose failure your diff did not cause is still yours to fix when you find it. Establish the cause from the failing run and each parent’s history first, then regenerate or repair in a small PR of its own, and merge it as soon as it is green. | Do not blame the last merge because it is the last merge. Check whether the parent was already red. | .

369.title: Why — the failure modes this prevents
369.content: . | Stepped-on work. A branch that hoards uncommitted work collides with siblings the moment it lands. Continual push surfaces intent from minute 1 so siblings triage around it. | Lost work on session reclaim. Cloud sessions are ephemeral; an uncommitted change vanishes when the container is reclaimed. Push it. | Opaque progress. “What’s the status?” should be answerable from the PR body, not a chat scrollback. The checklist is the source of truth. | Un-takeoverable tasks. If you go idle/blocked, a sibling can pick up a continually-committed, checklist-annotated PR; they cannot pick up an opaque local branch. | .

370.title: Checklist (run this as you work)
370.content: . | PR open? If not: branch → stub commit → push → open it now. | Anything uncommitted older than ~20–30 min? Commit + push it. | Does the PR-body status checklist reflect the current state? | Any sibling whose files I just started touching un-notified? One intent line (not a stream). | Blocked or going idle? Update the checklist + a one-line “blocked on X / handoff-ready” note so a sibling can continue. | .

371.title: Relationship to other skills
371.content: . | pr-description (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc): what the PR body says ABOVE the status checklist (the problem, why, approach, constraints, solution, usage, what is not done), for a reader who was not here. | /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — cross-PR triage (scope map, sibling intent, cherry-picks, ledger). continual-progress keeps your PR legible so /coordinate (yours or a sibling’s) has something to triage. | A folio’s own AGENTS.md may carry these rules for that repository, and a stricter merge gate — litlfred/qou §”Branch + PR workflow” is the worked case. This skill is the platform-side statement; where a folio is stricter, the folio wins. | /todo-manager — the session work-plan; the PR-body status checklist (invariant 3) is its externally-visible projection, so a watcher needs no access to the session’s work item queue. | .

373.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
373.title: Contributor feedback on a working draft
373.content: Process_ContributorFeedback · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . A document is still being written, and the Authoring Committee gives feedback on it in a shared Contributor Feedback sheet. This is what happens to ONE change set, one row of that sheet: a member starts it with a title, the sections it is about and their feedback; the agent proposes a direction; an Editor lets the agent edit; the agent makes the edit in the row’s one pull request, whose staging preview shows what changed; the committee answers on the row; and an Editor lets the agent merge. If the row’s feedback changes after the agent wrote its proposal, the proposal is marked stale and the row’s Ready for agent goes back to No, so the agent proposes again and an Editor decides again. The sheet’s colours follow the lanes: Blue for the committee, Green for the agent, Orange for the Editor. Skill: review-sheet-script. i i i i i i i i i

385.title: Working on materialized content — copy it out
385.content: Skill copy-out-materialized: Materialized content is read-only. To work on it you take a copy into your own folio/, and the copy records what it is a copy of — the local-provenance edge, which is not the upstream one. Named by: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes . Materialized content is a copy of somebody else’s bytes, and this repository does not edit it in place. The contents of a materialized <stub>/<sub-graph> are immutable, and the rule is enforced: to work on them, copy them into your own folio/. Diagram: copy-out-materialized.bpmn. Schema: the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer above this one — named here, not linked). Where they disagree, the schema wins and this file is wrong.

386.title: What the rule protects, and what it does not
386.content: It protects the CLAIM. A materialized record asserts “these bytes are what upstream published”. Editing them in place leaves that assertion standing over bytes it no longer describes — and check:materialized-fixity is what catches one that happened, by hashing the bytes against the digest the record carries. It does not protect against the copy being wrong, stale or badly chosen. Those are the five gates’ job, at materialisation time (materialize-remote), and a copy-out re-opens none of them: you are copying something this repository already decided it may hold.

387.title: Who may copy out
387.content: Any reader. This is deliberately not a permission: refusing a copy would not protect the original, because the original is protected by being read-only. A gate here would only stop people working. What copying out does NOT confer is the right to publish. The copy inherits its source’s restrictions and copyright verdicts, and it is a new artefact in your folio whose publication is your folio’s decision, judged the way any other authored content is.

388.title: Where the copy goes
388.content: Into the copier’s own folio/, with provenance — never a scratch area, which makes the copy publishable by accident: a directory nobody declared is a directory nobody gates.

389.title: The copy records what it is a copy of
389.content: This is the part that is easy to leave out and impossible to reconstruct later. materialization.provenance is a pair: . | field | points at | . | upstream | the remote thing — a URI, upstream | . | local | the original in this repository it was taken from | . A copy-out writes local. It does not overwrite upstream, and it does not reuse upstream for the local original. Without local, one rename later a copy is indistinguishable from original work. That is the whole failure this step exists to prevent, and nothing downstream can repair it: the information was never written down.

390.title: The copy is NOT read-only
390.content: A materialized node is frozen because it is a claim about somebody else’s bytes. A copy in your own folio/ is yours, makes no such claim, and is ordinary authored content — so it is writable, and its directory’s readOnly is false. If it were frozen too, the copy-out would achieve nothing, and the next person would need a copy of the copy.

391.title: The exception is “say what you did”, not a list of who may skip
391.content: The exception — for publication workflow purposes and the like — is a rule, not an allowlist of writers that would go stale: . A step that rewrites a materialized artefact records the new fixity in the same change. Then check:materialized-fixity passes and the record describes what is actually there. A step that rewrites without updating fixity fails, correctly, because it has forked upstream without saying so — which is exactly what the rule exists to prevent. The check asks a question about BYTES and never about who wrote them, so it needs no attribution of a commit to a process step. Where it applies . refresh-materialized.bpmn’s Task_Apply is the one step in the declared corpus that rewrites bytes a materialization record describes, so it writes the new fixity in the same change; otherwise a correct run of it would fail the gate as an unannounced edit. No publication process writes to materialized content. kg-to-portal.bpmn’s S_Sign signs a subgraph cut from the KG — derived content, not held upstream bytes. So the publication case is a rule with no instance yet, stated here rather than drawn as a step no diagram does, because a declared-but-absent step makes a consumer report a clean run over nothing.

392.title: What to check afterwards
392.content: . | bun run cat check:materialized-fixity — the original still hashes to its recorded digest. If it does not, the copy-out was an edit in place. | bun run cat check:read-only-graphs — your folio’s directory is not accidentally declared read-only, and the source’s still is. | .

394.doc: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else's bytes
394.title: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes
394.content: Process_CopyOutMaterialized · strict · 5 step(s) . Somebody wants to change content this repository holds a read-only materialized copy of: copy it into their own folio/, recording which original it came out of. Materialized content is read-only, and that is enforced, not advised. STRICT, and the reason is narrow. Only one step here is a gate, and it is Gateway_Frozen: whether the target is read-only at all. Everything after it is mechanical. What makes the process strict is that skipping it does not fail loudly — an edit in place succeeds, and is only caught later by check:materialized-fixity hashing bytes against the digest their record carries. A process whose omission looks exactly like compliance cannot be advisory. The copy-out re-opens NONE of the five materialisation gates. Those were answered when this repository decided it may hold these bytes at all (materialize-remote.bpmn); copying something already held is not a second acquisition. What the copy does inherit is the restrictions and copyright verdicts — the copy is a new artefact in the copier’s folio, and publishing it is that folio’s decision. The three states, the five gates and the provenance pair are folio-assistant-core/schemas/materialization.ts. Nothing here restates them. i i i i i

400.title: Corpus — committing an accepted edit
400.content: Skill corpus-commit-contract: The contract the corpus role is held to when an accepted edit is committed into it: take the write only on the editor’s acceptance, as one change with its QA sidecars, under the commit-hygiene requirement and with no relaxing of that policy. The narrowest contract the editing diagram requires. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: Editing and HCI validation . corpus (declared below this layer) is played by a mechanical actor: the versioned content store, which is written to and decides nothing. A role played by a machine is still a role, and its skills are its contract: the responsibilities it must perform, which a test can hold it to. This skill is the part of that contract this layer’s diagrams rely on, and nothing more.

401.title: Where the diagrams lean on it
401.content: Lane_Corpus in editing-hci-validation names this role and holds one activity, Task_Commit. What that lane’s documentation and the task’s say is the whole contract.

402.title: What it must do
402.content: . | Receive the write only after the editor accepts. Task_Commit is reachable from no path except Gateway_EditorDecision’s accept branch (the lane’s documentation). A change the editor discards, or one that has not reached the editor, never reaches the corpus. | Take the change together with its QA sidecars. “Only now does the change become corpus content, together with its QA sidecars” (the task’s documentation): the block and the findings about it arrive as one change. | Hold the commit to the commit-hygiene requirement (req:commit-hygiene), and allow no relaxing of it: the task’s policy is relaxable="false", because this is the one step that is irreversible in a way nothing upstream is. | .

403.title: Not its responsibility
403.content: Drafting the change, validating it, or deciding whether to accept it. Those happen in the author’s, the pipeline’s, the reviewer’s and the editor’s lanes before anything reaches the corpus. Resolving the bean afterwards is the work plan’s.

404.title: Tests
404.content: The test in tested-by: drives the editing process with the harness’s workflow engine and checks line 1 (the commit is enabled only after accept), and checks that the diagram binds the lane to this role and carries line 3’s policy. Line 2 and the content of the commit-hygiene statements are not exercised: no code in this layer performs the commit.

406.title: Corpus-Grep Skill
406.content: Skill corpus-grep: Pre-declaration corpus check. Before declaring any item “open”, “gap”, “TODO”, “open problem”, “pending derivation” — or asserting in chat that something is unresolved in the corpus — run the four-path grep checklist. A source file’s ## Status note lags the corpus by weeks; the corpus is the source of truth. An item is open only after all four paths come back empty (modulo the originating file itself). Named by: Hand back to the discussion . Disambiguation. This skill formalizes the backward check (“has this already been resolved somewhere in the corpus?”). Its forward complement is the formalize-first discipline (“can a structural claim prune the hypothesis class before I run a wide search?”). Run corpus-grep before declaring an item open; run formalize-first before launching an expensive numerical scan. The two are duals — backward against known results, forward against the hypothesis class.

407.title: Role
407.content: Gate every “this is open / unresolved / a gap” declaration behind a mechanical four-path search of the corpus. The originating source file’s status note (## Status, Open question, Phase 3 open, a TODO in a code or formal-source file, a PR-description “still open”) is not authoritative — prior agents routinely land a resolution as an audit doc, an adjacent chapter’s block, an implemented witness script, or a coordination ledger entry weeks before the source file’s note is updated. This skill catches that lag.

408.title: When to run this skill (STRICT)
408.content: Run the checklist before any of the following land in a durable artifact (audit doc, content block .md/.ts, code or formal-source comment, PR description, coordination ledger) or are asserted as fact in chat: . | “X is open” / “Open X” / “open problem” / “open question” | “TODO: derive X” / “pending derivation” / “still missing” | “this is a gap” / “no proof exists” / “not yet implemented” | “X is not wired into compute” / “nothing computes X” | . If you are about to type any of those about a corpus topic, stop and run the four paths first.

409.title: When NOT to run it (scope boundary)
409.content: The checklist gates factual corpus-status claims only. It does not gate, and must never be used to suppress: . | Skeptical assessments — “this looks fitted”, “this is numerology”, “hidden degrees of freedom here”. | Outside-view critique of a derivation’s rigor. | Reception / publishability / referee forecasts. | . Those are critical-distance judgments (see the repo’s Critical-distance license), not open-item declarations, and are never gated by this skill. Voicing them in chat does not require running corpus-grep first.

410.title: The four-path checklist (run all four)
410.content: | # | Path | What it catches | . | 1 | grep -rln <topic> docs/audits/ | Owner-authorised resolutions land as audit docs ahead of the source file’s status note being updated. | . | 2 | grep -rln <topic> content/ (full tree) | Related conjectures / propositions cross-cut chapters: a block in one chapter may answer a question raised in another. | . | 3 | grep -rln <topic> folio-assistant/computations/ | Implemented code may already discharge the content. | . | 4 | docs/coordination/<theme>.md | The coordination ledger — a prior agent may have already closed the item. | . Search the full content/ tree, not just the chapter you started in. The whole point of path 2 is that the resolution lives somewhere you did not expect.

411.title: Mechanical recipe
411.content: Pick a TOPIC that is the keyword / regex of the claim (an identifier, a label fragment, a phrase — e.g. delta_lambda, bring_color, c_3.*Taylor, kashaev.*density). Then run all four paths in one sweep: . TOPIC='delta_lambda' # ← keyword or regex for the claim under test for d in docs/audits content folio-assistant/computations docs/coordination; do if [ -d "$d" ]; then echo "=== $d ===" grep -rln -e "$TOPIC" "$d" 2>/dev/null fi done . Prefer the harness Grep tool (output_mode: "files_with_matches", one call per path or a single call with path set to the repo root and a glob) over shell grep when running inside an agent — results integrate with the permission UI and file links. The shell snippet above is the portable fallback. Widen the topic if the first pass is empty: try a synonym, the formal declaration name, the block label, the function name, and the witness-JSON key. A single spelling is not a clearing.

412.title: Decision procedure
412.content: . | Any non-trivial hit in (1)–(4) ⇒ the item is NOT open. Read the hit, then document the existing resolution instead of declaring a gap. Cite the file (audit doc / block .md / witness / ledger entry) that resolves it. | All four empty, modulo the originating file itself ⇒ you may declare the item open. “Modulo the originating file” means: a hit that is only the source file you are auditing does not count as a clearing — it is the very note you already mistrust. | Unsure whether a hit is the resolution ⇒ open the file and read it. A filename match is a lead, not a verdict. Treat a hit as resolving only if it actually discharges the claim (an audit verdict, a proved block, a passing witness, a ledger “CLOSED”). | .

415.title: Covered is not reachable — and check:tools cannot tell you which
415.content: Skill covered-is-not-reachable: A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism is reachable from no Tool node. Read before concluding from check:tools that a command is reachable, and before adding a Tool node or a maintains claim. Named by: Code node review . A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from nothing. check:tools reports the skill as covered and is right to: coverage is a relation between a Tool and a skill, never between a Tool and a command. For example, kg-export can be satisfied by a publishing node, a serving node and schema carriers while no node runs an export; translation-manager by extract, inject, status, signoff and validate nodes while none reaches the round-trip QA.

416.title: The two questions, kept apart
416.content: “Does this skill have a Tool?” — bun run cat check:tools, and bun run cat tools:coverage for which of the uncovered ones warrant one. “Is this command reachable by asking the graph?” — no instrument answers this yet; it has to be measured by hand. A skill showing as covered is not evidence that its code is reachable. Do not use the first question to answer the second: the cause of an invisible mechanism is structural, because nobody asks the second question.

417.title: What to do when you meet one
417.content: Add the node for the mechanism. Then two things not to do: . | Do not widen an existing node’s satisfies to make the gap look closed. That makes the graph assert a node does something it does not. | Do not give the new node the same I/O as an existing one unless it really is a substitute. Alternatives are derived from a shared skill plus an identical I/O signature (deriveAlternatives), and export-then-publish-then- serve are complementary steps, not competing arms. | .

418.title: Two reasons NOT to write maintains
418.content: maintains.artefact is a single path. A generator that writes one file per subject — gen-skill-docs, gen-schema-docs, gen-block-jsonld — has no single artefact to name. A declaration naming one file out of tens is worse than absent: it looks like a complete provenance record. A maintains claim asserts the artefact is published. Verify that by reading the build, not by assuming: cat-harness/ns.jsonld is a real claim because .github/workflows/docs-site.yml writes it. Remove a claim in the same change that retires its artefact: a claim outliving its artefact is the same 404 from the other side. An artefact nobody publishes is exactly the 404 the drift check exists to prevent. And the drift check only covers its own producer . kg:schema:check reconciles maintains both ways, but its unproduced direction runs only over artefacts whose declaring Tool invokes bun run cat kg:schema, because a maintained artefact is not necessarily produced by the schema exporter. So a maintains claim on any other producer’s artefact is unchecked: it can rot to a 404 and nothing notices. The fix — not yet built — is to assert every declared artefact is present after _site/ is assembled, with could-not-determine kept distinct from present.

419.title: Adding a Tool type is fail-closed, and that is deliberate
419.content: check:tools refuses a command-line input whose type could express a shell payload, against the membership list in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts. A newly added type is absent from that list and therefore unsafe by default. Adding it is a deliberate step, not an oversight to route around — and the fix for an enumerable input is the enum, never a looser type that happens to pass. Where the enum duplicates a union declared elsewhere, guard it in both directions: satisfies catches a member that stops being valid, and a conditional type catches a member added to the union and not here. An unavoidable duplicate is fine; an unchecked one is not — see directory-conventions.

420.title: Five cases, most invisible to the instruments
420.content: | case | what exists | what is missing | what sees it | . | 1 | a skill | a Tool | check:tools, tools:coverage | . | 2 | a skill and Tools for its neighbours | a Tool for the mechanism | nothing — this skill | . | 3 | a mechanism | any skill stating the capability | nothing | . | 4 | a skill, a mechanism, a Tool | a command — it runs in-process only | nothing | . | 5 | a skill, a mechanism, a command | anything that invokes it | nothing | . Case 5 is case 4’s inverse — the entry point is present and the callers are absent — and it is discussed under §Reachability is PLURAL below, because the useful question there is how many dispatch points this should have. A script whose only references are its own usage string and a line of skill prose telling a human what to type is case 5: its mechanism is inlined in prose.

421.title: The third case: a mechanism with no skill at all
421.content: A generator that renders theme and avatar nodes into the site’s stylesheets is a textbook maintains pair, and yet no generic skill need state the capability. tools:coverage cannot see this: it enumerates skills and asks which lack Tools, so a capability nobody has stated is absent from the list it walks. (site-presentation-assets is the skill that now states that one.) . satisfies requires at least one skill, so a node cannot be written without one: . | Do not stretch a neighbouring skill to make the node validate. The resulting satisfies edge is simply false. | Do not write the skill as a wrapper for the command. A skill states a capability generically and names no script; one that exists to give a script somewhere to point is a Tool with front matter. | . Authoring the skill is a design act — a claim about the platform’s capability vocabulary, inherited by every dependent layer — so it goes to the owner rather than being decided in passing. Write the skill before the nodes. Once the gap is closed, remove any note announcing it: an agent that believes a stale gap either avoids the capability or rebuilds it.

422.title: The fourth case: a mechanism with no command, reachable in-process only
422.content: Cases 1–3 are about a missing node or a missing skill. This one has both, and is still unaskable: the mechanism has no command, so no CI job and no person can run it. For example, checkFolioProfile in pipeline/profile-check.ts catches what schema validation structurally cannot — a block valid against its own schema but wrong for the folio’s content profile, because adapters partition disjointly while profiles nest. Its only caller is the MCP tool registration, so it is reachable by an MCP-connected agent and by nothing else: not a gate, not a sweep, not a person at a shell. Every instrument that asks “can this be reached” answers yes. Ask which callers, not whether. “Reachable from MCP” and “reachable from CI” are different claims, and a durable verdict needs the second. Giving a library function its first command . Prefer a qa-sweep axis to a one-off check script: a sweep verdict is durable where a printed one is not — a printed verdict cannot distinguish “wrong since it was written” from “broken in the commit under review”. Watch the library’s defaults. checkFolioProfile resolves through readFolioProfile, which turns an undeclared profile into "paper" — correct for a validator, which validates against the wider vocabulary, and wrong for a reporter, which must use readDeclaredFolioProfile or report pass on a folio that declares no content type at all. A library’s defaulting is usually what erases the third state. When you give a library function its first entry point, the value it resolves for its own use is not the value a verdict may report. Check which of the two you are reading — by running it, not by reading it.

423.title: Reachability is PLURAL — “which caller should this have?” presumes one
423.content: One mechanism can have several dispatch points, so the question to ask is not which caller should this have but: . What should be able to start this — and is each of those a trigger or a Tool? . The two are different objects, and which one a dispatch point is follows from who initiates: . | dispatch point | it is a | because | . | a named command | Tool | a caller invokes it; that is what a Tool node IS | . | a BPMN activity | trigger | the process fires it when the step is reached | . | a QA sweep axis | trigger | the sweep fires it per subject | . | a schedule or a watcher | trigger | time or an event fires it | . None of them is an alternative to another, by the same argument deriveAlternatives makes about sharing a skill: they are different ways the same work gets started. Enumerating the dispatch points also finds the ones already built. For each candidate, check whether it exists (an activity may already carry the skill, so workflow_next already hands it to an agent), whether it is possible (a sweep cannot run a check whose verdict originates outside it), and only then what is missing. Presented as a choice, the options waste proposals; enumerated as dispatch points, they are a short audit with one action. Read the mechanism’s entry point before proposing dispatch points. A name and a position in a diagram say what something is for; an argument list says what it does — for example, whether it performs a check or only records a verdict somebody else produced.

424.title: The same failure one level out: a KIND, not a mechanism
424.content: Ask what is missing of a kind of node and the same mistake appears: counting kg-qa sidecars over the work item store, finding zero, and calling work items unaudited when several gates audit them. Coverage is a relation between an instrument and the question it was built for — see audit-coverage, with bun run cat audit:coverage as the second question.

432.title: CRDM — the data-modelling phase
432.content: Skill crdm-data-model: The CRDM data-modelling phase — when in the requirements process a model is built, what it is built from, who confirms it, and what it hands to the phases either side. The technique it invokes is data-modelling; this skill carries only the sequencing and the sign-off. Named by: CRDM data model . This skill says WHEN and WITH WHOM. It does not say how to model. That is data-modelling, and it is deliberately free of CRDM so a folio modelling data outside a requirements process can read it without inheriting a methodology it is not running. Where the two disagree, the technique wins and this page is wrong.

433.title: Where it sits, and why there
433.content: Between requirements (phases 2–4) and sign-off (phase 5). Requirements are statements about things; the model says what the things ARE. The entities come from the business-process analysis (phase 2), and phase 5 must not sign off requirements whose nouns were never pinned. Drafted too early, the model is invented from nothing; drafted too late, two stakeholders approve the same sentence meaning different things. Call_DataModel in crdm-requirements.bpmn is the callActivity after Call_Requirements and before Call_Signoff.

434.title: What it consumes
434.content: | from | what | . | phase 1, needs | the domain vocabulary the BA actually used | . | phase 2, BPA | the activities — every verb whose object is a candidate entity | . | phases 3–4, requirements | each requirement’s nouns, which the model must be able to express | . A requirement the model cannot express is a finding, not a modelling failure. It means the requirement is about something nobody has named, and the remedy is to name it. That is why this phase sits after requirements rather than before.

435.title: The sign-off, and who gives it
435.content: The agent drafts; the BA confirms the entities are the ones they meant; the stakeholders confirm the cardinalities. Those are two different questions and are asked of two different lanes on purpose: . | Are these the things? — a naming question, and the BA owns the domain vocabulary. | Is it really one per? — an operational question, and the people who run the process know where the exceptions are. | . The agent asks both and decides neither: the BA knows the domain, the agent does not guess, because a wrong cardinality is invisible until the data arrives.

436.title: What it hands on
436.content: A declared model, readable by a tool, per step 6 of the technique. Phase 5 signs off requirements against it: whether each requirement is expressible, not only whether it is wanted.

437.title: The loop, and when to leave it
437.content: Like every other CRDM phase this one loops until confirmed, and the gateway is the phase. Leave when the BA recognises the entities and the stakeholders have answered every cardinality — not when the model looks complete, because an unanswered cardinality is a hole exactly where the exceptions live.

438.title: Not decided by this skill
438.content: Whether the model is expressed as Zod, JSON Schema, a class diagram or prose is placement’s question and the folio’s choice. This phase requires only that the artefact is declared, so the next phase can read it rather than be told about it.
