1052.title: ig-render-jekyll
1052.content: Skill ig-render-jekyll: Rendering a FHIR IG’s content through the just-the-docs pipeline instead of mounting the IG Publisher’s finished HTML — the JSON-only representation contract, navigation derived from sushi-config.yaml, and the LHS rail. Read before adding a representation, a menu entry, or a page kind. Named by: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs . Skill id: ig-render-jekyll · Package: fhir-ig-base · Layer: fhir-harness . Render an IG’s pages as folio pages — markdown with front matter, through Jekyll and just-the-docs — from the Publisher’s structured output, never its finished HTML. Publisher HTML has no front matter, so the navbar, language bar, QA badges and translation surface cannot reach it; a folio page gets them all. Whether an IG repository gets this rendering is asked when it is adopted (default yes); see ig-build-pipeline §”Who starts a build”.

1053.title: The three contracts
1053.content: 1. JSON only . The Publisher emits JSON, XML and Turtle; only JSON is taken, wrapped in JSON-LD / JSON Schema. RDF, where needed, is projected from the JSON-LD. A representation that arrives and is not taken is recorded as a refusal. Not linked either. The site does not link a resource’s .xml or .ttl copy: JSON-LD nodes carry only JSON encodings, and the site.data artefact variables only url.json. The refusal record still counts what each IG published in those forms. 2. Navigation is derived, never authored . sushi-config.yaml already carries both maps the site needs: . | pages: — an ordered map of source file to title. That is the page order. | menu: — the grouping, including nested subsections. | . Derive the navigation from them. Do not hand-author a nav file or write entries back into sushi-config.yaml. When the config names a page that does not exist, that is a finding, not a reason to create a placeholder. 3. LHS rail, and the theme is captured rather than replaced . Navigation goes in the left-hand rail, not the FHIR IG’s top bar. The rest of the IG theme — CSS, typography, resource-page furniture — is captured into the theme layer rather than discarded. Nav position is a layout setting; nav contents are derived per build.

1054.title: What the render reads in the IG repository
1054.content: Only what the repository declares. Every reader on this path (build-ig-site, ig-site-data, ingest-ig-menu, ingest-ig-chrome, ig-repo-site) goes through scripts/ig-read-scope.ts, which honours contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json; anything outside it is not rendered. A repository with no section is read whole, with a warning. See ig-build-pipeline §”What this layer reads”.

1055.title: Where the variables come from
1055.content: artifactVariables (build-ig-site.ts) writes the per-artefact Liquid variables from the artefact index to _data/, read by the same Jekyll run: site.data.fhir.artifacts.<ResourceType>__<id> with url (canonical, page, json), text, link.html and elements.<key>, plus artifact_categories, artifacts_listed and artifact_lists. An element key the index does not hold is reported as not sourced, never written empty. The families and keys follow WHO’s generate_smart_liquid.py, a build script outside this layer, without its smart__ prefix: that prefix is WHO’s, and this layer does not know about WHO.

1056.title: What parity means, and what it does not
1056.content: Parity is a checklist of asset types and page kinds. A page kind the Publisher emits no data for cannot be rendered.

1057.title: Thin pages, the default (--full-pages to opt out)
1057.content: Every IG page is a thin HTML shell that loads its content from the JSON-LD graph, unless a build passes --full-pages. The shell is cat-harness-tools’ thinPageHtml. Artefact pages (gen-ig-pages.ts) . | Page address: artifact/<Type>-<id>.html, self-canonical. | The asset is a JSON-LD node, artifact/<Type>-<id>.jsonld, with no .json twin (every reader fetches the .jsonld), written by ig-artifact-jsonld.ts from the index (kind ig-artifact-jsonld; QA ig-artifact-jsonld.ts check over the built site). It uses the FHIR RDF class, dcterms, schema.org and PROV, and mints nothing. The page names the node as alternate. Its encodings list the reduced <Type>-<id>.json at the site root first (local), then the full copy in the AST cache by raw URL (mirror), then the IG’s published file (upstream); artifact/index.jsonld names each root file on its entry (schema:contentUrl; fhir-harness#359). | One shared renderer. assets/ig-artifact.js fetches the node, then the resource’s full copy (the mirror, else the local one), draws the description, facts, identity table and elements, concepts or includes, and hands the narrative and JSON to ast-resource.js. The page carries only its title, key and a <noscript> link to the node and resource. | The rail is linked: folio-navbar: linked, and the rail pass (rail-standalone-pages.ts) links its style and scripts rather than inlining them. | The tab views are thin pages too, written beside the page wherever the site serves the artefact’s JSON: a compiled copy (--compiled-data) or, failing that, the Publisher’s own <Type>-<id>.json carried as data (--publisher-data <dir>, from the docs root). An IG repository’s site (ig-site:compose) passes only --compiled-data .: the AST’s copy, served once at the root as <Type>-<id>.json. Each view keeps the Publisher’s file name: . | -definitions: the snapshot’s element table, differential marked; | -mappings: each mapping declaration with the elements mapped to it; | the JSON view (.profile.json for a StructureDefinition, else .json), drawn by ast-resource.js; | -examples, for every StructureDefinition: the instances claiming it in meta.profile, or a note that there are none. | . Each uses the same shell (thinArtifactView) and renderer; the artefact’s page links them in a tab bar, and the narrative’s links to them are relinked. The change history, testing, XML and Turtle views are neither rendered nor published. The IG API view pages stay full pages. | Nothing under comparison-v*/ is published. ig-site:publisher-pages serves the AST’s data and reads no Publisher output. | In an IG site the docs root is the site root, so --compiled-data . points each resource at ../<Type>-<id>.json from artifact/. No ast-data/ mirror is published. | . The artefact list and the table of contents (build-ig-site.ts) . | One index node, artifact/index.jsonld (family folio-ig-artifact-index-jsonld/v1, same kind), lists every artefact once, in the Publisher’s order, each entry naming its node and carrying only what a list row shows; check holds it to the artefact index and each node. | artifacts.html is a thin shell over that node: a jump list of categories, a filter, then every category open (nothing collapsed), anchored #artifacts-<slug>. | What a list draws: . | The IG’s own ImplementationGuide is “This guide”, drawn first (#artifacts-this-guide), never as a “Not categorised” row; the toc lists it first too. | A category that mixes resource types is sub-headed by type (#artifacts-<category>-<type>; the Publisher’s “Other”: Basic, Questionnaire, DocumentReference…), and the jump list counts each type. | A table draws only the columns its rows fill. An instance (an artefact with no canonical URL) has no description, so the index copies what the resource states: its meta.profile (dcterms:conformsTo, drawn as the last path segment, linked when it is in the same IG) and its code (dcterms:subject). A definition’s core profile (shareablevalueset) is not shown. | . | toc.html is a thin shell. The IG’s own pages (sushi-config.yaml pages:, landing page first) stay in its HTML; the artefacts under each category are drawn from the index node. | Both are written by stageIgSite when StageOptions.artifacts.index is given, which stage-ig-sites.ts does unless --full-pages. Staging thin a site whose artefact pages were generated with --full-pages (no index node) is refused. | . The narrative pages (composeIgSite) . | The IG’s prose stays in the HTML, rendered by Jekyll; composed into a host site, the page wears thinIgLayout (_layouts/ig-thin-<instance>.html) instead of the host’s layout, so none of the host’s chrome (harness bar, SVG sprite, sidebar nav, inline scripts) is written into it. | Everything around the prose is linked: assets/ig-artifact.css, assets/ig-topbar.css, assets/ig-source-links.js and the rail (folio-navbar: linked). The IG’s top bar, edit links, footer and TOC declaration stay. | The thin page has no host search box or QA badges; it has its own search box and language picker block (below). | . The footer stays in view . Every IG page ends with the Publisher’s footer (ig-footer.liquid on the Jekyll pages, ig-artifact.js on the thin pages, one igSiteFooter object for both): publisher and copyright year, package#version, FHIR version, the build day, and Links: Table of Contents | QA Report | Version History | License, each value read from the IG’s package, sushi-config.yaml or AST and left out when none holds it. Unlike the Publisher’s, it stays at the bottom of the window (owner, 2026-11-06): it is the body’s last box, after <main> on every IG page, position: sticky (ig-artifact.css), so it spans the width beside the rail, the page scrolls under it and nothing is left behind it at the end of the page. The body is a column at least the window’s height with <main> taking the free space, so on a page shorter than the window the footer lands at the window’s bottom too. In print both are off: the footer is static, once, at the end. “QA Report” is qa.html, the harness’s QA report (ig-qa-page.ts): the FHIR QA the build holds (the Publisher’s qa.json carried with the AST, the AST’s record and validity) and the knowledge graph’s (cat-harness-tools kg-qa-report.ts). Search and the language picker . The folio rail replaces the theme’s side menu (#site-nav is dropped; IG_DROPPED in stage-local-ig.ts), and the IG’s top bar carries a search box over the IG’s pages and artefacts (ig-search.ts): . | ig-repo-site.ts compose writes the index, assets/ig-search.json (each IG page’s title and full text; each artefact’s title, id, name, key, canonical and description), and the client, assets/ig-search.js. The index is fetched on the box’s first focus, never on page load. | The box (form.ig-search, input #search-input) is in the composed pages’ .ig-topbar and the thin pages’ header.iga-top. It is not .search, so docs-ui leaves it in the top bar. A build that does not write the files (gen-ig-pages without --search, StageOptions.search unset) writes no box. | Any other built page lacking a box (for example an IG API hub page or openapi/index.html) gets one: publisher-pages puts a bar at the top of its body (header.ig-search-top: the IG’s name, the box, the picker’s slot; stampSearchBox, withSearchBar). The pass skips assets/ and runs only when the site serves a search index. | The language picker sits beside the box, in the empty <span data-fa-slot="locale"> that follows it, which docs-ui fills. A site with no IG bar keeps the picker in docs-ui’s band. | docs-ui draws the picker from a page’s fa-translation-meta block, which publisher-pages writes (cat-harness-tools lib/translation-meta.ts) into every built page lacking one, from the IG checkout’s translation declaration; set-html-lang.ts reads it afterwards. | Translated pages (fhir-harness#382). When the IG declares translations/ in contentTypes.ig.include, each catalogue translations/<locale>/pagecontent/<page>.po is injected into its page (cat-harness-tools injectMarkdown, the segmentation the catalogue was extracted with) and staged at <locale>/<page>.md, the path the picker opens. The page and its translations carry lang, available_locales and, on a translation, translation_status and translation_source; the thin layout writes the picker’s block from them, so the picker links each language that exists. A span with no translation stays in English. A locale is verified only when translations/<locale>/status.json records a sign-off; otherwise unverified, and docs-ui shows its notice. Translated pages are out of the menu, and relative links climb out of the locale folder unless they point at a page translated into the same locale (scripts/ig-page-translations.ts). | . The root parity guard (cat-harness-tools site-parity.ts) refuses to publish a build lacking the search box or language block over a root that had them. The opt-out . gen-ig-pages.ts --full-pages and stage-ig-sites.ts --full-pages build full pages (composeIgSite(…, { fullPages: true })). Pass both or neither. --thin is a no-op; --thin --full-pages is refused.

1058.title: What this does not replace
1058.content: Which AST the pages are drawn from. An IG repository’s site is drawn from the AST on its cache branch, cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>, which a Publisher run on a runner refreshes; the publish refuses an AST not valid for the commit. See ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle”. The Publisher still runs: validation, dependency resolution and terminology expansion are its job and are not reproducible from cached output.

1060.title: index.config.json: what this checkout instantiates
1060.content: Skill index-config: index.config.json at an instantiation root says which harnesses the checkout instantiates, where each one comes from (local, or a remote mount pinned to a SHA), each layer’s config INLINE in its entry (a legacy <name>.config.json is only imported until --inline retires it), and which harness / is. Covers instantiated against declared, landing resolution and its error case, index.lock.json and its legacy fallback, the reserved index stem, the generated .gitignore block and its gate, and index-config:migrate (with --inline) for separated repositories. Named by: Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Remote-mount a dependency . The schema is folio-index-config/v1 in cat-harness/schemas/kg/index-config.ts. The index is the ONE config. Each layer’s config is written inline in its instances[] entry. A <name>.config.json is a legacy file: imported only as a migration step, then retired with index-config:migrate --inline --write. Never create one — not to make a tool find a recipe, not for a new layer. If a reader only finds config in the file, that reader is the bug; fix it to read the index entry first. index.config.json holds three facts about how a checkout is instantiated: which harnesses are instantiated, which one is / (a checkout has one <base>/index.html), and where each one comes from, so each is stated once rather than spread across every root config. When it exists at the root it is authoritative. When it is absent, readers fall back to the root *.config.json files, their site.landing flags, and remoteMounts on the root declaration. { "$schema": "folio-index-config/v1", "instances": [ { "name": "folio-assistant", "source": { "local": { "at": "." } } }, { "name": "cat-harness" }, { "name": "my-ig", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "owner/my-ig", "ref": "<40-char sha>", "overrides": { "my-ig": { "whole": true } }, "trust": { "consent": { "...": "..." } } } } }, { "name": "my-guide", "contentType": "document", "site": { "build": { "sourceSteps": ["site:document"] } } } ], "site": { "landing": "cat-harness" } } .

1061.title: Instantiated is a different fact from declared
1061.content: A declaration (<name>.json) says what a layer declares. It travels with the harness into every checkout that uses the harness. An index.config.json entry says the layer is instantiated in this checkout. Without an index, a <name>.config.json at the root says the same thing. Tiles, the landing and the hub listing are all drawn from the instantiated set, which instantiatedHarnessNames(root) returns. Never derive that set from declarations or from a directory listing. The dependencies of an instantiated harness are not instantiated just because a mount’s closure brought them in. They keep a group of their own rather than disappearing. A harness that a KG subscription chose is instantiated the same way: kg:instantiate adds its entry, with its config inline, when the checkout has an index (and only without one writes a root <name>.config.json).

1062.title: Inline, over a legacy import while one remains
1062.content: Each entry’s effective config is built like this: . | Start from a legacy imported file, while one remains. That is import when it is given, else <name>.config.json, and only if the file exists. The target state is that no such file exists. | Overlay every other key of the entry (everything except name, import, source and _comment) as an inline HarnessConfig field. Objects merge key by key, and arrays and scalars are replaced. Inline fields win. | . effectiveInstanceConfig(root, name) computes it. readHarnessConfig(dir) returns it for any layer that an index lists, walking outward from the layer root and stopping at the first directory that holds either the index or the layer’s own config. A layer the index does not list is read from its own config file. Readers that are handed a root and a name (the site recipe in build-instance-site.ts) use readInstanceConfig in cat-harness-tools/scripts/instance-config.ts, which reads the same way and REPORTS every legacy file it reads. Retiring the files is index-config:migrate --inline --write: each imported file is folded into its entry by exactly the overlay above, so no effective config changes, and the file is deleted. index-config:inline:check fails while one remains.

1063.title: Local or remote
1063.content: . | source absent: local, at <name>/. | source.local.at: local, at that path. Use . for the layer declared at the root. | source.remote: a remote mount. It is a remoteMounts entry minus harness, which is the entry’s name. It reuses RemoteMountSchema instead of restating it, so it has ref (not pin), overrides.<name>.whole and .path, note, trust.consent and track, and every field added to RemoteMountSchema arrives with no edit here. | . There is one read path and one write path for remote mounts: . | Read: readDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot) returns the index’s remote entries when an index exists, else the declaration’s remoteMounts. If both carry mounts it throws and names both files. It never picks one. | Write: writeDeclaredMounts(instanceRoot, mounts) always writes index.config.json, seeding the index from the checkout first if there is none. It refuses while the declaration still carries remoteMounts. Nothing writes remoteMounts on a declaration. | .

1064.title: Which harness / is
1064.content: resolveLandingInstance(root) is the only reader. It applies these rules in order: . | condition | / is | . | the index is unreadable | invalid: the gate fails. There is no fallback to the flags, because the index was written to override them | . | the index’s site.landing names a layer it lists | that layer (by: "index") | . | the index’s site.landing is "hub" | the neutral hub: the harness listing and the todo panel | . | the index’s site.landing names a layer it does not list | invalid: the gate fails, and it is never a silent fallback | . | no site.landing (or no index), one layer | that layer (sole) | . | no site.landing, several layers, exactly one config flags site.landing: true | the flagged one | . | several flagged | the hub | . | none flagged | ambiguous: check:landing-instance fails, because the answer is never guessed | . | nothing instantiated | none: a state of its own, not a default | . gen-landing-data.ts and sync-docs-harness.ts ask this resolver. They do not use their own location. check:landing-instance also checks that the index and the root *.config.json files agree: . | A root config that the index does not import fails the check: without the index it would instantiate a harness, with it it does not, and nothing picks between them silently. | An import that names a missing file also fails the check. | An entry with no config file at all is the target state, and passes. | A legacy file an entry still imports is reported every time. It passes while it is a pending migration (every key it holds is either not inline or inline with the same value). It fails when the entry overrides one of its keys with a different value: the file’s value is then dead text that a reader of the file alone takes for the config. | .

1065.title: A harnessed repository runs its checks on its own pull requests
1065.content: Instantiating a harness in a repository includes turning its checks on there, through one reusable workflow the harness owns, never a copy per repository, so a layer is judged on its own pull requests and not only when an index re-pins it. Switching off a repository’s builds must not switch off its gates. The workflow is the tools layer’s .github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml. A repository calls it from a workflow of about fifteen lines that runs on pull_request: . jobs: checks: uses: <owner>/<tools-layer>/.github/workflows/layer-pr-checks.yml@main with: mode: layer # or `index`: the repository is its own index instance: <instance> # layer mode: its directory in the folio-assistant index path-in-repo: <instance> # where the instance sits in the repository ('.' at the root) . | layer mode is for a repository that an index mounts, such as cat-harness or the DAK layer. The workflow checks out folio-assistant and puts the PR in place of the locked mount. | index mode is for a repository that is its own index: an IG repository over the DAK layer, smart-ra, or a folio. Its own index.lock.json is replayed. | The gates are the harness’s graph checks over the repository’s own layer, plus every check:* / *:check script of that layer and its whole dependency harness (its transitive needs). Each is named <owning-instance>:<script>. | A PR fails only on what it newly breaks. Each gate and test runs on main and on the PR. Anything already red on main is listed, never hidden, and never counted against the PR. | . A layer PR that declares a new directory is red on two index gates it cannot clear. The index README lists every declared directory, so the PR leaves index:render:check and readme:sync:root:check stale, and only the index re-pin that takes the PR regenerates the README. Read those two as expected when they are the only new failures, and run them green in the index re-pin instead. Disabling a repository’s automatic builds is not disabling its checks. When an IG repository’s automatic gh-pages or IG Publisher triggers are switched off (the onboarding question in the FHIR IG layer’s ig-build-pipeline), the harness caller stays on.

1066.title: The exemptions of the index’s own workflows
1066.content: .github/workflows/ belongs to the index, so the steps CI runs there that the local gate set does not are exempted HERE, under gateExemptions.steps, each with a kind and a reason (GateExemptionsSchema, the same shape an layer declaration carries). They land in the same change as the workflow step, never ahead of it in a layer: an exemption for a step CI does not yet run matches nothing, and gates-workflows.test.ts refuses a stale exemption as it refuses an unclassified step. "gateExemptions": { "steps": [ { "match": "bun run cat state:push -- --id health", "kind": "ci-only", "reason": "…" } ] } . A layer still exempts its OWN scripts and steps in its own declaration.

1067.title: index.lock.json, and the legacy name
1067.content: The lock records what the declared mounts resolved to. It is generated by mount:remote and kept as a separate file. The legacy name is <root-instance>.mount-lock.json. The rules for each reader and writer: . | Writers write index.lock.json. mount:remote first renames a legacy lock onto the new name, so the old file is moved, never dropped. | Readers take index.lock.json first, then fall back to the legacy *.mount-lock.json, so downstream folios and old branches still replay. The readers are: . | mount-from-lock.ts | mountedInstanceRoots | mountedUnder in git-corpus.ts | mount:remote:check | . | Both files present is an error that names both. Two locks are never merged. | . mount-from-lock.ts imports only node:*, so it restates the rule inline and its test holds it to lockFilesIn. A re-pin ends with one commit per layer, and moves pins only forward (owner ruling, 2026-11-06, card “Pin target”, A). Every layer the change needs is pinned in the same re-pin, and the re-pin PR holds the pins and nothing else: a change that needs the new pins stacks on it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). The one exception is a change mutually dependent with the re-pin, where neither passes alone. It may share the PR, and the body says why. The rules are in remote-mount §”Re-pinning”.

1068.title: The reserved index stem
1068.content: index.config.json ends in .config.json, so a scan that treats “each root *.config.json is a harness” would find a harness called index. The index stem is therefore reserved across the board: . | rootConfigStems skips every index.* file. It is the one root scan; every other reader calls it or instantiatedHarnessNames. | findDeclarationFile skips every index.* file too. | The index schema refuses a layer named index, and hub, because that is the landing keyword. | . Do not add another copy of the scan: a new copy is how the reserved name leaks back in.

1069.title: The generated .gitignore block
1069.content: # BEGIN index mounts (generated from index.config.json — do not edit) /my-ig/ # END index mounts . The block holds one /<path>/ line per remote layer in the index, where the path is overrides.<name>.path, else <name>/. After those it lists every further layer root the lock records, because a mount’s closure can land layers that the index never names. Three things write the block: . | mount:remote | writeDeclaredMounts | index-config:migrate --write | . check:index-ignores fails when the block is missing or disagrees with the index. When an index exists, mount:remote does not append to .git/info/exclude: a local exclude rule is invisible to every other clone, so a path the committed block does not cover is reported as not ignored. Without an index, it still appends there.

1070.title: Converting a checkout: index-config:migrate
1070.content: bun run cat index-config:migrate # print the index it would write, and its findings bun run cat index-config:migrate --write # write it; move remoteMounts; write the block; rename the lock bun run cat index-config:migrate --check # exit 1 when --write would change anything (a gate here) bun run cat index-config:migrate --inline --write # also fold each <name>.config.json into its entry, and delete it bun run cat index-config:inline:check # exit 1 while any imported <name>.config.json remains bun run cat index-config:migrate --root <clone> # a separated repository's standalone checkout . The converter reads only the files under --root, so it runs on a standalone clone of any separated repository. | Which root configs it imports: a root <name>.config.json is imported only when name is a layer the checkout declares (at the root or one level down) or mounts. Anything else becomes an unmatched-config finding and is not imported. A repository cut from a fork, for example, can carry the fork’s own <fork>.config.json; importing it would instantiate a harness the repository does not hold. | Re-runs: it is idempotent. A re-run moves only the remoteMounts entries that the declaration has gained since the last run. An entry the index already holds identically is dropped from the declaration. An entry the index holds differently throws, and you reconcile it by hand. | .

Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

On main that work is a merge train: composes it from the queue, attributes and ejects on red, lands at the tested SHA. On a route-keyed ref it is coalescing: batches the writes arriving in one window into a single write. Decides nothing the reprioritisation table or the owner has not -- placement is computed by merge-priority.dmn, and landing waits for the owner's release, given in the steward's own session as one card per batch. Records decisions on queue entries and windows, never the host's facts. On main the lane is conditional: it is held while two or more active sessions have ready PRs in the same repositories and their merges slow each other down (contended runners, or PRs that conflict with or supersede each other), and lapses when that stops. With none active the sibling sessions elect one by a fixed rule (the owner of the P0 PR, else the earliest-created active session); a lone session is its own steward. 1505.title: Glossary
1505.content: Derived: every term this instance's swimlanes define — the role's title and description, the lane names that bind it, and whether the term has been retired. This is an index, not the documentation. It says what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a process is for, when you would be in it, and what it is not, is authored beside it and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. Filter this table | Artefact | What it declares about itself | . | Activity logglossary-ledger.json | The agent activity log. A MECHANICAL role: it is written to at task start and task end, and emptied by an actor — one entry, all of them, or on a periodic sweep — and it decides nothing. Modelled on work-plan and corpus, the two existing stores; its skill is the contract it is held to. Its entries are held in the layer's unpublished store and never reach a published graph; the activity-log skill names the location, which is deliberately not repeated here because a role description IS published.notation role/logfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Actorbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_LogMessage/lane/Lane_Actorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Adjudicatorglossary-ledger.json | Settles a criterion whose reviewer entries disagree, and records WHY. Inherits reviewer because an adjudicator is a reviewer with one added entitlement — the adjudication permission — and the separation is the point: a reviewer reports, an adjudicator settles, and a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. The KNOWLEDGE spreads (several roles carry the adjudication skill, because each has to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint); the ENTITLEMENT does not, and lives on the actor as a permission.notation role/adjudicatorfirst seen 2026-09-22status current | . | Administratorglossary-ledger.json | Administers the role graph itself: who exists, what they may act as, and what they may do. The ONE lane whose activities change the substrate every other diagram's lanes bind to — which is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit. Declared 2026-09-20 on the owner's answer that administration is a swimlane; role-model.md's rule is that a role is never invented to make a diagram drawable, so it waited for that.notation role/administratorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_HumanAgentDiscussion/lane/Lane_Agentfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | Archimateglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/archimatefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Attestation serviceglossary-ledger.json | Signs a QA report's run hashes over an API. A MECHANICAL role, and the one that DISAPPEARS when the actor performing it cannot reach out — which is why the signing process carries a second, human lane rather than a retry.notation role/attestation-servicefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Attestationsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/attestationsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Auditorglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/auditorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Authorglossary-ledger.json | Writes and revises folio content. The position, not the person: an editor and a guideline developer both act as author when they are changing a block.notation role/authorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | The session agent doing the work. The broadest skill set here, and the one whose membership most needs auditing.notation role/authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring Committeeglossary-ledger.json | The people writing a document with its editor, while it is still a working draft: contributors who give feedback through the Contributor Feedback sheet, one change set per row, in their own Blue column. They recommend; an Editor decides, through the sheet's Ready columns. Added 2026-10-31 by the owner, so the drafting sheet names a process role rather than a job title, as the public-comment sheet names the Feedback Review Committee. The lane it binds is in folio-assistant-core/processes/content/contributor-feedback.bpmn and authoring-a-document.bpmn.notation role/authoring-committeefirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Auto docsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/auto-docsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Back-translatorglossary-ledger.json | The checker of a translation round trip: renders a sample of the target-language text back into the source language from the target text alone, with no tools and without seeing the source. It rules on nothing. Its rendering is the intermediate the adjudicator reads (untainted-verification, rule 1: neither party sees what would let it shortcut).notation role/back-translatorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Basic CDN siteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Basic cdn site (node kind)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bean notesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/bean-notesfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Binary releasesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/binary-releasefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Block kindsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/block-kindsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board positionsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/board-positionsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board rendererglossary-ledger.json | Draws a board and performs what the reader has already decided: reads each kind's declared zoom threshold and the layout layer, swaps a card for its avatar, projects an open window onto the canvas, and carries out a confirmed relocation. 1603.title: auto-docs index
1603.content: Derived documentation over a declared sub-graph. Each entry below is generated from the repository on every build, so it is what the tree actually holds rather than what anybody remembered. These are indexes, not the documentation. They say what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a thing is for, when you would reach for it, and what it is not, is authored beside them and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. | Decisions …every DMN decision table a declared `processes` graph holds, with the decision's own name | Docs …every AUTHORED documentation page an instance publishes, with the title and description its own front matter declares | Processes …every BPMN process, with its own documentation, its lanes, and the skills its activities name | Roles …every role a declared `scenarios` graph defines, with the description it declares | Schemas …every schema module a declared `schemas` directory holds, with the first sentence of its module docblock | Skills …every skill markdown file, with the description it declares in its own front matter | Tasks …every named activity in a declared `processes` graph — task, user, service, manual, script and call activities | Tools …every Tool module a declared `tools` directory holds, with the first sentence of its module docblock | .

1609.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1609.title: The load-bearing idea, in the specification’s words
1609.content: “The System Package Data Exchange (SPDX®) specification defines an open standard for communicating bill of materials (BOM) information for different topic areas. SPDX defines an underlying data model as well as multiple serialization formats to encode that data model.” — §1 Scope (sec-007) . Its scope lists, among others, “software composition”, “software build information”, “provenance and integrity”, “licenses and copyrights, including a curated list of licenses and exceptions”, and “security vulnerabilities, defects, and other quality data” (§1). It is profiled. “The Core Profile is mandatory. All others are optional” (§5.2, sec-015): Core, Software, Security, Licensing, Dataset, AI, Build, Lite and Extension. A producer conforms at a profile, not to the whole. The Lite Profile “captures the minimum set of information required for license compliance in the software supply chain” (§5.10, sec-023). Everything is an Element with creation info. CreationInfo requires specVersion, created and createdBy (Figure A.1). The specification qualifies created in a way that matters here: “The dateTime created is often the date of last change (e.g., a git commit date), not the date when the SPDX data was created, as doing so supports reproducible builds” (CreationInfo, sec-044, where the page split carries it; also sec-072). A generator that uses the source commit’s date writes the same document twice for the same commit. Serialisation is JSON-LD with ONE global context. “The SPDX global JSON-LD context file must be used universally for all SPDX documents in JSON-LD format that adhere to a specific SPDX version … "@context": "https://spdx.org/rdf/3.0.1/spdx-context.jsonld"” (sec-032). There is also a “canonical serialization”: “a single, consistent, normalized, deterministic, and reproducible form” (sec-029). That is the form to hash and sign. “Known unknown” is not the same as absent. For licences: “a missing hasDeclaredLicense is not the same as a relationship to NoAssertionLicense since the latter is a ‘known unknown’ whereas no assumptions can be made from a missing hasDeclaredLicense relationship”, and “A written explanation of a relationship to a NoAssertionLicense MAY be provided in the comment field for the relationship” (Licensing, sec-210).

1610.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary

Each is ours, read against the held text, and none is adopted. | house fact | SPDX 3 term | fit | . | licence.json status: stated + id | simplelicensing_LicenseExpression via hasDeclaredLicense | exact, once ids are validated against a pinned License List | . | status: unknown + searched[] | hasDeclaredLicense → NoAssertionLicense, the search log in the relationship’s comment | exact. The three states survive: SPDX’s absent relationship is our absent record | . | bun.lock, python-deps.ts | software_Package + purl (packageUrl) + dependsOn | exact for npm. Python is blocked: requirements*.txt pin no versions | . | kg-to-portal’s manifest of digests | software_File with verifiedUsing: Hash inside a software_Sbom | exact | . | a published layer’s needs[] / FHIR dependsOn | dependsOn between software_Packages | exact, but only GENERATED from one authoritative record (#592) | . | folio-tool-run/v1, attribution.ts toolchain / inputDigest | build_Build (buildType, configSourceDigest, parameter, environment) | close, and it competes with prov-o-provenance for “what ran” | . | a QA or test report about a released package | ExternalRef with externalRefType: qualityAssessmentReport, “A reference to a quality assessment for a package” (sec-123) | exact as a POINTER. The report stays ours | . | bun audit advisories | security_Vulnerability + security_Vex*VulnAssessmentRelationship | exact, and a VEX not_affected needs a person’s decision | .

1611.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1611.title: What it refuses, with reasons
1611.content: . | A QA verdict store. SPDX 3.0 has no verdict class. A result is an Annotation (“An assertion made in relation to one or more elements”, free-text statement; sec-039) or a relationship (hasEvidence, hasTest, testedOn). A house sidecar holds {criterion, result, reviewer, field_hash} per criterion, many reviewers over time, with four-state freshness. Serialising that into SPDX turns validated fields into a string. 3.1 changes the first half of this, and the change is recorded rather than smoothed over: the RC1 schema has functionalsafety_EvaluationResult (evaluation ∈ {pass, fail, inconclusive}, a required evaluationBasedOn → RequirementVerification with verificationMethod ∈ {analysis, assessment, audit, demonstration, inspection, review, test, other}, and a required rationale), plus a Core Requirement class. That is a verdict class. It makes an SPDX export of a certification report plausible, once 3.1 is final. It does not make SPDX the store, for the remaining reasons: the records are mutable, they would churn, the class sits in a functional safety profile whose semantics a non-safety QA run would be borrowing, and “stale” and “absent” have no SPDX term (inconclusive covers only could-not-determine). | A second execution log. “What ran, as whom, under which plan” is prov-o-provenance’s, by owner decision. A release document that must say how it was built references the PROV record, or generates build_Build from it. It never authors one beside it. | The AI profile for agent authorship. ai_AIPackage describes a model distributed as a package (training, energy consumption, limitations). The platform ships no model. Who wrote a block is provenance. | Authoring SPDX by hand, or committing it where its facts already live. A document generated from bun.lock that is also committed is a second answer to “what are we running”, the failure upstream-pins.json names. | .

Not compared. | Which buildType IRIs to use. The Build profile requires one (buildType: anyURI[1], Figure A.7) and leaves it to the producer. | How to sign. SPDX carries verifiedUsing integrity methods. Signing the document is outside it, and is qa-report-signing.bpmn’s question. | .

1613.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1613.title: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
1613.content: ← All methodologies . spdx-3 — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Describing an artefact that LEAVES this repository so that a party who does not run our tooling can check what is in it, what it depends on, under which licences, and that it arrived intact — a release, a signed package, a published layer’s dependency set, the licences of what we redistribute. It answers what is this, what is it made of, who supplied it, under what licence, with what known vulnerabilities. It does NOT answer what happened inside the repository or who answers for it (prov-o-provenance), what an actor may do (odrl-policies), how a node is serialised internally (json-ld-serialisation), or whether a block passed its QA criteria (the house QA schemas; see §”What it refuses”). Origin. The Linux Foundation and its Contributors, with SPDX Model contributions from OMG, “System Package Data Exchange (SPDX) Specification Version 3.0”, OMG formal/24-11-01, March 2025 (https://www.omg.org/spec/SPDX); its model is the SPDX 3.0.1 model (Annex A points at https://spdx.org/rdf/3.0.1/spdx-model.ttl). Licensed Community-Spec-1.0, with pre-existing portions CC-BY-3.0. SPDX® is a registered trademark of The Linux Foundation. SPDX 3.1, a release candidate since 2026-01-26, is held only as a secondary source (a 2025 conference deck, CC-BY-SA-3.0) and as its RC1 machine-readable schema queued in uploads/, NOT as a specification. 1614.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1614.title: Specification-compiled agents
1614.content: Adopted 2026-09-23, on the owner’s “ingest into library for use as evidence and skills as subgraph on processes in cat-harness”. The authors’ own sentence for the mechanism: . “we compile an industry standard BPMN 2.0 process model into a ReAct style control graph. Each BPMN node provides a typed tool contract and a node local policy, while the control plane enforces branches and joins, scopes context per node, and applies contract derived runtime validation with targeted retries.” .

1615.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1615.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
1615.content: The control flow is COMPILED from a specification the model did not write, so the model never rediscovers the plan at runtime. Everything else in the paper follows from that. The model still reasons — it is a ReAct agent, not a state machine — but it reasons locally, inside a node, against a typed contract, with the branches and joins enforced by something that is not it.

1616.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1616.title: Three principles, and they are separable
1616.content: The paper names them together; they are three distinct commitments and a reader may take one without the others. | principle | what it does | what it costs | . | constrained execution | branches and joins come from the diagram, not from a plan the model produced | the diagram must exist and be right | . | targeted context management | each node sees the minimum it needs, rather than the accumulated transcript | somebody must decide, per node, what that minimum is | . | modular decomposition | prompt, tools and orchestration are generated as separate artefacts | more upfront authoring than a single prompt | . The second is the one with an argument behind it rather than an intuition. The paper cites evidence that model performance degrades as more of the context window is consumed, and observes that a generalist system cannot scope context per subtask because it does not know, at construction time, what each subtask will need. A specification does know — which is why scoping is available to this design and not to the other.

1617.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1617.title: What the paper measured
1617.content: Ten workflows, 9 to 52 nodes, all deterministic, spanning e-commerce, costing, risk, labelling, news, social, promotion, tournament registration and weather. Ten successful agents per workflow per system, evaluated across all control-flow paths — 300 agents over 30,543 test cases, from 371 generation attempts. Baselines: Roo and Cline. AutoGen, MetaGPT and FLOW were tried and produced nothing executable — MetaGPT emitted prompts and tools but no agent, AutoGen needed manual wiring even with GraphFlow, FLOW produced decompositions rather than code — so they were excluded rather than scored, which is the honest handling. Aggregates (Figure 4), specialist vs Cline vs Roo: . |   | specialist | Cline | Roo | . | tool-use exactness ↑ | 57.7 % | 48.6 % | 38.1 % | . | tool-call errors ↓ | 1.27 | 3.19 | 3.22 | . | latency (s / effective step) ↓ | 2.49 | 6.59 | 9.08 | . | process adherence ↑ | 54.7 % | 51.6 % | 42.4 % | . | repair iterations ↓ | 0.00 | 1.85 | 2.04 | . | total tokens | 53.8 k | 1 021.8 k | 1 468.6 k | . The two robust results are the last two rows, and they are robust because they are not close: zero repair iterations across every successful generation, and an order of magnitude in tokens. Those are properties of the pipeline rather than of the generated agent, which is why they do not vary the way the run metrics do.

1618.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1618.title: What the figures say that the prose does not
1618.content: Read off Figure 3 directly, 2026-09-23, as part of ingesting the images. This is a reading of the paper’s own chart, not a claim about the authors’ work, and it is recorded because the surrounding text does not say it. The paper writes of tool-use exactness that “the per-workflow breakdown in Figure 3(a) confirms this advantage holds consistently across all ten workflows regardless of complexity.” Figure 3(a) does not show that. On three of the ten the specialist system is not best: . | workflow | specialist | Cline | Roo | . | Cost | 49.6 | 76.0 | 67.6 | . | Tournament | 46.2 | 99.4 | 94.9 | . | Weather | 81.8 | 90.1 | 61.0 | . Tournament is not a near miss — it is 46.2 against 99.4. The same two workflows invert in panels (b) and (d): on Cost the specialist has the most tool-call errors (1.43 against 0.55 and 0.34) and the lowest process adherence (57.2 against 87.1 and 76.2), and Tournament repeats both. And the aggregate advantage is carried disproportionately by two workflows. On Risk the specialist shows 0.20 tool-call errors against 13.19 and 11.94, and 98.6 % exactness against 0.4 % and 0.9 %; Social contributes a smaller version of the same. A mean over ten workflows, two of which contain an order-of- magnitude gap, is a mean dominated by those two. Separately, §4.3.1 gives the aggregate repair figures as “2.08 for Roo and 1.89 for Cline” where Figure 2(d) is labelled 2.04 and 1.85. Small, and noted only because this node quotes one of them. None of this makes the method wrong. It makes the aggregate run metrics the wrong thing to quote, and it is the reason the section above marks the generation metrics as the robust pair. It also suggests a real question the paper does not ask: what do Cost and Tournament have in common that inverts the result? Looking at their diagrams, both are shallow and branch-heavy — the regime where a compiled control graph has least to contribute, because there is barely a plan to rediscover.

1619.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1619.title: What this checkout already does, and where it differs
1619.content: methodology-adoption §”Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools” requires this comparison before any tool is proposed. Read from the repository, not assumed: . | the method asks for | this checkout has | gap | . | BPMN 2.0 as the authored control flow | processes/, 69 diagrams, .bpmn as the source of truth | none — this is already the premise | . | a control plane that enforces branches and joins | workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_gate / workflow_complete, with workflow_complete refusing a step that is not enabled | none of substance | . | a node-local policy | cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement, relaxable, cat-harness.processes:decision, cat-harness.processes:judgement — four mechanisms, already finer than the paper’s one | this checkout is AHEAD | . | a typed tool contract per node | <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> names the instruction body; there is no typed input/output contract | the real gap | . | context scoped per node | not modelled. A step returns a skill; nothing says what the agent may or must see | the second real gap | . | contract-derived runtime validation with targeted retries | nothing. A step that goes wrong is not caught by the control plane | follows from the first gap | . | compilation to an executable agent | nothing, and deliberately: the diagrams here govern agents rather than generating them | out of scope, not a gap | . The last row is the one to be careful about. The paper’s system emits a deployable service; this repository’s engine runs alongside an agent doing the work. Those are different products of the same specification, and adopting the method here means taking the first three principles, not the code generator.

1620.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1620.title: Where this rendering stops
1620.content: . | No implementation is adopted. ReAct, FastAPI, LangGraph and Langfuse are the paper’s tools, not obligations. | The benchmark is not adopted. Ten workflows the authors built themselves, and they say so: “author-constructed workflows may introduce design bias”. A benchmark of somebody else’s processes measures their processes. | The numbers are not adopted as evidence for anything here. See the figures section: three of ten workflows invert, and the aggregate is dominated by two. What survives is the shape — zero repair iterations and an order of magnitude in tokens — and even those were measured on that corpus. | The deterministic scope is inherited, not argued away. Every workflow evaluated is deterministic by construction. The authors state the limit plainly; this node does not extend the result past it, and deterministic-and-agentic is where the open question lives. | “Specialist beats generalist” is not a conclusion this node draws. The paper compares one specialist pipeline against two general coding assistants operating unconstrained at their defaults, and says future work will examine “more heavily optimised baseline configurations”. That is a fair comparison of realistic low-configuration usage and it is not a claim about ceilings. | .

1621.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1621.title: The owner’s own statement of the two ends
1621.content: library/kg-folio-asst-2026-09-30 is the owner’s deck of 2026-09-30. It is cited as evidence of intent, not of effect. Slide 7 draws the axis this node sits on: “BPMN Execution Skill: given a Process, Context, State, Role utilize one or more Skills in order [to] execute a Task”, run by either of two Tools. One is an open-source BPMN engine with “state and swimlanes strictly enforced”. The other is “an agentic swarm with ungoverned state”, mitigated by mechanical and agentic QA/QC reports. This node is the method for the first end. The deck measures nothing, so it says where the owner wants the harness to go and nothing about how well either end works. That is what the paper above is for. The diagrams this method executes are OMG BPMN 2.0.2 (formal/2013-12-09), recorded as library/omg-2013-bpmn-2-0-2. The entry identifies the exact specification and its clause outline, so a citation can name a clause and page. It holds none of the text, because OMG’s licence forbids posting copies on a network.

1622.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1622.title: See also
1622.content: . | specification-compiled-agents — the part an agent here acts on. | deterministic-and-agentic — the open research agenda this is evidence for, and the four mechanisms this repository already has. | hybrid-llm-deterministic — the same shape at a different grain: emit a rule, validate it, run it. | .

1623.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1623.title: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
1623.content: ← All methodologies . specification-compiled-agents — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A process is already written down as a diagram, and something must now EXECUTE it. Use it when the control flow is external and authored — a BPMN process, a DMN table, a pipeline someone drew — and the question is how an LLM should act inside it. It answers where the plan comes from, never what the plan should be: authoring the diagram is bpmn-authoring, deciding a branch from a table is dmn, and choosing between options is kepner-tregoe. Its companion is hybrid-llm-deterministic, and the two are the same shape at different grains: that one has the model emit a RULE that machinery validates and runs; this one has the model act inside a CONTROL GRAPH that machinery derived from a specification. Reach for this one when the artefact that constrains the model already exists as a diagram. Do NOT reach for it where no specification exists, or where the process is genuinely open-ended. The paper’s own evaluation is scoped to deterministic workflows and says so; a setting with ambiguity, stochasticity or open-ended human decision-making is outside what it measured, and outside what this node claims. Origin. Harris Borman, Herman Wandabwa, Fusun Yu, Sandeepa Kannangara, Justin Liu, Anna Leontjeva and Ritchie Ng, “Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution”, Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Published as a workshop paper at SCALE, ICML 2026 (PMLR 306); arXiv:2607.14456v1 [cs.SE], 16 July 2026. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. It is a SYSTEM paper reporting one implementation against a benchmark its own authors built, so what is adopted below is the METHOD, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. §”What the figures say that the prose does not” carries a reading of the paper’s own charts that changes how its headline numbers should be used, and it is the reason this node quotes almost none of them. 1624.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1624.title: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM)
1624.content: Adapted from the Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII) and PATH. The harness’s CRDM requirements workflow (crdm-requirements-workflow (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) and specification template (crdm-requirements-template) adapt PHII’s Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) and PATH’s 2012 application of CRDM to health information systems, combining their process-centric requirements method with the platform’s own agentic facilitation, codebase impact analysis, work-plan decomposition, and pull-request sign-off gates. | Canonical SKOS glossary concept: https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/glossary/platform/collaborative-requirements-development-methodology (docs/assets/glossary/cat-harness--platform.skos.jsonld) | . | Ingested source | What it establishes | Library entry | . | PHII (2021/2023), Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems (https://phii.org/crdm/, 10 pp.) | The three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, and swimlane Task Flow Diagrams | library/phii-2023-crdm | . | PHII (2016/2021), 5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (EHR Toolkit, 6 pp.) | Functional vs. non-functional requirement grammar (“The system must or should…”), the three-level priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have), nine requirement quality criteria, and three validation techniques (Desk checking, Walkthrough, Peer review) | library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide | . | PATH & PHII (2012), Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (36 pp.) | Domain-scale application of CRDM: a four-column Process Framework (Table 1), swimlane Task Flow Diagrams across facility and community pools with numbered activity narratives (Appendix 1), Activity-Linked Functional User Requirements (Appendix 2), and General System Requirements (Appendix 3) | library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm | . | IETF BCP 14 — RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017) | Normative conformance keywords (MUST / SHALL, MUST NOT / SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY) in uppercase | library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels, library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | .

1625.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1625.title: 1. The PHII and PATH CRDM method
1625.content: PHII developed CRDM as a process-centric methodology grounded in business process management that brings multi-disciplinary subject matter experts (SMEs) together to document how work is performed, redesign how it should be performed, and derive what an information system must do to support that work (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 1–3; path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, pp. 4–7). 1.1 The three concentration areas . PHII organises CRDM around three sequential concentration areas (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 2–9): . | Concentration area | Guiding prompt | Core artefacts | What happens | . | 1. Business Process Analysis (BPA) | Think: How do we do our work now? | Business Process Matrix (process goal, inputs, activities, outputs, actors/roles, business rules, issues/opportunities) and Task Flow Diagrams (swimlane diagrams showing the sequence of tasks across pools and actors) | SMEs map current-state operations end to end, making implicit workflows, hand-offs, and decision points explicit (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 3–6). | . | 2. Business Process Redesign (BPR) | Rethink: How should we do our work? | Redesigned Business Process Matrix and updated Task Flow Diagrams | Before automating anything, participants examine the current-state model to eliminate bottlenecks, redundancies, policy barriers, and information gaps (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 7–8). | . | 3. Requirements Definition | Describe: How can an information system support our work? | Functional User Requirements (anchored to numbered task-flow activities) and Non-Functional / General System Requirements | Every activity in the redesigned task flow is examined to state the information system capabilities needed to support it, followed by structured SME validation (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 8–9; phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, pp. 1–5). | . 1.2 PATH (2012): domain-scale health information system artefacts . PATH & PHII (2012) demonstrate how CRDM scales across a clinical and public health domain (path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm): . | Process Framework (Table 1, PDF p. 8): Inventories all domain business processes across functional columns (Patient Administration, Patient Care, Patient Fees and Accounting, Planning, Management & Surveillance) and selects priority processes for deep modeling (sec-009-outputs-of-the-crdm-process.md). | Task Flow Diagrams with Activity Narratives (Appendix 1, PDF pp. 11–20): Draws each priority process using a ten-element notation (Pools, Swim Lanes, Start Event, End Event, Sequence Flow, Activity, Subprocess, Decision, Multi-Page Connector, Annotation) paired with numbered activity details and narratives (sec-013-appendix-1-business-process-flows.md). | Activity-Linked Functional User Requirements vs. General System Requirements (Appendices 2–3, PDF pp. 21–36): Groups functional requirements by process and numbered activity ID, and separates cross-cutting system requirements (security, audit logging, reporting, interoperability, offline operation) into a dedicated general system requirements catalogue (sec-014-appendix-2-requirements.md, which also holds the general and nonfunctional requirements). | . 1.3 Quality criteria and validation techniques . PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, pp. 3–5) checks every requirement against nine quality criteria — Correct, Unambiguous, Complete, Consistent, Ranked for importance and/or stability, Verifiable, Modifiable, Traceable, and Comprehensible — using three validation methods: . | Desk checking: Individual review of the specification against the business process models and quality criteria. | Walkthrough: Facilitated step-by-step group traversal of task flows and requirements with the SMEs who perform the work. | Peer review: Independent structured inspection by peers to catch ambiguities, omissions, and conflicts before sign-off. | .

1626.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1626.title: 2. How the harness adapts PHII and PATH CRDM
1626.content: The relation between crdm-requirements-workflow and PHII/PATH CRDM is adapts: Phases 1–3 and the SME validation walkthrough follow PHII/PATH CRDM directly, while the facilitation channel, Phase 4/4b codebase impact and dependency analysis, Phase 5 work-item and filing decomposition, and Phase 6 pull-request sign-off are the platform’s own extensions. | Workflow phase / mechanism | Relation to PHII & PATH CRDM | What follows PHII/PATH CRDM vs. what is the platform’s own | . | Facilitated elicitation channel (crdm-requirements-workflow § Core Principle) | Platform adaptation of CRDM workshop facilitation | PHII/PATH run multi-stakeholder SME workshops facilitated by a human business analyst. The harness adapts this into an LLM agent acting in the Business Analyst role (Role_BusinessAnalyst) conversing with the human SME (Role_SME) over an issue/PR thread before any code is modified. | . | Phase 1: Needs Assessment & Problem Framing | Follows PHII CRDM (Business Process Analysis — context & scope) | Establishes the business problem, actors/personas (Role_*), scope boundaries (in-scope vs. out-of-scope), and information inputs/outputs, matching PHII’s Business Process Matrix header and PATH’s process framework scoping. | . | Phase 2: Business Process Analysis & Redesign | Follows PHII & PATH CRDM (Concentration Areas 1 & 2: BPA + BPR) | Models current-state (“as-is”) and redesigned (“to-be”) workflows using swimlane task-flow diagrams (BPMN 2.0 / Mermaid) across pools and actor lanes, paired with a gap analysis table (bottlenecks, redundancies, missing rules). | . | Phase 3: Requirements Definition (Functional, Non-Functional & Data Model) | Follows PHII & PATH CRDM (Concentration Area 3) + BCP 14 keywords | Derives atomic Functional Requirements (FR-001, …) linked to redesigned process steps, Non-Functional / General System Requirements (NFR-001, …), business rules/decision tables, and domain data entities with cardinalities and validation criteria. | . | Phase 4: Impact Analysis & Effort Estimation | Platform’s own extension | Inspects the repository’s existing schemas, skills, BPMN/DMN models, UI components, pipelines, tests, and downstream consumers across 7 impact dimensions to identify breaking changes and t-shirt effort estimates. PHII/PATH CRDM is technology- and codebase-agnostic and has no code impact phase. | . | Phase 4b: Capability Area Grouping, Dependency Ordering & Formalize-First Rule | Platform’s own extension | Groups requirements into capability areas (CA-1, CA-2, …), orders them by a dependency DAG, and enforces the platform’s formalize-first rule (formalizing existing implicit behavior before adding net-new capabilities). | . | Phase 5: Work Breakdown, Work Items & Specification Filing | Platform’s own extension (+ PHII Walkthrough / Peer review) | Writes the specification to docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and upon filing to docs/requirements/<slug>.md per requirements-filing-and-organisation), decomposes work into agent work items (beans/) and human todos (todos/), and conducts the SME walkthrough on the proposal PR. | . | Phase 6: Implementation & Merge Sign-Off | Platform’s own extension | Implements approved requirements on a feature branch, publishes a branches/<branch-slug>/ preview, verifies every acceptance criterion against automated gates, and requires explicit human owner sign-off before merging. | .

1627.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1627.title: 3. Priority scale and normative conformance keywords
1627.content: In CRDM and in the harness’s requirement template (crdm-requirements-template), implementation priority and normative conformance level are two distinct fields with different semantics and different standards origins: . 3.1 Priority weighting (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) . PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 2) and PATH (2012) (path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, p. 1 / Appendix 2) rank requirements by relative implementation importance using a three-tier priority scale. The harness aligns its three priority labels one-to-one with PHII’s scale: . | PHII / PATH priority rank | Harness template label | Meaning when sequencing or trading off scope | . | High | Must-have (High / Must-have) | Essential to the core business process; the system cannot satisfy the process goal without this capability. | . | Medium | Should-have (Medium / Should-have) | Important for operational efficiency or completeness; expected in standard operation, though a temporary workaround may exist. | . | Low | Nice-to-have (Low / Nice-to-have) | Desirable enhancement that improves convenience or secondary workflows when resources permit. | . 3.2 Normative conformance keywords (SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT) . While PHII’s informal prose grammar phrases requirement statements as “The system must or should…” (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 1), the harness’s separate Conformance field (SHALL / MUST, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT / MUST NOT) uses uppercase normative keywords governed by IETF BCP 14: . | RFC 2119 (Bradner 1997, library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels): Defines MUST / SHALL (absolute requirement of the specification), MUST NOT / SHALL NOT (absolute prohibition), SHOULD (recommended; valid reasons may exist in particular circumstances to ignore, but full implications must be understood and weighed), SHOULD NOT (not recommended), and MAY (truly optional). | RFC 8174 (Leiba 2017, library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words): Clarifies that only UPPERCASE words carry the RFC 2119 normative meanings; lowercase “must”, “should”, and “may” in surrounding prose carry only their normal English meaning. | . Keeping Priority (High / Must-have, Medium / Should-have, Low / Nice-to-have) separate from Conformance (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT) avoids conflating when a capability is scheduled for delivery (priority) with how strictly an implementation must behave once it claims conformance to that requirement (BCP 14 modality).

1628.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1628.title: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
1628.content: ← All methodologies . crdm — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Eliciting, structuring, prioritising, and validating functional and non-functional requirements from current-state and redesigned business processes before implementation begins. Use it when a capability, specification, or workflow spans actors and tasks that must be analysed and redesigned first so every requirement traces to a concrete business activity. Not a replacement for filing and lifecycle governance (requirements-filing-and-organisation), interchange standards mapping (requirements-standards-assessment), one-off option trade-offs (kepner-tregoe), recurring decision logic (dmn), or architecture decision records (madr). Origin.
