1701.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1701.title: Assessment of open standards for requirements and bootstrap mapping
1701.content: Status: evaluated and recommended, NOT adopted into bootstrap. Issue #1164. Owner, 2026-09-23, choosing markdown front matter for requirement documents: “1 for now. need bean to assess open stds for requirements/methodologies that fit in”. The bootstrap Requirement (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) is deliberately free of outside concepts. This methodology assesses open standards across three categories — interchange formats, statement templates & grammars, and quality models — evaluating their licensing, governance, serialization overhead, and exact field-by-field fit to the bootstrap Requirement. It concludes with concrete architectural recommendations on layer placement and verifies the no-outside-concept boundary.

1702.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1702.title: 1. The bootstrap baseline: the six parts of a requirement
1702.content: In the bootstrap and harness architecture, a requirement is defined by six essential parts (formalized in Issue #2405, FR-007/FR-008, and documented in skills/content/requirements-planning/requirement-definition.md): . | Identifier (id): A globally unique URI/slug (req:<slug>), with each individual requirement statement addressable as req:<slug>#<key> and each success criterion addressable as req:<slug>#<key>/<criterion>. | Title & Label: A concise human-readable heading (title for the document, label for each atomic statement). | Statement & Conformance (requirement, conformance): Exactly one sentence that a reviewer or test can say yes or no to, qualified by an RFC 2119 conformance verb (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT). | Rationale / Benefit (benefit, description): The justification explaining why the obligation exists and what value it delivers. | Parent & Lineage (derivedFrom): Direct upstream references in the specialization/conformance lattice. | Acceptance & Verification (successCriteria[]): At least one concrete success criterion (criterion) with an explicit verification method (verification ∈ {test, inspection, review, analysis}). A requirement without a success criterion can be filed and never judged. | . A requirement document is authored in Markdown with YAML front matter or stored as JSON, and grouped into a RequirementSet (reqset:<slug>) tracking stages (draft → proposed → approved → planned → in-progress → delivered → accepted), member decisions, work plans (work items), and recorded human sign-off attestations.

1703.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1703.title: 2. Survey of open standards
1703.content: Category A: Interchange formats . 1. ReqIF (OMG Requirements Interchange Format v1.2) . | Origin & Governance: Object Management Group (OMG formal/2013-10-01), originally standardized by ProSTEP iViP. Also ISO/IEC 17506:2022. | Licence: Open specification, royalty-free (RF). | Maturity: High. De facto interchange standard in automotive, aerospace, and defense systems engineering (supported by IBM DOORS / DOORS Next, PTC Integrity, Siemens Polarion, Dassault, Eclipse ProR). | Serialization Overhead: Very high. XML-based schema with extensive metamodel indirection: REQ-IF → CORE-CONTENT → DATATYPES → SPEC-TYPES (SpecObjectType, SpecRelationType) → SPEC-OBJECTS → SPEC-RELATIONS → SPECIFICATIONS (SpecHierarchy). Attributes require multi-level XML wrappers (<ATTRIBUTE-VALUE-STRING>, <THE-VALUE>). Line-based Git diffs of raw ReqIF XML are unreadable. | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | SpecObject maps to a bootstrap Statement (or an atomic Requirement). | SpecObjectType defines attribute metadata. | ReqIF.Name maps to title / label. | ReqIF.Text maps to requirement (statement text). | SpecRelation (type derives or parent) maps to derivedFrom. | Verification items can be modelled either as separate SpecObjects linked via SpecRelation (type verifiedBy), or as structured attributes on the SpecObject (VerificationMethod, SuccessCriteria). | . | Verdict: Excellent for enterprise import/export projection; totally unsuitable for native storage or authoring in Git. | . 2. OSLC-RM (OASIS OSLC Requirements Management v2.1 / OSLC Core 3.0) . | Origin & Governance: OASIS Open Standard. | Licence: OASIS Royalty-Free (RF) on Limited Terms. | Maturity: High in ALM/PLM linked-data ecosystems (IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management, Siemens, Eclipse Lyo). | Serialization Overhead: Moderate to High. RDF graph representations (JSON-LD, Turtle, RDF/XML). Relies on URI dereferencing, Linked Data Platform (LDP) protocols, and ontology vocabularies (oslc_rm:, dcterms:). | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | oslc_rm:Requirement resource type. | dcterms:identifier maps to id / key. | dcterms:title maps to title / label. | dcterms:description maps to requirement statement text. | oslc_rm:derivedFrom and oslc_rm:elaboratedBy map to derivedFrom / dependsOn. | oslc_rm:validatedBy links to test artifacts or verification definitions. | . | Verdict: Natural fit with knowledge-graph / JSON-LD export pipelines (ns.jsonld, kg-export), but introduces unnecessary REST/graph server assumptions if forced into the local authoring loop. | . Category B: Statement templates and grammars . 3. EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) . | Origin & Governance: Alistair Mavin, Philip Wilkinson, Adrian Harwood, Mark Novak (Rolls-Royce plc / IEEE International Requirements Engineering Conference 2009). | Licence: Unencumbered, open methodology. | Maturity: High. Widely adopted across aerospace, automotive, medical device, and agile systems engineering. | Serialization Overhead: Zero. Operates directly on the requirement statement natural language text. | The Five EARS Patterns: . | Ubiquitous: “The <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “The harness SHALL validate every block against its declared schema.” | . | Event-driven: “When <trigger>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “When a plan is requested, the agent SHALL produce a requirements document and work plan.” | . | State-driven: “While <in a state>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “While the requirement set is in draft stage, the tool SHALL allow modification of statement keys.” | . | Unwanted behavior: “If <trigger/error>, then the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “If a statement lacks success criteria, then check:requirements SHALL emit a validation finding.” | . | Optional features: “Where <feature is present>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “Where LaTeX tooling is installed, the adapter SHALL generate typeset math blocks.” (Complex requirements combine While, Where, When, and If clauses). | . | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Fits directly inside the requirement string in bootstrap Statement. | The <system> noun maps to actors / harness components. | Conformance verbs align 1:1 with RFC 2119 / bootstrap SHALL, SHOULD, etc. | Can be validated deterministically by regular expressions or syntax AST checkers in check:requirements without altering the data schema. | . | Verdict: The optimal statement syntax pattern for authoring requirements in the harness. | . 4. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Requirements engineering) . | Origin & Governance: Joint ISO/IEC/IEEE standard. Replaced and consolidated IEEE 830, IEEE 1220, and IEEE 1233. | Licence: Formal international standard (copyright held by ISO/IEEE; concepts open for reference). | Maturity: Definitive international benchmark for requirements engineering. | Serialization Overhead: Zero (process and semantic standard, not a file format). | Core Elements: . | Requirement Construct (Clause 5.2.4): Defines standard syntax comprising Conditions, Subject, Conformance Verb (“shall”, “should”, “may”), Action/Object, and Constraints. | Verification Methods (Clause 6.4): Explicitly standardizes the four fundamental verification methods: . | Test: Quantitative verification using automated or manual test cases with controlled inputs and measured outputs. | Inspection: Visual or manual verification by examining the product, code, or documentation without executing it. | Analysis: Verification using mathematical models, calculations, simulations, or formal logic proofs. | Demonstration: Qualitative verification of observable operation under specified scenarios (analogous to review). | . | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Bootstrap’s verification method enum (test, inspection, review, analysis) is an exact 1:1 realization of ISO 29148’s verification quartet (with review representing demonstration/adjudication). | Traceability relations (derivedFrom, dependsOn) align with Clause 5.2.7. | . | Verdict: The conceptual foundation for the harness’s requirement definition. | . 5. IEEE Std 830-1998 (Software Requirements Specifications — SRS) . | Origin & Governance: IEEE Computer Society. | Status: Officially withdrawn and superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2011/2018. | Licence: Historical IEEE standard. | Maturity: Historic benchmark, but obsolete in modern systems engineering. | Fit to Bootstrap: Premised on large, monolithic, document-centric Software Requirements Specification (SRS) manuals (Section 1 Introduction, Section 2 General Description, Section 3 Specific Requirements). Bootstrap requirements are atomic, graph-linked statement nodes in Git rather than monolithic text chapters. | Verdict: Superseded. Retained only for historical traceability; all modern harness mappings should cite ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018. | . Category C: Quality models . 6. ISO/IEC 25010:2011 / 2023 (Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation — SQRE) . | Origin & Governance: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 7. | Licence: Formal international standard. | Maturity: Universal international taxonomy for software quality characteristics and Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs). | Structure: Defines 8 product quality characteristics (expanded to 9 in 2023): . | Functional Suitability (completeness, correctness, appropriateness). | Performance Efficiency (time behaviour, resource utilization, capacity). | Compatibility (co-existence, interoperability). | Interaction Capability / Usability (recognisability, learnability, operability, aesthetics). | Reliability (maturity, availability, fault tolerance, recoverability). | Security (confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity). | Maintainability (modularity, reusability, analysability, modifiability, testability). | Portability (adaptability, installability, replaceability). | Safety (2023 addition: operational risk, hazard mitigation). | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Bootstrap Statement differentiates kind: "functional" and kind: "non-functional". | For kind: "non-functional", bootstrap requires a category string. | ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics provide the canonical controlled vocabulary for this category field (e.g. security, performance-efficiency, maintainability, reliability). | . | Verdict: Strongly recommended as the controlled taxonomy for non-functional requirement validation in cat-harness. | . 7. INCOSE Guide for Writing Requirements (INCOSE-TP-2010-006-04, 2023) . | Origin & Governance: International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE). | Licence: INCOSE copyright; educational / professional guidance. | Maturity: Universal de facto standard for requirements authoring quality and automated linting rules. | Structure: Defines 9 Requirement Characteristics (Necessary, Appropriate, Conforming, Singular, Feasible, Verifiable, Correct, Conforming, Complete) and 40+ specific quality rules: . | Singularity: One requirement per statement; no compound sentences with “and/or”. | Verifiability: Must state conditions that can be definitively verified. | No ambiguous words: Avoid vague terms (“user-friendly”, “rapid”, “cost-effective”, “easy”, “robust”). | No escape clauses: Avoid “where possible”, “as appropriate”, “to the extent practical”. | Active voice: Clear subject acting upon an object. | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Directly justifies the bootstrap requirement rule: “one sentence a reviewer can say yes or no to” and “at least one success criterion with a verification method”. | Provides the precise linting rules for automated QA criteria in check:requirements. | . | Verdict: Strongly recommended as the rule basis for requirements quality linters. | .

1705.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1705.title: 4. Architectural assessment: complexity, cost, and layer placement
1705.content: Why nothing is adopted into bootstrap (the no-outside-concept rule) . Bootstrap (bootstrap/) is the foundational, zero-dependency substrate of the entire folio-assistant platform. It defines the core data contracts and schemas that every tool, harness, and workspace inherits. | No External Dependencies: Bootstrap cannot import or depend on heavy XML parsers (for ReqIF), RDF/triple-store engines (for OSLC), or specialized NLP libraries. | Git Hygiene and Line-Oriented Diffs: Markdown front matter (.md) and lean JSON files (.json) produce readable, clean Git diffs on PR reviews. ReqIF XML produces massive, unreadable multi-thousand-line diffs for minor attribute changes. | Speed and Portability: Validating bootstrap schemas via Zod is nearly instantaneous in Bun or Node. It introduces zero runtime overhead. | Conclusion: Any standard mapping or projection must live in higher layers (cat-harness, or a content layer above it). Injecting outside formats into bootstrap would violate the repository’s foundational architecture. | . Architectural layer placement . The diagram below illustrates the strict separation of concerns across layers: . ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 2: Projection & Integration Adapters (tools / folio-assistant) │ │ - ReqIF Exporter/Importer (.reqif XML for DOORS, Polarion, Cameo) │ │ - OSLC-RM Linked Data Provider (JSON-LD / RDF / LDP) │ └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ maps to/from ┌──────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 1: Harness Validation & Quality Linters (cat-harness) │ │ - EARS Pattern Validator (checks statement regex / grammar in CI) │ │ - INCOSE Requirements Linter (flags vague words, compound sentences) │ │ - ISO 25010 NFR Category Checker (validates non-functional categories)│ │ - check:requirements gate & requirement-set adjudication │ └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ validates ┌──────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 0: Bootstrap Substrate (bootstrap/) │ │ - Pure Markdown Front Matter + Zod Schema │ │ - Zero outside concepts, zero external dependencies │ │ - 6-part requirement structure: id, title, statement, conformance, │ │ derivedFrom, successCriteria (test, inspection, review, analysis) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ .

1706.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1706.title: 5. Concrete recommendations
1706.content: . | Maintain Markdown Front Matter + Zod as Native Format: . | The current Markdown front matter format for requirement documents (and JSON for programmatic requirement nodes) is optimal. | It is human-readable, machine-checkable via strict Zod schemas, and perfectly suited for Git pull request workflows. | Do not replace the front matter format with ReqIF XML or raw OSLC RDF. | . | Implement EARS Grammar Verification in cat-harness: . | Add an EARS pattern checker into check:requirements (or as a dedicated script scripts/check-ears-patterns.ts). | Every requirement statement should be checked against the 5 EARS patterns (Ubiquitous, Event-driven, State-driven, Unwanted behavior, Optional features). | This provides immediate authoring feedback and enforces rigorous syntax without changing the underlying data schema. | . | Standardize NFR Categories on ISO/IEC 25010: . | In cat-harness validators, enforce that for statements with kind: "non-functional", the category field belongs to the ISO/IEC 25010 quality taxonomy (security, performance-efficiency, compatibility, interaction-capability, reliability, maintainability, portability, safety). | . | Build Projection Adapters in Higher Layers on Demand: . | When interoperability with enterprise requirements tools is required: . | Develop tools/reqif-adapter: converts RequirementSet and Requirement nodes into standard OMG ReqIF 1.2 XML packages and vice versa. | Develop tools/oslc-rm-adapter: exposes requirement graphs via OSLC-RM JSON-LD contexts mapped through ns.jsonld. | . | Keep these tools isolated from the core bootstrap package. | . | .

1707.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1707.title: 6. What this methodology refuses
1707.content: . | Refuses adopting ReqIF XML or OSLC RDF into bootstrap/. Bootstrap must remain free of external interchange baggage. | Refuses monolithic document SRS models (IEEE 830). Requirements in this platform are atomic, graph-addressable statements (req:<slug>#<key>). | Refuses requirements without success criteria. A requirement without an explicit verification method (test, inspection, review, analysis) and criterion is unauditable and refused by CI gates. | Refuses ad-hoc NFR categories. Non-functional categories must adhere to the established ISO/IEC 25010 quality model. | .

1708.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1708.title: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
1708.content: ← All methodologies . requirements-standards-assessment — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Evaluating how requirements authored or verified in the harness map to or from open industry standards, interchange formats, statement grammars, and quality models — and deciding which transformations belong in higher harness layers (cat-harness, and content layers above it) while keeping the bootstrap Requirement schema strictly self-contained and free of external dependencies. It answers how bootstrap requirements translate to ReqIF, OSLC-RM, EARS, ISO 29148, and ISO 25010, what each standard costs in serialization and semantic complexity, and where mapping adapters must live. It does NOT govern runtime execution logs (prov-o-provenance), decision table structures (dmn), software package bills of materials (spdx-3), or access policy enforcement (odrl-policies). Origin. Survey and comparative assessment of formal and open requirements standards: OMG Requirements Interchange Format (ReqIF 1.2, formal/2013-10-01); OASIS Open Services for Lifecycle Collaboration Requirements Management (OSLC-RM 2.1 / OSLC Core 3.0); Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax (EARS: Mavin et al., IEEE RE 2009); ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering); IEEE Std 830-1998 (Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148); ISO/IEC 25010:2011/2023 (Systems and software engineering — Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation — System and software quality models); INCOSE Guide for Writing Requirements (INCOSE-TP-2010-006-04, 4th Edition, 2023). Evaluated against the bootstrap Requirement schema (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json, Issue #1164). 1709.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
1709.title: RASCI — the fifth letter, and when it earns its place
1709.content: Adopted on the owner’s ruling, 2026-09-23 (issue #1004), as a parallel track to raci, not a replacement for it. methodology-adoption: “Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them… pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.” A process here declares which it is written in, and declaring nothing means raci.

1710.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
1710.title: ⚠ This rendering is not backed by a source
1710.content: No RASCI source is ingested here, and nothing below is asserted on a source’s authority. What follows is the method as commonly understood — weaker than a cited rendering, and marked as weaker on purpose. check:methodology-evidence reports this node as unbacked, correctly. Do not remove that finding by pointing evidence at the RACI paper. It was searched: zero occurrences of rasci, racsi, supportive or five roles. Citing it here would be the failure methodology-adoption §”Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched” names, made worse by the citation being checkably about something else.

1711.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
1711.title: The five letters
1711.content: | letter | means | direction | . | Responsible | does the work | may be several | . | Accountable | carries the decision; answers for the outcome | exactly one | . | Supportive | contributes effort or resources to the work, without owning the deliverable | may be several | . | Consulted | asked for input before | two-way | . | Informed | told after | one-way | . Four of these are raci’s and are not restated here — the node is raci.md, including the exactly-one-Accountable constraint, which RASCI inherits unchanged.

1712.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
1712.title: What S is, against its two neighbours
1712.content: S is not a weaker R. The line is ownership of the deliverable, not quantity of effort: a Supportive party may do more work than the Responsible one and still be S, because the deliverable is not theirs to hand over. S is not a Consulted who happened to help. C is asked for input and gives an opinion; S does work. Collapsing them is the same error as collapsing C into I — it turns a contribution into a conversation, and the chart still reads as complete. The test: if this role stopped participating, would the activity be late (S), or merely less well informed (C)? A role whose absence changes nothing but opinion was never S.

1713.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
1713.title: When NOT to use it
1713.content: A five-letter chart where every S column is empty is worse than a four-letter one, because it advertises a distinction the author did not actually make. The fifth letter is justified by a Supportive party existing, not by wanting a more complete-looking matrix. raci remains the default here for exactly that reason.

1714.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
1714.title: How this platform applies it
1714.content: S is declarable; R still is not — and the asymmetry is structural rather than an omission. A BPMN activity sits in exactly one lane, and that lane is Responsible. So the lane is a discriminator, not a description: R is the owning lane, S is a declared role that is not it, and no case can be both. This was checked against the corpus before the letter was added — no activity anywhere declares involvement="responsible" — so the premise holds and S inherits no ambiguity from it. It buys real expressiveness rather than a letter for its own sake: BPMN cannot place one activity in two lanes, so before this there was no way to say “this role also does the work here”. A process opts in: . <bpmn:process id="Process_X"> <bpmn:extensionElements> <cat-harness.processes:involvement vocabulary="rasci"/> </bpmn:extensionElements> . and may then declare <cat-harness.processes:raci ref="<role>" involvement="supportive"/>. In a process that has not opted in, a supportive is a reported breach — neither coerced to a neighbouring letter nor silently dropped. That refusal is what makes this a choice rather than a spelling rule; check:raci and the raci-involvement-vocabulary QA criterion carry it, and the skill skills/process/raci/raci.md holds the platform overlay both vocabularies share.

1715.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
1715.title: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
1715.content: ← All methodologies . rasci — declared by cat-harness — cited, not ingested . Applies when. Who is involved, when a role does the work without owning the deliverable. Use it where a separate Supportive party is real — someone who contributes effort or resources to an activity that another role answers for. If no such party exists, use raci instead: a fifth letter nobody fills is a column that makes the chart look more considered than it is. Like raci it answers who, never what or whether — a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, situation analysis is swot. Origin. NOT ESTABLISHED FROM ANY SOURCE HELD HERE, and that is stated rather than guessed. RASCI (also written RASIC) is the five-letter member of the responsibility-assignment-matrix family from project-management practice. No text for it is ingested in this repository and none was reachable when this node was written. The one RACI source this checkout does hold — library/dusengumuremyi-2026-ai-mediated-raci — was searched and contains ZERO occurrences of rasci, racsi, supportive or five roles, so it backs raci and expressly not this. The candidates are the same paid standards and books listed in raci’s §”The primary is still not held”. See literature-search. Node file: rasci.md .

1716.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1716.title: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1716.content: This methodology node completes work item folio-assistant-qh1s (Issue #1164): a literature search over requirements-management practice across the five lifecycle dimensions (organisation, identifiers, traceability, change, and retirement), the explicit adoption or rejection of candidate methodologies through methodology-adoption, and the proposed executable BPMN filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) put to the owner before automation is built. Whereas sibling methodology requirements-standards-assessment.md (work item folio-assistant-1gf7) assessed open interchange and syntax standards (ReqIF, OSLC RM, EARS, RFC 2119 / RFC 8174, IEEE 29148, Planguage, SysML, Gherkin) to map their constructs onto bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json, this node governs how requirements are organised, identified, traced, amended, superseded, and retired as they are filed into docs/requirements/ once docs/requirements/ grows past a flat hand-maintained list.

1717.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1717.title: 1. Literature search over requirements-management practice
1717.content: Per literature-search, every surveyed source is recorded below with its provenance/access status (ingested library/<bib-slug> node where held on disk, or external standard / open-source specification where copyright or scope keeps the full text outside library/) and with what it offers here across the five dimensions of work item folio-assistant-qh1s: . | Organisation — how a growing corpus of filed requirements is structured and navigated without breaking path stability. | Identifiers — how requirements and sub-clauses receive durable, collision-free, human- and machine-addressable IDs in a distributed Git workflow. | Traceability — how backward lineage (to proposals, user needs, and L1 sources), horizontal dependencies (between requirements), and forward verification (to work items, skills, processes, and test attestations) are recorded and checked. | Change — how in-scope amendments versus scope-altering replacements are distinguished, reviewed, and versioned. | Retirement — how obsolete or superseded requirements leave active force without breaking historical links or audit trails. | . 1.1 Summary matrix across the five filing dimensions . | Source | Provenance / library status | Organisation | Identifiers | Traceability | Change | Retirement | . | ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering, Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, 6.5) | Proprietary ISO/IEEE standard; assessed via public clause structure (no full-text redistributable PDF in library/) | Separates stakeholder requirements (StRS) from system/software requirements (SyRS/SRS); organises by system architecture or functional domain | Unique, persistent requirement identifier (id) independent of document section position | Clause 5.2.7 mandates bidirectional traceability: backward to source/parent need, forward to design elements and verification records | Clause 6.5 requires formal change control, impact analysis over dependent items, and baseline sign-off | Explicit lifecycle status attribute (retired / obsolete / superseded); historical records retained for audit | . | Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson, Mastering the Requirements Process, 4th ed.) | Commercial book / template; assessed via published Volere atomic “Snow Card” specification | Groups requirements by functional area / business event / concern rather than implementation module; pairs functional with non-functional categories | Atomic requirement number + type code + event/use-case reference on each Snow Card | Each card records Source / Originator, Supporting Materials, Dependencies, and a mandatory measurable Fit Criterion | History log on the card tracking creation, amendments, and re-verification | Explicit archived / retired state with reason when business rules change; card number is never reused | . | IREB CPRE Foundation Level (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals, 3rd ed.) | Standard RE body of knowledge; external textbook | Contrasts tree-structured chapter hierarchies against faceted / attribute-driven views over atomic requirement objects | Recommends immutable object identifiers decoupled from chapter headings so restructuring views never renumbers requirements | Defines three explicit trace link directions: pre-RS / backward (to origins), post-RS / forward (to artefacts/tests), and within-RS / horizontal (dependsOn, refines, conflictsWith) | Configuration management and baseline versioning; change impact propagation along trace links | Status state machine (draft → agreed → validated → implemented → deprecated/retired) | . | Doorstop (Browning & Adams, Doorstop: Text-Based Requirements Management Using Version Control, JOSS 2014; github.com/doorstop-dev/doorstop) | Open-source Git-native requirements tool (lgpl-3.0); external software reference | Stores one text file per requirement (YAML or Markdown-with-front-matter) inside version-controlled directories representing document trees | Prefix + identifier per file, addressable in git diffs; supports sub-links and hierarchical parent pointers | Parent/child trace links stored directly in requirement front matter; detects suspect links when a parent requirement changes | Git commits and pull requests are the change-control log; review happens in PR diffs alongside code and tests | active: false / normative: false front-matter flags retire an item in place without git rm, keeping git blame and incoming links intact | . | Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (Nygard 2011; Kopp et al., adr.github.io/madr/, already adopted in methodologies/madr.md) | Adopted harness methodology (methodologies/madr.md) | Flat directory of Markdown files (docs/decisions/ or docs/proposals/), indexed by concern or status in index.md | Filename slug (<slug>.md) serves as the stable human-readable identifier | Cross-references related decisions, issues, and motivating forces in front matter and body | Append-only / immutable intent: minor clarifications edit in place; substantive reversals file a new record that supersedes the old | Explicit status transitions: proposed → accepted → deprecated | superseded by ADR-XXXX; old files are never deleted | . | W3C PROV-O (PROV-O: The PROV Ontology, W3C Recommendation 2013, adopted in methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md) | Ingested in library/w3c-2013-prov-o | Graph of prov:Entity nodes linked by typed provenance relations independent of filesystem nesting | Stable IRIs (req:<slug>, req:<slug>#<key>) identifying each entity | prov:wasDerivedFrom (parent/source lineage), prov:wasGeneratedBy (filing/test activity), prov:wasAttributedTo (actor/sign-off) | prov:wasRevisionOf and prov:specializationOf distinguish revisions from distinct derived entities | prov:wasInvalidatedBy and prov:invalidatedAtTime model retirement/supersession without erasing the entity from the provenance graph | . | RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017 — BCP 14 key words) | Ingested in library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | Separates normative statements (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) from explanatory prose within a specification | Statement-level addressing (statements[].key → req:<slug>#<key>) so each normative keyword clause is individually citable | Pairs each uppercase keyword statement with its own successCriteria and verification witness | Changing a statement’s modality (SHOULD → MUST) is a normative change requiring re-sign-off | Retiring or relaxing a MUST statement requires explicit normative adjudication | . | Specification-Compiled Agents & Issue-Driven Work Plans (arxiv-2404.04834v4; hmans-2026-beans-readme) | Ingested in library/arxiv-2404.04834v4 and library/hmans-2026-beans-readme | Connects declarative specifications to executable agent work items (beans/) and automated verification gates | Cross-graph IDs: req:<slug> linked to work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) and process IDs (Process_*) | Closed-loop compilation: requirement statement → work-plan work item → implementing skill/process → test attestation | Specification edits trigger deterministic re-check (check:requirements) across all linked sets and attestations | Completed work items archive when closed; filed requirements remain in-force as the persistent invariant until superseded or retired | . | IEEE Std 830-1998 (IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) | Historical IEEE standard (superseded); external baseline | Monolithic single-document SRS organised by deep numbered outline (3.1.1.1 Functional Requirement 1) | Positional section numbers (§3.2.4.1) tied to document outline location | External traceability matrices (spreadsheets) mapping section numbers to test cases | Document-level revision history table at the top of the monolithic SRS | Striking out or deleting sections in a new SRS edition, causing section renumbering unless placeholder sections are kept | . 1.2 Detailed source notes: what each source offers this harness . 1.2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, and 6.5) . | What it offers here: . | Attribute canon (Clause 6.5): Defines the essential metadata attributes every managed requirement needs beyond its statement text: unique identifier, requirement status, source/origin, rationale, priority/modality, verification method/criteria, and trace links. Our bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json directly embodies this attribute set (id, title, status, proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, statements[], beans, skills, processes, supersededBy). | Bidirectional traceability (Clause 5.2.7): Establishes that forward traceability alone (requirement → test) is half a system; backward traceability (requirement → originating proposal/need/source via proposedIn and derivedFrom) is what prevents gold-plating (orphan requirements with no stakeholder origin) and explains why a constraint exists when an agent later considers changing it. | Change and retirement discipline: Distinguishes an approved baseline from working drafts (RequirementSet.stage: draft → proposed → approved → accepted in bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json) and requires any transition into or out of active force to carry human sign-off. | . | . 1.2.2 Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson) . | What it offers here: . | Atomic “Snow Card” structure with Fit Criteria: Volere’s primary contribution is insisting that a requirement is not filed until its Fit Criterion (our statements[].successCriteria) is written beside the description (statements[].statement). A requirement whose fit criterion cannot be stated is still a proposal or open question. | Organisation by semantic concern / business domain: Rather than organising requirements by the code file they touch or chronological filing date, Volere organises requirements by functional domain / concern area so a reader auditing one domain sees all governing invariants together. In cat-harness, the eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) already partition skills, processes, schemas, and tests; projecting filed requirements under those same eight concern groups in docs/requirements/index.md aligns requirement navigation with the rest of the knowledge graph. | . | . 1.2.3 IREB CPRE (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals) . | What it offers here: . | Decoupling identification and storage from presentation views: IREB highlights the classic failure mode of hierarchical specifications: when chapter structure is used as both the file path and the requirement ID, reorganising chapters breaks every incoming reference. Storing atomic requirements at stable paths with immutable IDs (docs/requirements/<slug>.md → req:<slug>) while providing faceted views (grouped by concern group, by RequirementSet, or by lifecycle status in docs/requirements/index.md) gives both stable URIs and structured human browsing. | Three-axis trace topology: Clarifies the distinction between backward trace (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal trace (dependsOn between peer requirements), and forward trace (beans, skills, processes, and verification attestations). | . | . 1.2.4 Doorstop (Browning & Adams, JOSS 2014) . | What it offers here: . | Git-native file-per-requirement architecture: Doorstop proved that storing requirements as individual text files with YAML front matter and Markdown prose in the same Git repository as the implementation eliminates external ALM database drift. Every requirement filing, amendment, or retirement travels in the same pull request as the code, process diagram, and test attestation that implements or verifies it. | In-place retirement (status: retired / superseded): Doorstop retires requirements by flipping a front-matter status field rather than deleting the file (git rm), ensuring that historical commits, test runs, and child requirements never point to a missing file. | Suspect-link awareness: Doorstop flags downstream items when an upstream requirement changes. In our harness, check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts) provides the deterministic equivalent: it verifies that every derivedFrom, dependsOn, and supersededBy target exists, that no cycle exists in derivedFrom, that no in-force requirement depends on a retired or superseded requirement without updating its own lineage, and that every RequirementSet at approved or accepted has a matching human requirement-signoff attestation and only in-force members. | . | . 1.2.5 Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) . | What it offers here: . | Proposal-to-Requirement continuity (git mv + proposedIn): In cat-harness, a feature starts as a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (where options are weighed using Kepner-Tregoe, SWOT, and MADR). When the feature ships and is signed off, git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md promotes the file in place, preserving its slug, its git log --follow history, and the options analysis that justified it, while proposedIn records the commit SHA and path of the proposal before the move. | Immutable supersession chain: When a shipped requirement’s fundamental contract is replaced by a new design, the old requirement file is not overwritten into a different contract; instead, the new proposal is filed as docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md, and the old requirement’s front matter is updated to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | .

1718.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1718.title: 2. Candidate methodologies: adopted vs rejected with reasons
1718.content: Following skills/process/process-core/methodology-adoption.md, we do not invent an unattributed house method. We adopt four orthogonal practices from the surveyed literature—naming their origins, what is taken, what is left behind, and how each binds into bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and check:requirements—and we explicitly reject five candidate practices with documented reasons. 2.1 Adopted methodologies . M1 — Doorstop + MADR git-native file-per-requirement and two-level semantic identifiers (req:<slug> and req:<slug>#<key>) . | Origin: Doorstop (Browning & Adams 2014) for one-file-per-requirement in Git with YAML front matter + Markdown body; MADR (methodologies/madr.md) for human-readable <slug>.md filenames; RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md) for statement-level normative clauses. | What is adopted: . | Each filed requirement lives in its own Markdown file at docs/requirements/<slug>.md with id: req:<slug> matching its filename stem (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Individual normative clauses inside a requirement are declared in statements[] (key, modality, statement, successCriteria) and addressed as req:<slug>#<key> (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*#[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, every <slug> is globally unique: a slug exists either as an unshipped proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md or as a filed requirement in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, never both (check:requirements refuses a collision). | . | What is left behind and why: . | Doorstop’s auto-incremented numeric filenames (REQ001.yml, REQ002.yml) are left behind because concurrent feature branches in a multi-agent repository collide on sequential integers and opaque numbers hide meaning in prose and test logs. | Doorstop’s content-hash “fingerprint” clearing on whitespace edits is left behind because explicit lifecycle status + human requirement-signoff attestations (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/) provide stronger, semantically intentional governance than raw byte hashes. | . | . M2 — Faceted concern-group organisation (code-lists/concern-group.json) over flat docs/requirements/<slug>.md storage (Volere + IREB faceted view) . | Origin: Volere functional-area grouping (Robertson & Robertson) combined with IREB CPRE’s separation of stable storage identifiers from faceted navigation views (Pohl & Rupp), bound to the harness’s eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json. | What is adopted: . | Physical storage stays flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md: Every filed requirement sits directly in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, preserving 1:1 path parity with docs/proposals/<slug>.md for git mv, keeping req:<slug> → docs/requirements/<slug>.md resolution O(1) without directory searches, and ensuring check:requirements (mdFilesIn) reads 100% of filed requirements. | Logical organisation in docs/requirements/index.md groups by two orthogonal views: . | By Concern Group (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct from code-lists/concern-group.json), so a reader or agent working in a concern domain sees every in-force invariant governing that domain. | By Requirement Set (RequirementSet) and Lifecycle Status (in-force vs superseded / retired), so CRD baselines and historical records are cleanly separated from active invariants. | . | . | What is left behind and why: . | Physical subdirectory nesting (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) is rejected (see R3 below) so that reclassifying a requirement’s concern group or cross-cutting scope never breaks markdown links or requires a second git mv. | . | . M3 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 + IREB + W3C PROV-O three-axis bidirectional traceability . | Origin: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Clause 5.2.7 (bidirectional traceability), IREB CPRE (backward / horizontal / forward trace links), and W3C PROV-O (library/w3c-2013-prov-o, methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md). | What is adopted: . | Backward traceability (to origin and parent sources): . | proposedIn: required on every requirement promoted from docs/proposals/<slug>.md (commit SHA + path: docs/proposals/<slug>.md), binding prov:wasDerivedFrom to the exact pre-move proposal revision. | derivedFrom: array of parent req:<slug> IDs or library/<bib-slug> L1 sources from which this requirement is derived (checked for existence and acyclicity by check:requirements). | . | Horizontal traceability (between peer requirements): . | dependsOn: array of req:<slug> IDs that this requirement relies on at runtime or design time (checked for existence by check:requirements). | . | Forward traceability (to work items, implementation, and verification): . | beans: work-plan work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) that delivered or amended the requirement. | skills and processes: the Skill and Process (Process_*) nodes that implement the requirement. | Verification & Sign-off: test runs (test/runs/) and attestations (test/attestations/) citing req:<slug> or req:<slug>#<key>, plus RequirementSet membership and human sign-off attestations in test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json. | . | . | . M4 — MADR / ISO 29148 immutable lifecycle for change, supersession, and retirement (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired) . | Origin: MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Clause 6.5 configuration & change control. | What is adopted: . | Four lifecycle states (status in requirement.schema.json): . | proposed: drafted in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or in a RequirementSet at draft / proposed / approved stage) awaiting final delivery and acceptance sign-off. | in-force: shipped, verified, and accepted by human BA/owner sign-off; actively binds the codebase and knowledge graph. | superseded: replaced by a newer requirement; must carry supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (enforced by requirement.schema.json allOf rule and check:requirements). | retired: no longer applicable (the feature or constraint was intentionally removed without replacement); supersededBy is omitted, and the retirement rationale and authorising issue/bean are recorded in the document body. | . | Change decision rule (Amendment in place vs Supersession): . | In-scope amendment (edit in place, keep req:<slug>): When clarifying prose, adding a statements[] sub-clause, tightening a successCriteria check, or updating skills/processes/beans links without reversing the core invariant, edit docs/requirements/<slug>.md in place and record a fresh requirement-signoff attestation if its RequirementSet is approved or accepted. | Scope-reversing replacement (file req:<new-slug>, mark old superseded): When a new proposal reverses or fundamentally replaces an in-force requirement’s contract, file the new proposal at docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md (status: in-force, derivedFrom: [req:<old-slug>]), and update docs/requirements/<old-slug>.md to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | Set membership consistency: Because check:requirements enforces that an approved or accepted RequirementSet may only contain in-force (or proposed at approved stage) members, superseding or retiring a requirement requires updating any RequirementSet that lists it (replacing the old ID with req:<new-slug> or removing the retired ID under a re-signed set amendment). | . | . 2.2 Rejected candidate methodologies (with reasons) . | Candidate methodology | Verdict | Reason for rejection in this harness | . | R1 — IEEE Std 830-1998 monolithic SRS & positional section numbering (§3.2.1.4) | Rejected | Tying a requirement’s identifier to its outline position in a single monolithic file causes cascading renumbering whenever a section is inserted, split, or reordered. Renumbering breaks req: URIs in test runs, attestations, and work items, and a single monolithic SRS file creates constant Git merge conflicts across parallel agent branches. | . | R2 — Centralised sequential integer IDs (REQ-0001, FR-0042) | Rejected | In a distributed multi-agent Git workflow (worktrees, branches, subagents), two branches filing requirements concurrently will allocate the same next integer (REQ-0043) unless gated by an external lock server. Even when unique, opaque integers convey no domain meaning in test logs or prose compared to req:<slug>#<key>. (Note: FR-NNN may still appear as a local table label inside a single CRD proposal during discussion, but the canonical graph identifier is req:<slug>#<key>.) | . | R3 — Physical subdirectory sharding (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) | Rejected (kept as faceted index view in docs/requirements/index.md instead) | 1. check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts, mdFilesIn) scans docs/requirements/ and docs/proposals/ non-recursively and enforces a 1:1 slug namespace between docs/proposals/<slug>.md and docs/requirements/<slug>.md.2. Many proposals span multiple concern groups (e.g., sdlc + process); forcing a single directory path would make paths brittle when concern boundaries evolve.3. Faceted grouping in docs/requirements/index.md delivers the navigational benefit of Volere/concern-group organisation with zero path churn. | . | R4 — ReqIF XML / OSLC RM RDF triples as the primary authored store | Rejected (consistent with requirements-standards-assessment.md) | XML UUID graphs and raw RDF triples are unreadable in GitHub PR reviews and cannot be naturally co-authored as prose + front matter by humans and agents. Our YAML front matter (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) exports cleanly to JSON-LD (bootstrap/ns.jsonld) without burdening authors with XML. | . | R5 — Destructive deletion (git rm) of superseded or retired requirements | Rejected | Deleting docs/requirements/<slug>.md when a requirement is retired or superseded breaks historical provenance: past test/runs/, test/attestations/, beans/, and derivedFrom links would become dangling references. Keeping the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md with status: superseded (supersededBy: req:<new-slug>) or status: retired preserves referential integrity across the graph. | .

1719.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
1719.title: 3. Proposed filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn)
1719.content: To fulfil Criterion 3 of work item folio-assistant-qh1s (“a filing PROCESS proposed as BPMN, to be put to the owner before it is built”), the executable BPMN diagram sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (Process_RequirementsFiling) models the end-to-end process for filing, organising,superseding, or retiring a requirement in docs/requirements/. 3.1 Where Process_RequirementsFiling sits in the lifecycle . In the CRDM lifecycle (skills/process/crdm/crdm-requirements-workflow.md): . | Phases 1–4 (crdm-needs.bpmn, crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn, crdm-data-model.bpmn, crdm-signoff.bpmn) produce and sign off a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and optionally a RequirementSet moving from draft → proposed → approved). | Phase 5 (crdm-deliver.bpmn) builds and verifies the MVP in code, skills, and processes. | At Phase 6 (crdm-close.bpmn), when the feature ships and stakeholders/BA confirm acceptance criteria are met, Process_RequirementsFiling (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn) governs the transition of the proposal into docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or the amendment, supersession, or retirement of an existing filed requirement). | . 3.2 Lanes and responsibilities . | Lane | Role (partitionElementRef) | Responsibility in Process_RequirementsFiling | . | BA / Feature Requestor (Lane_BA) | business-analyst | Reviews the filed requirement’s organisation, traceability links, normative statements, and any supersession/retirement transition (BA_ReviewFiling), and issues the human sign-off decision (approve, amend, reject, defer, cancel) required by check:requirements before a RequirementSet can reach accepted. | . | Authoring Agent (Lane_Agent) | authoring-agent | Executes the deterministic filing steps: classifies the requirement’s concern group and filing mode (A_ClassifyFiling), moves or updates the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (A_PromoteOrUpdate), binds the Requirement front matter (A_BindFrontMatter), updates superseded/retired records (A_UpdateLifecycle), indexes the requirement in docs/requirements/index.md (A_UpdateIndex), runs check:requirements (A_RunCheck), and records the human sign-off attestation (A_RecordFilingSignoff). | . 3.3 Step-by-step walkthrough of sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn . | A_ClassifyFiling — Classify filing mode, concern group, and req:<slug> identifier (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Determine which of the three filing modes applies: . | New filing from proposal: promoting docs/proposals/<slug>.md → docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | In-place amendment or supersession: amending an existing docs/requirements/<slug>.md or superseding req:<old-slug> with req:<new-slug>. | Retirement: retiring an obsolete docs/requirements/<slug>.md (status: retired). | . | Assign the primary concern group from code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) for indexing in docs/requirements/index.md. | . | GW_FilingMode — Which filing transition? (cat-harness.processes:judgement): . | Branches on the three modes: promote (from docs/proposals/<slug>.md), amend-or-supersede (on an existing requirement), or retire (marking an active requirement retired). | . | A_PromoteOrUpdate — git mv proposal to docs/requirements/<slug>.md and capture proposedIn (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | On the promote branch, record the pre-move commit SHA (git log -1 --format=%H -- docs/proposals/<slug>.md), execute git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md so Git history stays unbroken, and populate proposedIn: { commit, path: "docs/proposals/<slug>.md" }. | . | A_BindFrontMatter — Bind Requirement front matter, statements, and 3-axis lineage (skill: specification-management): . | Validate or author the YAML front matter against bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>, title, status: in-force (or proposed prior to acceptance sign-off); | statements[] with stable #<key>, RFC 2119 modality (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), normative statement, and measurable successCriteria; | Backward lineage (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal dependencies (dependsOn), and forward implementation links (beans, skills, processes). | . | . | A_UpdateLifecycle — Update superseded or retired requirement records and RequirementSet membership (skill: specification-management): . | When superseding req:<old-slug> or retiring a requirement, set status: superseded + supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (or status: retired with retirement rationale in prose) on the old file without deleting it, and update any RequirementSet in docs/requirements/*.set.json so no approved/accepted set retains a non-in-force member. | . | A_UpdateIndex — Organise entry in docs/requirements/index.md under its concern group and status (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Add or update the requirement’s row in docs/requirements/index.md under its code-lists/concern-group.json section (for in-force requirements) or the Superseded and Retired Requirements archive table, and regenerate directory READMEs (subgraph-readmes.ts). | . | A_RunCheck — Run check:requirements gate (skill: specification-management): . | Execute bun run cat check:requirements to verify schema validity, slug uniqueness across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, derivedFrom acyclicity, resolution of all derivedFrom / dependsOn / supersededBy / skills / processes references, and RequirementSet invariants. | . | GW_CheckPassed — Does check:requirements pass?: . | If fail, loop back to A_BindFrontMatter to fix schema, collision, or broken-link findings 1721.doc: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1721.title: Correspondence analysis: the SVD of the standardised residuals
1721.content: Adopted 2026-09-29 (work item ansc, issue #1482), as option G of the LSI work, and measured against LSI on this repository’s one ground truth before being adopted.

1722.doc: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1722.title: Its sources: what is held
1722.content: | source | held | what this node takes from it | . | Qi, Hessen & van der Heijden 2023 | ✅ library/qi-hessen-vanderheijden-2023-ca-vs-lsa | the definition (§2.2), the retrieval use and the transition formula, the weighting and α variants (§3), the worked example the engine is tested on (Table 1, Fig. 1) | . | Greenacre 1984 / 2017 | ❌ not held | cited by Qi et al. for the method; nothing here depends on it beyond what Qi et al. restate | . | Benzécri 1973 | ❌ not held | the origin, for attribution only | .

1723.doc: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1723.title: The load-bearing idea, in the paper’s words
1723.content: “the solution of LSA is a mix of the associations between documents and terms, and marginal effects arising from the lengths of documents and marginal frequencies of terms” — and “CA ignores the information on marginal frequency differences between documents and between terms from the solution by preprocessing the data, and it only focuses on the relationships between documents and terms” (§2.1).

1724.doc: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1724.title: The method, as Qi et al. define it (§2.2)
1724.content: | # | step | definition | . | 1 | proportions | P = F / N for the document × term count matrix F; row masses r = P1, column masses c = Pᵀ1 | . | 2 | residuals | S = D_r^{-½}(P − E)D_c^{-½} with E = rcᵀ, the expected proportions under independence. ‖S‖² is the total inertia, “the Pearson χ² statistic divided by sample size” | . | 3 | SVD | S = UΣVᵀ; keep k | . | 4 | coordinates | standard Φ = D_r^{-½}U, Γ = D_c^{-½}V; documents at ΦΣ, terms at ΓΣ. “Euclidean distances between the rows of ΦkΣk … approximate χ²-distances between the rows … of F” | . | 5 | margins removed | Σ_i r_i φ_ik = 0 = Σ_j c_j γ_jk — every dimension is orthogonal to the margins | . | 6 | new document | the transition formula (eq. 8): “a new document d … can be projected onto the k-dimensional subspace by placing it in the weighted average of the column points using (d / Σ d_j) Γk” | . | 7 | variants | weighting the raw matrix before CA (§3.1) and a singular-value exponent α (§3.2): coordinates ΦΣ^α | . What the paper found: on four datasets, “CA always performs better than LSA” in mean average precision, under each of four feature extractions; weighting the input “can improve CA; however, it is data dependent and the improvement is small”; α “often improves the performance of CA; however, the extent of the improvement depends on the dataset and the number of dimensions”; and “cosine similarity performs better than the Euclidean distance and dot similarity” (§6).

1725.doc: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1725.title: Measured here, 2026-09-29
1725.content: On the one ground truth this repository has — the epics 250 open work items were already filed under, leave-one-out over 21 epics, on the work item store as it stood before the LSI-driven re-filing (after it, LSI would be scored against its own proposals): . | method | agree | paired with | only this one | only the other | exact McNemar | . | CA, raw, k=100 | 146 | LSI, raw, k=100 (136) | 27 | 17 | p = 0.17 | . | CA, raw, k=100 | 146 | LSI, log-entropy, k=100 (149) | 13 | 16 | p = 0.71 | . | CA, raw, k=200 | 157 | LSI, log-entropy, k=200 (153) | 19 | 15 | p = 0.61 | . The direction agrees with Qi et al. on the same feature extraction (CA over raw-count LSA); the size is not significant at n = 250; and weighted LSI closes the gap. Neither method is shown better at filing work items, so the filing default stays lsi and this node is a parallel track, not a replacement. Two observations on the IRIS replica library (342 sections), recorded as observed here, not as claims from a held source: . | LSI’s dimension 1 places all 342 sections on one side — a margin, as Qi et al. describe. CA’s dimension 1 splits them 46 / 296 — a contrast. The paper’s central claim holds on this corpus. | CA’s leading dimensions are carried by the most distinctive profiles: the style manual’s list of place names, and the Lorem-ipsum and font-specimen pages. The χ² metric weights a rare profile heavily. That makes CA the sharper instrument for finding outlier pages, and a noisier one for reading themes. | .

1726.doc: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1726.title: What this platform adopts, and what it refuses
1726.content: Adopted: steps 1–6 on the RAW counts (the paper: processing the raw matrix “is considered an integral part of CA”); cosine for comparison; α and a weighted input available as options, off by default, because the paper finds their gain data-dependent and this repository measured none that is significant. Refused, for the same reasons as lsi and with the same numbering: a CA cosine is never merged with a lexical match (1); a dimension is not a topic until a person names it (2); CA output never writes a relation (3); it is never evidence for a claim in content (4). And one of its own: . | A unit with no indexed term is not placed. Its profile is undefined, so its row is taken as zero — it is dropped from the analysis and scores 0 against everything, rather than being given a made-up position. | .

1727.doc: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1727.title: How it is performed here
1727.content: pipeline/ca.ts, sharing lsi.ts’s term matrix and randomized SVD (Halko et al.) so that a comparison is between decompositions and not between vocabularies. The residual matrix is never formed: products with S and Sᵀ are one sparse product plus a rank-one correction each. ca.test.ts checks it against the paper’s Table 1: the first two principal inertias (0.475, 93.2 %; 0.017, 3.4 %), their sum equal to χ²/N, jaguar between the cat and car terms, every dimension centred on the masses, and the transition formula returning each document to its own coordinates. bun run cat lsi:epics --method ca runs it on the work item store; the skill is lsi-indexing.

1728.doc: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1728.title: Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts
1728.content: ← All methodologies . correspondence-analysis — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. The same question as lsi — which units of a prose graph are close in what they are about — when the answer must not be dominated by how LONG a unit is or how COMMON a term is. CA removes those margins by construction, so it is the method to reach for when LSI’s first dimensions are margins (a first dimension with no negative pole) or when the question is which units are UNUSUAL — outlier pages, specimen text, a list among prose. It answers which units have similar term profiles, relative to independence. Like lsi, every output is a PROPOSAL. Not for choosing between the two methods by blending them (methodology-adoption §”Parallel, not composable”), not for a controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), and not for any decision. Origin. Correspondence analysis is Jean-Paul Benzécri’s (L’Analyse des Données, 1973) and is set out in Michael Greenacre, Theory and Applications of Correspondence Analysis (Academic Press, 1984) and Correspondence Analysis in Practice (3rd ed., 2017). Its application to information retrieval, and the comparison with latent semantic analysis this node rests on, is Qianqian Qi, David J. Hessen and Peter G. M. van der Heijden, “Improving information retrieval through correspondence analysis instead of latent semantic analysis”, Journal of Intelligent Information Systems (2023), doi:10.1007/s10844-023-00815-y — open access, ingested whole and read. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/qi-hessen-vanderheijden-2023-ca-vs-lsa | . Applied by skills: . | l1-document-ingestion | l1-document-ingestion | lsi-indexing | . 1729.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1729.title: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation: score against where experts agree, and read the panel
1729.content: Adopted 2026-09-26 (work item 0js9). Both sources were ingested through the library pipeline and read before this node was written.

1730.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1730.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
1730.content: Experts agree about what a work is about far more than about how to say it, so an evaluation must score those two layers separately. It must also take its answer key from where independent experts agree, not from one of them. The source makes this a measured premise rather than an assumption. Its concordance study (section “Consensus ground truth”) compares the headings that three research libraries assigned independently to 465,187 works that all three catalogued. It finds two layers. At the concept level (the heading’s root, before the first --), the three share a heading 93.3 % of the time and share nothing 0.2 % of the time. At the exact, fully subdivided level, only 39.4 % assign identical sets, and 35.6 % of all assertions come from just one of the three. In the source’s words: “most disagreement is granularity — which subdivisions, how specific — not topic”. Those figures are the source’s measurements on its corpus. They are quoted here as the reason for the design, not as constants this platform relies on.

1731.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1731.title: The method, as the source constructs it
1731.content: 1. The answer key is a consensus of independent judges. A work is admitted only if at least two cataloguing agencies independently assigned headings. The source enforces independence “at the level of the cataloging agency (MARC field 040), not merely the holding library, so that a copy-cataloged record imported from another institution does not count as a second judgement”. The rule is “strict and never relaxed to enlarge the dataset”. 2. Disagreement is kept, not resolved. Each heading carries a vote: the number of judges who asserted it. Three answer views are released: per-judge (the raw evidence), union (the default, which “rewards finding any heading a professional used”), and unanimous (the strictest). Every result states which view it was scored against. 3. Provenance before validity. A heading string can look valid in the vocabulary and still come from somewhere else. The source keeps a heading only when its record says it is from the target vocabulary. That removes “most of a quarter of candidate headings whose strings look like valid LCSH but whose provenance is not — a distinction string-validity checks miss”. 4. Normalise before comparing. NFC, lower-casing, a canonical subdivision separator, collapsed whitespace, and no trailing period, “so systems are judged on substance, not typography”. 5. Two match modes, always both. Every measure is computed under exact match (the full subdivided heading) and concept match (the root only). The gap between them is diagnostic: “a high concept but low exact score means the system found the right topic but not the authorised subdivided form — a different, specifiable error from a topical miss”. 6. A panel, not a headline. “The central methodological commitment is that no single number is trustworthy on its own.” Set metrics (micro and macro precision, recall, F1) for generation; ranked metrics (recall@k, P@k, R-precision, MRR) for retrieval; each under both match modes; and each broken down by language and by heading type, which the source calls “the panel’s most important safeguard”. 7. Never score what the system could not have reached. Retrieval is scored against the gold headings that exist in the retrieval vocabulary. The reachability ceiling is reported explicitly. Records with no reachable gold are excluded and counted, not scored as zero. “So that a heading that cannot be retrieved is never scored as a miss.” . 8. Stage-wise, where the system has stages. Where a system retrieves, reranks and then selects, each layer is scored separately. Recall at the first stage is “the ceiling for everything downstream”. The source rejects a frozen candidate pool because it “would bake in an arbitrary retriever’s choices”. 9. Human agreement is a reference, not a ceiling. One cataloguer reproduces roughly 87 % (exact) or 93 % (concept) of their peers’ consensus, so “a non-trivial share” of a system’s misses are headings a second cataloguer would also have omitted. The source deliberately does not turn this into a recall ceiling, because a ranked list of 200 and a short final set “measure different things”.

1732.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1732.title: Why the panel is not optional: the source’s own worked case
1732.content: The source’s section “The metric panel is necessary” shows a single aggregate getting the answer wrong. Its fine-tuned embedder wins on exact recall@200, but a hosted model wins on concept recall@200. The fine-tune wins on Korean, Arabic, Japanese, Chinese and German, and the hosted model still wins on English and Russian. “A benchmark reporting a single aggregate F1 would have asserted a clean victory and been wrong about its shape.” This is the case for step 6. It is not a claim about either model, and this node makes no such claim.

1733.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1733.title: What it refuses
1733.content: . | Never score against one indexer’s record as though it were the truth. A single library’s headings make “a noisy gold standard”. The concordance numbers are the reason. | Never report one number. Not a headline F1, not one match mode, and not an aggregate without the language and type breakdowns. | Never count an unreachable heading as a miss, and never leave out the count of what was excluded. | Never treat a hashed or held-out answer set as contamination-proof. The source is explicit that hashing over a finite public vocabulary is “a speed-bump, not a guarantee”, and that genuine control “would require a private evaluation server”, “with residual risk reported, not assumed away”. | Never compare results across vocabulary versions as though they were comparable. The vocabulary and cataloguing practice change. The source versions and dates its benchmark for this reason, and notes that the change affects exact match more than concept match. | .

1734.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1734.title: The parallel design, and why it is not this node
1734.content: methodology-adoption: parallel tracks are recorded, not blended. SemEval-2025 Task 5 (arXiv:2504.07199v3) evaluates with a single catalogue as gold: subject annotations by TIB’s own subject specialists, 17 of them across 28 disciplines. Its primary metric is recall, averaged over k from 5 to . | It adds a qualitative track in which subject librarians label each predicted subject as correct (Y), irrelevant but technically correct (I), or wrong. That track is scored twice: once counting Y and I as correct, and once counting only Y. The organisers note that their precision “would never amount to one” at larger k, because records carry about five true subjects. | . This is a sound design for its setting: a single institution, a specialist team, and a shared task with a deadline. What it does not have is steps 1 and 2 above. With one catalogue as gold, the concordance finding says that a large share of “misses” at exact level would be headings another professional would also have phrased differently. The two-case qualitative reading is the part of SemEval’s design that LCSHBench does not yet have. LCSHBench lists “the qualitative expert track” among its deferred components. Where this platform needs expert ratings, it uses SemEval’s protocol as SemEval’s, cited as such. It is not grafted into the consensus method as step 10.

1735.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1735.title: Where this rendering stops
1735.content: methodology-adoption step 2 requires both halves, so both are given here. Adopted: steps 1–9, the refusals, and the two-layer premise as the reason for them. Not adopted: the benchmark itself. Its corpus, its three source catalogues, its answer hashing, its embedders and its fine-tuning recipe are one instantiation for LCSH. The owner’s instruction, 2026-09-23: “start with process, determine most appropriate tools.” Nothing in the method depends on LCSH. A vocabulary without multiple independent indexers cannot supply step 1, and that is a reason to say the evaluation is single-judge, not to pretend otherwise. Not assessed: the source’s fine-tuning result. The source calls it “preliminary”: it was run on a development subset, not the held-out test, and at the first stage only. No claim about any system’s performance rests on this node. The concordance percentages quoted above are the source’s measurements, attributed as such, and nothing here uses them as parameters.

1736.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1736.title: How this platform applies it
1736.content: It does not apply it yet. Nothing here assigns subject terms, so nothing is evaluated this way. The nearest existing machinery is the QA-sidecar discipline. It shares this node’s refusals: never render “could not determine” as clean, and never quote one number without its basis. That is agreement in spirit, not an application, and it is recorded so nobody mistakes it for one.

1737.doc: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1737.title: Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score
1737.content: ← All methodologies . consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Judging how good a set of controlled-vocabulary assignments is, when qualified people would themselves disagree about the exact answer. Use it to evaluate a subject-indexing system, compare two of them, or decide whether one is good enough to draft for a human reviewer. It is also for any labelling task whose gold standard is expert judgement with a subjective surface. It answers how to measure. It does not answer how to produce the assignment, which is skill-pipeline-subject-indexing, a parallel node. Not for certainty of evidence behind a recommendation (grade), and not for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe). Not applicable where the answer is decidable, meaning a single correct output a checker can verify, because then there is no disagreement for a consensus to absorb. Origin. Kwok Leong Tang, “LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment” (arXiv:2606.04382v1), 2026. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. The method is rendered from that paper. The parallel design it is contrasted with is the one used by the shared task the other ingested subject-indexing papers were entered in: D’Souza, Sadruddin, Israel, Begoin & Slawig, “SemEval-2025 Task 5: LLMs4Subjects — LLM-based Automated Subject Tagging for a National Technical Library’s Open-Access Catalog” (arXiv:2504.07199v3), TIB Hannover. It was ingested and read too, so that design is described from its own text. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2606.04382v1 | library/arxiv-2504.07199v3 | . 1739.doc: ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions
1739.title: Its sources: what is held, what is not
1739.content: | source | held | what this node takes from it | . | ODRL Information Model 2.2 (W3C REC, 2018) | ✅ library/w3c-2018-odrl-model-2-2 | the model, its classes and every MUST quoted below | . | ODRL Vocabulary & Expression 2.2 | ❌ not held | the Common Vocabulary actions (display, modify, …) and their includedIn; the JSON-LD context. The includedIn values in ODRL_ACTIONS are not verified against it here | . | post-REC errata | ❌ not held | none | . A caution on section references.
