4421.title: KG to public portal
4421.content: Generated from cat-harness/processes/kg/kg-to-portal.bpmn by gen-processes-viz.ts — do not edit here. All processes · cat-harness processes .

4422.title: Rendering the knowledge graph
4422.content: Skill kg-viewer: Render a published knowledge-graph document so a person can read it — faceted index, node detail, followable edges, and an honest account of what the document is missing. Host-agnostic; the publishing is a separate Tool. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . kg-export serialises the layer’s graph to one JSON-LD document. This skill is making that document legible to a person. The two are separate capabilities — serialising is mechanical and host-agnostic, rendering is a design problem, and posting the result to a host is a third thing that belongs to the pages-publish Tool.

4423.title: The page is generated, not committed
4423.content: The viewer must fetch the graph document, and that document is named after the repository — <stub>.jsonld, never a generic kg.json. A committed page would have to either: . | Hardcode one layer’s stub, so a platform script works in exactly one repository; or | Compose the name at runtime from the URL or a convention, which breaks the “resolve, do not compose” rule: a consumer should never have to manipulate a string to find a document. | . So the exporter, which already knows the stub, writes it into the page. The page resolves nothing. It fetches the document relative to its own location. The page is <site>/<stub>/index.html and reads ../<name>/<stub>.jsonld (the document’s own path, under its layer’s directory, the host’s included), so the same bytes work on the canonical site and under branches/<slug>/ with no configuration, no --base-url, and no build-time branch. A staging build that needed a different page would test something other than what ships. Which documents the site publishes, and where: instance-publication §”What each layer publishes”.

4424.title: No dependencies, and that is a requirement rather than a preference
4424.content: No CDN, no framework, no build step — one HTML file. A page that needs a third-party fetch to render cannot be opened from a file or reviewed offline or from a restricted network, and adds a third party to the trust boundary of a page that displays this repository’s own data. “No CDN” means no THIRD party’s. A script or stylesheet this site publishes itself, shared by many of its own pages, is the opposite case and is what the next section requires.

4425.title: Every asset has its own IRI — a materialized path, loading published JSON-LD
4425.content: Four rules, for every viewer that shows addressable things: . | Every addressable asset has its own IRI, and it is a PATH — <viewer>/<instance>/<id>/. Never a query string (?entry=, ?id=) and never a fragment (#<id>) as the asset’s address. A fragment may still point INSIDE a page; it is not an asset’s name. | The IRI is a real file on gh-pages, returning 200, written by the viewer’s generator and compared by its --check. No 404.html routing, no SPA fallback: a URL that works only because a not-found page rewrote it is a 404 to every crawler, cache and standards-following client. | The page at that IRI is a thin shell: identity only (a small JSON config block naming the published data and the asset’s id), a rel=canonical, a rel=alternate type=application/ld+json to the asset’s published JSON-LD where there is one, a <noscript> link to that data, and the viewer’s SHARED stylesheet and script by reference. No content of the asset is written into it; the script loads it from the KG JSON / JSON-LD the site already publishes. If the asset’s own serialisation is not yet published, publish the KG’s existing one — do not invent a format. A shell is a few KB; never inline shared chrome into each one. | An old #<id> link is legacy: the shell normalises it ONCE to the path IRI with history.replaceState (or navigates, when the asset belongs to another page), and nothing new emits it. | . The asset and its rendering are two resources with two IRIs . This is the one place the rule is stated; other skills point here. | The asset’s IRI is extensionless, …/<kind>/<id>, and its @id says so: absolute, instance-qualified, under the site root the docs are served at; its JSON-LD is published at the IRI plus .jsonld. A library entry’s is <site>/assets/library/jsonld/<instance>/source/<id>, minted by ONE function (schemas/library/library-iri.ts) that both the @id’s writer and the file’s publisher call, so the two cannot drift. | The rendering has its own IRI — the viewer page — and it points to the asset: rel=alternate type=application/ld+json, and if the page ever carries JSON-LD of its own, about/mainEntity naming the asset’s @id. | The asset never references its renderings — no subjectOf, no foaf:page, no viewer URL in its JSON-LD. Renderings change with every visualiser; the asset would have to be rewritten each time. | A rendering’s IRI is DERIVED from the declared visualiser for the graph kind (the harness’s visualisers, at <base>/<harness>/<visualiser>/ computed by visualiserRoute), never authored into the asset. If an index of renderings is useful, generate it; never store it in the asset. The library does exactly this: each entry in the GENERATED projection (assets/library/index.json) carries view — the site-root path of the page that renders it (another layer’s declared root route for an entry that layer renders; else the entry’s own library page) — and the row’s slug links there, so clicking it opens the entry’s visualiser. | . Reference implementation: gen-library-viz.ts (viewerHtml, VIEWER_JS, VIEWER_CSS) and scripts/lib/library-address.ts; browser check test/library-entry-iri.e2e.ts. A library entry’s DOCUMENT view — TOC, pages with printed labels, figures, sections, checks — is scripts/lib/library-document.ts: a projection read from the ingestion schema plus the browser code that renders it, kept in one module so a test runs the same text the page runs.

4426.title: Do not draw the whole graph
4426.content: The instinct is a force-directed node-link diagram of everything. Resist it. At the size of a real layer (on the order of a thousand nodes) it renders as a hairball that answers no question, while costing a layout library and a frame budget. The questions people actually arrive with are local: . | What is this node? → a detail panel with every property. | What does it point at? → edges rendered as controls you can follow. | What points at it? → back-links, computed at load rather than published. An inverse index stored in the document is a second copy of the edge set that can disagree with the first. | What else is of this kind? → facets, with counts from the document’s own counts rather than recounted. | . A one-hop neighbourhood diagram for the selected node is worth drawing, because at that scale a picture beats a list. Cap it; a node with two hundred neighbours is a list, not a diagram.

4427.title: Render what the document is missing, in the document’s own terms
4427.content: A viewer must surface what the graph lacks rather than display everything as though it were all part of the graph. Two things the export reports and the viewer must not swallow: . | undeclaredTerms — property names absent from the @context. Every one is dropped when the document is processed as the JSON-LD it claims to be, and kg-export exits non-zero rather than publishing a new one. Mark them in the detail panel; do not silently show them as ordinary properties. Keep the marking even while the list is empty — it is the guard that makes the next one visible, and a viewer for this layer is a viewer for any layer, including one whose export is older or whose context is thinner. | danglingLinks and problems — a link with no target node, and a source that could not be read. | .

4428.title: Three states, on the page as everywhere
4428.content: A document that could not be fetched is never drawn as an empty graph. On screen the two are identical and they mean opposite things: “this layer has no nodes” versus “I could not read it”. Say which. The same applies to a property that is absent versus one that is present and empty.

4429.title: Provenance belongs on the page
4429.content: The export carries sourceCommitSha, sourceCommitAt, sourceTreeDirty and, for a preview, a PreviewGraph type and a canonicalDocument link. Show them. A reader looking at a staged graph must be able to tell it is staged from the data, not from an injected banner that a JSON file would not carry anyway — and sourceTreeDirty is the difference between a graph a SHA reproduces and one it does not.

4430.title: Translate the chrome from the GENERATOR, never from the page
4430.content: A generated artefact is not a translation source. Its generator is. Run an extractor over the emitted HTML and the .pot fills with the generator’s OUTPUT: regenerate for any reason — a new node kind, a changed commit line — and every reference churns while no string has changed, and every sign-off is invalidated by the regeneration rather than by an edit. So the viewer’s own words live in a declared table in the source (scripts/kg-viewer-strings.ts): the English text, which IS the msgid as everywhere else here, plus the translator comment naming where it appears and what each {placeholder} will hold. bun run cat translate-kg-viewer --extract turns the table into translations/<locale>/kg-viewer.pot through the shared formatPot, and the generator reads each .po back through the shared parsePo and embeds the catalogues. There is no inject step: generating the page is the injection, and a second artefact would serve nothing. --check separates two things that look alike. Drift fails: a .pot that no longer matches the table, a translation that dropped a {placeholder}, an entry for a string the page no longer says. Coverage only reports: a string nobody has translated is the ordinary state of a translation in progress, and the page falls back to English string by string.

4431.title: Say where the translation stops
4431.content: Chrome-only translation is half a translation, and the half that is missing is the half the reader came for. Node titles, descriptions and property names arrive in the graph document in whatever language the corpus is written in; no catalogue in the viewer can reach them. Draw that boundary on the page, in the language the reader chose, so the reader can tell a missing translation from a corpus that is simply English; silent about it, the reader reads the gap as a defect or as a claim. Three states, never two, as for an unreadable document.

4432.title: A language switcher is a UI control
4432.content: It is bound by ui-accessibility like everything else, and four things are easy to get wrong: . | Label each option in ITS OWN language — Français, العربية, 中文 — and set lang on the control. That is what a reader scanning for their language looks for, it leaves no accessible name to mistranslate, and it is what lets a screen reader switch voice. | Translate the accessible names too. A page whose visible text is Spanish and whose aria-labels are English is a page that is translated for sighted readers only, and nothing on screen says so. | Announce the change. The panel is rewritten in place and the reader’s cursor has not moved. | Turn the page, not just the words. A right-to-left language needs dir on the document, and the layout has to be checked in it — axe over an RTL render catches what an LTR one cannot. | . Do not invent a second locale mechanism. The docs site already stores the reader’s choice in the fa-locale key; read that, let a lang query parameter override it for a shared link, and fall back to the browser’s own preference. Offer only what the page can show. A catalogue with nothing translated is not a language the viewer can render, and listing it would promise a translation the reader would not get.

4433.title: Verifying it
4433.content: A rendered artefact is not verified by reading its source: nobody can assess a rendering from a description of it, including the agent that wrote it. “The HTML looks right” is not evidence that the document loads, that an edge is clickable, or that a failed fetch says so. Drive the real page in a real browser. test/kg-viewer.e2e.ts is the worked example, and it asserts against the generated artefacts rather than a fixture, so a test cannot agree with a stand-in while disagreeing with what ships. It generates them if absent, so the suite runs from a clean checkout. Look at it, too. Take a screenshot: layout problems such as a long nested property (a Tool’s io) pushing the rest of a node off screen are caught only by looking, because no test reports that a property makes a node unreadable. Nested objects are collapsed behind a disclosure for that reason.

4434.title: kg-viewer (skill)
4434.content: The skill kg-viewer as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/kg-viewer.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

4435.title: L1 document ingestion
4435.content: Skill l1-document-ingestion: The detailed method for turning a DOCUMENT in uploads/ into a complete L1 entry in library/<bib-slug>/ — which rung reads it and why, what a complete L1 entry holds, why an inferred structure is refused rather than guessed, and the archive, dataset, narrative, image and vector-label arms. Refines the harness’s basic library-ingestion flow; one entry point: bun run cat ingest. Named by: Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph . This is a refinement, not the entry point. The harness’s library-ingestion skill carries the basic flow every asset takes — an upload is accepted, its metadata goes into the knowledge graph, and the asset lands in library/ if it is materialized — together with the two entry points, the upload’s retirement to fsh-guts/, and the remote half. This skill is what happens next when the asset is a document whose text and structure are wanted as L1 source content: reading it into sections, blocks and sidecars that check:l1-complete can judge. The rung code — scripts/ingest-document.ts, the pdf-*.py rungs, notebook-structure.ts and OCR — lives in the harness. This skill is the METHOD that chooses among them; invoking harness code from here is a downward edge. The executable form is processes/library/l1-document-ingestion.bpmn, which calls the harness’s basic Process_Ingestion first and then the four ingest-* phases beside it.

4436.title: The whole path is two commands
4436.content: bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # rung + every derived arm, into ingest-staging/ bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> --promote # the L1 gate, then into <lib>/<slug>/ . Staging prints the second line for you, built from your own arguments. --promote writes the entry’s JSON-LD nodes, for that entry only, with the same buildEntryNodes the corpus generator uses. They are minted for the destination, not for staging: an entry’s layer is read off where it sits, and ingest-staging/ belongs to whichever layer holds it. You do not need gen-library-jsonld or check:l1-complete --write after promoting — the first is done, and the second’s verdicts live on the qa-reports branch rather than on main.

4437.title: Which rung, and why there is more than one
4437.content: | rung | when | what it produces | . | pdf-structure.py | any PDF with a text layer | the outline’s chapters; with no outline, the inferred contents when it is trusted, else one section per page | . | pdf-pages.py | a page tree by hand: --first-page-label, or --from-ocr text | one section per page | . | pdf-ocr.py | text extraction yields almost nothing | a text layer to then page-split | . | pdf-tables.py | tables or figures matter | what pdf-structure/v1’s Section does not carry | . | slides-structure.py | the package declares a PPTX or ODP deck | one section per slide, images.json, accessibility.json | . | referenced-source.py | --reference given: the licence forbids a copy | referenced.json only — identity, sha256, outline; no text | . | text-structure.ts | the source is text files — Markdown, MDX, XML — usually fetched from a repository at a commit | text-structure/v1: a Markdown file divided by its own ATX headings outside fenced code, any other file one verbatim section, located by file and line range; images recorded by digest, never sectioned | . | notebook-structure.ts | the file is JSON with a numeric nbformat and a cells array — a Jupyter notebook, decided by content, never by the .ipynb name | notebook-structure/v1: one section per markdown heading, located by cell range; code kept as fenced code and never run; outputs not kept, and structure_note says so | . A notebook is a variant, not a PDF with odd pages. structure.json has a shared base (cat-harness-tools schemas/content/document-structure.ts): the PDF format is one variant, unchanged, and the notebook format is the other. A reader that needs only sections reads either through structureOf(), which says where a section is as {pages} or {cells}. A page-aware reader gets nothing from a notebook, rather than a cell index mistaken for a page number. The decision is mechanical: . | toc_source: outline → pdf-structure (9789241548960-eng, 250 sections) | toc_source: none, source.text_source: embedded → pdf-structure, which keeps its inferred contents only when they pass the trust tests and otherwise writes pages (wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng lands on pages that way) | a junk outline (milnorlink) → pdf-pages: pdf-structure would read the outline it found rather than infer one | toc_source: none, source.text_source: ocr → pdf-ocr then pdf-pages --from-ocr (who-pub-tps-931) | .

4438.title: Slide decks — PPTX and ODP
4438.content: A deck is a zip that declares its type ([Content_Types].xml, or ODF’s mimetype member), so it routes on the sniff, before the archive rung, exactly as a workbook does. slides-structure.py writes the same pdf-structure/v1 shape a paged PDF gets — one section per slide, page_start == page_end == <slide>, granularity: "slide" — so l1-blocks.ts, the manifest and check:l1-complete read it unchanged. Two differences from the PDF rungs: . | A slide’s title is its title placeholder, or it is Slide N. Never the largest text box: that is the inferred-TOC failure below in a new format. It is also an accessibility finding, because a slide with no title placeholder cannot be navigated to by name, so the two questions share one answer (title_source: placeholder | none in each section’s front matter). | No image is a page-scan. A full-bleed picture alone on a slide is the slide’s content, not a scan of text already extracted. | . accessibility.json reports, per check, what the package can answer — slide titles, alt text (with editor auto-captions such as “Description automatically generated” counted as failing, since nobody wrote them), decorative marks, language tags, document title, speaker notes — and says undetermined for the three it cannot: reading order, images of text, contrast. It gives no overall score. A single number would weigh a missing title against a missing alt text, and nothing supports that weighting. Two copies of one deck? Compare before you choose which to ingest: . python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/slides-structure.py --a11y-only DECK.pptx DECK.odp . Prefer the copy that wins the per-check comparison. An export can lose what the author wrote (an ODP export of Google Slides can drop all alt text and keep the language only on the default style), and the format’s reputation does not tell you which way a particular export went. Image descriptions go in the library’s image-verdicts.json as for a PDF. Put the inspector in attribution.<doc-id> when they are not the file’s inspected_by; without it the deck inherits the first inspector’s name and date.

4439.title: A source whose licence forbids a copy — record it, do not ingest it
4439.content: Some sources may be read but not reposted. The OMG BPMN and DMN specifications permit use on condition that a copy “will not be copied or posted on any network computer or broadcast in any media”. A normal ingest commits every section’s text to a public repository, which breaks that condition. It does so silently, because nothing in the text layer says so. bun run cat ingest FILE.pdf --reference IDENTITY.json --library <name> . IDENTITY.json holds the title, version, document number, date, publisher, URL and the licence clause, read off the document. A missing field is refused, never guessed. The entry holds referenced.json — the exact bytes’ sha256, the embedded outline (clause titles and pages, so a citation can still name a clause), a folio-materialization/v1 record in state referenced, and why the text is withheld — plus a manifest with an empty contains, and a licence.json quoting the clause. The choice is the caller’s, never inferred. Whether a licence permits posting is a reading of the licence, not of the bytes. check:l1-complete knows the kind, and refuses a referenced entry that holds sections/, blocks/ or images/. That would be the copy this kind exists not to make. A publication, not a file — an external reference. A FHIR implementation guide is a website and a package, not one PDF, so there are no bytes to hash. Its referenced.json takes the published variant of source (schemas/referenced-source.ts): kind: "published", url, canonical, package_id, version, and read_from / read_at naming the local record the identity was read off — no sha256, rather than a made-up one. links names where a reader goes instead (the publisher’s page, and a site_path on this site such as the layer’s artefact index), and the library viewer shows them on the entry’s row. Write it by hand — there is no file to run referenced-source.py on — then gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry for the manifest. The licence follows the usual rule: stated only with a basis, else unknown with where you looked. Example: the WHO SMART Trust IG’s entry in the DAK layer’s library/.

4440.title: A source published as text in a repository — read it at a commit
4440.content: The Gherkin reference, the MCP specification, the hmans/beans README and FHIR R5’s TestPlan resource are published as Markdown or XML in git repositories. Printing one to PDF so a PDF rung can read it makes the recorded sha256 identify a rendering nobody published, so they take their own rung instead: . bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.md --text --library <lib> # rung + l1-blocks, into ingest-staging/ bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.md --text --library <lib> --promote # the L1 gate, then the entry and its KG nodes . --text is the CALLER’s statement that the file is text: text has no magic bytes, so the extension is never read, and a binary handed in as text is refused as undetermined. Through cat ingest it takes the notebook’s derived arm (l1-blocks), and --promote writes the entry’s JSON-LD nodes, as for every rung. Do not stop at the rung. Run alone, text-structure.ts leaves an entry with no manifest.jsonld and no section or block nodes. A source read at a commit, with its upstream.json and several files, still runs the rung directly: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/text-structure.ts -o <library> --doc-id <slug> \ --base <checkout> --upstream upstream.json [--title T] [--image F]... FILE... and then, without fail, l1-blocks.ts -o <entry> and gen-library-jsonld.ts --entry <entry>, as for a notebook. What it decides: . | Divided by the author’s headings, or not at all. A Markdown file splits at its own ATX headings, outside fenced code. A # comment inside a gherkin block is not a heading. Any other text, and anything that opens with <, is one section, fenced verbatim. Nothing is rendered: shortcodes and JSX stay as written, and structure_note says so. | upstream records the exact revision: repository, 40-hex commit, ref, path, and in words whether that revision is the published text or a working copy. A default branch is often neither, and a reader cannot tell which from a URL. Keep the clone out of the repository tree. The bytes can be fetched again from the commit, so none go to uploads/ or fsh-guts/. | Several files are one source when the publisher ships them as one, as with a specification version that is a directory of pages. Each file keeps its own sha256. The source’s sha256 is the sha256 of their sha256sum listing, so sha256sum -c against a checkout verifies the entry without this code. | .

4441.title: From a library entry to a folio document — seed it, and its graph comes with it
4441.content: A folio whose working document starts from a source (an outline, a draft, a report) is SEEDED from the library entry, not from the raw file: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/seed-folio-from-library.ts \ --entry library/<doc-id> --slug <folio-doc> [--title T] [--author A]... [--force] . Any structure.json variant works. The top heading level becomes the chapters, deeper levels nest as sections, and a section’s own text becomes one prose block. No kind is guessed: a persona or a requirement is the folio’s own enrichment step. Every block carries meta.source (library, section, locator, method: "library-seed"), and the seed ENDS by writing each block’s .jsonld with gen-block-jsonld’s own code. A folio-specific seed script that writes blocks must end the same way, or its site publishes no graph. A seed is one-time: an existing document is refused unless --force, which discards hand edits. The original is never touched: the library entry and the folio’s nodes are DERIVED, and both are checked (gen-library-jsonld --check, gen-block-jsonld --check) so neither can drift unseen.

4442.title: A source’s glossary and abbreviations — candidates, read by one tool
4442.content: Every L1, DTH and DAK source reads its glossary the same way, with the Tool glossary-from-source, never with a script of its own: . bun run cat glossary:from-source --out glossary/<scheme>.glossary.json \ --id <scheme> --title "<title>" --from library/<doc-id>/sections . --from reads every section whose title names a glossary, definitions, terms, abbreviations or acronyms, and each numbered section under a glossary section (a specification that prints one term per heading). A folio block can be named with --terms or --abbreviations. Each row becomes a candidate term, verbatim, with source: <file>#L<line>; an acronym becomes the notation of the term it expands. The scheme is merged: a term a person has adopted or edited is never changed. Only a person moves a term to authored (glossary-terms). --check keeps the candidates in step with the L1 entry.

4443.title: A source’s reference list — its own bibliography, read by one tool
4443.content: Every source that prints a reference list gets its own bibliography, read the same way with the Tool references-extract (step Task_References of ingest-build-l1-kg.bpmn), never with a script of its own: . bun run cat references:extract --instance . [--entry <doc-id>] [--check] . It reads the L1 sections of each library entry. A list is a whole section whose title is a reference-list heading, or the lines after such a heading inside a section (chapter-end lists), in the six UN languages and Portuguese (References, Bibliography, Further reading, Références bibliographiques, Referencias, Литература, المراجع, 参考文献, …). Numbered lists are split on their own numbers; unnumbered ones where an entry closes and the next opens. Page numbers, running heads and section tabs between entries are skipped; a list ends at an annex, chapter or glossary heading, a table or figure, or a contents leader. Each entry becomes a folio-reference/v1 node in the instance’s declared references directory, keyed <doc-id>.<section>.<n>: provenance: extracted, derivedFrom the section file, and printed the entry exactly as the source prints it. Only fields read without guessing are set: URL, DOI, ISBN, issued (the work’s year, not the access date), accessed, and type: article-journal for a journal’s year;volume:pages. No title or author is parsed, because WHO, Vancouver and author-year styles disagree on where a title ends; the bibliography shows printed instead. A cited IRIS handle the library holds gets heldAt. An entry longer than any citation (the list ran into the text after it) is left out rather than kept wrong. The bibliography page lists the nodes under the document they came from (bibliography/library/<doc-id>/). Re-run the tool after a section is re-derived; --check fails when a node is stale or has no list left to come from. Nodes with any other provenance are never touched.

4444.title: Requirements and normative statements — every DAK and DTH source
4444.content: Requirement extraction is a general part of L1 ingestion for DAK and DTH sources, as a Stage B aspect: cat ingest runs extract-candidates.py --aspects-only on every staged entry, and each requirement the source states becomes a typed node in the entry’s graph, derivedFrom its L1 section. A folio’s requirement block then CITES that node. It does not restate it with an id of its own. The mount is the gate. The requirements aspect lives in the DAK layer (its scripts/extractors/dak-requirements.py), so it runs in DAK and DTH repositories and nowhere else. With no aspect mounted the arm writes nothing. No new schema: the existing kind that fits the source. Requirement schemas come in more than one style, some core and some the DAK layer’s: . | the source prints | kind | layer | . | a DAK requirement row, <CODE>.FXREQ.<n> / .NFXREQ.<n> | functional-requirement / non-functional-requirement | DAK layer | . | a system’s shall/must/should in prose (“The registry shall …”) | functional-requirement, no id | DAK layer | . | a row of a table of system functions | functional-requirement, source_kind: function-table-row (by hand today) | DAK layer | . | a row of a table of information needs, an item of a list of reports or functions, a figure caption naming a function | functional-requirement, source_kind: information-need-table-row, function-list-item, figure-caption (by hand today) | DAK layer | . | an indicator | indicator | DAK layer | . | any other normative sentence | recommendation, strength in rfc2119-requirement-level or grade-recommendation-strength | core | . Ids come from the source or there are none. number is the id exactly as printed, and it lands in the node’s meta.source_number. A requirement that prints no id has none. The node’s @id is derived from the section and the order the items appear in (<kind>-<section>-NN), never from a made-up label such as an agent-assigned FR-xx. A requirement from a source is a reference, not a definition: it contributes to a definition but does not make one. The nodes carry provenance: ingested and route_to: l2-dak-authoring. The folio that cites one decides what it means for its own system, and a person promotes it. Then account for everything. Run l1-coverage with the entry’s requirement candidates as --captured. Every normative sentence the aspect did not propose is either a missing capture or an exclusion a person signs off. A requirement written by hand, from a table no extractor reads yet, uses the same candidates.json shape: kind, source_kind, number (or null), name, statement verbatim, section_file, section_title, pages, formalization_candidate: false, route_to. Leave out document_class, validated and disposition. Those describe the WHOLE document, and the manifest reads them as such. Then run gen-library-jsonld --entry.

4445.title: An inferred chapter tree is refused, not guessed
4445.content: The failure this rule prevents is silent. Without an outline, a heading-detector can infer a table of contents — and an inferred TOC is confidently wrong in a way the output does not show. Two cases: . | WPR-RDO-2020-003-eng.pdf — 11 of 13 inferred sections were named after a different publication, because page 22 reproduces a sample table from one as a design example. | WHO_PUB_TPS_93.1.pdf — inferred entries took page numbers from the contents pages, so 26 of 42 sections came out under 500 characters while 37,923 characters landed in one section misnamed 18-usetul-reference-books. | . So pdf-pages claims no chapter tree and says so in structure_note. A page is a determined division; an inferred chapter was not. Same third-state rule the rest of this repository keeps: a structure that could not be determined is never rendered as one that was. The route pdf-structure.py takes itself . With no outline, the inferred contents is used only when it passes all three tests, in order (inferred_toc_trust): . | concentration: at most 60% of its entries may start on the two commonest pages — a list read off a page is not the document’s structure; | mean confidence ≥ 0.6 (TOC_MIN_MEAN_CONFIDENCE), each entry’s confidence being how much independent evidence agreed — a contents page, the body, a heading style, a numbering run; | headings with bodies: from 5 sections up, no more than 25% of the sections the tree would cut may hold under 50 characters (TOC_MAX_EMPTY_SHARE, TOC_EMPTY_SECTION_CHARS), front matter not counted — a tree of empty sections is logo lettering, a sample table’s column heads or a cover’s address block, not chapters. | . Otherwise — refused, or nothing inferred — the entry is split one section per page (page-001, “Page 1”, the shape pdf-pages.py writes), with granularity: "page", toc_source: undetermined or none, toc_undetermined_reason, and a structure_note saying why. Both inputs are recorded whether or not they passed: diagnostics.toc_inferred_entries and diagnostics.toc_inferred_mean_confidence and diagnostics.toc_inferred_empty_share. What the floor does and does not catch. The mean is a weak predictor of quality. A mean of exactly 0.60 means no entry was corroborated by anything but its style, and “at least 0.6” lets it through, so read a font TOC at 0.60 before citing it. The floor’s real work is on the regex fallback, whose entries carry no confidence and count as 0. The third test is the one that catches a poor font tree; a poor tree with an empty share just under 25% is too close to good ones to separate by this measure.

4446.title: A text layer that is not text
4446.content: Owner, 2026-11-11 (who-iris, card Q-ODD-1 = A): “force OCR when a page’s text layer fails a quality check”. A text layer can carry plenty of letters and still not be the page’s words, and the character count the router used to look at cannot see it. cat-harness-tools/scripts/_text_quality.py checks EVERY page against the document’s languages (--lang-hint, else the catalogue’s dc.language.iso). Each check was measured on an IRIS PDF: . | The text layer | Seen on | What the check counts | . | accents through the wrong code page (“dΘclaration”) | 10665/231031, French | words mixing Greek and Latin letters, in a Latin-script document | . | Persian in the wrong Arabic code points | 10665/94830-per | Arabic-script letters outside the language’s alphabet | . | words split by kerning (“au g m ente”) | 10665/83270, French | a lone lower-case letter between two lower-case words | . | fake bold, each word printed twice | 10665/66977-chi | words equal to the word before | . | a font with no Unicode mapping | 10665/232378, Arabic | letters among characters that are not digits or table punctuation | . The router runs the check in its probe. When any page fails, the document goes to pdf-ocr+pdf-structure: pdf-ocr.py reads every page and pdf-structure.py --ocr takes the OCR text for the failing pages only, keeping the outline and the text layer of the rest. They are listed in structure.json source.ocr_pages, each with its reason; text_source stays embedded. When most pages fail and there is no outline, the whole document is read from OCR (pdf-ocr+pdf-pages), as for a scan. A page that holds two scripts. OCR reads a page in the script its detector names, so a French article’s Arabic abstract (10665/117378) came out as “er ie obus AU ball”, and the Latin URLs in an Arabic toolkit’s references (10665/75211-ara) as Arabic letters. A page whose mean word confidence is under 70 is read again with each other installed script added (ara+eng, fra+ara), and the most confident read is kept when it gains 10 points. On the Arabic references page the confidence went from 54 to 86 and the URLs read correctly; a page of plain Arabic keeps its first read.

4447.title: An outline that is not contents, and a section too long to be a block
4447.content: Owner, 2026-11-11: “split single blocks that hold a whole book”. Eight IRIS PDFs came out as one section of 10,000 to 101,000 words, every one because an outline was present, was taken as the document’s answer, and located no heading on any page: . | Word bookmark names: _tyjcwt, _Hlk62546849, _GoBack, _TOC_250000 (10665/353150, 353151, 259268, 341997); | “Blank Page” (10665/385385), or the names of the files merged into the PDF (10665/44118: 9789241547727_eng_Chapter1-4); | a Russian edition carrying its English outline (10665/331525-rus). | . pdf-structure.py drops machine bookmark names from the outline, and sets the outline aside when nothing is left or when under half of what is left names a line the pages print (diagnostics.outline_rejected says which). The contents are then inferred, and must pass the three tests above, else the document is split by page. A section that still holds more than half of a document of 20 pages or more (and over 8,000 words), or over 20,000 words anywhere, is cut at the headings inferred inside it, else one section per page (diagnostics.oversized_split). A re-ingest renumbers the section ids of an entry cut this way, so its block summaries go stale and are redrafted. Titles that do not match their text . Four IRIS entries had section titles that did not match the words under them. pdf-structure.py now tidies an INFERRED table of contents before it splits (diagnostics.headings_tidied; an outline entry is never touched): . | A title cut to its last line (“sanitaria universal”, 10665/354399): a title that opens in lower case is rejoined with the lines above it, up to the bare number that opens it (“1.2 Función de la salud digital … cobertura sanitaria universal”). With no number above it, it is dropped. | A body word set apart by a font (“un”, “comme”, “On”, 10665/264857), and a reference’s first author in capitals (“YOUNG,”): dropped. | A diagram’s labels (an annex flowchart, 10665/329296): two or more sections on one page, each with fewer than 30 words, are dropped as headings and their words stay with the section before them. | . A page whose PDF draws its side panel and body before its headings (10665/342236) put every section one heading late. When the outline’s first heading on a page sits in the later half of the page’s text, and the page read in print order (top to bottom, a band of columns left column first) puts it near the top, that page is read in print order (diagnostics.pages_read_in_print_order). The document’s language is recorded, not read from the slug . structure.json source.languages holds the languages the ingest was given (--lang-hint). A reader asks it, not the slug: an item’s first edition keeps the bare slug whatever its language, so 10665/202203, which is Russian, has no -rus.

4448.title: Footnotes and their marks
4448.content: Owner, 2026-11-11: “also foot notes/marks”. The pdf-footnotes.py arm reads the page layout after l1-blocks.ts and writes footnotes.json (folio-document-footnotes/v1, schemas/content/document-footnotes.ts): . | a mark is a superscript span (or one small and raised) whose text is 1-3 digits, a letter, or * † ‡ §; | a note is a line in the lower 40% of the page, smaller than the body text, that opens with a mark; the small lines after it continue it; | a mark calls the note with the same mark on its page, else on the next. | . Only a note that a mark calls is a footnote, with every marks[] place that calls it (page and the words before the mark) and the block that holds its page. A small line opening with a number is as often a table row or a running footer (10665/311941: 159 such lines, none called), so those are kept as uncalled_notes, and marks with no note as unlinked_marks; nothing is dropped. The section text is not changed. OCR’d pages have no fonts and are listed in pages_unread. check:l1-complete reports the counts (footnotes) and fails only on a file that will not parse or names another entry. Numbered citations ([12], or a superscript 12 whose reference is in a list at the end) are not footnotes; a superscript one shows up in unlinked_marks, where a reference-list extractor can pick it up.

4449.title: Errata: errors in the source’s own text
4449.content: Owner, 2026-11-11 (card Q-ODD-1 = A, and “add to L1 doc schema errata”). Reading the blocks to summarise them finds errors that are in the publication, not the extraction: a workshop report titled June 2006 whose introduction says June 2005 (10665/205022), a Spanish edition announcing “nueve recomendaciones” where the English lists ten (10665/354399). The block is never changed. The agent records each one in library/<bib-slug>/errata.json (folio-document-errata/v1, schemas/content/document-errata.ts): . | Field | What it holds | . | id | e1, e2, … never reused | . | kind | error, inconsistency (two places or two official editions disagree), residue (a placeholder, an editor’s comment, contents page numbers “xx”), translation (an official translation says what its original does not) | . | block / page | where it is printed; at least one | . | quote | the words as printed, verbatim | . | reading | the reading the evidence supports, when there is one | . | evidence | what shows it, in a form a person can check | . | narrative | the note a reader sees, a draft naming its model until a person confirms it in bun run cat narratives | . The file is authored, so a re-ingest keeps it. An extraction defect (garbled OCR, a block cut in the wrong place) is not an erratum: re-derive the entry. Decisions about a document (personal data in a participant list, a “do not distribute” notice) are not errata either; ask the owner. check:l1-complete reports errata (errata) and fails only on a file that does not parse, names another entry, or points at a block the entry does not have.

4450.title: What a complete L1 entry holds
4450.content: library/<bib-slug>/ structure.json "$schema": "pdf-structure/v1" — doc_id, toc_source, granularity, sections[], structure_note, source{} (see below; source.text_source says embedded|ocr) sections/ one Markdown file per section, front matter + body blocks/ the block projection consumers read manifest.jsonld @id, @type folio:SourceDocument, contains[], provenance summaries.json agent summaries of prose blocks, a QA sidecar (see below) footnotes.json footnotes and the marks that call them (pdf-footnotes.py arm) errata.json errors in the source's own text, authored (never a rung's) ocr/ page-NNN.txt, only where the source was scanned . bun run cat check:l1-complete is the gate. It reports three states, never two: a requirement met, unmet, or not yet derivable — the last because the per-format arms (images, audio, tables, archives) are tracked separately and a check that cannot run must not read as a pass. Then publish its statements. Once the entry is complete and promoted, every statement extracted from it is published in the folio’s working artifact and in the shared extraction viewer, each linked to the entry and its section, and CI keeps those pages current. That is a standard step, the same for every content type: publish-extracted-statements.

4451.title: A manifest’s title — the authority order, and never the page-1 parse
4451.content: A library entry’s manifest.jsonld title is the first of these the entry has: . | rank | meta.title_source | read from | . | 1 | dc-record | dc.title of the Dublin Core record that the catalogue node naming this entry (libraryId) points at through metadataRef | . | 2 | referenced | referenced.json identity.title | . | 3 | pdf-info | structure.json metadata.docinfo.Title, the PDF Info /Title, when it is not junk | . | 3 | text-heading | structure.json metadata.title of a text or notebook structure: front-matter title:, --title, or the level-1 heading | . | 4 | slug | the entry id. Nothing better exists, and check:library-qa reports it as title-missing | . The page-1 front-matter parse is NEVER a title. On a pdf-structure/v1, metadata.title is parse_front_matter’s guess at which lines of page 1 are the title, and it guesses wrong (a running head, a repeated word, a status block). A plausible wrong title passes every check that has no second source. A slug is honest about being a placeholder and gets flagged. The parse may still feed search and the section files’ doc_title. text-heading shares rank 3 because it is the same kind of fact as /Title (the source naming itself, in its format’s own metadata). The two are exclusive by variant, so no entry ever has both. A tabular record’s title is its source file name, which is never a title. Junk /Title (pdfInfoTitleJunk): shorter than 3 characters or no letters; untitled and its kin; Microsoft Word - …; an arXiv stamp (arXiv:0909.4061v2 [math.NA] …); anything ending in a file extension; the source’s file name or stem; the slug. A junk value falls through to the next source. It never becomes the title. Records (ranks 1–2) are taken as written, because a cataloguer’s choice is not a program’s default. Record the Info dictionary at ingest. pdf-structure.py and pdf-pages.py write metadata.docinfo. Backfill an older entry with python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-pages.py --docinfo-into <entry> <pdf>. It refuses unless the PDF’s sha256 is the one the entry recorded. One resolver, cat-harness-tools/pipeline/library-title.ts (resolveLibraryTitle, TITLE_AUTHORITY), is used by both gen-library-jsonld.ts and check-library-qa.ts. The manifest records meta.title_source and meta.title_from, and the QA check re-derives the order from the entry’s files. So a manifest that claims pdf-info while a catalogue record exists is reported as title-implausible, not believed.

4452.title: source{} — the technical facts, written by whichever rung ran
4452.content: Every rung writes source on structure.json, from the single definition in scripts/_tech_meta.py: file, full 64-hex sha256, bytes, mtime (the SOURCE’s, UTC to the second — not the ingest time, because what tells you a re-fetch got something new is the file changing), mimetype_sniffed and mimetype_source. Both rungs add text_source, embedded or ocr: ONE field and ONE vocabulary for where the section text came from. pdf-structure also adds pages and extractor. The mimetype is sniffed from the leading bytes and never falls back to the extension. An extension is a claim by whoever named the file; the magic bytes are what the content is, and a .pdf that is really an HTML error page extracts to nothing while every downstream verdict is about the wrong document. Unrecognised bytes give mimetype_sniffed: null with mimetype_source: "unrecognised": a guess that agrees with the filename is indistinguishable from a real sniff. bun run scripts/ingest-document.ts <pdf> --refresh-meta backfills an existing entry. It reads the indent off the file rather than choosing one: the two rungs write at different widths, and hardcoding either reformats every entry the other authored.

4453.title: provenance — who wrote it, and the closed union that makes omission impossible
4453.content: Every block declares how its text came to be. The vocabulary is schemas/attribution.ts, and it is closed: . | the literal "ingested" — verbatim source text. There is no author to name; the document it came out of is recorded by source{} above. | an Attribution — kind (script | agent | human), id, and optionally version, model, session, date, skill. | . An agent must name its model, structurally. “A model described it, version X” is what a reader needs to weigh a narrative, and what makes the set re-generatable when that model is superseded, so AttributionSchema refuses an agent attribution with no model. The vocabulary is the QA reviewer’s, not a second one. block-qa.ts re-exports ATTRIBUTION_KINDS as QA_REVIEWER_KINDS; the same three participants review and author. What is not shared is QaReviewer itself, most of which is about whether a criterion’s cached verdict is stale. What the gate can and cannot enforce . check:l1-complete checks two things per block, and the second is the point: . | provenance parses as a Provenance. An open string, a malformed attribution, an agent with no model — all unmet. | A block of an authored kind must not claim "ingested". | . LIBRARY_BLOCK_ORIGIN classifies each library block kind as extracted or authored, and a test asserts it is total over what actually occurs in library/ — so a narrative arm cannot land a new kind without classifying it, and classifying one authored arms requirement 2 immediately. Closing the union does not stop an arm asserting something false. It makes the omission impossible: a new arm has to choose, and choosing "ingested" for a generated description is a false statement rather than a missing field. A zero narrative count is reported, never silent. The authored branch is proved to fire by fixtures in scripts/tests/attribution.test.ts, not by the corpus, and each of the three branches is mutation-checked — removing it fails a named test.

4454.title: Archives — the entry list is data, and the rung is chosen by CONTENT
4454.content: A tar or zip in uploads/ is opaque to every grep in the corpus: a search for a filename inside one finds nothing, and that absence is indistinguishable from the file not being there. scripts/archive-contents.py writes library/<slug>/contents.jsonld — one schema whatever the container (schemas/archive-contents.ts), so a consumer reads archives without knowing whether it was tar or zip. Per entry: path, bytes, sha256, mtime, mimetype_sniffed, mimetype_source — the source{} vocabulary above, reused verbatim, because an archive entry is not a different kind of thing from a loose file. The mimetype is sniffed from the entry’s own leading bytes, never from its name, for the same reason it is outside an archive. Four entry states, not two: a directory carries no size and no digest (a zero would be a measurement nobody made); an unreadable member is mimetype_source: "unreadable", which is not an empty file; a symlink or special is listed with its kind rather than dropped. Dropping directories would make an archive of empty ones indistinguishable from an empty archive. A file the sniffer does not recognise as an archive is refused — an empty entries[] would read as an empty archive, a different fact. The rung is chosen before anything opens the file as a PDF . planFor sniffs first, so a zip is never reported as a PDF with a missing backend. A file named .pdf that is really a zip takes the archive rung, which is the case only a sniff can decide. What the gate checks, and the determined zero . Which entries the requirement applies to is derived, not guessed: source. mimetype_sniffed is already on every entry, so “this came from a zip” is a recorded fact. An archive entry must carry a contents.jsonld that validates against the declared schema. An entry that is not an archive reports not an archive (<mimetype>) — said out loud rather than passed in silence, because “nothing to check here” and “the check never ran” are different facts. The requirement is proved to fire by fixture archives built in scripts/tests/archive-contents.test.ts, and each of its four branches is mutation-checked.

4455.title: Datasets — findable by their headers, and the narrative nobody wrote
4455.content: scripts/tabular-records.py writes library/<slug>/tabular.jsonld: sheet names, the header row, and the shape of each sheet. header_vocabulary is the union across sheets, and it is the field a grep for a column name lands in — without it a dataset is stored but not findable, and a failed search is indistinguishable from the dataset not having that column. The record is real JSON-LD, and so is contents.jsonld. Both arms emit the published content context (the URL lives once, in scripts/_content_context.py, pinned to CONTENT_CONTEXT_URL by a test), and every key is a declared term. The facts a consumer queries across documents — format, the counts, header_vocabulary — are real terms; the nested structures that are ours — sheets, entries, the technical metadata, the narrative — are @json literals, because that is how their nulls survive: rows: null means “could not be counted” and narrative.text: null means “nobody has written one”, and JSON-LD drops a null anywhere else. The schemas still accept an older record with no @context, since folio repositories hold them. Stdlib only (zipfile + xml.etree, csv). This repository declares no Python dependencies — no requirements.txt, and CI installs only ruff — so a tool needing openpyxl would pass locally and fail there. Everything this arm needs is in xl/workbook.xml and each sheet’s <dimension>. The narrative is a state machine — drafted by an agent, confirmed by a person . cat-harness-tools schemas/content/narrative.ts: not-authored → draft → confirmed, with rejected as a real fourth state. Two attributions, because they are two acts. drafted_by is who wrote the words; confirmed_by is who accepted them. The question a reader most wants answered is not “did a machine touch this” but “has a person agreed to it”. An agent cannot confirm its own draft — confirmed_by.kind must be "human", structurally. Without that, confirmed degrades into “an agent said so twice”. But a rule about who may act cannot be enforced by a rule about what is written. In an agent container git config user.name is the agent’s, so the CLI could record the agent as a human reviewer and the schema could not see it. reviewer() therefore refuses outside a terminal: a person confirming at a prompt has one, an agent’s subprocess and CI do not. This stops accident, not fraud — it makes it impossible to confirm a narrative while going about other work. rejected keeps its reasons. A rejected draft silently re-offered wastes the reviewer’s time; one that vanishes lets the next agent redraft the identical thing. Reviewing: bun run cat narratives . Numbered list, numbered reasons: a review step that demands a typed sentence is one that will not happen, and then confirmed means “nobody got round to objecting”. bun run cat narratives # what is waiting on you bun run cat narratives:confirm 1 bun run cat narratives:reject 1 --why 2 # or --why-text "..." . check:l1-complete’s narrative-review validates every narrative-bearing file. A draft is reported, not failed: it is work waiting on a person, and failing it would make an unreviewed queue indistinguishable from a broken arm. A null rows/columns is likewise not an empty sheet: shape_source says whether the shape was read, counted, or undetermined. Summarising prose blocks — a QA sidecar, drained slowly . The block stays verbatim. A prose block is the source’s text, provenance: "ingested", and re-ingestion regenerates it. A summary is an agent’s account of that text, so it lives beside the blocks in library/<slug>/summaries.json (folio-block-summaries/v1, schemas/block-summary.ts): one record per block, holding block, source (the section file), source_hash and a narrative. That narrative is the state machine above, not a second one: draft, confirmed by a person only, rejected with a reason, and an agent author must name its model. source_hash makes a changed source read as STALE. It is the sha256 of the section text the summariser was shown (proseBody). Re-ingest a document and any section whose text moved puts its summary back in the queue, marked stale. bun run cat narratives shows it and refuses to confirm it. The queue is derived, so nothing enqueues. Every prose block in every declared library is in it until it has a current draft or confirmation. A rejected draft is back in it, and its rejection reason travels with it. bun run cat summaries # the backlog, per entry bun run cat summaries:next -- --n 5 [--entry <slug>] # next K blocks WITH their text, as JSON bun run cat summaries:record -- drafts.json # write drafts; validated, all or nothing . drafts.json is {drafted_by: {kind: "agent", id, model, session}, drafted_at, lang?, drafts: [{block, source_hash, text, lang?}]}, with source_hash echoed from summaries:next. lang is a BCP 47 tag and defaults to en. record refuses a state other than draft, a hash that no longer matches, and a block that already has a current summary IN THAT LANGUAGE. A draft in a language the block does not have yet is added beside the others, which are kept unchanged. Drain K at a time during ingestion work, not all at once: a thousand unreviewed drafts at once is a buried reviewer. Write in your own words, from the block’s text only, adding nothing from outside it. Length scales with the source: . | source text | summary | . | under ~150 words | 1 short sentence | . | ~150–600 words | 2 sentences, short to medium | . | ~600–2,000 words | 3 medium sentences | . | over ~2,000 words | 4 sentences, medium to long | . If the extraction put the wrong text under a heading, summarise what is there and say so. The backlog is reported by check:l1-complete (block-summaries) and on the library page. It is advisory, never a gate. What the gate does fail is a sidecar that does not parse, names another entry, or holds a record for a block or source that is not there. Special pages get one sentence saying what the page is: a cover, title page, copyright or cataloguing page, a blank or near-blank page, a table of contents, an index, a reference list. Garbled OCR, text in the wrong script, or text that does not match the block’s title is summarised as far as it can be, and the summary says so (“the extracted text of this page is garbled OCR; it appears to be a table of …”), so a reviewer sees an extraction defect instead of a confident account of noise. A block too long to read whole (a whole book extracted as one block) is summarised from its start, its headings and its end, at the 4-sentence length, and the scope is taken from the headings. Report the block as an extraction defect: it should have been split. Summaries in every language . A block’s summary is owed in every configured language: the layer’s translation.supportedLocales, which defaults to the six UN languages (ar, zh, en, fr, ru, es) (owner, 2026-11-11). The slot holds one narrative per language, each reviewed separately in bun run cat narratives. The order is: . | English first, from the block’s text, as above. | The document’s own language, when it is not English, also written FROM THE SOURCE TEXT, not from the English. It uses the document’s own terminology and checks the English against the source; when the two disagree, the source wins and the English draft is reported for redrafting. An edition in a language outside the configured set (Portuguese, Persian…) still gets one in its own language. | Every other configured language, translated from the current summary, as below. | . bun run cat summaries # also prints the translations owed, per language bun run cat summaries:next -- --lang fr --n 50 [--entry <slug>] # summarised blocks with no fr summary, WITH their current summaries bun run cat summaries:record -- drafts-fr.json # drafts carry lang: "fr" . check:l1-complete reports the missing languages in its block-summaries detail. Like the summary backlog, it is advisory. Translating a summary . Say the same thing, in the same length. Translate the current summary faithfully and naturally: nothing added, nothing dropped, and its notes kept (garbled text, blank pages, a figure that does not match). It is a translation of the summary, never a new summary of the block. Use WHO’s established terms in the target language (ВОЗ, منظمة الصحة العالمية, 世界卫生组织, OMS; World Health Assembly as each language’s official name). Proper names, test and drug names (Xpert MTB/RIF, PrEP) and document codes (A42/10, EB95/8) stay as written. A title with no official translation stays in its original language. Use the target’s own conventions: decimal commas in fr, es and ru, logical-order Unicode for Arabic and Persian (Persian letters ی and ک), Simplified Chinese with full-width punctuation. Check before recording: every block and source_hash copied exactly, the text is in the target script, and it is not the source summary unchanged. Record one language per file: record refuses the same block twice in one file. The Document panel — what a reader browses . Every entry carrying a structure.json gets a Document panel in the library viewer, built from the ingestion schema by cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts and published as assets/library/entries/<id>.doc.json (folio-library-document/v1) by bun run cat library:viz. Tabs: Contents (the TOC as a tree, collapsed below the first level that branches, each inferred entry’s confidence, linking to its section), Pages (physical page, printed label, sections starting, figures), Figures & tables, Sections (the summary, else an extract — the section’s own opening text, labelled as such and cut at a word), Checks (contents vs body, numbering gaps, page-label conflicts). Because it reads the schema, a new field in structure.json reaches every library at once; a field an older ingestion lacks shows “not recorded — re-ingest”, never an empty table. For a withheld entry the panel keeps structure, page labels, figure and table captions (labels, like TOC titles) and our summaries, and omits only section body extracts. Keywords — from the LSI weights, per section and per document . Keywords are extracted content, so they never live in the ingest record (cat-harness#1144). bun run cat library:keywords builds them at publish into the derived keywords graph: one folio-keywords/v2 JSON-LD node per entry under the site’s assets/keywords/<instance>/<slug>.jsonld, with an index.json beside them. Nothing is written inside library/<slug>/; the route is declared builtAtPublish, and derive:publish runs the writer. Up to 12 for the document and up to 8 per section, fewer for a short section (one per ~20 content tokens, at least 3). Each node holds six variants side by side, so they can be compared: . | Variant | Method | Weighting | Terms scored | . | lsi-log-entropy-surface (default) | lsi | log-entropy | the words the text uses | . | lsi-tfidf-surface | lsi | tf-idf | the words the text uses | . | lsi-log-entropy-latent | lsi | log-entropy | latent scores, any term of the library | . | lsi-tfidf-latent | lsi | tf-idf | latent scores, any term of the library | . | lsi-log-entropy-latent-rerank | lsi | log-entropy | latent scores, only the words the text or its headings use | . | ca-latent | correspondence-analysis | raw counts | latent scores, any term of the library | . The default is read from the same log-entropy matrix the LSI index is built from (keywordsOf in pipeline/lsi.ts), so a keyword means “frequent here, rare across this library” exactly as the index does. A latent variant scores terms by the rank-k reconstruction (k = 100), so it can propose a term the text never uses (synonymy, Deerwester et al. 1990); it scores the top 300 candidates. Correspondence analysis tends to favour rare proper names (authors, publishers), which the comparison shows. The Document panel computes the default variant in memory and shows it as chips, green where a heading also names the term (evidence: ["heading"]): the document saying it of itself. Withheld entries show them: they are derived terms, like captions, not the text. The library-keywords check in bun run cat health reports entries without keywords and any legacy keywords.json still committed. What the scoring does: . | Two-word phrases from truly adjacent tokens said at least twice; a stop word, punctuation, or a line break before a capital (a table cell, a heading) breaks the run — “Development” over “Systematic review team” is two cells, not “development systematic”. | A word said once in a text of 100+ tokens is not a keyword, unless the section’s heading names it; heading-named terms score double. | Generic words the index keeps but that say nothing about a topic (“anyone”, “aims”, “take”, “-ly” adverbs) are excluded from keywords only. | Plurals fold: “evidence reviews” does not follow “evidence review”. | . Limits: no part-of-speech tagging, so a rare verb can still surface in a short section; a library of fewer than 3 sections gets none. A WITHHELD entry in the viewer — its summary, else the gate, never “no content” . An entry whose library root’s withheld.json names it is listed but publishes no verbatim text: gen-library-viz reads its blocks with verbatim: false. “Not ours to show” must not look like “nothing was extracted”: . | A row shows the section’s summary when one exists, labelled as a summary and never as the source text. Summaries are our writing and stay published. | Otherwise, a withheld row says the gate: “Withheld — copyright not granted”, naming every gate that refused (“copyright and restrictions not granted”), with a link to the catalogue record — its published page first, its upstream URI second, no link rather than a guessed one. | Anything else with no content keeps the neutral “(no content carried)”, because for those it is true. | A banner tops a withheld entry: why the text is not shown, which gate refused, the record link, and how many sections have summaries (“0 of 121 sections summarised”). No banner on any other entry. | . Withheld is READ, never inferred from emptiness. The flag, the gates and the record come from withheld.json — folio-withheld/v1 carries an optional structured gates[] and record{id, page, uri} beside the reason sentence, which the layer’s generator writes from its own data (the IRIS catalogue: gen-iris-pages.ts, from the catalogue’s publication gates). A list that carries only the sentence still works: the row then says the sentence. The row and banner code is scripts/lib/library-withheld-view.ts, embedded in the page verbatim so library-withheld-view.test.ts runs the same text the browser does; library-withheld-viewer.e2e.ts opens the rendered page. Drafting the summaries is a separate backlog: bun run cat summaries:next -- --entry <slug> serves a withheld entry’s text to the summariser like any other. Describing a document’s images — and why it is an ARM, not a step you run . pdf-images.py classifies by geometry, which answers exactly one question: is this image the whole page, or something on it. It cannot tell a logo from a chart. The finer roles come from LOOKING, and that judgement is data — <library>/image-verdicts.json, one entry per image, reviewable line by line. bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # stage; reports what is unmet # look at ingest-staging/<doc-id>/images/, write the verdicts into # <lib>/image-verdicts.json, then: bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> # re-stage: the arm applies them bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE.pdf --library <lib> --promote . Re-running ingest is the second step, not a separate apply command. --promote refuses an entry whose image-descriptions requirement is unmet, and the stand-alone narrative writers (apply-image-verdicts.ts, narratives.ts) resolve their targets through directoriesForGraph(root, "library"), i.e. only in promoted libraries. Applying the verdicts as an arm in staging is what lets a document be both described and promoted. Applying by hand works exactly once. pdf-images.py opens the sidecar with "w" — no existence check, no merge — so the next ingest overwrites the descriptions, and overwrites them quietly: the file still parses and still validates, it simply has no narratives in it any more. Running the application as the fourth arm, after pdf-images.py, makes a re-run RE-APPLY instead — the sidecar is rebuilt from the PDF and the committed judgement is laid back over it. --staging <entry-dir> --library <lib-dir> is available directly if you need it, and --library is required: a staging directory does not say which library a document is being promoted into (a queue does not determine a library). An absent verdicts file exits 0, because the first ingest necessarily runs before anybody has looked at the images; image-descriptions is the gate that refuses, not that script. An orphaned verdict — one naming an image the sidecar does not have — still fails, in either mode. Every narrative it writes lands as draft. Only a person confirms one. A role threshold is OPTIONAL, and its default is NONE . A coverage cutoff may sort images into roles (figure vs furniture) only when a caller supplies one. | By default nothing is thresholded. With no value supplied, every role call comes from an inspection verdict as above, naming who looked. | A caller may supply one. An image whose role it decides must record that basis: the value, and that the value was caller-supplied rather than inspected. A thresholded role must never be readable as an inspected one. | Ship no number. No config default, and no value in docs, tests or examples presented as recommended. Per-image coverage does not separate the classes, and a cutoff placed in one corpus’s empty stretch is fitted to that corpus and says nothing about others. | . Reading a figure: the text layer is not the figure . Two traps, both of which produce a wrong description: . A diverging axis’s SIGN cannot be read from the text layer. get_text returned 0.2 0.4 0.6 below the zero of a Delta Pass Rate bar with no sign at any codepoint — matplotlib draws U+2212 as a vector path, so the minus exists in the rendering and not in the text. Rendering the region showed -0.2 -0.4 -0.6 plainly. A verdict trusting the extraction would have called a -0.6 endpoint +0.6. And the direction is a fact about the axis, not about the colours. The recorded inspection said a bar ran “blue low to red high”. Its ticks said Pass Rate, 1.0 at the top in dark blue: blue was HIGH. A reader given the original sentence reads every heatmap in the paper inverted — worse than no description, because a missing one is visibly missing. So: render the region and read the ticks. Two images that look alike need the same check each: a third “repeated legend” can be a different, signed scale. The figure that is DRAWN — pdf-vector-labels.py, the other arm . pdf-images.py answers “what does this page PLACE”. A WHO conceptual figure — a framework, a maturity model, a taxonomy, a process flow — is drawn in path operators and text, so it places nothing, and the raster arm is silent about it truthfully. 9789240120747-eng declares six captioned figures, places zero images, and image-descriptions reported “0 image(s), 0 describable and all described” over it: a determined empty that is true about raster and misleading about figures. The vector arm runs beside the raster one in withDerivedArms and writes vector-labels.json — every positioned text line on a page that declares a figure, with its rectangle in the visible frame, its fonts and sizes, and whether it intersects a drawing. Read the sidecar, not a count. Three things it deliberately does not do: . | It does not say which labels belong to the figure. intersectsDrawing is recorded and never filtered on. On 9789240120747-eng page 34 it separates perfectly; on 9789240010567-eng page 25 it is false for thirty labels that are plainly figure content, because they sit in the white space between the drawn boxes. | It does not group above the MuPDF LINE. A block on that same page holds six circled numerals 200 pt apart across three different diagrams. | It does not compare its counts to anything. Declared figures and recovered labels are not commensurable. | . So when you describe such a figure, the labels are your evidence and the grouping is your judgement — which is the same split as image-verdicts.json, one level over. The rule from the section above holds here with more force, not less: render the page and look at it. The arm recovers what the text layer says; it cannot tell you that the arrows run clockwise. The determined empty is still meaningful: who-rhr-1806-eng records zero pages because it contains no Fig. or Figure mention at all. A document with no text layer returns pages: null with a reason instead — the one place this arm could otherwise report a clean run over an unread scan. An .xlsx IS a zip — ask the container . The magic bytes of an OOXML or ODF document say application/zip, which is true and useless: it would send every spreadsheet to the archive rung to be listed as a bag of XML parts. The magic cannot tell them apart, so _tech_meta.sniff_zip_package asks the container, which declares itself — OOXML by [Content_Types].xml plus the part names, ODF by its mimetype member. Same principle as the byte sniff, one level in. sniff_effective_mimetype is the single answer the router (planFor) and the recorder both ask, so they cannot disagree. A CSV has no magic bytes at all, so routing one cannot be a sniff and must not become an extension guess. is_tabular_text asks the only content question available: do the first rows split into the same number of fields, more than one? Prose, a single column and anything ragged all answer no — a one-column “table” is indistinguishable from a list of lines. Proved on fixtures built at test time, all five branches mutation-checked.
