4461.doc: L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph
4461.title: Steps
4461.content: Every one of the 16 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Basic ingestion (harness)CallActivity_Basic | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/library-ingestion | The harness’s document-ingestion.bpmn: accept the upload by a declared route, extract its metadata into the KG, and catalogue the asset in library/ — placed if materialized, recorded as referenced if not. Everything below refines that result for a document. Called, not copied. | . | Detect media type, mint a doc idTask_Detect | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Sniff the media type rather than trusting the extension, and mint the doc id from the page-1 arXiv stamp where there is one, else from the filename. | . | Establish the licence from the uploadTask_Licence | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | EARLY: before any derivation, because library/ is holds: content and anything derived first is committed, so refusing it later is a deletion nobody may take unasked. This step sees only the upload itself — the licence recorded in its intake.json (the same stated / unknown record a library manifest carries) and whether a LICENSE file sits beside it. It never infers a licence from extracted text. The verdict is stated, unknown, or UNDETERMINED, and undetermined is never reported as cleared: the pipeline proceeds and says so, because a licence that only extraction can reveal is a later check’s to find. | . | Extract structureCallActivity_Extract | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — extract structuredocument-intake | See ingest-extract-structure.bpmn. | . | Derive content from the assetsCallActivity_Derive | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assetsdocument-intake | See ingest-derive-content.bpmn. Most of this subprocess is not implemented yet. | . | Ingest the themeCallActivity_IngestTheme | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — ingest a themetheme-art-intake | See ingest-theme.bpmn. The subprocess derives one Theme node with kind sticky|webpage|publication, and refuses a source it cannot complete rather than emitting a partial theme. | . | Open the beanCall_BeanOpen | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Process_BeanOpenbean-coordination | Process_BeanOpen: check before you create, find out whose the bean is, and claim it — or leave it alone when it is someone else’s. The one place a claim is drawn; the gateway after this reads which end it reached. | . | Close the beanCall_BeanClose | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Process_BeanClosetodo-manager | Process_BeanClose: end the bean in a state that says why — complete and archive it, scrap it with its reasons and archive it, or record the blocker and hand it back. The one place resolve and archive are drawn; placed straight before the end so the engine’s resolve sees nothing left but the archive step. | . | Build the L1 knowledge graphCallActivity_BuildKg | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graphdocument-intake | See ingest-build-l1-kg.bpmn. | . | L1 completeness gateCallActivity_Gate | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gatel1-document-ingestion | See ingest-l1-completeness-gate.bpmn.Skill-backed by l1-document-ingestion: its section“What a complete L1 entry holds” names check:l1-complete as the gate andstates its three results.The gate contains one adjudication (Task_FlagDrift: real, spurious or source-wrong), and its own Task_Verdict records the answer as a reason against the verdict before returning. So both answers reach this step, and nothing here branches on them; Gateway_Complete branches on the gate’s completeness verdict instead. | . | Record the gap as a beanTask_OpenBean | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | todo-manager | A missing derived artefact is a tracked gap, not a silent omission. The document stays in uploads/ until the gap closes. | . | **Move into library//**`Task_Promote` | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | The folder name IS the bibliography citation key, so a citation and a directory are the same string. | . | Publish the extracted statementsCallActivity_PublishStatements | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Publish extracted statements with source linkspublish-extracted-statements | THE ENTRY IS COMPLETE HERE, so its statements are published here. Every statement the extraction captured from this entry (a recommendation, a requirement, a candidate a person still has to rule on) becomes readable in two places: the folio’s working artifact, in the pages its content profile renders, and the shared extraction viewer. Each one links back to the library entry and to the section it came from.WHY IN INGESTION AND NOT LATER. A statement nobody can read beside its source is reviewed from memory, or not at all. Publishing when the entry is promoted means a reviewer can check every extracted statement against its source the moment it exists.The sub-process is the same for every content type. The content type decides only how its pages look, through its adapter. An entry that yields no statements (a referenced source, a dataset) passes through it with nothing to publish, and says so. | . | Summarise prose blocks, in every languageTask_SummaryQueue | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | A QA sidecar of general document ingestion, drained slowly.Nothing is written to ENQUEUE a block: the queue is derived (every prose block in every declared library, minus those whose summaries.json record is a current draft or confirmation), so a promoted entry is in it the moment its blocks are. A re-ingested document whose text changed re-enters it on its own, because the record’s source_hash no longer matches.What an agent doing ingestion work does here is DRAIN a few: bun run cat summaries:next -- --n K hands it the next K blocks with their text, it writes a short summary of each in its own words, and bun run cat summaries:record writes them into library/<bib-slug>/summaries.json as drafts naming the agent and its model. The block itself stays verbatim and ingested.A library can ask for a summary in more than one language (who-iris: the six UN languages, owner 2026-11-11): the English draft, one in the document’s own language read from the source, and translations of the English into the rest, each its own narrative in the block’s slot. Method: skill l1-document-ingestion, “Summarising prose blocks”.ADVISORY, never a gate: this step does not hold up Task_Citeable, and check:l1-complete reports the backlog (block-summaries) without failing on it. Confirming or rejecting a draft is a person’s act, in bun run cat narratives. | . | Record errata in the source’s own textTask_Errata | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | Owner, 2026-11-11 (who-iris, card Q-ODD-1 = A, and “add to L1 doc schema errata”). Reading the blocks to summarise them finds errors that are in the publication itself, not in the extraction: a title that says June 2006 over an introduction that says June 2005, a Spanish edition announcing nine recommendations where the English lists ten. The block stays as printed. The agent records an erratum in library/<bib-slug>/errata.json (folio-document-errata/v1): the kind, the block or page, the words as printed, the reading the evidence supports, the evidence, and its note as a draft narrative a person confirms in bun run cat narratives. An extraction defect is not an erratum: it is fixed by re-deriving the entry. ADVISORY: check:l1-complete reports errata and fails only on a file that does not mean what it says. Method: skill l1-document-ingestion, “Errata: errors in the source’s own text”. | . | Available to cite as an L1 sourceTask_Citeable | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Every knowledge-graph reference to this source now resolves through library/. Authoring and review consume it from here – see authoring-a-document.bpmn. | .

4464.title: l3-fhir-authoring
4464.content: Named by: Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review . Skill id: l3-fhir-authoring · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Named by l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Author FSH profiles, Compile FSH to FHIR JSON) and ig-incremental-build.bpmn (SUSHI on the restricted tank). Derive the L3 layer — machine-readable FHIR artefacts — from an authored L2 DAK, using FHIR Shorthand and SUSHI. Sourcing. FHIR, FSH and SUSHI are HL7’s; the SMART Guidelines L1–L4 model is WHO’s. This skill states how they are wired in this harness — which lane, which inputs, which binaries the package installs — and defers to the FHIR and FSH specifications for what a conformant artefact must look like.

4465.title: Inputs and outputs
4465.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/l3-fhir-authoring/: . | in — artifactType (required), sourceModel (required), fshOutputDir, igRoot | out — fshFiles (required), sushiResult (required), generatedResources | . L3 is derived, not authored from scratch, so sourceModel is required: an L3 artefact with no source behind it is a profile nobody can review against what it was meant to encode. The layer above chooses the source in its own process: that process maps its model and then CALLS l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Process_L3Fhir), which starts at “Source model ready”. Neither this skill nor that pipeline names the model, because this layer may not (AGENTS.md). CQL — clinical decision logic — is part of this skill, not a separate one; cql-library is one of the input schema’s artifactType values.

4466.title: The toolchain
4466.content: sushi-compiler and ig-publisher are capabilities this package declares (providesCapabilities in package-manifest.json, defined in scenarios/capabilities/): . sushi --version # sushi-compiler, requires node-runtime java -jar "$IG_PUBLISHER_JAR" --version # ig-publisher, requires java-runtime . If a capability probe fails, the step was not run — never that it passed.

4467.title: Deriving rather than retyping
4467.content: When the layer above carries transforms in the render direction — from its own model to FSH, or to rendered tables — use them rather than hand-writing what a transform already emits, and read that layer’s own tooling skill for how they behave. Whatever they emit is still FSH this skill owns: a collision between two emitted files is a finding to decide (a duplicate input, or two sources legitimately contributing the same thing), never one to let overwrite silently.

4477.title: Library ingestion — the basic flow
4477.content: Skill library-ingestion: The BASIC ingestion flow every asset takes: an upload is accepted, its metadata goes into the knowledge graph, and the asset lands in library/<slug>/ if it is materialized. The two entry points (a drop in uploads/, or materializing an asset a remote graph lists), what happens to the upload afterwards, and why content-type methods refine this flow from above rather than living in it. Command: bun run cat ingest. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Wireframe design review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Public comment on a review draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links . uploads/ and library/ are two stages of one pipeline. uploads/ is the incoming queue — raw files as dropped, not L1 and not greppable as corpus. library/<slug>/ is where an ingested asset lives, and every knowledge-graph reference to a source resolves through it. Why that bites: the corpus-grep checklist searches library/ only, so a file still in uploads/ makes a clean grep mean “nobody has done this” when the source is right there. That is how a held result gets re-derived.

4478.title: The flow — four steps, and no content-type decision
4478.content: cat-harness holds only the basic, high-level ingestion workflow, with very little process context assumed: the uploaded asset’s extracted metadata goes into the KG, and the asset into library/ if materialized. library/processes/document-ingestion.bpmn (Process_Ingestion) is that flow, executable: . | Accept — the bytes reach the declared uploads/ queue by a declared route (upload-routes; names per upload-naming; arrival noticed by uploads-watch). | Extract metadata into the KG — asset-extraction: a container’s INDEX goes in, its contents do not unless asked for. | Materialized? — the state vocabulary is schemas/kg/materialization-state.ts: referenced, materialized or unknown, with no default. | Place in library/<slug>/ — this skill. A referenced asset is still catalogued: its record says where the bytes are and that we hold none. | . The flow calls no subprocess and decides nothing about content type. Which reader a PDF needs, what a complete L1 entry holds, how images or datasets are described — those are refinements, and they live in a layer above this one. The mechanism is inversion: a higher-layer process CALLS Process_Ingestion as its first step and continues with its own work. Nothing here names a refinement, because there is no BPMN extension point in the corpus and a harness process naming a higher one would be an upward edge. methodology-from-source.bpmn’s Call_Ingest is a harness caller of the same flow.

4479.title: TWO entry points
4479.content: Things enter the library through uploads/ → library/ document ingestion, or through materializing an asset listed in an external KG that a dependent harness declares. |   | drop | materialize | . | the source is | a file somebody put in uploads/ | an asset listed in a remote graph a dependency declares | . | decided first | how it is read (a refinement’s choice) | the five gates, and a purpose | . | entry | bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE | materialize-remote.bpmn | . Neither is a shortcut past the other. A materialized asset still arrives as bytes that have to be read, so it re-enters at exactly the point a dropped file does. Materialization adds what happens before there is a file: may we hold it, what does holding it cost, for what purpose, and what if the source goes away. Entry one is bun run cat ingest uploads/FILE (--dry-run says what it would do, and why). Entry two starts from remoteGraphs in a layer’s declaration (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts, RemoteGraph): assets listed there are referenced — we know they exist and where, and hold none. materialize-remote.bpmn asks purpose (working or archival), then the five gates, then fetches; the asset lands in library/ with its provenance and fixity, and a refusal leaves the node referenced rather than failing. A reference is not a fetch: the KG viewer follows a remote graph to show its hierarchy without materialising anything — navigable without being held. Who owns which half . | This layer owns the basic flow and the reading CODE — the pdf-* rungs, ingest-document.ts, notebook-structure.ts. Reading bytes is platform work, and OCR stays here. The method that chooses among them is a refinement above. The flow itself cannot move up: uploads and library are graph typologies this layer declares, and a flow above would make the harness’s own library writable only from a layer above it — a wrong-direction, and circular, dependency. | The remote half’s gates belong to the content layer above. Only the state vocabulary lives here; the five gates, the purposes and the record binding them stay with the layer that owns content, because each gate is a decision about content. A harness that cannot hold content must not own the vocabulary for deciding to acquire it. | The large-datasets package owns the question before both (library/skills/large-datasets/): how to enumerate a corpus and ask it for a subset (source-descriptor.ts). Neither entry point can start until something says what is out there. | Further down the tree, a dependency’s declared remoteGraphs is what makes the second path reachable at all, inherited the way directories are. | .

4480.title: A held PDF gets its page-1 cover BEFORE the upload is retired
4480.content: The picture of a PDF entry is library/<slug>/cover.png, page 1 rendered by pdf-cover.py — never its first figure, which can be any picture from deep in the document. With no cover, the entry shows the book glyph. | A new ingest writes it: ingest-document’s cover arm runs last. | An entry without one gets it from bun run cat library:covers. Run it in the checkout that holds the PDF (the composed index, whose uploads/ may be another repository’s), and commit the cover into the repository that holds the entry. | Run it before the upload is retired. Once the PDF moves to fsh-guts/uploads/, library:covers no longer finds it and skips the entry as “not held”. | bun run cat library:covers:check fails on a held, unwithheld PDF that has no cover. | .

4481.title: After ingestion the upload is RETIRED — never left, never deleted
4481.content: Three places, and only uploads/ is temporary: queued uploads/FILE; derived library/<slug>/, which may not hold the source bytes (check:l1-complete reports an unexpected child); archived fsh-guts/uploads/FILE beside a folio-fsh-guts/v1 sidecar whose movedFrom and movedOn are load-bearing. Never rm an ingested upload: it is the only working-tree copy of the source. bun run cat check:uploads-retired finds unretired ones by sha256 against every declared library, never by filename, and refuses rather than passes when no library records a hash. It reports and never moves anything. Rename an upload before its first ingest — the slug follows the name. The full rule — why the library cannot be the destination, the sidecar convention, the blocking and advisory families, and renaming — is in library-ingestion/uploads-retirement.md.

4482.title: When an ingested document names what else the library needs
4482.content: Some documents say what they rest on, by number, in a section the content type defines — and then the library is not complete until it holds those too. The flow above is run again for each, and the citing document’s graph is regenerated once they are in, so a cited source the library HOLDS is described from its own metadata rather than from a one-line reference. The content type owns which section that is, how its citations resolve, and how a cited source is acquired (for instance from a DSpace repository); it says so in its own authoring skill. This layer owns only the rule: the flow above runs once per cited source, and the citing document’s graph is regenerated after.

4483.title: A second representation sits DOWNSTREAM of the entry
4483.content: A content type may describe an ingested document a second time, in its own schema — a WHO guideline is also an L1 knowledge graph. The library is upstream of L1: L1 points upstream, never downstream. So that representation is derived from the entry and points at the entry’s nodes (the source document, its sections, its blocks); nothing in the library points back, and the entry is never rewritten for it. It inherits whatever sectioning this flow produced, so a better reader here improves it without a change there. Whether a document gets one is recorded on its intake (classifications), by a person, by the process that acquired it, or by a rule — the content type owns which, and its skill says how.

4486.title: Liquid templates — layout only, every fact from the graph
4486.content: Skill liquid-templates: Authoring a Liquid template in this repository — a README template the subgraph-readmes Tool renders with liquidjs, or a Jekyll include on the just-the-docs site. Where templates live (inside a declared directory, reached through its id), what a template may read (only what the Knowledge Graph hands it), the leading comment the generator reads as the file’s description, includes, whitespace control, escaping, and regenerate-then-commit with the --check gate. Read it before adding or changing any .liquid file or anything under docs/_includes/. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Two engines run Liquid here, and they produce different kinds of output. Know which one you are writing for before you write a line: . |   | README templates | site templates | . | engine | liquidjs, run by bootstrap-tools’ subgraph-readmes (jekyllInclude: true, strictFilters: true) | Jekyll, run by docs-site.yml with the pinned just-the-docs remote_theme | . | lives in | templates/readme/ beside the writer, in the tools repository (bootstrap-tools/scripts/templates/readme/) | cat-harness/docs/_includes/ — just-the-docs’ extension points (head_custom.html, footer_custom.html, nav_footer_custom.html) plus our own | . | output | <directory>/README.md, committed, read on GitHub where no Liquid runs | _site/, never committed, published to Pages | . | data | only what the generator passes: subgraph, instance, kg, files, subdirs, summary | site, page, include, and _data/*.json written by the pipeline | . | verified by | bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check — the diff is the output | building the site: rendered-verification, bun run cat preview:site | .

4487.title: Where a template lives
4487.content: Beside the writer that renders it, in the tools repository. The README templates are part of bootstrap-tools’ scripts/ subgraph, at bootstrap-tools/scripts/templates/readme/, and the writer finds them with TEMPLATES, a path relative to its own file. A template is part of the toolset: somebody who wants different READMEs uses a different toolset over the same content, and a harness that wants its own layout passes its own templates directory to plan(). They are files OF the scripts/ subgraph, not a directory of their own: a declared directory nested inside another is refused by check:layout-norms. Never an inline template string in a .ts file and never a .liquid file outside a declared directory: a template nobody declared is one no checker looks at, and its README row cannot say what it is.

4488.title: What a template may read — and what it must not compose
4488.content: A template arranges facts; it never states one. Every word that is not layout comes from a variable the generator read from the Knowledge Graph: the directory’s declared title and description, each file’s own account of itself, a relation a diagram records. No count, URL, name or claim typed into a template — each is a second answer free to drift from the first, which is readme-sections §”Resolve links; never compose them” one level down. | Computation belongs in the generator, where it is tested: counting, grouping, choosing a link target, collapsing a long list. The template sees results (subdirs[].count, summary), not inputs to derive them from. | A missing value is shown as missing, never papered over: {{ subgraph.title | default: subgraph.id }} and “No description is declared for …” are the pattern. The generator records the gap as a QA finding in test/results/subgraph-readmes.qa-results.json (a derived result, stored on the qa-reports branch by qa-publish); the template must not make it look filled. | A new variable is a generator change first. Add it to the object passed to renderFile, list it in the template’s comment, then use it. | .

4489.title: Versions are variables, never numbers
4489.content: A version typed into a template is stale on the next bump. Read it: . | README templates get release: version (every layer declares one), and — for a layer declaring an iriBase — major, agent (for identifiers) and human (for pages), both <iriBase>v<major>/. Empty strings where not declared: test with != "", and show nothing rather than a guess. | Site templates read site.data.harness.releases.<instance> — the same four fields for every layer, written by sync-docs-harness into _data/harness.json under the docs:harness:check gate. | . Link a person to human and name an identifier with agent. They are one address today — every address carries the major only, and the pin, not the address, fixes the exact release (instance-publication §”Release IRIs”) — but the field still says which audience a link is for.

4490.title: The leading comment IS the file’s description
4490.content: Open every template with a {%- comment -%} block. Its first sentence is what the directory README’s “what it is” column shows for the file (describe() in bootstrap-tools/scripts/readme-graph-sections.ts), so write it for a reader of that table — “The file table: files directly in the directory, then its subdirectories.” — and put the variables it reads in the lines after. No comment and the row says only “a template”.

4491.title: Includes
4491.content: jekyllInclude: true gives Jekyll’s syntax: {% include files.liquid %}, the file name unquoted and with its extension. An include with no parameters sees the including template’s variables (files.liquid reads files directly); a parameter passed as {% include x.liquid key=value %} is read as include.key, as in Jekyll. Split a template when a part is reusable or when a reader would want its own row for it — not to hide logic.

4492.title: Whitespace — check the output, not the template
4492.content: {%- and -%} strip the whitespace on that side of the tag, and that is how a template emits clean Markdown. It is also how a separator the output needs disappears — a stripped space between two HTML attributes makes the page print its own markup as text, past every gate (continual-progress §”A template is not a page”). Strip freely inside a tag’s own lines; think before stripping next to a table row’s newline, the blank line before a heading or table, or an attribute boundary. subgraph-readmes also collapses three or more newlines to two, so do not fight blank lines with stripping.

4493.title: Escaping
4493.content: . | strictFilters: true — an unknown filter is an error, not a silent pass-through. No custom filter is registered. | A value bound for a table cell is escaped before it reaches the template — the generator’s cell() turns | into \| and folds newlines. A new cell-bound field goes through it; a raw | from a file’s description splits the row. | Liquid syntax in prose that Jekyll will build must sit inside a raw block. gen-skill-docs wraps every skill page in one, so a skill may quote {{ }} and {% %} freely — but never the closing endraw tag itself, which ends the block early. A generated README that sits under a site source (cat-harness/docs/, root docs/) may be read by the site build too; if a KG value there can carry Liquid, build the site and look before assuming either way. | .

4494.title: An undefined variable is a message, not silence
4494.content: Jekyll renders an undefined variable as the empty string and says nothing; strict_variables says something by FAILING the build and by changing what renders (the exception aborts the whole tag, else branch included). docs/_plugins/liquid-undefined-warn.rb does neither: every lookup runs as Liquid runs it, and at the end of the build each path that was ABSENT is printed as a warning with its count and pages, site.data.* first. A lookup inside a condition or under | default is not reported — there the template asked — nor an include’s own parameter (include.x, optional by convention), a field of a variable that is there and nil (its cause is reported once, where it went undefined), or a path liquid_undefined_ignore in _config.yml lists: a THEME’s optional settings, which site-chrome/_config.yml names for just-the-docs. Without those exclusions the report is mostly noise over a few real gaps. FOLIO_LIQUID_UNDEFINED_REPORT=<file> writes the same record as JSON; liquid_undefined: off in _config.yml turns it off. It runs only where plugins do (bundle exec jekyll, as an IG repository’s own site and preview:site build); the github-pages build is safe mode and loads none.

4495.title: Markers — the platform owns the region, the folio owns the file
4495.content: subgraph-readmes writes only between <!-- kg:subgraph:begin --> and <!-- kg:subgraph:end -->, creates a README holding just that region when there is none, and leaves an unmarked README alone and reported. The rules are in readme-sections; do not restate them in a template.

4496.title: Regenerate, commit, and the gate
4496.content: bun run cat readme:subgraphs # render every declared directory's README + the QA sidecar bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check # fail on a stale README or sidecar — CI and the pre-commit hook . Changing a template changes every README it renders; commit them with the template, in one commit. So does adding or removing a file in any declared directory — that directory’s table changed. readme:subgraphs:check runs in code-quality-gates.yml and in cat-harness-tools/scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit; it is part of bun run cat gates.

4499.title: Literature search — finding the source a citation points at
4499.content: Skill literature-search: Finding the source a node cites but does not hold — memory first, then this repository, then open-access services. Always produce a DIRECT download link. Read before recording that a citation cannot be found, and before appraising any source you have not opened. Its central rule: a blocked network is not a missing document, and the two must never share a report. Named by: Options analysis . A node cites a source. Nothing in any declared library holds it. This skill is the step between those two facts and library-ingestion, which takes over once a file exists. It runs on a measurable trigger, not a feeling: a origin, evidence, source or bibliography reference whose target does not resolve to an entry in any library the layer declares. The methodology graph is where this bites hardest — methodology-adoption requires that an adopted methodology be “external and named”, with “an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body” — and a front-matter string nothing can follow satisfies that requirement only on paper.

4500.title: Look in this order, and stop at the first hit
4500.content: 1. Memory. The memory graph and agent memory under .claude/agent-memory/. A source located once and found unreachable is worth recording; re-deriving that costs the same search twice and reaches the same wall. 2. This repository. Every declared library and uploads directory, not one of them. A layer may declare several — ask the declaration, do not assume a path. A file sitting in uploads/ is found but not ingested, which is a different finding from not found, and it is the cheapest possible outcome: hand it to library-ingestion and stop. 3. Open-access services. DOI resolution through the publisher, then the open-access aggregators and repositories — Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Crossref, DOAJ, CORE, arXiv, PubMed Central, Zenodo, HAL, and a standards body’s own site where the origin names one. archiving-arxiv and archiving-web-pages cover the fetch once a URL is in hand. Open access only. What this finds is committed into a library in a public repository, so a paywalled PDF is not a candidate whatever its availability to the person searching. When only a paywalled copy exists, that is an outcome to report (below), not a licence to take it. A publisher’s own free-to-read landing page, a preprint, an author copy in an institutional repository and a standards body’s public specification are all fine.

4501.title: Always give the direct link
4501.content: Every outcome carries a direct download link — the URL that yields the file itself, not a search page, not a DOI landing page, not “search for it on X”. A landing page is acceptable in addition, never instead. The person reading this has limited hand function; “you can find it by searching” converts a finished search into their work, which is the whole thing this skill exists to absorb.

4502.title: Three outcomes, and the middle one is the point
4502.content: There are three, not two, and collapsing the middle into the third is the failure this skill is written to prevent. 1. Found and fetched . The file is in uploads/. Hand to library-ingestion and say which service it came from, so the provenance is checkable. 2. Found, but this agent cannot fetch it . The document exists, its location is known, and something in the way this agent is running stopped the transfer — a proxy refusal, a TLS failure, a robots policy, a rate limit, a login wall, a network the container cannot reach. Report this as a located document, never as a missing one. Say all of: . | what the item IS — full citation: authors, year, title, venue, volume, pages, DOI. Enough that a person recognises it without opening anything. | what it contains, in a sentence, and its extent if known (pages, format). This is what lets the person judge whether it is worth their trouble. | the direct download link, as above. | why the fetch failed, in plain words — “the agent proxy returned 403”, “the publisher requires a login”, “the host is not reachable from this container”. Not “could not retrieve”. | what to do with it: drop the file into uploads/ and the ingest runs. | . Then record it in the work plan as blocked on a fetch, with what it waits on — bean-blocking’s rules apply, expiry included. A network restriction is a fact about this agent, not about the literature. Reported as “not found” it becomes a fact about the world, and the next agent re-runs the identical search, hits the identical wall, and reports the identical wrong conclusion. Worse, a methodology whose source was found and blocked reads exactly like one whose source does not exist, and the first is a five-minute human action while the second may mean the methodology should not have been adopted. 3. Not found . Nothing open-access resolves to it. Say what was searched — the services, not “a search was done” — and what the closest candidates were and why each was rejected. A rejected candidate with no record is a dead end the next agent walks back into, which is bean-coordination’s argument for scrapped over deleted, applied to a search. “Not found” for a source that is merely paywalled is wrong. That is outcome 2 with “the only copies are behind a paywall” as the reason.

4503.title: Never fill the gap with recall
4503.content: Do not paraphrase, summarise, quote or characterise a source you have not opened. Not from training, not from a secondary source, not from an abstract read in a search result, unless the abstract is what you say you read. This is the rule the whole evidence base rests on. A methodology file that renders a method from the agent’s recollection and cites a paper nobody fetched is worse than one with no citation at all: it carries the authority of a reference while resting on nothing, and there is no way for a reader to tell it apart from a faithful rendering. Where a source is read through another — a review paper reporting a primary one — say so at each claim. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: Humphrey, Weihrich, Dealtry, Wheelen & Hunger, Hill & Westbrook, Mintzberg and Dess et al. are all read through one review, every attribution is marked second-hand, and the file says the origin of the method is contested rather than repeating the usual story as fact.

4504.title: What this skill does NOT do
4504.content: . | It does not appraise. Certainty of a body of evidence is evidence-appraisal against the grading system the folio declares, and for a health recommendation that is grade. Finding a paper says nothing about whether it is any good. | It does not ingest. library-ingestion owns uploads/ → library/, and the ingest chooses its own rung. | It does not decide which methodology to use. That is methodology-adoption, which this skill feeds: the evidence behind a methodology is an input to selecting it. | It does not judge whether a gap matters. It reports the gap. Whether a methodology with no reachable source should still be adopted is the owner’s call, and deletion-requires-confirmation’s posture applies — report, with what is missing, and wait. | .

4505.content: . | library-ingestion — the next step, once a file exists | methodology-adoption — what requires an origin in the first place, and the selection question this feeds | evidence-appraisal — appraising what was found | evidence-review — separation of appraiser from drafter | bean-blocking (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) — recording outcome 2 so it does not read as abandoned | .

4507.title: Logging what you are doing
4507.content: Skill log-message: Say what you are doing, to the Logger, in a form a reader can act on. Five required fields and one optional body; an incomplete message is not logged. Callable from any task in any process, and required by some. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness, Log a message . You are the author of a log line; the Logger is where it goes. The Logger records and decides nothing, so it cannot know who acted: you supply actor. It is carried out as a sub-process: nobody starts there. A task in another process calls it, and the calling task’s diagram says so; this skill does not list its callers or the process that implements it.

4508.title: The message
4508.content: Five strings, all required, and one optional markdown body. | field | what it answers | shape | . | timestamp | when | an ISO-8601 instant, e.g. 2026-09-20T14:03:11Z | . | actor | who was acting | the acting actor’s id — never the Logger’s | . | process | inside which process | a process id, e.g. my-process | . | task | at which step of it | a node id within that process, e.g. A_DoTheThing | . | message | what happened | one line, no newline | . | body | the detail, if any | markdown, optional | . All five are required: each answers a question a reader would otherwise guess. body is the one place free prose belongs. A diff, an error, the contents of a file that was not where it should have been. Keep message to the line somebody scanning will read, and put everything else here.

4509.title: When to log
4509.content: Optionally, from any task in any process. You need no permission and no element in the diagram: an actor saying what it is doing is always in order. Required where a diagram says so, which it says by drawing the call explicitly — a callActivity whose calledElement is Process_LogMessage. If the diagram drew it, logging is a step, not a courtesy. The difference between the two is only whether the caller drew it. It is the same sub-process either way, and it takes the same six fields.

4510.title: If you cannot complete the message
4510.content: Do not log, and say that you could not. The End_NotLogged branch is a real outcome, not an error path to route around. A line missing its actor or its task still looks like a record, and a reader cannot tell it from a complete one. The same holds if the Logger is unreachable: say so, in the place you would have logged to, and carry on with the task. Logging is not a gate. A failure to log is never a reason to abandon an install.

4511.title: The one destination bootstrap has
4511.content: The discussion with the human actor. A Bootstrapping Agent has no log file, no service and no work plan — the only place it can put a line where a person will see it is the conversation it is already in. There is no command: the agent writes the six fields into the conversation. A harness that installs a real log sink adds a Tool for it; this skill still says what a message is.

4512.title: What this skill is NOT
4512.content: A log line says what an actor did at a moment; it is not a record of work still outstanding. Logging is also not asking: if a step needs a judgement, that is confirm-harness, and no number of log lines substitutes for it.

4519.title: Log a message
4519.content: Generated from bootstrap/processes/log-message.bpmn by gen-processes-viz.ts — do not edit here. All processes · bootstrap processes .

4520.title: The Logger’s contract
4520.content: Skill logger: The contract a Logger keeps: accept a complete log message, record it unchanged where a person can read it, attributed to the actor the message names. A mechanical Actor plays this Role; this is what it must do, and what it can be tested against. Named by: Log a message . A Logger plays a Role, and this is the Role’s contract. The author of a log line follows log-message. This skill is the other side: what happens to the line once it arrives. It sits in the Logger lane of log-message.

4521.title: Responsibilities
4521.content: . | Record a complete message unchanged. All five fields log-message requires (timestamp, actor, process, task, message), and body when given, are recorded as received. No field is rewritten, truncated or filled in. | Attribute it to the actor the message names. The line says the actor field’s value acted. It never names the Logger. | Put it where a person can read it. In bootstrap that is the discussion the human actor is already in. A harness that installs a log sink adds a Tool for it, and this contract still holds. | Say when it cannot record. If the destination is unreachable, the failure is reported to the author, so log-message’s “say that you could not” can happen. A message is never dropped silently. | .

4522.title: Tests
4522.content: Bootstrap runs nothing, so the test named in tested-by: lives with the toolset. It checks line 1 (the fields match log-message, and only a complete message reaches the Logger lane). Lines 2–4 concern the destination, the discussion, and are not tested.

4523.title: Not its responsibility
4523.content: Composing the message, judging whether it is complete, or deciding what happens next. Those happen in the acting Actor’s lane before anything reaches the Logger.

4525.title: LSI indexing — the platform’s application of methodologies/lsi.md
4525.content: Skill lsi-indexing: Build, read and audit a Latent Semantic Indexing index over a declared prose graph — a library, the skills, the work items, docs — to find units that discuss the same thing in different words, near-duplicates, outlier clusters, and a proposed home for unfiled work. Every output is a proposal; LSI never writes a relation. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . The method is the node, not this file. lsi carries what LSI is, its sources, and the six refusals. This skill says how to run it here and how to read what comes back. Where the two disagree, the node wins.

4526.title: When to reach for it
4526.content: | you are asking | use | . | “which nodes contain these words?” | graph-search — lexical, exact, no score | . | “has anyone worked this topic in other words?” | bun run cat lsi query "<text>" --instance <i> --graph <g> | . | “is this new bean / section a restatement of an existing one?” | the sidecar’s nearDuplicates | . | “what is this graph about, as a whole?” | the sidecar’s dimensions (read both poles) | . | “is there junk in this library — boilerplate, specimen text, a bad page?” | the sidecar’s narrowDimensions | . | “which epic does this bean / branch / PR belong under?” | bun run cat lsi:epics | . Run the lexical search FIRST. LSI supplements an empty or thin lexical result; it never replaces a lexical hit, and its hits are always reported under their own label (latent only vs lexical+latent) — refusal 1.

4527.title: Commands
4527.content: bun run cat lsi index --instance <instance> --graph library # build + write the sidecar bun run cat lsi index --instance <instance> --graph library --doc 9789241548960-eng # one document bun run cat lsi query "certainty of the evidence" --instance <instance> --graph library bun run cat lsi:audit # which graphs need one; is each fresh? bun run cat lsi:epics --out <file.md> [--prs <open-prs.json>] # epic-filing proposal bun run cat lsi:near "<planned bean title>" # before `beans create` bun run cat-harness-tools/pipeline/graph-search.ts "<q>" --latent # lexical + graph, THEN a separate latent list . From an MCP host: the lsi_query tool (Tool node lsi-query), with the query as text and optional instance / graph. On a shell the query goes on STDIN (echo "<q>" | bun run cat lsi query --instance <iris-replica> --graph library), because free text never goes on a command line. A unit is the graph’s own chunk: a library section (what ingestion already produced), otherwise one markdown file. Units under 20 tokens are skipped — too little vocabulary to place.

4528.title: Beyond the beans: other graphs in lsi:near
4528.content: lsi:near also searches every graph a layer declares under lsiUnitProviders in its <instance>.json: content blocks (core) and Lean declarations (sci). It prints one list per graph. Scores from two separately built indexes are not comparable, so the lists are never merged into one ranking. Each list starts with explicit references: a block @id or a Lean name written in the query text. These are deterministic and unscored. The latent hits come after them, labelled lexical+latent or latent only. A graph that could not be indexed is shown as not searched, never as “no hits”. bun run cat lsi:near "<planned bean title>" --graphs blocks,lean-decl --root lean-decl=<lean dir> .

4529.title: Cross-document links — a floor, and hubs reported, not penalised
4529.content: bun run cat lsi links --instance <i> --graph <g> proposes links between units of DIFFERENT documents in one graph: each unit’s best other-document match, only at cosine ≥ 0.5 (LINK_FLOOR), with the units that are “nearest” to many others listed as hubs to discount. Most units get no link when the median best match is low, and that is the honest answer. There is no hub PENALTY. A CSLS-style penalty (2·cos − r(a) − r(b)) made ranking worse on reader-labelled pairs (real-vs-spurious AUC 0.96 with plain cosine, 0.75–0.79 with the penalty): a hub is often central because it is genuinely on-topic. The floor is a house number fitted to 15 labelled examples.

4530.title: Keywords — the per-unit view
4530.content: The weighted matrix says which terms characterise each unit before the index reduces it to k dimensions. keywordsOf(matrix, cols, texts, top, headings) keeps that view: a unit’s (or a pooled set of units’) top terms and two-word phrases, from the same weights. Its first consumer is bun run cat library:keywords (per library section and per document, written as keywords.json and shown in the library viewer). The scoring rules are documented with keywordsOf in pipeline/lsi.ts, and the ingestion skill that runs it says when (skill_fetch l1-document-ingestion, §”Keywords”). Reuse it for any unit set the index covers — work items, chapters — rather than writing a second term weighting.

4531.title: Correspondence analysis — the parallel track
4531.content: correspondence-analysis is a separate method over the same term matrix (pipeline/ca.ts): the SVD of the χ² residuals, so no dimension carries document length or term frequency. bun run cat lsi:epics --method ca runs it on the work item store. It is not significantly better or worse than LSI at filing work items (exact McNemar p = 0.17–0.71), so LSI stays the default. Reach for CA when an LSI dimension 1 has no negative pole, or when the question is which units are UNUSUAL — CA’s leading dimensions go to the most distinctive profiles. Pick one per question; never average the two scores.

4532.title: On ingestion — the index refreshes itself
4532.content: bun run cat ingest … --promote ends by re-indexing the library it wrote into and printing, for the promoted document only, its near-duplicate section pairs and any narrow dimension it carries. Advisory: an index is not part of L1, so a failure prints “not refreshed — this is not a pass” and the ingest still succeeds. Read the lines while the document is fresh: a narrow dimension on a new document is almost always boilerplate, specimen text or a mis-extracted page, and it is cheapest to mark now.

4533.title: Where to LOOK at an index
4533.content: Its health is in the repository health report: bun run cat health, check lsi-indexes. It lists every declared prose graph that needs an index and lacks a fresh one, with the command that builds it, and each stored index’s narrow-dimension and near-duplicate counts. Its content (the dimensions as two poles, the near-duplicate pairs, the narrow-dimension units) is the sidecar below; read it with lsi query or open the file. bun run cat lsi:viz writes the Indexing evidence page at /cat-harness/lsi/ (/lsi/ is its declared alias). Until cat-harness#1144 it drew the indexes; the owner (2026-11-08) made it the evidence chain instead. For each indexing method (this one, correspondence-analysis, skill-pipeline-subject-indexing, consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation) it shows the held papers it rests on, the skills that declare uses-methodology for it, the Tools that satisfy those skills, and the processes that call them. It also lists the indexing skills that apply no method, such as glossary work and lexical search, as having no evidence yet. So a skill that reads this index (keywords, lsi:near, graph-search --latent) gets the papers as its evidence by declaring uses-methodology: lsi. cat-harness DECLARES the page (visualisers entry lsi, renderedBy: lsi-viewer), so it appears on the navbar and the central Published graphs page with no further wiring. The page is excluded from every index’s units.

4534.title: Where the index lives, and what is stored
4534.content: test/results/lsi/<instance>/<graph>.lsi.json — the fingerprint, parameters, retained variance, per-dimension pole terms, each unit’s three nearest neighbours, and the findings. Not the vectors: a rebuild is about a second per few hundred units, and a float dump is not reviewable. That path is the working copy, and nothing under it is committed. The record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch (main/<sha>/, pr/<n>/<sha>/). The readers cope with its absence: with no test/results/lsi/ in the checkout, the verdict rebuilds the index in memory and judges that run, writing nothing, and the health check reads the indexes by ref through qa-store (main). Anything but a hit is unknown, never “no index is missing”. The Indexing evidence page is never committed. It is declared under builtAtPublish in cat-harness.json (docs/en/cat-harness/lsi/), because it joins every instance’s methodologies, skills, Tools and processes, so it moves with the index’s pins, not with one commit. It reads no stored index; --detail and --ref are accepted and ignored. A merge strategy does not stop a generated file conflicting, even when the file is reproducible and take-base plus a regeneration converges. An SVD rotation is globally sensitive: one sentence added to one skill rewrites most of a sidecar’s dimensions and neighbours, so there is no small diff to merge. A declared strategy (derived-results/take-base) settles how a conflict is resolved, never whether one arises. Ask of a conflicting generated file “what is this file’s record, and is main it?” Where the answer is no, take the file off main. State graphs are indexed on demand, never stored. The beans graph changes on nearly every commit; a stored index would be stale on every PR and a merge-conflict magnet. lsi:epics rebuilds it each run.

4535.title: Reading a sidecar
4535.content: . | retained — share of ‖A‖²_F the rank-k approximation keeps. It is not a quality score; a low value on a large heterogeneous graph (work items: ~45 %) is expected. | Dimension 1 is usually a margin. Qi et al. (2023): LSA’s first dimensions mainly carry document length and overall term frequency. A dimension with no negative pole is that signature — skip it when reading themes. | dimensions — a dimension is a contrast, so read the positive and negative poles together. Refusal 2: it is not a topic until a person names it. | narrowDimensions — a dimension ≥ 80 % of whose mass sits on ≤ 3 units (or 1 %). Almost always non-prose: Lorem-ipsum layout filler, font specimens, a mis-extracted page. Treat as an ingestion finding. | nearDuplicates — cosine ≥ 0.95. In the work item store these are work items filed twice. A duplicate work item is scrapped with a pointer, never deleted (bean-coordination). | .

4536.title: The need-an-index audit
4536.content: bun run cat lsi:audit walks every declared graph of a prose kind across every layer and writes test/results/lsi-need-an-index.qa-results.json (qa-results/v1). | result | means | . | n/a | below the threshold — not judged, which is not the same as fine | . | fail | needs an index and has none, or its fingerprint no longer matches | . | pass | has a fresh index | . The threshold (≥ 100 units and ≥ 20,000 words) is a house number with its basis stated in scripts/lsi.ts; the method gives no corpus-size rule. It reports and does not gate (exit 0), like check:methodology-evidence; --strict exits 1 for a caller that has decided; no CI step runs it yet. The same verdict in the audited record — kg:audit’s tool-downstream-fresh . LSI is the first member of the downstream-tool family. The lsi-index Tool node declares downstream, and every bun run cat lsi index writes a folio-tool-run/v1 record — outcome and input fingerprint, on success AND on failure — under test/results/tool-runs/lsi-index/. The verdict reads three states: . | state | meaning | green? | . | fresh | a successful run’s recorded fingerprint matches the graph now | yes | . | stale | the graph changed since the recorded run | no | . | not-run / failed | no run record, or the last run failed | never | . A sidecar on disk with no run record is not-run: a file is not evidence the run that should keep it current succeeded. kg:audit carries this as tool-downstream-fresh on the lsi-index Tool (minor), one finding per graph, using the same verdict function as lsi:audit. Its finding text carries no counts, so the kg-qa sidecar moves only when a verdict flips. Two chains keep the indexes fresh, so the criterion stays quiet in ordinary work: . | a skill edit — skill:register runs lsi:skills before kg:audit, and CI checks it with lsi:skills:check; | an ingest — --promote re-indexes the library (§”On ingestion”). | . A graph that needs an index and has none is a standing minor finding on the lsi-index Tool, so “needs one and has none” is a fact in the audited record.

4537.title: Epic filing — the qou hierarchy, proposed by evidence
4537.content: The qou project-management skills (todo-manager, session-intent) require every piece of work to sit under a parent work item. lsi:epics proposes that parent for each open work item with no epic, each unmerged branch and each open PR: . | explicit first — a parent: chain that reaches an epic, or a work item id named in a branch’s commit messages (case-insensitive, merge commits excluded); | latent second — cosine to each open epic’s centroid (the epic plus all descendants of every status, each normalised; leave-one-out for the work item being scored). A branch or PR is folded in from its name and commits. | . It prints a calibration line: of the work items already under an epic, how often LSI’s best guess is the current epic (about 59 % against 21 classes, flat across k = 50–250; log-entropy beats tf-idf). Read every proposal in that light. A disputed filing is not a misfiling. A work item filed by symptom (translation catalogues under CI RELIABILITY because they turned main red) may be filed by LSI by subject (TRANSLATION). Both are defensible; which axis an epic means is a decision for the owner, not for the score. Never apply the proposal in bulk. beans update <id> --parent <epic> is done one work item at a time by somebody who read both the work item and the epic.

4539.title: Materialize on demand
4539.content: Skill materialize-on-demand: After bootstrap, a person asks for part of a remote subgraph to be held locally. Check what is already here (cache:index), put a number on the ask before anything is fetched, then run materialize-remote. Eviction is a report, never an act. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links . Bootstrap brings an agent to a working harness. It does not bring the corpus, and must not: a remote source such as IRIS runs to about a million files and hundreds of gigabytes. What arrives is the reference; a person asks, as they come to need it, for parts of subgraphs to be materialized. This skill is that ask. The gates are not here; they are in materialize-remote, once.

4540.title: 1. What is already here
4540.content: bun run cat cache:index # summary and eviction candidates bun run cat cache:index --all # every copy . Read the columns for what they are: . | column | values | what it means | . | size | recorded · measured · directory · absent | measured is the file now, not when it landed. A directory is counted through its parts. absent is not zero. | . | fetched | a date, or not recorded | only the record’s materializedAt | . | last read | not recorded, always | nothing records reads; file access times are not used, because they are often off or reset by a checkout. | . | freshness | fresh · expired · no-expiry · permanent | from freshness(). no-expiry is a finding: a working copy nobody gave a lifetime. | . If what they want is already held and fresh, stop: point them at it.

4541.title: 2. Put a number on the ask BEFORE anything moves
4541.content: Asking must not mean hundreds of gigabytes arrive without a number first. Before calling materialize-remote: . | Name the subset in the source’s own terms: its identifiers, or a subset strategy its descriptor (in the owning layer’s declared sources/, e.g. the IRIS replica’s sources/) supports. | Close it over dependencies if the descriptor says the subset is not self-contained (subsetIsSelfContained: false, mathlib). The size that matters is the closure’s. | State the size and its basis: from the descriptor’s enumeration, or a measured listing. If neither gives a number, say that. The SIZE gate refuses on an unknown, and so should this conversation. | Say what it would add to the cache total from step 1. | . Then ask the person, with the number in front of them.

4542.title: 3. Materialize
4542.content: Run Process_MaterializeRemote. Its five gates decide; this skill does not second-guess them. A refusal leaves the content referenced, with the reason recorded. That is the process working, not failing.

4543.title: 4. Eviction is a report
4543.content: cache:index lists candidates: expired first, then no-expiry working copies, largest first. An archival copy is never a candidate. Nothing is removed by the tool or by you. Show the list with sizes and reasons, and let the person decide (deletion-requires-confirmation).

4545.title: Materializing remote content
4545.content: Skill materialize-remote: Landing remote content locally — the five gates, the three states, and the two purposes. One process, shared by catalogue import and harness bootstrap, plus the refresh that is not a re-import. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Getting started, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Publish extracted statements with source links, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . One process for every caller that lands remote content locally. | caller | remote source | held locally | refresh | . | the IRIS replica | IRIS | selected items | refresh-materialized | . | bootstrap | a harness | the cat-harness checkout | upstream-pins.json | . bootstrap/workflows/initialize-harness.bpmn fetches a harness that is remote content and lands it locally; upstream-pins.json exists because that copy goes stale. Diagrams: materialize-remote.bpmn and refresh-materialized.bpmn. Schema: the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer above this one — named here, not linked). Nothing here restates either — where they disagree, the schema wins and this file is wrong.

4546.title: Ask the purpose FIRST
4546.content: working or archival, before any gate, because three of the five mean different things under each. |   | working | archival | . | what is kept | derived content — sections, OCR | the original bytes | . | retention | expires; re-fetchable | no expiry, by design | . | sourceLoss | unanswered | discharged | . | fixity | not needed | required | . A process that gated first and asked afterwards would be judging a copy whose obligations it did not yet know.

4547.title: The five gates
4547.content: Each is a decision a person makes; none is answerable from a file. A gate that only warns is a gate nobody fails. | Size — what fraction, and what the whole would cost. Refuse when you cannot tell: “three items” with no denominator is not a size answer. | Restrictions — “no restrictions known in context” is a state, not a green light. unknown is never rendered as permitted. | Copyright — per bitstream, and separately for the derived work. LICENSE-CONTENT.md exists here and the ingestion pipeline does not read it. | Retention — what expires this copy. A copy with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one. | Source loss — what survives if the origin goes. Only an archival copy discharges this. Origins do disappear: a regional repository instance can be merged away, taking its handles with it. | .

4548.title: Three states, and no default
4548.content: referenced (it exists, we know where, we hold no bytes) · materialized · unknown. A node that has not declared one is invalid, not unknown — “the author did not say” and “the author said they could not tell” are different facts, and only the second is actionable. A refusal is the process working. The node stays referenced, the graph still knows it exists, and the refusing gate’s basis is recorded so the next agent does not re-litigate it.

4549.title: Refresh is not re-import
4549.content: Three answers, not one: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both. A materialized copy edited in place is not a copy — overwriting it destroys work whose existence was never established; check:materialized-fixity detects it. An archival copy is never refreshed. Re-fetching it discards the state it exists to keep. It gets a fixity check instead — has our copy rotted — which is a different question with a different remedy: restore from backup, never re-download.

4550.title: Before you enumerate anything
4550.content: cat-harness/schemas/library/source-descriptor.ts answers the question that comes before the gates: how to enumerate a corpus and ask it for a subset. Check subsetIsSelfContained first — when it is false (mathlib), close the request over its dependencies before gating, because the size being gated is the closure’s, not the request’s.

The three states (referenced / materialized / unknown) and the five gates are schemas/materialization.ts in folio-assistant-core. Nothing here restates them. i i i i i i i

4553.title: How it connects
4553.content: . | Called by: Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph | Calls: none | Names the materialize-remote skill without calling this process: Refresh materialized remote content — activity-calls-skill-process asks whether each should be a call activity. | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Skill: materialize-remote | Running instances: none recorded | .

4554.doc: Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess
4554.title: Lanes — who acts
4554.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Contributor (human or agent) | user | One task, asked first for a reason: working vs. archival is not just an input to the five gates that follow, it changes what three of them MEAN — an archival copy is the only one that can discharge source loss, and a process that gated before asking this would be judging a copy against obligations it did not yet know applied. | . | Ingestion engine (agent, runs unattended) | ingestion-agent | Runs the five gates in a fixed order and reaches Task_Fetch only after Gateway_Gates finds none of them refused. Before the first gate it resolves the request against the source DESCRIPTOR (Task_Enumerate), because the size being gated is the closure’s, not the request’s — size, restrictions, copyright, retention, source loss — so this lane’s job is not one decision but five independent ones, each of which can send the process to Task_StayRef on its own. It does not get to average them: unknown on any single gate is enough to keep the node referenced rather than materialized. | .

4555.doc: Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess
4555.title: Steps
4555.content: Every one of the 7 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Declare the purpose: working or archivalTask_Purpose | Contributor (human or agent) | materialize-remote | working or archival, and it is asked FIRST because three of the five gates mean different things under each. An archival copy keeps the original bytes, never expires, requires fixity, and is the only thing that discharges sourceLoss; a working copy keeps derived content and discharges none of that. A process that gated first and asked afterwards would be judging a copy whose obligations it did not yet know. | . | Enumerate the source descriptorTask_Enumerate | Ingestion engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | Resolve the request against the source’s descriptor (one per corpus, in the declared sources/ of the layer that owns it, e.g. who-iris/sources/), read against cat-harness/schemas/library/source-descriptor.ts BEFORE any gate. Three things come from it and none may be guessed. (1) Which subset strategies the source supports — supportsSubset(). (2) Whether a subset stands on its own: when subsetIsSelfContained is false (mathlib), the request is closed over its dependencies here, and every gate after this one is asked about the CLOSURE, because a subset that omits what its members depend on is not a smaller corpus, it is one that does not build. (3) What enumerating the whole costs — enumerationCost(), which is undefined when the descriptor has no measured denominator; SIZE then refuses rather than estimates. A source with no descriptor is not an error here: it is an unknown, and SIZE refuses on it. The descriptor is CALLED here rather than restated. | . | Size the take and the wholeTask_Size | Ingestion engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | What is being taken, and what the whole collection would cost. REFUSES when it cannot tell: ‘three items’ with no denominator is not a size answer. 0.7 TB is the measured reason the IRIS import is by reference. | . | Answer the other four gatesTask_AnswerGates | Ingestion engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | Restrictions, copyright, retention and source loss, each answered permitted, refused or unknown. They are four answers to one decision, and Gateway_Gates reads them with size through decisions/materialization-gate.dmn.RESTRICTIONS. ‘No restrictions known in context’ is a STATE, not a green light. GateVerdict is three-valued for this reason alone, and unknown is never rendered as permitted.COPYRIGHT. What the licence permits for THIS bitstream, and separately whether it permits the derivation. LICENSE-CONTENT.md exists in this repository and the ingestion pipeline does not read it.RETENTION. A copy with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one — the same argument bean-blocking makes about a block with no expiry. An ARCHIVAL copy is the exception and it is a specification rather than an omission: freshness() reports it permanent, not no-expiry.SOURCE LOSS. Not hypothetical. The one IRIS record this repository holds carries a handle on iris.wpro.who.int, a regional instance merged into the global one. 4558.title: MCP assembly — many Tools, one service, one namespace
4558.content: Skill mcp-assembly: Compose several Tool nodes into one MCP service — naming, collisions, grouping and versioning. Read when a service will expose more than one tool, or when two layers’ tools land in the same namespace. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . mcp-projection maps one Tool node to one MCP tool. This is what happens when there are several, which is the normal case and where the problems are: a flat namespace shared by tools from a layer, its dependencies, and whatever else the agent has mounted.

4559.title: Naming — the model reads these, so they are an interface
4559.content: An MCP tool name is what a model pattern-matches against when deciding what to call. It is not an identifier that merely has to be unique. <subject>_<verb>, lower snake case. bean_claim, bean_list, folio_render. Subject first, because an agent scanning tools/list is looking for the thing before the action, and because it groups related tools adjacently in a flat list with no grouping mechanism. | Verbs are from a closed set, and a new one needs a reason: list, get, create, update, delete, run, check, sync. bean_fetch beside folio_get costs a model a guess on every call. | Never encode the transport, the vendor or the binary. github_pr_create names a forge in a name a skill is supposed to reach generically; the neutral pr_create with per-forge Tool nodes behind it is the shape skills-and-tools asks for. | Never version in the name. bean_claim_v2 beside bean_claim asks the model to choose, and it will sometimes choose wrong. See versioning below. | .

4560.title: Collisions are refused, not resolved
4560.content: Two Tool nodes projecting to one name is an error at assembly time, not something to paper over by prefixing the loser. ContributionRegistry and GraphTypologyRegistry follow the same rule: automatic disambiguation means the name a caller gets depends on load order, and load order is not something anybody reasons about. Refuse, name both contributors, and make somebody choose. One exception, and it is the diamond case: the identical Tool node reached twice through a dependency graph is a no-op, not a collision. Identical means same id, same io, same invoke — not merely the same name.

4561.title: Prefixing across layers
4561.content: A layer inherits its dependencies’ Tool nodes the same way it inherits their skills. When two different layers contribute a tool of the same name, the collision rule above applies — but the fix is a declared prefix on the contributing layer, not an ad-hoc rename at the consumer: . fa_bean_claim # folio-assistant's qou_bean_claim # the folio's, if it genuinely has its own . A prefix belongs to the layer and is written down once, so the same tool has the same name everywhere it appears. A consumer that renames what it imports produces a namespace nobody else’s documentation matches.

4562.title: Versioning
4562.content: The service is versioned; the tool name is not. A breaking change to a tool’s schema is a version bump on the server, announced in its metadata, not a second tool beside the first. When both must run at once — a migration window — run two servers, not one server with two generations of tool. The agent’s mount configuration then says which it is talking to, which is a place a human can look, rather than the model choosing from a list where both look plausible.

4563.title: Grouping, given MCP has none
4563.content: MCP’s tool list is flat: there is no namespace, no category, no folder. The kg/ grouping this harness uses for skills has no counterpart in the protocol. So the grouping has to survive in two places instead. The name carries it via the subject-first rule — bean_* sort together and read as a family. The description carries the rest: the first clause of tools[].description should make the subject unambiguous without the name, because a model that has truncated or reordered the list is reading descriptions. Do not attempt to recreate grouping with separators (bean/claim, bean.claim). Clients render names literally and some validate them against a restricted character set, so a separator is a portability bug.
