4565.title: MCP contract — the projected service must match what it was projected from
4565.content: Skill mcp-contract: Verify an MCP service’s tools against the Tool nodes and skill declarations they came from — I/O equivalence in both directions. Read before shipping a projected server, and when a tool call fails with an argument the schema said was fine. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . mcp-projection emits a server. This checks the emitted server still agrees with its sources, which is a different activity and needs its own gate: a projector that is correct today drifts the moment a Tool node is edited and nothing re-runs it.

4566.title: What is being checked, and against what
4566.content: Four checks, and they fail in different directions: . |   | source | checked against | . | schema equivalence | ToolDefinition.io | the served inputSchema / outputSchema | . | coverage | the layer’s Tool nodes | what tools/list actually returns | . | satisfaction | ToolDefinition.satisfies | the skills that claim the capability | . | authority | ToolInvocation.by | the role graph — was this actor, in this lane, allowed to run it | . Schema equivalence is not string equality. JSON Schema has several spellings of one constraint, and a generator may legitimately change spelling between versions. Compare accepted instance sets, not serialised text — at minimum: same required keys, same types per key, same enum members, same nullability. A test asserting the JSON blob is byte-identical fails on a harmless zod-to-json-schema upgrade and teaches everyone to re-baseline it without reading, which is worse than having no test. Coverage is the direction that goes quiet. A tool dropped from tools/list does not error — the model simply never calls it, and the capability silently disappears. So the check is: every Tool node with a projectable invoke arm and met requires appears in tools/list, and every listed tool traces back to a node. An unexpected extra is as much a finding as a missing one; it means something is being served that nothing declares. Satisfaction is the KG edge, and it is the one nobody checks. A skill says “claim the item before you work”. satisfies is what says which Tools can do that. If no served tool satisfies a skill the layer ships, an agent will read the skill, find no mechanism, and improvise, which is the failure the skill/Tool separation exists to prevent. Report it; do not fail on it by default, because a skill may legitimately be satisfied by a manual Tool with nothing served.

4567.title: Three states at the check, too
4567.content: . | Agrees — the served tool matches its node. | Deliberately absent — requires unmet, or invoke.mcp only. Expected, and must be reported as why, not merely as absent. | Could not check — the server would not start, tools/list errored, or an io.*.schema reference does not resolve. Never rendered as agreement. This is the same rule check:ci-health follows: a checker that cannot see has not found that nothing is wrong. | .

4568.title: When a call fails but the schema said it was fine
4568.content: The common cause, and worth checking before anything else: the schema describes what the tool accepts, not what the underlying command accepts. A ToolDefinition whose io.inputs was written by hand against an imagined CLI will type-check, project cleanly, serve happily, and fail on invocation. So the contract check is necessary and not sufficient. Equivalence between io and inputSchema proves the projection is faithful; it proves nothing about whether io describes the real tool. That second question is answered by exercising the tool, and a Tool node that has never been called is unverified however green the schema check is — say so rather than implying coverage the check does not have.

4569.title: Status
4569.content: The source side exists; the served side does not. schemas/tools/tool.ts, schemas/tools/tool-types.ts and the Tool nodes under tools/ are real, and bun run cat check:tools does the satisfaction check in this table’s third row: every satisfies resolves to a skill that exists. Schema equivalence and coverage wait on a served projection: the projector exists as a library (mcp-projection §”Status”) but is registered on no running server, so there is no served tools/list to compare against. Because io ports reference a shared $defs document by absolute IRI rather than restating a structure per tool, “these two Tools accept the same input” is identity rather than a structural comparison. That is what makes the equivalence check in row one tractable when it is written.

4571.title: Adopting a methodology, and choosing between them
4571.content: Skill methodology-adoption: How a named external methodology enters the knowledge graph, and how an agent picks which one applies. Read before following a judgement method, before adopting a new one, and before writing a house method instead of adopting one. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Options analysis, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, SWOT situation analysis, Wireframe design review, Questionnaire wireframe review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A methodology is somebody else’s work, adopted whole. It is not a house process with a citation bolted on. The graph carries them as a distinct kind so that adopting one, replacing one and removing one are all ordinary operations. Methodologies are parallel ways of achieving the same process, chosen by context; each is formalised on its own and kept independent, so that other skills can incorporate it as a sub-graph.

4572.title: Parallel, not composable
4572.content: Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them. A composite — this one’s vocabulary, that one’s record, a third one’s filter — is a house method that cites nobody, and it inherits none of their authority while claiming all of it. So: pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.

4573.title: Choosing which applies
4573.content: First: is this a judgement, or a process? . Ask before the ladder. The ladder below is about how to decide something; a request for a change is not yet a decision but work needing agreed requirements before anything is built. Sent down the ladder, it lands on the catch-all rung and produces an options analysis for a question nobody has framed yet. Is somebody asking for a change, such that requirements have to be agreed before it is built? . If yes, the question is who is asking, and does the answer depend on what a folio says? . | A change to the platform’s own capability — a tool, a schema, a pipeline, a skill, a gate — raised by somebody building the tooling, whose answer does not depend on any folio’s subject matter → the software-development process methodology. | Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, tied to a folio’s domain → the stakeholder requirements methodology. | . Both answer request → agreed requirements, so they are parallel and must not be blended — the refusal below applies to this pair first and hardest. Which is which is stated in each one’s applies-when, not here, for the reason in §”Why this skill does not name them”. If no — the change is agreed and the question is how to decide something within it — continue to the ladder. Then the ladder . Ask in this order. The first yes decides. | Do the criteria recur, with the same inputs having to produce the same answer? → the computable methodology. A one-off tabled as if it recurs asserts a repeatability it does not have. | Is the question the certainty of a body of evidence behind a recommendation? → the evidence-grading methodology. Note this is about evidence, not about a design choice that happens to be uncertain. | Is the context a work item recording a decision? → the decision-record methodology. It constrains the record, not the method, so it composes with (1) or (4) rather than competing. | Otherwise — a one-off choice among candidate options → the decision-analysis methodology. | . If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence. Say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit: either is how a house method gets in. Why this skill does not name them . Naming each methodology here would couple this skill to the set, and the set is meant to be extractable: a methodology can be lifted out, or replaced, without a prose edit here. So the declared set is the contents of the methodology graph, read from the layer’s declaration. Ask for it; do not remember it.

4574.title: Node, skill, or both?
4574.content: An adopted methodology can produce up to two artefacts: . | you are writing | it is a node in the methodology graph | it is a skill | . | what the method IS — its vocabulary, its constraints, what it refuses | ✅ | ❌ | . | how to PERFORM it here — the extension element, the gate, the procedure | ❌ | ✅ | . | a house process with no external origin | ❌ | ✅ — and do not dress it as an adoption | . Most adoptions produce both, and the split is the same every time: the node is the method, the skill is this platform’s application of it. The skill names the node and does not restate it, because two files carrying one definition is two copies free to drift. Three worked cases: . | raci — both. The four letters and the one-Accountable rule are the method (node); reading R from the BPMN lane, the cat-harness.processes:raci element and check:raci are this platform’s application (skill). | crdm — both (methodologies/crdm.md). PHII’s three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, swimlane Task Flow Diagrams, and PATH’s activity-linked requirement structure are the external method (node, backed by library/phii-2023-crdm, library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, and library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm); agentic facilitation, 7-dimension code impact analysis, work-item decomposition, and pull-request merge sign-off are this platform’s adaptation (crdm-requirements-workflow and crdm-requirements-template). | swot — both. | . A methodology in use with no node is invisible to the graph: check:methodology-evidence and every other reader of the methodology graph count nodes, not skills.

4575.title: Adopting a new one — the ingestion process
4575.content: . | Establish it is external and named. A methodology has an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body. If it has none, it is a house process — write it as a skill and do not dress it as an adoption. | Render it faithfully, and say where the rendering stops. The file carries what the method says, not a summary of what we liked. Where this platform adopts part of a method and refuses part, both halves are stated with the reason — a silent omission misrepresents the standard. | Declare its applicability. applies-when in the front matter, phrased so the selection question above can reach it, and saying what it is not for. | Place it by ownership, not by convenience. A domain-neutral method belongs to the harness; a domain method belongs to the repo that owns the domain. The separation plan decides, and the placement must make extraction literal — the directory lifts out, its declaration entry goes with it, and nothing else moves. | Declare the directory. A methodology outside a declared directory is invisible to every tool that reads the graph. | State its refusals. The part of a method a platform must not do is as load-bearing as the part it follows, and it is the part a later agent will breach first. | Ingest the source and cite it as evidence. origin names the work; evidence: library/<bib-slug> points at a copy a reader can open from this checkout. Use literature-search to find it and library-ingestion to bring it in. Where the source cannot be fetched, that is an outcome to report — a located-but-unreachable document, never a missing one — and the node keeps its origin with no evidence until somebody closes the gap. | .

4576.title: Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools
4576.content: A source that presents a method through an implementation is presenting two things, and only one of them is the methodology. Render the method first, then decide which tools — existing or to be added — this platform should use to perform it. A node that adopted the source’s tool stack would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method, and it could never be falsified: the tools would work and the method would never be examined. hybrid-llm-deterministic is the worked case. Its source demonstrates the method in one tool with one model and one expression language; the node renders the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards and the bounded-truncation technique, and §”Where this rendering stops” names every tool it declined to adopt and why. The method survives replacing all of them, which is the test of whether you extracted a method at all. Ask it as: what would still be true if they had built it differently? What survives is the methodology. What does not is their engineering, and it belongs in the skill if anywhere — where this platform’s own tool choices already live. And say what the source does NOT establish. A demonstration is not an evaluation. Where a paper shows an approach working once, with no baseline and no measurement, the node records that no performance claim rests on it. Doing otherwise manufactures a finding the authors did not make — the same failure as §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”, arriving through a citation instead.

4577.title: An origin nobody can open is not evidence
4577.content: A methodology’s justification is being somebody else’s named, external work, so its origin must resolve to a source a reader can open. bun run cat check:methodology-evidence is the axis that makes this visible, and test/results/methodology-evidence.qa-results.json is where it is recorded. It reports and does not gate on a missing source: whether a methodology whose source nobody can open may still be used is the owner’s call, and a gate failing on the whole corpus at once would be switched off. It does fail on front matter that does not validate, and on an evidence pointing at a bib-slug no library holds, because a citation that claims to resolve and does not is worse than none. The evidence is an input to SELECTION, not only to adoption. options-analysis.bpmn’s A_CheckEvidence reads it before the chosen methodology is applied. Adoption happens once; selection happens at every decision, and a source can stop being reachable in between. A contested origin is recorded as contested. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: the usual attribution is repeated everywhere and its own source says no academic reference supports it, so the node declines to name an inventor: flattening that into a fact would carry the authority of a citation while resting on nothing.

4578.title: Refusals
4578.content: . | Never blend two methodologies into one procedure. Parallel means parallel. | Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A citation with no rendered method is an appeal to authority that no reader can check. | Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform adopts the structure and refuses the arithmetic: a total reads as a measurement, and the weights were invented. This is the same rule as never quoting a count from prose as though it were evidence. | Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. Whichever methodology was used, the alternatives and why they lost are part of the output — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted. | Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched. Read the source, or say you read it through another and mark each attribution second-hand. See literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. | .

4586.title: Remote-mount a dependency
4586.content: Process_MountDependency · strict · 6 step(s) . Laying a harness — and every layer it needs — down from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories, with a lock that says exactly what arrived. You are in this process whenever a folio or harness needs a layer it does not hold: a downstream folio built on a content layer above this harness, a separated layer whose foundation lives elsewhere. The downstream names the harness, its repository and a 40-character pin as a source.remote layer in its root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration, never both); everything else is read from the harness’s own declaration at that pin. Every layer reached ends in one of three states — mounted, missing, could-not-determine — and the third is never reported as the first. The skill is remote-mount. i i i i i i

4592.title: Mount a declared subgraph
4592.content: Process_MountSubgraph · strict · 6 step(s) . Making a declared subgraph’s content available at its declared path, whatever its content source. You are in this process whenever a step is about to read or write the contents of a declared subgraph — beans, todos, fsh-guts, or any directory a declaration names. The source is resolved once, by declaredSubgraph (schemas/kg/harness-config.ts) through resolveSubgraphSource (schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts): the layer config’s subgraphSources override by id, then the entry’s source, then a legacy storage, then the directory default. The gateway is on the source KIND, and its flows are the only places the kinds differ. A directory subgraph is already where its path says, and writing it is an ordinary commit. A branch subgraph is mounted from the declared branch’s tip into its path, and written back by splicing onto the tip without force. A remote subgraph is another repository’s tree at a pinned commit, laid down by Process_MountDependency and read-only here. An npm subgraph is an npm package or tarball retrieved via kg-retrieve-npm or npm. A kind with no flow here is refused. i i i i i i

4598.title: Multi-locale translation
4598.content: Process_MultiLocaleTranslation · advisory · 13 step(s) . Translate one or more layers into several locales at once, as a team: one source-language lead, one translator per locale, an untainted round trip, and the owner’s merge window. The result is unofficial, on main, and kept current by a watcher. You are in this process when more than one locale is being produced from the same source at the same time. translation-workflow is the machine half for one catalogue and human-translation-workflow is the path to an official, signed-off translation; this process is the team around them. It extracts ONCE: every locale starts from the same templates, merged to main in one source PR before any locale begins, and no translator re-extracts. Each locale then lands as its own PR to main, never into the source branch, and a source PR’s branch receives nothing after it merges. Two things are never done in a translation: fixing the source (a source-text error is reported as one issue to the lead), and editing a FHIR resource inline (terms go into one CodeSystem supplement per locale). Officiality is not decided here: every catalogue is written unofficial, and a person makes it official through human-translation-workflow. i i i i i i i i i i i i i

4604.title: normative-statements
4604.content: Named by: Authoring a document . Carry a recommendation, requirement or rule in a document folio — the thing an L1 health-policy guidance note, a standard, or a terms-of-reference document exists to state.

4605.title: The problem this addresses
4605.content: A normative statement is the block readers cite, implementers trace to, and reviewers sign off individually, so it needs a label, a stable identity and a place in the dependency graph. It is not a theorem: nothing proves it, and its authority is the issuing body’s.

4606.title: What to do
4606.content: Use a recommendation block: one statement per block, with a label, a title, and its strength as a code. // folio/<slug>/<chapter>/rec-cold-chain-audit.ts import { recommendation } from "@folio/schemas/builders"; export default recommendation({ label: "rec:cold-chain-audit", title: "Audit the cold chain quarterly", strength: { list: "grade-recommendation-strength", code: "conditional" }, uses: ["rec:scope", "prose:cold-chain-terms"], about: ["hi:cold-chain-management"], }); . The block’s .md holds the statement itself, and its label becomes the anchor every cross-reference targets ([see](#rec:cold-chain-audit)). | label: a prefix of your folio’s own choosing, kept consistent across the corpus. The platform reserves none: the kind’s node says prefixEnforced: false. rec: is recognised, never required. Pick a prefix once and write it down in the folio’s own AGENTS.md. | title: the short form the document’s index and any cross-reference will show. | strength: a code in a declared code list, not free text. Core declares two: . | grade-recommendation-strength: strong or conditional, GRADE as the WHO handbook for guideline development applies it; | rfc2119-requirement-level: must, must-not, should, should-not, may, from BCP 14. | . A folio whose issuing body grades differently declares its own folio-code-list/v1 in its code-lists/ rather than editing these. The check is “resolves in the scheme”: strengthFinding in folio-assistant-core/schemas/recommendation-strength.ts. State the strength in the prose too, in the issuing body’s own words, because readers read the prose. | uses[]: the blocks a reader must have read to act on this one. That means definitions of terms it uses, the scope statement it sits under, and the evidence summary it rests on. This is what makes “what else changes if this recommendation changes?” answerable. | about[]: optional labels of the DAK health-interventions this recommendation is about. It is a link, not a merge: the two vocabularies stay separate, and nothing in this one depends on the DAK adapter. | . Keep one statement per block. A block holding three recommendations cannot be cited, reviewed, superseded or traced individually, and splitting it later means renumbering everything that referenced it. Converting a labelled prose block. Change the builder call from prose to recommendation and add strength. The label, title, uses[] and .md stay as they are, so no reference breaks.

4607.title: When the statement comes from a source
4607.content: A normative statement or requirement that a SOURCE makes is already a node in that source’s L1 entry (l1-document-ingestion, “Requirements and normative statements”), with the source’s own number in meta.source_number. Cite that node from the block’s meta.source, and keep the source’s number in the title or prose. Do not mint a new id that looks like the source’s: a reader cannot tell the two apart.

4608.title: What not to do
4608.content: . | Do not use definition. It is a math kind: its lean field is required, so the block will not validate in a document folio at all. | Do not use a bare prose block. It validates, but no criterion can tell it is normative. | Do not use theorem or proposition for a good-practice statement. They are outside this profile and content_profile_check rejects them. | Do not encode the recommendation number in the label alone. Numbers are renumbered between editions; the label must survive that. Put the published number in the title or the prose. | .

4610.title: NPM Knowledge Graph Distribution
4610.content: Skill npm-kg-distribution: Package, release, distribute, and retrieve Knowledge Graphs using npm tooling and tarballs: declare package.json as an authored pre-packaging asset in the Knowledge Graph, build .tgz packages via bun pm pack, record publications as folio-binary-release/v1 state documents hosted on GitHub binary releases, and retrieve remote Knowledge Graphs using npm install for both unhydrated source graph and hydrated materialized graph views. Named by: Mount a declared subgraph . Knowledge Graphs in the folio ecosystem can be distributed and consumed as npm packages — packaged tarballs (.tgz) containing either the authored source graphs, pre-compiled hydrated graph views, or both. |   | where | . | the packaging tool | pack-tarball (bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts) | . | the retrieval tool | kg-retrieve-npm (bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts) | . | the release schema | schemas/sdlc/binary-release.ts (folio-binary-release/v1) | . | asset verification | cat-harness-tools/scripts/check-declared-assets.ts | . | related skills | remote-mount, kg-export, package-release (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc), kg-subscription | .

4611.title: 1. package.json as an authored pre-packaging asset in the KG
4611.content: A file that is not declared in <instance>.json is a file no check verifies, so package.json is declared as an authored Knowledge Graph asset that defines package identity, exports, dependencies, scripts, and the tarball inclusion whitelist (files array). Each layer that publishes an npm package declares package.json under assets in its <instance>.json: . { "id": "npm-manifest", "src": "package.json", "role": "package-manifest", "title": "package.json", "description": "The npm pre-packaging source manifest declaring package identity, exports, dependencies, scripts, and tarball whitelist." } . Why declare it under assets . | Verification at commit and mount time: check:declared-assets verifies that every declared asset exists on disk. | Remote mount resolution: remote-mount.ts and mount-from-lock.ts check out, lay down, and verify declared layer assets so that mounted dependencies carry their package identity. | Single source of packaging truth: package.json’s files field acts as the authoritative whitelist for what is bundled into the distribution tarball. | .

4612.title: 2. Packaging via bun pm pack & folio-binary-release/v1
4612.content: An npm package is built as a compressed tarball (.tgz) using bun pm pack: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts --root <instance-root> --destination <out-dir> . The packaging process: . | Reads the authored package.json to verify package identity (name and version). | Invokes bun pm pack --destination <dir>, which respects .npmignore and the files array in package.json. | Computes the exact file size in bytes and the SHA-256 digest of the .tgz tarball. | Generates and validates a folio-binary-release/v1 state node recording the release event. | . The folio-binary-release/v1 state node . A published tarball is represented in the Knowledge Graph as a folio-binary-release/v1 document (schemas/sdlc/binary-release.ts). A release record captures the publication event, never the binary payload itself: . { "$schema": "folio-binary-release/v1", "release": { "id": "cat-harness-v1.0.0", "version": "1.0.0", "tag": "v1.0.0", "publishedAt": "2026-10-08T18:30:00.000Z", "url": "https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/releases/tag/v1.0.0" }, "origin": { "kind": "github-release", "repository": "litlfred/cat-harness" }, "assets": [ { "name": "cat-harness-1.0.0.tgz", "bytes": 524288, "digest": { "algorithm": "sha256", "digest": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855", "verifiedAt": "2026-10-08T18:30:00.000Z" }, "fetchedFrom": "https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/releases/download/v1.0.0/cat-harness-1.0.0.tgz", "contentType": "application/gzip", "disposition": "published" } ] } . Key invariants: . | Never the bytes: The schema is .strict(). Content and blobs are rejected. | Verifiable fixity: SHA-256 digests and byte counts are required. | Provenance: fetchedFrom must state where the binary can be retrieved. | Dispositions: An asset’s state after publication is tracked (published, superseded, deleted-before-deploy). Any deliberate removal must provide a dispositionReason. | .

4613.title: 3. GitHub binary releases hosting .tgz tarballs
4613.content: Published Knowledge Graph tarballs are hosted on GitHub Releases: . | The git tag (v<version>) marks the exact source commit in the repository. | The .tgz package is uploaded as a release asset attached to the GitHub release. | The release URL follows the canonical scheme: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/v<version>/<package>-<version>.tgz | . This provides: . | High availability via CDN. | Immutability tied to the release tag. | Checkable fixity against the folio-binary-release/v1 document. | .

4614.title: 4. npm install as an alternative retrieval Tool for remote KGs
4614.content: Remote Knowledge Graphs can be retrieved into a workspace or consumer environment through three distinct mechanisms, each serving a specific architectural need: . | tool / mechanism | transport | granularity | best when | . | remote-mount | Git shallow blobless fetch at 40-char SHA | Transitive dependency closure of declared directories | Developing against dependencies whose TypeScript/code is imported directly | . | kg:subscribe | Substrate snapshot via HTTP | Selective subgraphs and on-demand assets through 5 gates | Consuming large external reference datasets (WHO IRIS, FHIR) | . | kg-retrieve-npm (npm install) | NPM package tarball (.tgz) via registry or GitHub release | Pre-packaged bundle with whitelisted files and optional pre-built views | Distributing versioned Knowledge Graph packages with immediate consumption | . Unhydrated source graph vs. Hydrated materialized graph views . When an npm package distributes a Knowledge Graph, it can provide two distinct graph views: . 1. Unhydrated source graph view . The authored source files as they exist in the repository: . | package.json pre-packaging manifest. | <instance>.json layer declaration. | Authored source directories: skills/ (markdown instructions), schemas/ (Zod/TS definitions), processes/ (BPMN diagrams), methodologies/, text-based metadata. | Binary media assets excluded: PNGs, JPGs, PDFs and figures under library/ and uploads/ are excluded via .npmignore during unhydrated packaging, keeping the base package compact (~2-5 MB). | Packaged as <package>-<version>.tgz. | Ideal for agents and developers authoring new knowledge, extending skills, or compiling the graph locally. | . 2. Hydrated materialized graph view . The complete, materialized Knowledge Graph artifacts and binary assets: . | Binary media assets included: Losslessly optimized library PNGs, figures, and covers. | Named subgraph JSON-LD (docs/subgraph/<instance>/<path>/index.jsonld). | Fully dereferenced hydrated JSON-LD (index.hydrated.jsonld). | Metadata indexes, RDF N-Quads, and pre-computed search indices. | Packaged via pack-tarball --hydrated as <package>-<version>.hydrated.tgz. | Ideal for read-only consumers, visualizers, semantic search engines, and portal deployments that require immediate access without installing compilation toolchains or running offline export pipelines. | . 3. The subgraph index package — one per pin . A third, narrow package carries a pin’s subgraph index files and nothing else: <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>, built by the subgraph-index-package Tool through pack-tarball and released as subgraph-index-<sha> on every push to main. A hydrated remote mount reads it; see remote-mount §”Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package”. Using kg-retrieve-npm . To retrieve and inspect a remote Knowledge Graph tarball or package: . # Retrieve and inspect both graph views from a tarball bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz # Retrieve and verify integrity against a folio-binary-release/v1 document bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --release path/to/release.json # Retrieve only the unhydrated source graph view into a target directory bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --view unhydrated --destination ./deps/my-kg # Retrieve only the hydrated materialized graph view bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/kg-retrieve-npm.ts path/to/package.tgz --view hydrated --destination ./static-kg . When verified against a folio-binary-release/v1 document, any mismatch in byte size or SHA-256 digest immediately refuses the package, preventing corrupted or tampered graph data from entering the consumer environment.

4616.title: Opening brief — brief the topic before you touch anything
4616.content: Skill opening-brief: Brief a work item or a topic BEFORE touching anything: what you are doing and why it is worth doing, what you already know and with what provenance, how you plan to do it and what would falsify the approach. Scales with irreversibility, not line count. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Options analysis, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, SWOT situation analysis, Wireframe design review, Questionnaire wireframe review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Record agent step, Review-log watch . This skill governs what you say before the work; turn-reporting.md (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) governs what you say during and after it; todo-manager.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) keeps the work item mechanics.

4617.title: Opening brief
4617.content: Claiming a work item records the work. Briefing it is what makes the work resumable. Both are required, and the brief comes first — before the first tool call, in the chat, not in the commit. AGENTS.md §”Opening a bean or a topic” states the rule and when it applies. This is the shape. When it applies — proportionality, so this does not become ceremony . The trigger is irreversibility and surprise, not line count. | A one-line fix with an obvious route needs no brief. Say what you are doing and do it. | Anything touching a shipped gate, a shared artefact, a formal declaration with consumers, or a number a reader sees — brief it. | Anything where you expect to be wrong some of the time — brief it, and say where you expect to be wrong. Research is the case this is most valuable for and most often skipped, on the grounds that the outcome is unknown. The unknown outcome is the reason to write down the route, not a reason to skip it. | . Why it is a rule and not a style preference . Sessions end mid-thread. Containers are reclaimed, context windows fill, a branch is picked up days later by an agent with none of the reasoning that produced it. The work item body and the commit are durable; the chain of inference that made them sensible is not, unless it is written down at the point where it was still obvious. An agent resuming cold should be able to read the brief and continue — not reconstruct its predecessor’s rabbit hole first. It catches wrong work before it is done rather than after. A route stated in advance can be corrected by the author in one line. The same route discovered in a finished diff costs a review cycle and, often, a revert. It is the same discipline as the question frame in interaction-modality §4.1, applied to work instead of decisions: a terse start, like a terse question, makes the author go and find context the agent already had. The four parts . 1. The problem, stated for someone who was not here. Expand every identifier on first use. Not “fixing qou-93hu” but “bean qou-93hu — the CriticalExponent conjecture carrier, whose only field is (3 * 4 : ℕ) = 12, a closed numeral identity with no exponent variable in it, so the class constrains nothing.” . 2. What you know, and how you know it. Every number with its provenance: . | provenance | how to say it | . | measured this session, on this tree | “measured just now: 22 of 22 seeded, 0 missed” | . | measured this session, on a DIFFERENT tree | “grepped 0 on claude/x before branching — not re-run here” | . | carried from a prior session | “recorded 2026-08-24 as 43 drifted; not re-measured” | . | asserted by a work item or a doc | “bean qou-q7lf says X — unverified” | . The last row is the one that bites hardest. A sibling’s work item is not a primary source, and neither is a source file’s ## Status note; both go stale, and a specific, recent, confidently-worded work item is exactly the kind that gets believed. “Measured this session” is not the safe case. A measurement is scoped to the TREE it was taken on, and git switch invalidates every earlier one without saying so. The number is real, recent, and yours; only the tree underneath it moved. So say which tree, and re-run anything load-bearing after a branch change — the re-run costs one command and it is the same command. Part 2 includes the result of the collision review in coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Starting new work”: the siblings that overlap, or “no overlap found” and what you checked. 3. The route and the gate. How you plan to do it, what you will verify against, and what would falsify the approach. A plan with no failure mode is not a plan; it is an intention. If the gate is a script, name it and its expected output. 4. What you are NOT doing. The adjacent defect you are leaving, the scope you decline to widen into, the thing you will flag rather than fix. Stating it up front is what stops it becoming either silent scope creep or a silent omission — and it puts the scope call where it can still be argued with, which is before the diff. Briefing a sibling or a subagent — pass interaction-modality on (STRICT) . When a coordinating session writes a brief to launch a child session (create_session, send_message) or a background subagent (Agent, invoke_subagent), the brief is the child’s only prompt until it reads the graph. A child whose brief omits how to ask the owner will default to asking in plain prose when it hits a permission wall or a design call. Every sibling brief and subagent prompt written by a coordinating session MUST carry the interaction-modality contract explicitly: . | If the child can reach the person directly (a sibling session with its own chat surface): every question to the owner goes out twice, in order — first the full question in chat (context, what differs, every identifier expanded, at most four numbered or lettered options with pros, cons, downstream impact and reversibility, recommended option first and marked (Recommended), and the stated default on silence), and second the tappable card (AskUserQuestion, request_decision, ask_question, or post_widget) carrying the same option labels. Never ask in prose alone, and never ask the person to type. | If the child is a background subagent or a sibling running beside a live discussion: it does not ask the person in prose either; it returns any owner-facing decision to the coordinating session in the hand-back-to-discussion schema format so the coordinator presents both the full chat block and the tappable card. | Pass it on: if the child itself spawns a helper or a subagent, its brief to that child must carry the same interaction-modality block. | . Before you offer options, check whether it is already ruled (STRICT) . Part two of the brief is what do I already know, with each measurement’s provenance. This is the half that gets skipped, because an unsettled question is more interesting than a settled one and nothing in a checkout announces that a decision exists. Presenting options for a settled question is worse than presenting none. It reopens a decision, spends the owner’s attention on it a second time, and the options offered will not be the ones already weighed. Four places to look, in this order: . | The proposals — the design corpus. They live in the docs/ of the layer whose stub needs them; today that is cat-harness/docs/proposals/ (opt-in cat-harness.proposals), and its index.md is where to start. Resolve the directory rather than remembering this sentence — a stub’s docs/ is where its proposals are, and this path is an example of the rule, not the rule. | The owner’s rulings, in work items and in the declarations that quote them verbatim. A _comment field in a *.json is frequently where a decision was recorded, because that is where it had to be obeyed. | The skill that owns the area — and read it, rather than recalling it. | The commit history — git log -S "<symbol>" over the file you are about to change, and a beans list | grep <topic> that does not filter to open items. A decision that shipped is invisible to every instrument that looks for pending ones — and a recent one is exactly when you are most confident your own reading is current. One git log -S answers it. | . Cite what you read, never what you remember. A half-remembered line used as an authority is the fake-reference failure activity-names-skill exists to prevent, one level up: it is unfalsifiable by the reader, because it sounds like something this repository would say. Worked example . Starting qou-93hu — the CriticalExponent §3b-cond hypothesis class in lean/QOU/AlgebraicSubstrate/ConditionalClasses.lean. The problem. Its single field is alpha_three_eq_four : (3 * 4 : ℕ) = 12 — a closed numeral identity with the values already substituted in, so no exponent variable occurs in it and rfl proves it whatever the physics. Four sibling carriers in the same file are vacuous too, but they are at least the right shape (parameter-quantified inequalities); this one has no quantifier and no free variable at all. What I know. Measured this session: bound as [C] in 5 files; the probe baseline records it proved-vacuous; the class’s own docstring already claims “α = 4/3”, so the target value is not something I need to invent. Not measured: whether any downstream proof depends on the field’s current type. Route. Make α a class parameter — class CriticalExponent (α : ℝ) : Prop where alpha_eq : α = 4/3. A Prop class cannot carry data, so α must be a parameter, not a field. Gate: lean-direct exit 0 on all three affected modules, plus a content probe proving ¬ CriticalExponent 2 — because inhabitability at 4/3 alone would not show the class constrains anything. Falsifier: if ¬ CriticalExponent 2 will not go through, the encoding is not doing what I claim and I stop. Not doing. The other four carriers need analytic setup their docstrings only gesture at — the author’s mathematics, not a cleanup. Also leaving the separate CriticalExponent in core-levi-form.lean, a different carrier in a different namespace. ~200 words, and it would have let a reader stop the work, redirect it, or pick it up cold. What a thin brief looks like, and why it fails . Starting qou-93hu — fixing CriticalExponent. Names the work item and nothing else. It does not say the field is a closed numeral identity with no exponent variable in it, so a reader cannot tell whether this is cosmetic or load-bearing; it does not say the class signature changes, so nobody can warn that every binder in two consumer modules moves with it; and it does not say what “fixed” will be checked against, so the agent is free to declare victory on a compile. Each of those omissions is a place the author could have intervened for the cost of reading one sentence. The failure this prevents . An agent that has spent an hour inside a problem writes in the private vocabulary it built along the way, and a reader — the author, or the next agent — has to reconstruct that vocabulary before evaluating anything. The brief is written at the one moment when the agent still knows which parts are non-obvious, because it has just finished finding them out. Cheapest correct move when you do not want to spend the words: do not start the topic. A task you cannot brief is one you have not understood well enough to begin. The brief’s durable form is the PR description. Once the work exists, pr-description (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) answers the same questions for a reader who arrives after it.

4619.title: Options analysis
4619.content: Process_OptionsAnalysis · strict · 5 step(s) . A decision reached by a NAMED methodology, with its rejected options recorded. Called as a subprocess, never run on its own. WHEN IT APPLIES: the trigger is opening-brief’s — IRREVERSIBILITY AND SURPRISE, not size. A reversible choice needs no subprocess; an irreversible one cannot skip it. A subprocess fired on every decision becomes ceremony, and ceremony is how a gate stops being read. WHY IT IS ONE SUBPROCESS AND NOT A BRANCH PER METHODOLOGY: the methodologies are parallel tracks selected by context, and the selection is a judgement made inside A_Select rather than a gateway. A gateway per methodology would assert the choice is computable from data, which is the claim dmn says to make only when the criteria recur. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it does not decide. It produces the options, their trade-offs and a recommendation; the decision and its authorisation belong to whoever owns the calling step. i i i i i

4621.title: Lanes — who acts
4621.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Business analyst | business-analyst | This lane’s deliverable is the recommendation together with the rejected options — a rejected option with no record is a dead end the next agent walks back into — but it never authorises anything; A_Record hands both to whoever called the subprocess, and the decision stays theirs. 4622.title: Steps
4622.content: Every one of the 5 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Frame the decision and check the triggerA_Frame | Business analyst | opening-brief | One sentence naming the KIND of thing being chosen, not the options — “which cache strategy”, never “A or B”. Then the trigger: is this irreversible, or would the answer surprise someone? If neither, say so and stop; the calling step decides without this subprocess. Stopping here is a correct outcome, not a skipped step. | . | Select the methodology by contextA_Select | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | Ask the selection question in order, first yes decides: do the criteria RECUR with the same inputs having to produce the same answer; is this the CERTAINTY of a body of evidence behind a recommendation; is the context a BEAN recording a decision; otherwise a one-off choice among candidates. If none fits, that is a finding — say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit.The declared set is the contents of the methodology graph. Ask for it; do not remember it. | . | Check the selected methodology’s evidence baseA_CheckEvidence | Business analyst | literature-search | Before applying a methodology, establish that the thing being applied is what it claims to be. A methodology is adopted because it is somebody else’s named, external work; this step checks that the origin it cites resolves to a source in a declared library, and reads the methodology-evidence QA sidecar for it.WHY THE CHECK IS HERE AND NOT AT ADOPTION. Adoption happens once; selection happens every time a decision is made. A source that was reachable when the methodology was adopted can stop being so, and a methodology adopted before this axis existed was never checked at all. Measured 2026-09-22: six methodologies cited an origin and NONE had that source in any library, so every selection made until then rested on an unverifiable citation.WHAT A GAP DOES AND DOES NOT DO. A missing source does NOT block the decision, and this step has no branch that stops the process — that would make a documentation gap into an outage, and the owner decides whether an unbacked methodology may still be used. It does two things: it runs literature-search to try to close the gap, and it puts the evidence state into the record A_Record writes, so a reader can tell a decision made on a verified method from one made on a citation nobody could follow.The third state is the one that matters. “Source ingested”, “source located but unreachable from here” and “no source found” are three different facts, and literature-search exists largely to stop the middle one being reported as the last. | . | Apply it, and state each option’s trade-offsA_Apply | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | Follow the selected methodology as written — adopted whole, not blended with another. At least two real options: one option is not a choice, and a straw option is worse than a short list because it makes the analysis look thorough while narrowing it.Never quantify the comparison to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform takes the structure and refuses the arithmetic: the weights are invented and a total reads as a measurement. | . | Record the chosen option AND the rejected onesA_Record | Business analyst | decision-audit | The rejected options and why they lost are part of the output, not an appendix. A rejected option with no record is a dead end nobody marked, and the next agent walks into it — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted.In a bean context the form is MADR’s. Which methodology was followed is named here, so a reader can check the method rather than take the conclusion. | .

4623.title: Decisions
4623.content: Every one of the 1 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Irreversible or surprising?GW_Trigger | A_Frame has always ENDED with this question — “is this irreversible, or would the answer surprise someone? If neither, say so and stop; the calling step decides without this subprocess. Stopping here is a correct outcome, not a skipped step.” Until this gateway existed, the diagram gave it NO WAY TO STOP: A_Frame’s only outgoing edge went to A_Select, so the prose promised a branch the model did not have.Found by adding the second caller, not by reading. With one caller the straight line looked fine; wiring editing-hci-validation made every write in that process run all four activities, and its corpus-gate tests failed with “Task_RecordDecision is not enabled. Enabled now: A_Frame.” That is the ceremony this process’s own documentation refuses — “a subprocess fired on every decision becomes ceremony, and ceremony is how a gate stops being read” — and it was unreachable as a criticism while the subprocess had a single caller.DELIBERATELY NOT DMN-BACKED, unlike the gateways that are. Irreversibility and surprise are judged, not computed: dmn says to claim computability only when the criteria recur with the same inputs having to produce the same answer, and “would this surprise someone” does not. So the outcome is supplied by whoever is at the step, exactly as Gateway_EditorDecision takes one. | yes → Select the methodology by contextno → Trigger not met — the caller decides without an analysis | .

4630.title: pcf-consent
4630.content: | Skill pcf-consent: Model IHE Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF 1.1.0, Trial Implementation) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use) resources referenced by canonical URL only, translate PCF Basic and Additional PurposeOfUse Consents plus the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets into W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policies (consentToOdrl()), and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown) across decide() / permits(), odrl:obtainConsent duties, IHE ITI-108 Consent Registry reads, and PROV-O decision records citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . Named by: Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review . Skill id: pcf-consent · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Layer: fhir-harness · Modules: schemas/pcf-consent.ts (consentToOdrl, decide, evaluatePcfPolicy, PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS), schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts (findAccessConsents, Iti108ConsentClient), schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts. Model patient privacy consent directives in FHIR Implementation Guides, translate them into W3C ODRL 2.2 policies, and evaluate three-valued access-control decisions (permit | deny | unknown). Standards and scope: . | Specifications: IHE IT Infrastructure Technical Framework Supplement — Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) 1.1.0 (Trial Implementation, 2023-08-04) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use, FMG maturity level 2). | Profiles: IHE PCF Basic (IHE.PCF.consentBasic) and Additional PurposeOfUse (IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate: extended HL7 PurposeOfUse codes and nested provision exceptions). The translator also handles IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced security-label sensitivity tags when declared. | Referenced by canonical URL only: never copy or re-author IHE PCF StructureDefinitions or ValueSets in an IG; pin the upstream packages in sushi-config.yaml and reference IHE profiles and value sets by their canonical URLs. | No IUA claim: do not claim conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA), and do not profile ITI-71 / ITI-103 OAuth token exchange; HTTP Authorization headers on ITI-108 reads are passed through opaque to the transport. | Trust-anchor neutral: any consent-bearing workflow or verifiable link depends on an abstract trust anchor (a national PKI, a regional federation, did:web, the Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN), …); none is hardcoded. | .

4631.title: 1. Model — Authoring IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent in a FHIR IG
4631.content: 1.1 Package dependencies in sushi-config.yaml . An IG that profiles, instantiates, or references IHE PCF consent directives or Verifiable Health Links pins the upstream IHE packages in sushi-config.yaml and references their artefacts by canonical URL only: . dependencies: ihe.iti.pcf: id: ihe_iti_pcf uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.pcf version: 1.1.0 ihe.iti.vhl: id: ihe_iti_vhl uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.vhl version: 1.0.0-comment . FHIR R4 Consent in an R5 IG (could-not-determine): ihe.iti.pcf@1.1.0 is an R4 (4.0.1) package. When an R5 (fhirVersion: 5.0.0) IG compiles against it and SUSHI or the IG Publisher rejects cross-version R4-in-R5 profile resolution, report that cross-version outcome explicitly as could-not-determine with the exact tool diagnostic rather than silently dropping the dependency or hand-copying the profile. 1.2 Canonical URLs (never re-declared locally) . Reference the IHE PCF profiles, value sets, and HL7 code systems by their canonical URLs exported in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts: . | Artefact | Canonical URL | Constant in schemas/pcf-consent.ts | . | PCF Implementation Guide | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF | PCF_IG_CANONICAL | . | PCF Basic Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic | PCF_CONSENT_BASIC_PROFILE | . | PCF Intermediate Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate | PCF_CONSENT_INTERMEDIATE_PROFILE | . | PCF Advanced Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced | PCF_CONSENT_ADVANCED_PROFILE | . | PCF Basic Purpose ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/BasicPurposeVS | PCF_BASIC_PURPOSE_VS | . | PCF Advanced Security Tag ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/AdvancedSecurityTagVS | PCF_ADVANCED_SECURITY_TAG_VS | . | HL7 v3 ActReason (PurposeOfUse) | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason | HL7_ACT_REASON_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 Confidentiality | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-Confidentiality | HL7_CONFIDENTIALITY_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ActCode | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActCode | HL7_ACT_CODE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ParticipationType | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ParticipationType | HL7_PARTICIPATION_TYPE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 ConsentScope | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope | HL7_CONSENT_SCOPE_SYSTEM | . | LOINC Privacy policy / Consent | http://loinc.org (59284-0) | LOINC_SYSTEM / LOINC_CONSENT_CODE | . 1.3 Required structure of a PCF Consent instance . Every conformant IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent resource carries: . | meta.profile: one of IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, or IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced (detectPcfProfile(consent) inspects meta.profile and falls back to structural inspection). | status: "active" for an enforceable consent directive ("draft", "proposed", "rejected", "inactive", and "entered-in-error" carry no active permissions or prohibitions). | scope: http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope#patient-privacy. | category: includes http://loinc.org#59284-0 (Consent). | patient: reference to the Patient subject (Patient/<id>). | dateTime and performer (the consenting patient or authorized representative, which becomes the ODRL assigner) and organization (the custodian organization). | sourceReference or sourceAttachment: the signed paper/electronic consent artifact or questionnaire response. | policy: policy[].uri naming the overarching privacy policy (such as one of the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit policy URIs). | provision: root provision (type: "permit" or "deny"), purpose codings from http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason (TREAT, HPAYMT, HOPERAT in BasicPurposeVS, or extended PurposeOfUse codes such as HRESCH, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, PUBHLTH, ETREAT, BTG, PATRQT), optional period, actor, action, dataPeriod, data, securityLabel, and optional nested provision.provision exceptions. | . No draft purpose vocabularies: W3C DPV is a Community Group report and is refused (dpv:* or /dpv returns false in isKnownHl7PurposeOfUse). Always use HL7 v3 ActReason PurposeOfUse codes.

4632.title: 2. Translate — consentToOdrl() and the Four Implicit Policies
4632.content: consentToOdrl(consent, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts translates a FHIR R4 Consent into a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policy (PcfOdrlSet). 2.1 Field-by-field mapping (Consent → ODRL Set) . | FHIR R4 Consent element | ODRL 2.2 Set element | Translation rule | . | id + meta.versionId | uid | consentPolicyUid(consent) → urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId> (or urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id> when unversioned). | . | performer[0] (fallback patient) | assigner | The party granting or withholding consent. | . | status !== "active" | permission: [], prohibition: [] | Non-active consents emit an empty Set, which evaluates to "unknown" (or defers to implicitPolicy). | . | provision.type ("permit" / "deny") | permission / prohibition | Root provision defaults to "permit" when provision.type is omitted, per FHIR R4 Consent.provision.type. | . | provision.purpose[] (v3-ActReason) | constraint (odrl:purpose) | Each HL7 PurposeOfUse code becomes { leftOperand: "odrl:purpose", operator: "odrl:isA", rightOperand: code }, so ontological parent codes (TREAT, HRESCH, ETREAT, …) permit their sub-concepts (CLINTRL, BTG, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, …) via broaderOrSelf over HL7_PURPOSE_OF_USE (IHE PCF Vol 3 §3:5.8.2). Non-HL7 local project codes become odrl:eq. Multiple purpose codings expand into one rule per purpose (logical OR). | . | provision.period (start, end) | constraint (odrl:dateTime) | period.start → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:gteq", rightOperand: start }; period.end → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:lteq", rightOperand: end }. Date-only bounds (YYYY-MM-DD) expand to 00:00:00.000Z (start) and 23:59:59.999Z (end). | . | provision.actor[].reference | assignee | One rule per actor reference; defaults to ANYONE ("*") when actor is omitted. | . | provision.action[] | action | "read" → "odrl:display", "correct" → "odrl:modify", "access" / "collect" / "use" / "disclose" (and default) → "odrl:use". | . | provision.data[] (meaning: "instance") | target | Direct resource references (DocumentReference/ex-doc, Observation/ex-obs) become rule targets. | . | provision.data[] ("authoredby" / "related") | constraint (pcf:author / pcf:encounter) | meaning: "authoredby" → leftOperand: "pcf:author"; meaning: "related" → leftOperand: "pcf:encounter". | . | provision.dataPeriod | constraint (pcf:dataPeriod) | Clinical data creation/effective period (odrl:gteq / odrl:lteq on pcf:dataPeriod). | . | provision.securityLabel[] | constraint (pcf:securityLabel) | Confidentiality / sensitivity tags (R, V, ETH, PSY, SDV, HIV, …) become odrl:eq or odrl:isAnyOf on pcf:securityLabel. | . | Nested provision.provision[] | permission / prohibition + conflict | Child provisions inherit parent period (intersected via mergePeriods). A root permit with nested deny exceptions sets conflict: "odrl:prohibit". A root deny with nested permit exceptions (e.g. dissent except for Break-Glass BTG) sets conflict: "odrl:perm". | . 2.2 The four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets . When a patient has no explicit active Consent on file (or when their explicit Consent has expired), IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 and §1:53.4.2.4 define four overarching jurisdictional baseline policies, exported in PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS and resolved by getImplicitPolicySet(uriOrAlias): . | Canonical URI (PCF_POLICY_*_URI) | Alias(es) | Constant | Semantics | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-basic-normal | "basic-normal" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BASIC_NORMAL_SET | Permit Clinical Treatment: permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA TREAT (including ETREAT, BTG, CLINTRL, POPHLTH); non-treatment purposes return deny. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-all-normal | "all-normal", "opt-out" | PCF_IMPLICIT_ALL_NORMAL_SET | Permit All Authorized (opt-out baseline): permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA PurposeOfUse. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-break-glass-only | "break-glass-only" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BREAK_GLASS_ONLY_SET | Break-Glass Only: prohibits all uses except when odrl:purpose isA BTG (medical patient-safety override). | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-deny | "deny", "opt-in" | PCF_IMPLICIT_DENY_SET | Deny All (opt-in baseline): prohibits all odrl:use until an explicit active Consent permits access. | .

4633.title: 3. Decide — Three-Valued Evaluation, ITI-108 Reads, obtainConsent, and PROV Citations
4633.content: 3.1 decide() and evaluatePcfPolicy() (permit | deny | unknown) . decide(consentOrPolicy, req, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts evaluates a PcfDecisionRequest (actor, actorRoles, actorGroups, action, and scope / top-level purpose, dateTime, target, securityLabel, dataPeriod, author, encounter): . | Active explicit Consent governs: if one or more active, non-expired Consent resources (or translated PcfOdrlSets) are supplied, any deny across them returns "deny" (odrl:prohibit), any "permit" (with no "deny") returns "permit", and unresolved scope operands return "unknown". | Missing Scope Operand is "unknown", never "permit": if a rule constrains odrl:purpose, odrl:dateTime, pcf:securityLabel, target, or assignee and the request omits that dimension, evaluation yields "unknown". Under conflict: "odrl:perm" (such as a root deny with a Break-Glass permit exception), if the exception’s constraint is unresolved, evaluatePcfPolicy() returns "unknown" rather than prematurely denying before purpose is supplied. | Expired or absent Consent: . | If options.implicitPolicy is provided, decide() falls back to the configured implicit-policy Set (IHE PCF Vol 1 §1:53.2.2 & §1:53.4.2.5). | If no implicitPolicy is configured: an expired active Consent returns "deny", and an absent or non-active Consent returns "unknown" — never a silent "permit". | . | . 3.2 Reading consents via IHE ITI-108 (findAccessConsents) . findAccessConsents(query) and Iti108ConsentClient in fhir-harness/schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts implement the IHE ITI-108 (Find Access Consent, [ITI-108]) RESTful search transaction (GET <baseUrl>/Consent) as a Consent Consumer: . | Search parameters (buildIti108SearchUrl): patient / patient.identifier, status (defaults to "active"), actor, purpose, security-label, period, date, data, _profile, and _count. | Client-side validity filtering (evaluateConsentValidity / filterIti108Bundle): every Bundle.entry.resource of type Consent is verified against FhirConsentSchema. Entries whose status !== "active", whose patient does not match the queried patient, or whose provision.period is expired (end < now) or future-dated (start > now) are excluded from consents and recorded in ignored[] with a structured Iti108IgnoredReason ("not-active", "expired", "not-yet-valid", "patient-mismatch", "invalid-period", "invalid-consent"). | Third-state failure handling (status: "unknown"): network failures, DNS errors, request timeouts, non-2xx HTTP responses, malformed JSON, non-searchset payloads, or OperationOutcome errors return { status: "unknown", reason, detail } — never an empty consents: [] that a caller could mistake for “no consent on file”. When passing an ITI-108 result into decide(), check result.status === "unknown" first and propagate "unknown". | . 3.3 Fulfilling odrl:obtainConsent duties on DSAs via injected createPcfConsentEvaluator . cat-harness/schemas/content/odrl.ts holds no FHIR resource types or pcf:* keys. A Data Sharing Agreement (@type: "Agreement") carrying an { action: "odrl:obtainConsent" } duty evaluates consent through an injected consentEvaluator: createPcfConsentEvaluator(consents, options) callback from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts, which returns { verdict, consent: { id, versionId, uid } } to permits() / permitsWithConsent() / decideWithConsent(): . | DSA + no Consent (or unreachable ITI-108 registry) → "unknown": when odrl:obtainConsent is due and no active matching PCF Consent (or consent-verification record) is provided, permits() returns "unknown". | DSA + matching deny Consent (or expired Consent) → "deny": when the patient’s PCF Consent denies the requested actor, action, purpose, or target, the decision is "deny". | DSA + matching active permit Consent → "permit": when an active, in-period PCF Consent permits the request’s actor, action, purpose, and target (and any other DSA constraints and duties hold), permits() returns "permit". | . 3.3a Consent rules for agreements . Four rules govern consent-based agreements. Rules 2 and 4 are enforced here; rules 1 and 3 are authored in the agreement itself (the dsa document kind and its lifecycle process in folio-assistant-core). | Legal basis. An agreement carries odrl:obtainConsent only when consent is its legal basis. Agreements resting on treatment, public-health law or a research waiver carry no such duty, and this evaluator is never asked. | Version pinning. A Consent names the agreement’s fixed-version URL in R4 Consent.policy.uri. createPcfConsentEvaluator counts a Consent only when that URI equals the agreement’s version (the agreement policy’s uid, or agreementPolicyUri); consentsCitingAgreement() is the filter. An amendment that widens use is a new version URL, so the old Consent no longer counts. An amendment that narrows use needs no new consent: pass the agreement’s DCAT 3 version chain as agreementVersions (each version’s ODRL policy and its dcat:previousVersion), and an older Consent still counts while every step back to its version is a narrowing amendment. isNarrowingAmendment() decides that from the ODRL rules alone: every newer permission sits inside an older one (same or narrower action, same target and assignee, each older constraint matched by one at least as tight, each older duty kept), and every older prohibition and obligation remains. A widening step, a missing version or anything it cannot compare (such as inheritFrom) stops the walk, and new consent is needed. | Plain language. Every agreement that needs consent publishes a plain-language summary, hashed with the agreement. That summary is what the person consents to. | Scale. The jurisdiction picks one of PCF’s implicit default policies (opt-in or opt-out) and passes it as implicitPolicy. Registry reads may be cached: new Iti108ConsentClient(base, defaults, { ttlMs }). An entry ends at its TTL, at the earliest provision.period.end of its Consents, or when consentWithdrawn(id) is called for one of its Consents. | . 3.4 Citing Consent.id + Consent.meta.versionId in PROV-O decision records . Every consent-based access decision recorded in the hash-chained W3C PROV-O decision log (cat-harness/schemas/content/prov.ts, cat-harness-tools/src/workflow/prov-record.ts) must cite the exact Consent resource version used: . | Use extractConsentCitation(consent) / consentPolicyUid(consent) from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts to obtain { id, versionId, uid, status, patient, performer, policyUris }. | Include the translated consent policy uid (urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId>) in "cat-harness:underPolicy" on the prov:Activity decision record alongside the governing DSA Agreement uid, and record the Consent’s id and meta.versionId citation so any auditor can verify which version of the patient’s consent directive was in force when the decision hash (cat-harness:recordHash chained via cat-harness:previousHash) was computed. | . 3.5 One-way renderer: ODRL 2.2 Agreement to FHIR R5 Permission (output only) . HL7 FHIR R5 Permission (Trial Use) is output only: W3C ODRL 2.2 is the source of truth and nothing reads Permission back. schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts provides odrlAgreementToFhirR5Permission(agreement, options) and fhirR5PermissionToFsh(permission, options): . | FhirR5PermissionSchema and its required value-set code lists are built from hl7.fhir.r5.core#5.0.0’s StructureDefinition-Permission.json and CodeSystem-*.json (permission-status, permission-rule-combining, consent-provision-type, consent-data-meaning), so no field outside FHIR R5 Permission is ever invented. | Maps conflict (prohibit / perm) to combining (deny-overrides / permit-overrides); assigner to asserter; shared dateTime constraints to validity; the agreement’s fixed-version uid and dcterms:source to justification.evidence / justification.basis; permission / prohibition to rule.type (permit / deny); target to rule.data.resource; assignee, action (consentaction), and purpose (HL7 v3-ActReason PurposeOfUse) to rule.activity; and delete duty roughly to rule.limit (v3-ActCode#DELAU). | Every ODRL 2.2, DCAT 3, or SPDX term with no exact home in FHIR R5 Permission (including @type, profile, inheritFrom, spdx:checksum, isA, exclusive lt/gt bounds, elapsedTime, refinement, and duties or duty constraints) is returned explicitly in dropped: DroppedOdrlTerm[] rather than dropped silently. | .
