4764.title: Remote-mount a harness
4764.content: Skill remote-mount: Bring a harness, and every layer it depends on, into a checkout that does not hold it, from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories with a lock: a source.remote entry in the downstream’s root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration) and mountDefaults on the harness. Covers when to mount and when to subscribe instead, why there are no submodules and no .deps/, the transitive closure through needs and gitlinks, overrides by id, the lock, and the three states. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review, Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs, Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Review and publish a folio, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment . How a downstream folio gets the layers it is built on: . | no git submodules, ever; | no .deps/, because a dot directory collides with GitHub’s conventions and with this repository’s own dot-prefix guard; | a remote mount is a declared directory with a remote source, pinned to a full 40-character SHA; | the defaults live in the harness’s own declaration, so a downstream never restates the paths; | a downstream may override them by id, never by path; | mounts are resolved transitively across the dependency closure; | code arrives through the mounted code directories. | . |   | where | . | the process | mount-dependency.bpmn; the per-subgraph view is the remote and npm flows of mount-subgraph.bpmn | . | the schema | cat-harness/schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts, plus the remote, npm and hydrated members of SubgraphSource (schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts); the per-pin index package is subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts | . | the tool | bun run cat mount:remote (--plan to resolve without writing), and bun run cat mount:remote:check (offline) | . | the entry point | bun run cat state:mount, which the session-start hook already runs | .

4765.title: Mount, subscribe or associate: choose first
4765.content: | you want | relation | what arrives | . | to build on a harness: run its scripts, import its schemas, read its skills as your own | remote mount (source.remote in index.config.json) | the harness’s declared directories and those of everything it needs, at one pin | . | to read another graph and hold chosen parts of it | subscription (subscriptions): the kg-subscription skill | a snapshot of its declaration, then parts you materialise one at a time through the five gates | . | to know of a harness and link to it | association (associatedHarnesses): the associate-harness skill | nothing | . | to retrieve or distribute as a package | npm distribution (kg-retrieve-npm, source.npm): the npm-kg-distribution skill | an npm .tgz tarball (unhydrated source or hydrated view) | . The test is whether your code imports theirs. If it does, mount. If you only read their content, subscribe: a subscription gates every part through copyright and purpose, and a mount does not, because the code it brings is the platform you are built on.

4766.title: The two halves of the declaration
4766.content: The harness side goes in the harness’s own <name>.json and is written once by the harness’s owner: . "mountDefaults": { "path": "cat-harness", "directories": ["schemas", "scripts", "skills"] } . What arrives is what the declaration NAMES: the declaration itself, the chosen directories, and the instance-scoped files in its assets (its README and AGENTS.md). A file the declaration does not name, such as a platform.ts beside it, never arrives. Code the mounted graphs import has to sit in a declared directory. Both fields are optional, and each absence has a meaning: . | path absent means the layer’s home path (livesAt.path, else its directory in its own repository). | directories absent means every declared directory whose content is in the checkout. A branch, family or remote source is somebody’s state, not part of the harness. | . The downstream side goes in the checkout’s root index.config.json, as the source.remote of the layer it brings in. Which layers a checkout instantiates, where each comes from, and the fallback for a folio with no index are index-config’s rule. This skill covers only what a remote source means once it is declared: . { "name": "<harness>", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "<owner>/<repo>", "ref": "<40-character sha>", "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "directories": ["schemas", "skills"] }, "bootstrap": { "skip": true } } } } } . The fields are a remoteMounts entry without its harness, because the layer’s name is the harness (RemoteSourceSchema in schemas/kg/index-config.ts). A folio with no index still reads remoteMounts on its declaration. Declaring a mount in both places is an error: readDeclaredMounts throws and names both files. bun run cat index-config:migrate --write moves the entries across. Every tool that writes mounts writes through writeDeclaredMounts, into index.config.json, and none writes remoteMounts. overrides is keyed by layer name, then by directory id: . | path moves a layer. | directories replaces its default list. An id may be one the layer declares in its <name>.json or from within one of those directories (a "subgraph": true entry of skills/skills.json, such as voices); both are resolved at the pin through instanceDirectories, the resolver every on-disk reader uses. A nested id mounts its own path alone. An id declared in neither place is refused, not dropped, and the refusal says where it looked. The same holds for the harness’s own mountDefaults.directories. An id may also be a concern name, a code from code-lists/concern-group.json such as sdlc. It expands to every kind-first member the layer declares, such as sdlc/processes/ and sdlc/skills/, read from each grouping kind’s own declaration file at the pin. Each member is locked as <directory id>/<code>. A code that none of the layer’s kinds declares is refused like any other unknown id. | After a review of hydrated metadata, `mount:remote –choose [:] --directories a,b --tools x,y` writes the choice into `overrides.` (the choice, never the state), so a fresh clone replays it. It ends the review: that layer mounts as files, so its `hydrated` is dropped. The pin and consent do not move. | skip leaves it unmounted, and the lock records it as an answer. | tools names Tools this layer declares, by id, and mounts each one runnable: its definition, its implementation and their import closure. The next section but one says what that brings. | hydrated: true (here, or on the entry for its harness) mounts each chosen directory as one file: its published index.hydrated.jsonld at the pin, a hydrated source. Read what is there, then choose what to mount as files. No declaration is laid down, and needs is not followed. Where that file comes from is the next section. With no directories, a hydrated mount offers every top-level in-checkout subgraph and ignores mountDefaults.directories on purpose: that list chooses which FILES a downstream gets, and a hydrated mount is the step before choosing. Each top-level file already carries its nested subgraphs inline (hasSubgraph), so a nested one is named only when you want it on its own. | .

4767.title: Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package
4767.content: A pin’s subgraph index files (index.jsonld, index.hydrated.jsonld under <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/) are published per pin in a package, and a hydrated mount fetches them through the Tool its source names (the hydrated source’s tool, which is remote-mount unless it says otherwise). | Not committed in each repository. The files are builtAtPublish: they are computed over the checkout’s other layers, so no commit can hold them current, and a committed copy turns every re-pin’s check red. | Not generated at mount time. The downstream would need the whole index, kg-export and the framing toolchain to read one file of metadata, which is the cost a hydrated mount exists to avoid, and two downstreams could frame two different files for one pin. | . What that means in practice: . |   |   | . | the package | <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>: the index files at their published paths, and subgraph-index.json (folio-subgraph-index/v1) giving each file’s sha256 and the repository, pin and harness | . | where | assets of the GitHub release subgraph-index-<sha> in the layer’s repository, with the tarball’s folio-binary-release/v1 record beside it. Every name is computed (subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts) | . | who publishes | the subgraph-index-package Tool, run on every push to main by the reusable workflow layer-publish-subgraph-index.yml (the tools layer); a harness opts in with one uses: line | . | what a mount checks | the pin’s git tree first (a commit that does carry the file still works); otherwise the package: the tarball against its record (size, sha256), the manifest against the repository, pin and harness asked for, each file against its sha256, then the same schema and subgraph-IRI check a tree file gets | . | the lock | a directory that came from the package records the tarball’s URL and sha256 and the file’s path in it (package), so mount:lock fetches the same bytes and refuses any others | . No release for the pin is missing, and the detail says the package was looked for. A package that fails a check is missing; one that could not be fetched is could-not-determine. Neither is ever an empty mount. The record travels with the tarball, so its digest proves the transfer, not the publisher: who may publish is the repository’s write access, the same trust the git tree at the pin already rests on.

4768.title: Tools: choose by id, mount runnable
4768.content: The workflow: load the Tools’ metadata, review it, then materialise a chosen set. The first step is a hydrated mount of the declaring layer’s tools directory. Its index.hydrated.jsonld holds every Tool whole, and each Tool is its own tools/<id>/ subgraph. The last step is tools on that layer’s override: . "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "tools": ["bean-query", "bpmn-checklist", "agent-memory"] } } . Three rules govern this step: . | A Tool brings both halves. Its definition is <tools dir>/<id>/<id>.ts in the layer that declares it, by the folder convention in schemas/tools/tool-folders.ts. Its implementation is what its invoke names: . | inProcess.module, found in the declarer or in a layer whose needs names it (resolveImplementingPath’s rule; two holders is refused); | the script a bun run cat <key> command resolves to through the layers’ checkoutScripts. | . A bare runtime command (gh, beans) or manual brings no code. Both halves arrive with their import closure. A definition without its code is not a Tool you can run, and code without the modules it imports does not load: either way the checkout is half-working. | One closure walker. The closure is bootstrap-tools’ importClosure (scripts/check-closure.ts). check:tools-closure and the staging cone use the same walk. Do not write a second walker: two of them give two answers to “what does this code load”. | Directory granularity. The mount brings every declared directory the closure touches, whole. It takes the most specific declared directory (a nested one such as skills/voices mounts alone) and never a single file, so the lock schema is unchanged. A closure file in no declared directory, and an import that resolves to nothing, are refused with the file named. Neither is ever dropped. | . With tools named anywhere in a mount entry, each layer of that entry mounts the directories the closure touches, plus any its override names in directories. It does not mount its default list. A whole layer stays whole. A Tool id the layer does not declare at the pin is refused at plan time. tools together with hydrated is refused, because metadata brings no code. What it costs. A Tool folder is not a declared directory: tools/ is, and most definitions import its lib.ts. So a definition arrives with the whole tools directory, which holds every Tool’s definition. The cost that matters falls on the implementation side, which brings the directories its closure touches (in the tools layer, typically scripts and src). Without tools, the tools layer mounts every in-checkout directory it declares. The end-to-end check is the remote-mount test “load tools metadata, choose three Tools, materialise them” in the tools layer.

4769.title: Why the default path is the home path
4769.content: At its home path, a mounted layer keeps its position relative to its siblings. Two things then follow with no extra machinery: . | instanceRootsIn scans one level deep, so it finds every mounted sibling and needs resolves exactly as it does in the monorepo. | A relative import such as ../../cat-harness/schemas/… finds the file it names. | . Moving a layer by override is allowed, and the overlay still finds it through the lock (mountedInstanceRoots, mountScopeFor). The override is then responsible for any import that climbs out of the moved layer.

4770.title: The closure
4770.content: . | The harness’s declaration is read from the pinned tree, not from this checkout. | Each needs name is looked for in the same tree. | If it is not there, the planner looks for a gitlink at that tree’s root. A submodule entry is itself a pin, so a need on bootstrap resolves to litlfred/bootstrap at the gitlink’s SHA. The downstream gets the bytes and never a submodule. | A need the downstream already holds as a local layer is local: it is supplied by the checkout and never mounted over. | A need found nowhere is missing. It is never dropped. | .

4771.title: The lock, and the three states
4771.content: index.lock.json sits beside the downstream’s index.config.json and is committed. It is generated by mount:remote and never hand-edited, which is why it is a separate file rather than part of the index. Readers also accept the legacy name <name>.mount-lock.json, and both present is an error. It records: . | the pins it was written for; | for each layer: the repository, the SHA, how the pin was found (declared / same-tree / gitlink), the declaration’s digest, each directory’s tree digest, and declared layer assets (such as package.json); | what was not mounted, and why. | . The mounted bytes are not committed. With an index, each mount path is ignored by a generated block in the root .gitignore, written from the index (check:index-ignores is the gate). A path that block does not cover is reported as missing, never patched locally, because a local exclude is invisible to every other clone. In a folio with no index, a path its rules do not ignore goes into the worktree’s info/exclude. Mount path and route collisions. A mount with no path override lands at <name>/ in the downstream root, beside the downstream’s own directories, and its site routes sit beside the site-wide ones. To prevent collisions on disk and in route space: . | Reserved names: RESERVED_ROOT_AND_ROUTE_NAMES in schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts declares the one authoritative list of reserved root directories and site route names: ["skills", "tools", "docs", "assets", "glossary", "api", "payload", "branches/", "beans", "todos", "fsh-guts", "uploads", "test", "build", "_site", "_docs", "_kg"]. | Mount path check: checkMountPathCollisions (run during planning in mount:remote and by bun run cat check:mount-collisions) rejects any remote mount whose effective path (path or <name>/) collides with: . | a directory the downstream declares in its own configuration; | a reserved root or site route name; | another mount’s path. When a collision occurs, the error states how to fix it: “set path” (on the layer’s overrides.<name>.path in index.config.json or source.remote.overrides). | . | Route rules: . | Canonical: every visualiser is reachable at <base>/<harness>/<visualizer>/. Every generated link uses that form unless an alias is declared. | Alias: <base>/<visualizer>/ exists only when a declaration opts in via alias: true or alias: "<alias>" in its Visualisation declaration (coverage.visualiser). The site build refuses an alias that collides with another alias, a harness route, or a reserved site route, and names both claimants. | The route rule itself is in schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes”. | . | . Every layer ends in exactly one state: . | state | means | exit | . | mounted | on disk, hashing to the lock | 0 | . | unverified-approver | mounted, on consent no mountApprovers list checked | 0, reported apart | . | missing | not on disk, edited since mounting, not in the tree, refused, or the lock is for other pins | 1 | . | could-not-determine | the fetch failed, a declaration or lock is unreadable, or a layer is reached at two pins | 2 | . Could-not-determine outranks missing, and missing outranks mounted. A fetch that failed is never an empty layer. A fresh clone: the root’s cat bootstrap . A downstream root’s cat script is bun .github/cat.ts, not the bare runner. The runner (scripts/run-script.ts of the tools layer) is itself a mount, so on a fresh clone it is not on disk.github/cat.ts checks for it and, when it is missing, runs .github/mount-from-lock.sh (which fetches mount-from-lock.ts at the commit the lock pins for the tools layer and replays the lock, verifying every tree digest) before it hands over with the same arguments. So bun run cat <name> works from git clone with no mount step. It checks only that the runner is present, so after a re-pin run bash .github/mount-from-lock.sh by hand to replace the stale mounts. instantiate-harness.ts writes both files from the tools layer’s templates/root-bootstrap/ and sets the cat script. A root set up before that keeps a cat script that runs the bare runner until the two files are copied in. Re-pinning: from a checkout mounted from the lock . A re-pin is mount:remote --seed <name>=<owner/repo>@<sha> (it writes the pin and its consent into index.config.json), then mount:remote (it lays the bytes down and rewrites the lock). Do it in a checkout whose mounts match the lock: a fresh one, or one replayed by .github/mount-from-lock.sh. A mount with local edits is left untouched by the next mount, at its old commit, while the lock’s top-level pin moves, so CI would keep testing the old layer. --seed refuses while a mount it moves has such edits, and mount:check reports a layer entry behind its pin as missing. After the re-pin, check that the moved layer’s sha in index.lock.json is the new pin. A pin only moves forward (owner ruling, 2026-11-06, card “Pin target”, A). When layers pin different commits of a shared layer, align them forward, bottom-up: start at the lowest layer, and move each shared layer to the newest commit that any layer needs. Stop when every lock names one commit per layer. Never move a pin back to an older commit so that two layers agree. A re-pin is a cross-layer set (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Pin together every layer the change needs, re-pinned to the current mains, and verify on a fresh mount (mount:remote --fresh). A layer can need another layer’s newer commit. For example, cat-harness#1100 removed routes that were listed by hand, because a content layer above it now derives them (builtOnHostSite). So cat-harness at 6dd3746 or later needs that content layer’s change, and the tools layer’s matching one, in the same re-pin. An asset that a layer commits must also match the tools recipe that generates it, such as cat-harness’s edit-links.js. A re-pin is its own PR (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “keep repins on own PR so easier to stack dependencies”). A re-pin PR changes the pins and nothing else: index.config.json, index.lock.json, the generated uses: pins, and what regenerates from them. It carries no feature change, no workflow logic and no fix. | A feature that needs the new pins is stacked on the re-pin PR (below) rather than riding inside it. | A fix that the re-pin needs lands in the layer that owns it, and the re-pin then only moves the pin. | Counter-example: folio-assistant#2985 carried #2999 (the shared ci-setup move) and its own caches:viz gate line inside the re-pin. | The one exception: mutual dependence (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card, about 08:43Z, “A. Allow the exception”). A re-pin may share a PR with a change only when neither can pass on its own. The PR body must say why. Example: a content layer re-pinned to cat-harness#1032 failed check:tools without its own PR’s library topic, and that PR alone declared the library topic twice against the old pin. A change that merely needs the new pins is not mutual: it stacks. | . A lower layer’s new gate must not break the next re-pin. A gate or check script added to a lower layer has passed a downstream dry run before it lands, so a re-pin moves pins and nothing else. When a re-pin nonetheless fails on a gate a lower layer just added, the fix goes into that layer, not into the re-pin (prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream”). Stacking across layers (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Work that needs an unmerged PR in a lower layer does not wait for it. Develop against that PR’s branch laid over a fresh mount. A draft PR may pin the dependency PR’s full 40-hex head SHA so that its CI sees the change. A branch is never pinned, as for any pin. That draft is never marked ready or merged while it pins an unmerged commit: once the dependency lands, re-pin to its merge commit on main. That move goes forward, so “a pin only moves forward” holds throughout. The re-pin refreshes layer health (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Layer health”, A). When a re-pin moves the tools layer, it regenerates the checkout’s layer health report at the new pins and publishes it. The health check fails a re-pin once the report is more than 26 hours old and the checker has moved. The tools layer implements it. The committer re-pins, locally, and CI only verifies. The person or agent who moves a pin does the whole re-pin in their own checkout: --seed, a fresh mount:remote, the regenerated agent surface (skill:commands, agent-memory, index:render), and the local checks. That same mount:remote then publishes the new lock’s layers cache ref (below) alongside the branch, with whatever credential pushes the branch. bun run cat layers:publish retries it, and --no-layers-publish skips it. CI never builds the ref when it exists: it fetches it and verifies it against the lock. Two writers are only fallbacks: . | the re-pin train, for layers nobody re-pinned; | main’s post-merge workflow, which rebuilds the ref for every push that changes index.lock.json. | . The layers cache: one fetch, every byte still verified . Replaying a lock fetches each pinned layer from its own repository. The layers cache is one git commit in the INDEX repository whose tree is the composed overlay a replay lays down: each locked directory at its mount path, each declaration and asset, and nothing an install, a state mount or a publish build wrote. | Ref: refs/cat/layers/<key>, where the key is the sha256 of the lock’s instances. refs/cat/layers/main moves with main’s lock. | Reader: mount:lock, and through it .github/mount-from-lock.sh, the session-start hook and every CI job, first tries ONE shallow fetch of the key’s ref, then of main. A layer whose copy verifies is laid down from it. A layer that does not verify, or a ref that is missing, is fetched from its own repository as before. --no-layers-cache (or CAT_LAYERS_CACHE=0) skips it, and CAT_LAYERS_URL points it at another remote. | Writer: the committer, through mount:remote or layers:publish. It refuses unless every mount reads current, then pushes the overlay. --main also moves main. --prune <n> keeps the newest n lock refs, main, and each --keep <key>, for example the lock of every open PR. | Gate: on an index-mode pull request that changes index.lock.json, the job layers-ref of the tools layer’s layer-pr-checks.yml runs layers:check --changed-from <base>. It only asks (git ls-remote) whether the new lock’s ref is at the repository, and fails when it is not. The build and the push stay on the re-pinner’s machine, never a runner (owner, 2026-11-08). A PR that leaves the lock alone owes nothing. | Shared fallback: an IG whose origin carries no refs/cat/layers/* can name a shared cache in .github/layers-url (one URL). The root bootstrap’s mount-from-lock.sh then sets CAT_LAYERS_URL to it. Only layers at the same pin hit; the rest are fetched as before. | . The lock stays the sole authority. The cache is untrusted. Every byte taken from it is checked against the lock: the declaration’s and each asset’s sha256, and each directory’s treeDigest. These are the same checks a fetched byte passes. So a stale main still serves every layer that did not move, and a tampered ref costs time, never correctness. Trust is unchanged: consent was checked when the lock was written, and the cache cannot add a layer the lock does not name. A replay that fails is reported loudly, not swallowed: a stale mount makes local checks pass falsely.

4772.title: A changed lock re-renders the agent surface
4772.content: A mount is not done when the bytes are on disk. A newly pinned layer can bring new skills, renamed skills and new agent-memory entries, but an agent does not read the layer: it reads what is generated from it. | surface | generated by | from | . | .claude/commands/<name>.md | skill:commands | every user_invocable skill in the mounted kg graphs | . | .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md, .agents/skills/, .agents/rules/ | agent-memory | the memory directories the mounted layers declare | . So when a mount:remote run changes the lock, it runs both generators from the checkout root before it exits, and a generator that fails fails the run. A re-pin commit then carries the new layers and the surface rendered from them. --no-agent-surface opts out; --check, --plan and --staging never run it, since they change no lock a commit would carry. The list lives in one place, AGENT_SURFACE_GENERATORS in cat-harness-tools/scripts/remote-mount.ts. A new generator of something an agent reads (a rule file, a settings hook) is added there, not to a checklist: a step a person has to remember is the step that gets skipped. The process step is Task_RenderAgentSurface in mount-dependency.bpmn, between writing the lock and checking against it.

4773.title: Trust: what lets a mount proceed (H8)
4773.content: A real mount needs a person’s consent for that pin (trust.consent); a --staging mount needs none. schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts has the rules. Four things to know: . | The lock records the basis for each layer: staging, or consent with who and when. mount:remote:check re-runs the trust check against the current declaration, so consent withdrawn later reads refused. | A gitlink needs consent of its own. A layer reached through a gitlink is another repository at another commit. Give its consent on overrides.<name>.trust, for the gitlink’s SHA. | Who may consent. Declare mountApprovers and a consent.by not on the list is refused. Without the list, mounts report unverified-approver: exit 0, but never shown as clean. A checkout whose mounts index.config.json lists declares the list there, as its top-level mountApprovers; declaring it on the layer declaration as well is an error. | A refused mount is not current. Its old bytes stay on disk (an agent does not delete them). The lock records them under unmounted as leftOnDisk, and the check reports them as not mounted. | . Standing consent: a site keeps itself on an upstream branch . Pins stay per site. A site may declare, on one layer’s trust.standing, that a named person consents to following a branch — {follows: "main", consentBy, consentAt, require?: "green"}. The repin tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/repin-standing.ts, run by its standing-repin.yml workflow) then moves that pin to the branch’s newest (green) commit and writes trust.consent for the new pin, by that person and marked standing. The mount accepts it only while the same rule is still declared: withdraw or edit it and those pins ask again. A pin moved by hand still asks again, rule or not.

4774.title: Publishing a remote-mounted downstream — provision gh-pages first
4774.content: A mount brings layers into a checkout; it provisions nothing on the downstream’s remote. A downstream that publishes a site needs a gh-pages branch before GitHub Pages can be switched on, exactly as a new repository does. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in the getting-started process (getting-started §5), with the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision (idempotent, never forced; without the flag it only reports unprovisioned and the exact command), then set Pages to “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)”. A worked example is in repo-conversion §5.

4775.title: Never
4775.content: . | Never add a submodule to get a dependency, and never clone into .deps/. | Never pin a branch or an abbreviated SHA. The schema refuses both. | Never move a pin back. Align layers forward to the newest commit any of them needs (§”Re-pinning”). | Never edit a mounted directory and expect a re-mount to keep the edit, or to throw it away. A re-mount leaves edited bytes untouched and reports them as missing. Move the edit upstream, or delete the directory and re-mount. | Never mount over tracked files, or over a directory that no lock says this mount made. Both are refused. | Never read missing or could-not-determine as “that layer has nothing in it”. A layer that is not mounted is absent from every overlay. | .

4779.title: Staging and release are the same step
4779.content: A preview is this with a root under the release root; a release is this with the release root. What differs belongs to the caller: who may start it, what must be reviewed or verified first, what else lives on the same host and must survive the push. That is why feature-staging and docs-site-publish both call this process rather than restating it, and keep their own steps — the slug, the render log, restoring the open previews, the publication-manager alert — around the call.

4780.title: Name the Tool, not its steps
4780.content: The general process has one call activity, bound by the Tool: the activity names this skill, the Tool for the chosen target satisfies it, and the Tool lists its own subprocesses — the diagram of its steps (skills-and-tools, bpmn-processes). The general skill never lists them. | target | Tool | its subprocess | its message | . | GitHub Pages | gh-pages | bootstrap-tools processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn | the commit merged onto gh-pages + the QA of what is staged and what is served | . A target may need provisioning before it accepts a push; the Tool’s subprocess owns that. For GitHub Pages a gh-pages branch has to exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it, so the gh-pages subprocess creates it first — the general step does not. Another CDN is another Tool with its own subprocess, and nothing here changes. A CDN in front of an origin is a layer, not a publication host (kg-to-portal): the publication root URL stays the origin’s canonical one even when a CDN serves it.

4781.title: What this is not
4781.content: Not the verification of what a build produced — that is publish-verification, and it runs before a caller hands its tree over. Not the decision to release — the content layer’s publication step and release-lifecycle. This step renders, pushes, and says whether the push landed.

4789.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages
4789.content: Skill render-kg-to-github-pages: Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, to GitHub Pages at a publication root URL, and report the push: a status (pushed, not pushed, could not determine) and one message carrying the deployed commit and the QA result. The same steps for a staging preview and for a release; only the root URL differs. Named by: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages . Inputs, each named by whoever starts the process: . | input | what | default | . | the Knowledge Graph | a layer root, the directory holding its <name>.json | none; required | . | Subgraphs | a list of directory ids from that declaration | the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | the declaration’s iriBase, else https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/ | . Output: a status and a message, and nothing else a caller must read. | status | when | . | pushed | the staged tree had no problem, the root URL answers, its README page (README.html) answers, and every document address answers | . | not-pushed | a check ran and failed: a staging problem, or a 404 at the root or at a document address | . | could-not-determine | nothing failed, but an answer was about the way here (403, 407, 5xx, no network) | . The message is one line a caller posts as it stands: pushed 1a2b3c4 to <root> — QA: staged ok (N files, M documents); root 200; README.html 200; documents M/M answer. The commit is which bytes are live: the commit on the gh-pages branch the site is served from. Staging and release are not two processes. A preview is this process with a root under the release root (…/branches/<slug>/, say) and a release is it with the release root. Anything that differs between them (who may start it, what must be reviewed first) belongs to the process that calls this one, never in here.

4790.title: The steps
4790.content: Drawn in processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Every command below is run from bootstrap-tools, with the layer as --root. | Resolve the inputs. Read the declaration; check every Subgraph id is one it declares; settle the root URL. An unknown id is refused, never rendered as a smaller site. | Make sure gh-pages exists and Pages serves it. Pages cannot be switched on to serve a branch that does not exist, so in order: . | git ls-remote --heads origin gh-pages; if absent, push an orphan placeholder (index.html + .nojekyll); | Pages on, Source = branch gh-pages, folder /: gh api -X POST repos/<o>/<r>/pages -f 'source[branch]=gh-pages' -f 'source[path]=/' when gh is signed in, otherwise the manual step (Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages, / (root)). bun run scripts/init.ts --root <instance> runs both as site:branch and site:enabled. This provisioning belongs to this process, not to the publication step that calls it. | . | Stage the rendering. bun run scripts/site.ts --root <instance> --out <dir> [--subgraph <id>]…: every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document at the IRI it names, the files as they sit, the README page as README.md — served at <root>/README.html — and index.html, a redirect to it. The redirect is only the default: a layer that carries its own index.html or index.md at its root gets that as its landing page instead. Every generated page opens with a notice naming bootstrap-tools and the script that wrote it, and its footer links the generator and its source rather than GitHub’s editor, which would edit the gh-pages copy the next publish overwrites. | Check what was staged. site.ts --check and bun run scripts/readme-book.ts --root <instance> --check. Any problem stops here: the report says not-pushed and names the problem, and nothing is deployed. A push of a tree known to be broken is not a push to report. | Deploy. Commit the staged tree onto gh-pages as a full replace with bun run scripts/publish-site.ts --site <dir> --remote <git url>: the layer’s Pages workflow runs it on a push to main, and an agent runs it with its own git credentials for a layer that carries no workflow (bootstrap). GitHub Pages builds the branch (Jekyll, unless .nojekyll). A rejected push is rebuilt and retried, never rebased. The gh-pages commit is the one the message names. | Check what is served, and report. bun run scripts/pages-status.ts --root <instance> [--url <root>] [--sha <commit>] [--subgraph <id>]… asks the root URL and every document address, and prints the message; --json gives the whole record. Exit 0 pushed, 1 not-pushed, 3 could-not-determine. | .

A harness above these tools may have several ways of putting a rendering in front of readers, and treat GitHub Pages as one of them; nothing here needs to know that, and nothing here names it. It does not decide who may publish, whether review has happened, or what happens to other previews on the same host: those are the calling process’s.

4799.title: Render logging — the publish branch keeps its own history
4799.content: Skill render-logging: Log every render to the publish branch — what was published, removed, restored or deliberately retained — to an append-only log that lives beside what it describes. Use when adding or removing anything on gh-pages, when asking “what happened to this preview”, or before writing a workflow step that deletes a published artefact. Named by: Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history .

4800.title: The question it exists to answer
4800.content: What happened to branches/<slug>, and why? . A preview can be cleaned up because its pull request closed, removed by a dispatch somebody confirmed, or deleted by an unrelated merge to main. Without a record on the publish branch itself, which one happened is not recoverable.

4801.title: Append-only, and never anything else
4801.content: A removal is a new entry, not the erasure of an old one. The pair — the rendered and the removed that follows it — IS the history. scripts/render-log.ts offers no verb that could lose an entry: no --remove, no --edit, no id to overwrite. The never-delete property is a shape of the tool, so a caller cannot be written wrongly. Emptying a log is a person’s decision, taken deliberately, with the confirmation every durable artefact here requires (deletion-requires-confirmation). No tool and no workflow does it.

4802.title: The four events, and why retained earns its place
4802.content: | event | what it records | . | rendered | published, or re-published over itself — so “when was this last built” needs no commit archaeology | . | removed | taken down. Requires a reason, refused without one | . | restored | carried across a full-replace deploy by restore-staging. Its own event, because “somebody pushed this branch” and “an unrelated merge nearly deleted it” are different facts | . | retained | a removal was considered and refused. Also requires a reason | . retained answers “why is this still up”: a preview still standing because a liveness signal fired leaves no trace otherwise.

4803.title: Where it lives, and why that is structural
4803.content: _render-log/<YYYY-MM-DD>.jsonl, at the root of the publish branch. Outside branches/, deliberately. The cleanup runs rm -rf "branches/$SLUG", and a branch named to collide with a directory under branches/ slugifies to exactly that name. A store outside branches/ is unreachable by that command whatever the slug says; a guard you have to remember is weaker than a location that cannot be reached. One file per UTC day, not one growing file and not one per entry. Six workflows publish to this branch; a read-modify-write of a single file loses whatever landed in between, and the tool appends a line rather than rewriting. One file per entry would make “what happened this week” a directory walk.

4804.title: It does NOT survive a deploy on its own — this is the part to get right
4804.content: docs-site.yml is a full replace: git rm -r --ignore-unmatch '*' over the whole branch, then copies _site in. It is the only one of this repository’s six gh-pages publishers without keep_files: true, and it is the one that fires on every push to main. So the log is carried across that deploy by restore-staging.ts, unconditionally — not gated on open pull requests the way previews are. A preview belongs to an open PR; a log entry about a closed one is exactly what nothing would carry, and exactly what a reader needs most. A log a deploy truncates is worse than no log, because a reader will believe its entries persisted. docs-site.yml runs restore-staging.ts from main, so a change to what the restore carries is not in force until it merges. --verify checks the carried prefixes as well as branches/, because a verifier blind to half of what the restore carried reports a clean run over the loss it exists to catch. A lost prefix is reported as not recoverable by re-running anything: a preview can be rebuilt from its workflow, and a record of what was already removed cannot. Only the prefixes the restore reported as carried are verified. A determined absent was never there to lose, and asserting on it would fail every deploy before the first entry is ever written. CARRIED_PREFIXES is where that is declared; it is a list, so another carried store is a new row, not a new code path. The carry runs before the preview check, so the log is carried even when there are no previews. A carry that could not be determined is not a warning. It collapses into the restore’s own unknown, exit 2, which fails the deploy step: continuing would run the full replace and delete the record. A determined absence — the branch is readable and has no log yet — is reported rather than omitted, because “there is no log yet” and “the carry never ran” look identical in a silent report and only the second is a defect.

4805.title: Who writes an entry
4805.content: Every path that can change branches/ writes one, and scripts/tests/workflow-yaml.test.ts asserts that by job rather than leaving it to be remembered: . | path | event | how it lands | . | feature-staging.yml → stage | rendered | the same commit as the deploy. The entry goes to the root _render-log/, never into _site, which would land it at branches/<slug>/_render-log/ — inside the directory a cleanup removes | . | feature-staging.yml → stage, preview cap | removed, one per rotated preview | the same commit as the deploy, written by staging-rotate.ts; the reason names the size budget, and the summary gives slug, age and size | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, confirmed | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, refused | retained | its own commit | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup-dispatch | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | docs-site.yml → restore | carried, not written | restore-staging.ts | . The reason is the gate’s own, never a restatement of one branch of it. cleanup emits merged | labelled | closed-unmerged-and-unlabelled and the entry carries that value. A hardcoded reason would name the wrong rule for some of them, and a wrong reason reads as evidence. A removal and its record are one commit. A separate log push can fail on its own and leave a preview that vanished with nothing saying why. The rendered and retained entries are continue-on-error. A preview that deployed and whose entry did not is a gap in the record, not a failed deploy, and failing the job there would turn a logging problem into a lost review surface. The step goes red in the run, so the gap is visible. A removed entry has no such fallback and needs none: it cannot fail separately from the removal it describes.

4806.title: Writing an entry
4806.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/render-log.ts --dir <gh-pages-checkout> \ --event rendered --kind staging-preview --path branches/<slug> --slug <slug> \ --summary "preview published" --branch "$BRANCH" --commit "$SHA" --run "$RUN_URL" . The tool writes into a directory and never pushes. The workflows that call it already hold a gh-pages checkout with their own retry and concurrency handling; a second pusher racing those is a new way to lose a deploy. One job knows how to push, this one knows what to write. Reading back: --read [--day YYYY-MM-DD]. It exits 1 when any line could not be read, and prints which — a short count must be visible as short, never passed off as complete. Same rule as ci-health: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean.

4807.title: A path is checked by VALUE, never trusted by provenance
4807.content: --path is refused unless it is / or a sequence of plain segments — no .., no leading /, no backslash. The staging slug sanitiser can emit .. (input .. gives output ..), and is safe only because git rejects every ref name containing it. That invariant holds for a slug taken from a ref and does not hold for one taken from a dispatch input — and cleanup-dispatch takes exactly that. So the check is on the value, not on where it came from.

4808.title: It is a specialisation of folio-log/v1, not a rival
4808.content: schemas/sdlc/log-entry.ts already answers “what does an entry look like”, and a render entry reuses those spellings: id, at, summary, detail, references, capture. Three things differ, each deliberately: . |   | activity log | render log | . | subject | what an agent did | what was published | . | store | fsh-guts/logs/, in the repo | the publish branch | . | published | no | yes | . An agent’s audit trail is not published; a record of what is on the publish branch belongs where its subject’s absence can be seen.

4809.title: Related
4809.content: |   |   | . | the process | staging-render-log.bpmn | . | the entry shape it specialises | schemas/sdlc/log-entry.ts, sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/activity-log.md | . | how the publish branch keeps the log across a deploy | scripts/restore-staging.ts | .

4811.title: /rendered-verification — look at it, then send the picture
4811.content: Skill rendered-verification: Confirm a UI change by LOOKING at it in a browser and sending the screenshots to the author, rather than describing it. Use whenever a change touches CSS, a Liquid/HTML template, a generated page, the navbar, a board, a sticky or any rendered surface — before claiming it works, and before asking the author to review it. Covers building the site locally, taking the REAL CI build off gh-pages when the question is theme chrome or layout, driving it with Playwright in this environment, measuring computed style rather than reading the stylesheet, hit-testing a control’s centre because visible is not usable, asserting the conditions so a check cannot pass over an unstyled page, and the defect classes that are invisible to a green gate set. Named by: Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file . continual-progress holds that a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. Neither can the agent that wrote it. A stylesheet is not a rendering, a generator’s output is not a page, and a green gate set is not a screenshot.

4812.title: The rule
4812.content: A change to a rendered surface is not done until you have looked at it in a browser and sent the author the picture. Not “ran the tests”. Not “checked the CSS”. Opened it, measured the computed result, and attached the image to the turn. Sending the screenshot is part of the rule, not a courtesy: an image lets the author disagree with you in one glance.

4813.title: Why a green gate set does not cover this
4813.content: Defect classes no test catches, because the source was right and the rendering was not: . | what happens | why the suite is green | . | a generator emits raw <h3>, kramdown assigns no ids, and every heading on a page shares one anchor | the generator’s own output looks right | . | two files hold their own copy of a shared size (a rail at 40px, a sidebar at 56px) | each file has a test asserting its own copy | . | a component renders with no colour | an invalid custom-property substitution fails silently — no parse error, no console warning, just the initial value | . | a region lays out below the viewport, rendered and unreachable | the markup is correct; a !important in the theme makes the flex column inert | .

4814.title: Measure the COMPUTED result, never the stylesheet
4814.content: getComputedStyle and getBoundingClientRect are the instruments. Reading the CSS tells you what was authored; only the browser tells you what won. Measure every time: . | display, flex, min-height on a region you believe is a flex child. A !important from a theme utility class silently makes every flex value below it inert. | scrollHeight against clientHeight. A region that “does not scroll” and a region whose content is ten times its height look identical in a screenshot of the top of it. | the resolved colour, not the declaration. A custom property holding a hue substituted into color-mix() yields rgba(0,0,0,0) and no error. | . Use a control. When you suspect a value is invalid, build the minimal element in the page and read it back, rather than reasoning from the spec: the probe is a measurement, and reasoning from the spec is a claim. const probe = document.createElement("div"); probe.style.cssText = "--h:268;background:color-mix(in oklab, var(--h) 28%, transparent)"; document.body.appendChild(probe); getComputedStyle(probe).backgroundColor; // rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) -> invalid .

4815.title: A before/after pair beats an after
4815.content: Build the base branch too and shoot the same element. Without it “the dividers have colour now” is unfalsifiable. git worktree add <dir> origin/main --detach is the cheap way; symlink node_modules and the docs vendor/.bundle into it rather than re-installing. When the pair goes to a reviewer rather than confirming the change to yourself, before-after-preview (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) governs it: one build with one variable where possible, stable capture, a k of n count with its method, the status line, and where the preview sits in the review processes. It also covers papers, FHIR IGs and slide decks.

4816.title: Running it here
4816.content: Building the site is preview:site, whose header carries the two things that make a naive bundle exec jekyll fail in this repo. It is not what CI builds — CI uses the pinned remote_theme, this uses the gem — so read a theme-chrome question off the staging preview (next section), not off this. Liquid and kramdown are identical, and so is our own stylesheet. Two environment facts: . | Serve it under its baseurl. _config.yml pins baseurl: "/folio-assistant", so every stylesheet is requested at /folio-assistant/assets/…. Serving the build directory at / returns 200 for the HTML and 404 for every stylesheet — and an unstyled page renders, so the failure looks like a CSS bug rather than a 404. Symlink <serve>/folio-assistant -> <build> and serve the parent. | Pin the browser. Chromium is pre-installed but its build number will not match whatever playwright-core resolves to, and playwright install is not available. Launch with executablePath: "/opt/pw-browsers/chromium". | . Drive the control a reader would drive. page.click(".side-bar .site-title") (the avatar, which opens and closes the sidebar from 50rem up), not element.classList.add(…). A state you set by hand is a state you have not tested the way in to. And check that the state actually changed. Setting data-fa-scheme directly does not switch the scheme — the real toggle is jtd.setTheme(name). A test that silently does nothing reports the old state as the new one. Assert the switch landed (for example, the sidebar background changed) before reading anything off it. Know what that toggle does: setTheme swaps the theme’s first stylesheet, so while the new file is in flight the page has no ground but the browser’s white canvas, and it flashes white. A scheme check that only reads the SETTLED page cannot see it — hold the new sheet in flight with page.route and read the ground then, as first-paint-scheme.e2e.ts does. The rule itself lives in theme-artefacts (opt-in cat-harness.platform-ui) §”The page ground: the first paint is DARK”.

4817.title: The REAL build is reachable — take it off gh-pages
4817.content: This environment’s proxy refuses litlfred.github.io, but feature-staging.yml deploys each preview into branches/<slug>/ on the gh-pages branch, and git reaches what HTTP cannot: . git fetch origin gh-pages S=claude-my-branch-slug # the deploy comment names it mkdir -p "/tmp/rv/folio-assistant/branches/$S" git archive "FETCH_HEAD:branches/$S" | tar -x -C "/tmp/rv/folio-assistant/branches/$S" cd /tmp/rv && nohup python3 -m http.server 8091 >/dev/null 2>&1 & # → http://127.0.0.1:8091/folio-assistant/branches/$S/<page>.html . That is the pinned remote_theme, the composed tree, the mounted layers and the post-Jekyll steps — the thing CI publishes. A whole preview is ~90 MB; git archive FETCH_HEAD:branches/$S page.html assets takes just what a page needs. Mount it at the branches/ path, not at the site root. A staged page requests /folio-assistant/branches/<slug>/assets/…, so serving the extract at /folio-assistant/ 404s every stylesheet.

4818.title: Assert the CONDITIONS, or the check passes over nothing
4818.content: An unstyled page still renders. It still answers elementFromPoint. It still returns PASS. A run mounted at the wrong path reports a pass over a page with zero stylesheets; what gives it away is the numbers beside the verdict, not the verdict. So every rendered check reports, beside its verdict: . | document.styleSheets.length — zero or one means the page is bare; | a count of responses with status >= 400, collected from page.on("response"); | the precondition the defect needs — the class, the state, the element count. If the bug only appears when fa-has-fullwidth is set, a run where it is unset has not tested anything. | . A check that cannot tell a styled page from a bare one is not a check: could-not-determine rendered as a pass. A COUNT over the built site needs its instrument validated first . Before trusting any “N of M pages have X”, run the instrument on a known positive AND a known negative, and on one positive of each way X can appear. Naive instruments give confident wrong numbers: an exact class match misses the theme’s own variant, a substring match counts the class name quoted in prose, a link count takes a stylesheet href as a way out. For navigated pages, the instrument that holds is <nav class="fa-nav" OR id="site-nav". For a site-wide count, the gh-pages route above scales. Use a --filter=blob:none --sparse clone of gh-pages, with sparse patterns for the files counted, and exclude branches/. All HTML is about 1.7 GB and takes minutes; one directory takes seconds.

4819.title: Visible is not usable — hit-test the control’s CENTRE
4819.content: A control can have the right size, the right colour and the right label, and still be un-clickable because something is painted over it — for example a wrapper that computes to height 0 because its only child is position: absolute, letting a flow sibling paint across the field. const b = el.getBoundingClientRect(); const hit = document.elementFromPoint( Math.round(b.x + b.width / 2), Math.round(b.y + b.height / 2)); const usable = hit && (hit === el || el.contains(hit) || hit.contains(el)); . Two ways this test lies: . | It resolves INSIDE the control. elementFromPoint returns the deepest element, often an <svg> or <span> within a button. hit === el alone reports a working control as covered — which is what the contains pair above is for. | It reports a preview-only overlay. The staging banner (a <div> with no class, z-index: 9999, a child of <body>) exists only on previews. Identify the coverer (document.elementsFromPoint(x, y).slice(0, 3)) before calling it a defect: what is on top decides whether it ships. | . Where the covered control is the ONLY route back to a state — the magnifier that reopens a collapsed search — being un-clickable means an action whose inverse is not reachable.

4820.title: Two environment facts that cost cycles rather than correctness
4820.content: . | Never pkill -f "http.server" from the shell running one. The pattern matches your own process group and kills the command issuing it — exit 144, no output, looks like the tool failed. Start each server on a fresh port in its own invocation instead. | Probe scripts must not be left in the repository root. check:undeclared-files fails the gate set on a stray probe.mjs. Playwright needs the script where playwright resolves, so write it to the repo root, run it, and delete it in the same command. | .

4821.title: What to send
4821.content: The frames that answer a question the author would otherwise have to ask: . | before and after of the same element, same viewport; | the surface in both colour schemes, if the change touches colour; | the state that is hard to describe — a region scrolled to its end, a menu open, an empty case. | . Caption them with what to look at, not with what they are. “The nav crushed to a 64px sliver, no home link” is a caption; “navbar screenshot” is a filename. SendUserFile is the mechanism; write into the working directory or the scratchpad, since a file the author cannot open is not a deliverable.

4822.title: Accessibility is measured here too
4822.content: Unique heading anchors and the 3:1 bar for meaningful non-text content are rendered facts: compute the contrast from the two resolved colours rather than from the tokens, because the token you authored and the colour that won are different questions.

4823.title: Listen for pageerror, or a crash reads as a missing feature
4823.content: A throw early in a page’s init() takes the rest of init() with it. The symptom is a feature that is simply not there — which looks exactly like a feature that did not mount — and a swallowed init is silent in a screenshot. So: attach the listener, and assert zero. page.on("pageerror", (e) => errors.push(e.stack || e.message)); . And check the base branch before you claim a crash is yours — or before you claim it is not. One run against a build of origin/main tells “something I just broke” from “a live defect nobody had reported”.

4824.title: A STATIC read of a client-rendered page is not verification — in either direction
4824.content: This skill stops a false red as well as a false green. Grepping a page’s committed HTML for content the page fetches at runtime proves nothing. The content is absent whether the page works or not. A library viewer, for example, carries DATA_HREF = "../../../assets/library/index.json", fetches it, and filters by layer. Its committed index.html never holds the entry names, so grepping it for them returns the same answer for a working page and a broken one. Loading it in Chromium settles it in one command. A false red files a bug against working code and sends the next agent to rewrite a correct generator, and because the report carries measurements it reads as thoroughly evidenced. If a page assembles any of its content after load, open it. The tell is cheap to check: a fetch, an XMLHttpRequest, a DATA_HREF, a <script> that writes into the DOM. Finding one means a static read cannot answer the question, and §"Running it here" above is how to answer it instead.

4825.title: What this does NOT replace
4825.content: The gate set. This is the layer above it: gates catch what is checkable from the source, and this catches what is only true once a browser has laid it out. A change that skips either is unverified.

4827.title: /repo-conversion — folio-assistant over a repo that already has a life
4827.content: Skill repo-conversion: Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn, Task_ScanRepo, Task_ChooseHarnessed and Task_ConfirmImport (both non-relaxable). Scanner: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts.

4828.title: 0. The one rule
4828.content: Scan, show, ask, then move — and never in any other order. The author’s repository is the thing of value; the scaffolding is replaceable. A wrong import is not fixed by a git checkout, because the author has to work out what the agent did. Task_ConfirmImport is marked relaxable="false" in the BPMN, and a content package may not declare it away.

4829.title: 1. Scan — read-only, and honest about its limits
4829.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts # human-readable report bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts --json # same, as facts . It walks the working tree (respecting .gitignore) and sorts what it finds into three buckets: . | bucket | means | typical | . | library | external source material — something somebody else wrote, that the folio will cite or ingest | PDFs, papers, scans, datasets, references/, papers/, sources/ | . | content | material authored here, that could become folio blocks | Markdown prose, docs/, notes/, drafts/, .tex | . | unclassified | it could not tell | everything else, and it is reported, not hidden | . unclassified is reported, never forced. A two-bucket scanner’s mistakes arrive as moved files; this one reports what it could not place, and the author disposes of it. The classification is by path convention and extension only. It does not read file contents or call a model, so the author can disagree with any row of it in one word. Outside-content candidate scanning — preserving evidence and refutations . In repositories with formal, analytical, or domain-specific content, crucial verification scripts, macros, and counterexamples often live outside the primary content tree (content/ or folio/); a conversion that carries only that tree drops the evidence that some claims are false. scan-repo-content.ts scans outside the content tree and classifies these artifacts into read-only candidate classifications (defined by the content-type layer’s conversion refinement skill), reporting source location, rationale, and linkStatus (linked when referenced by at least one content block, or unlinked when orphaned). Like the general scan, candidate scanning never writes, moves, or modifies files; it presents the candidates to the author and agent so decisions can be made before importing.

4830.title: 2. Show, then ask — three questions, all as selections
4830.content: Present the scan as counts and a handful of examples per bucket, never as a 1,400-line file list. Then three questions, each answerable by picking. Load interaction-modality first. Q1 — import at all? . | Import everything the scan found (recommended) | Import only the library bucket — sources now, prose later | Import nothing; just set up folio-assistant | Let me pick bucket by bucket | . Q2 — where does each group go? Only for groups the scan was not confident about, and only when Q1 was not “nothing”. Offer library/ vs content/ per directory, not per file (a per-file interrogation is the accessibility failure in interaction-modality §0). Q3 — leave in place, or reorganise? . | Leave everything where it is (recommended) — the folio references the files at their current paths. Nothing moves, every existing link still works, and the decision stays open. | Reorganise into library/ and content/ — tidier, and it rewrites paths. Offer this only on a clean working tree, do it in its own commit, and use git mv so history follows. | . Recommend leave in place by default: a broken relative link in somebody’s README is a defect.

4831.title: 2a. Markers — choose what the harness reads (declare, don’t slurp)
4831.content: A harness declares what it reads in a repository; it does not take all of its content. The principle is directory-conventions §”A marker declares what is read, and nothing else is”. The scan’s fourth section, markers, lists the content a harness COULD be told to read: a sushi-config.yaml (an IG: contentTypes.ig), a legacy dak.json (contentTypes.dak), .bpmn processes, a work items store, library/, uploads/, Lean (contentType: paper) and folio manifests (contentType: document). For each it gives the paths, whether it is already declared — declared, not-declared, or unknown when there is no readable index.config.json to ask — and the snippet that would declare it, with where it goes (index.config.json#contentTypes, or a local layer’s <name>.json#directories). Content types come from the registry (defaultContentTypes; an { indexSection } type is checked against contentTypes.<id>), directory facets are checked against the registered graph typologies, and only the evidence the registries cannot state is a short table in cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/content-markers.ts. Where each kind of content lives is directory-conventions. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers # the list bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers --json # same, as facts . A plain command: any agent host (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot) or a person at a shell runs it, with no MCP server. It writes nothing. Q0 — which of these should the harness read? (Task_ChooseHarnessed, non-relaxable). Ask it the interaction-modality way — the full question in the chat, then a tap card where the host has one, otherwise a numbered pick-list with its default stated. Never a typed reply. Offer only the markers that are not-declared (or unknown), one option each: . | None of these for now (the default) — nothing is declared; the scan can be run again any time | contentTypes.ig — sushi-config.yaml, input/fsh/, … (the FHIR IG) | directories: processes — processes/ (7 BPMN files) | Let me pick several — the same options as a multi-select | . The default declares nothing, and the agent never declares a marker the person did not pick. Declare exactly the picks — the scan’s suggestion snippet, at its suggestion.at — in the scaffolding commit, or in its own commit on a layer that already exists. After setup, too. The same question fits any layer at any time: “what else could this harness declare?” is --markers on the layer’s repository, then Q0. Rows already declared are shown for context and are not offered. A content type registered by a higher harness layer appears as a hint when that layer is not loaded, with a note saying where the type lives. Declaring a scoped content type is not a boolean flag: its include list states everything that layer’s readers will read, so confirm the list with the person and consult that layer’s build-pipeline skill for how additional paths are added later.

4832.title: 3. Dispatch the ingestion
4832.content: Ingestion proper is library/processes/document-ingestion.bpmn (and the content layer’s document-intake refinement skill when converting into a content folio). What this skill decides is how much parallelism, and it is a question for the author because it spends their tokens: . | scale | when | how | . | inline | under ~10 documents | do it here, no subagents | . | one agent | tens of documents, one kind | a single background agent, reporting per document | . | small swarm | hundreds, or several distinct kinds | dispatch-agent (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — 2–4 agents partitioned by directory, never by file count | . Partition by directory because a per-file partition puts two agents in the same manifest, and the conflicts cost more than the parallelism saves. Open one work item per ingestion front before dispatching — running the existence check in todo-manager.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) §”Check before you create” first — so a session that dies mid-import leaves a plan behind rather than a half-full library/.

4833.title: 4. The conversion itself
4833.content: Once Q1–Q3 are answered, folio_init against the existing directory. It refuses rather than overwrites where a file is already present, which on this branch is the common case (README.md, .gitignore, a docs/). Read its report rather than assuming; the files it declined to write are the ones you now merge by hand: . | AGENTS.md — if one exists, merge; do not replace. It is the most valuable file in the repository for the next agent. | README.md — never replaced. readme-sections.ts only writes inside marker pairs the author has opted into, so offer to add markers rather than content. | .gitignore — append the folio entries; keep theirs. | . If the remote is empty, push main first. A repository with work locally can still have an empty remote, and GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default. Run init-folio or push main before any feature branch. If main has no harness yet, land a setup-only PR first. A fork or an existing repository whose main has no index.config.json and index.lock.json gives the full PR checks nothing to compare against: the base side fails before any test runs, and the PR’s own gates are skipped. So open one small PR with only what folio_init writes and the pins, merge it, and only then branch for content. Draft-tier checks never build the base, so this does not show until the content PR leaves draft. The setup-only PR has a Tool: instantiate-harness. It pins the harness and every layer it needs, mounts them, commits the setup on harness/<harness>, opens that PR, and renders the branch’s preview at gh-pages:branches/<branch>/. On a repository with nothing mounted yet, run it from a fresh clone of the tools layer: . git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools /tmp/cht echo "<where the author consented>" | bun run /tmp/cht/scripts/instantiate-harness.ts \ --repo . --harness <owner/repo> --consent-by <who> [--plan | --local] . The setup also writes .github/cat.ts and .github/mount-from-lock.sh and sets the root’s cat script to bun .github/cat.ts, so after the merge a fresh clone needs no mount step: the first bun run cat … mounts the layers. --plan prints the closure and every step and writes nothing; --local commits on the branch and pushes nothing. The harness’s own adoption steps are its checkout scripts instantiate:<harness> (files it declares, committed with the setup) and prepare:<harness> (what the site is built from, never committed). For an IG on a FHIR harness these declare contentTypes.ig and build the IG’s first AST. A harness built on this platform may add adoption steps of its own for its kind of repository, for example about CI that already publishes a site on every push. Ask skill_list for the skill governing that kind before calling the conversion done.

4834.title: 5. Publishing — provision gh-pages first; an overlay needs it too
4834.content: An overlay never reaches getting-started §5 by itself, so this section repeats the one step a publishing route cannot skip: provision gh-pages before GitHub Pages is switched on. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in getting-started.bpmn, on the shared path after scaffolding and before the Pages build, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. The tool is pages-bootstrap: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts # reports `unprovisioned` (exit 3) and the exact command when gh-pages is absent bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision # pushes an orphan gh-pages: placeholder index.html + .nojekyll . --provision is idempotent and never forces a push, and nothing creates a remote branch without it. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — the script prints the source it expects. When the repository’s publish workflow pushes gh-pages, “GitHub Actions” is the wrong source: the workflow would push a branch Pages was never told to serve. The same holds for an overlay that remote-mounts its dependencies. A mount brings layers in; it does not provision anything on the downstream’s remote.

4835.title: 6. Anti-patterns
4835.content: . | Moving a file before Q3 is answered. | Reporting a two-bucket classification. If unclassified is empty on a real repository, suspect the scanner rather than celebrate it. | A per-file confirmation loop. See §2. | Swarming a 12-document import. The dispatch overhead exceeds the work. | Replacing an existing AGENTS.md or README.md. Merge, or leave. | Treating the scan as ingestion. It reads; it never writes. Ingestion is a separate process with its own diagram and its own gate. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. See §5. | Dropping outside-content math artifacts or unlinked audit refutations. Carrying only the primary content tree (content/ or folio/) drops outside proofs, computations, and refutations showing that some paper claims are false. See §1. | .

4837.title: Code node review
4837.content: Process_CodeReview · advisory · 4 step(s) . Judging changed CODE NODES — Tool definitions and schema definition nodes — on whether they are correct NODES, not merely correct code. You are in this process when what changed is a node that happens to be TypeScript. The distinction is the whole reason it is separate from ordinary code review: a file can compile, pass its tests, and still declare the wrong thing, name a skill that does not exist, or advertise a mechanism the pipeline does not actually invoke. The gateway picks by node KIND because the questions differ. A Tool is judged on whether its mechanism is the one that runs; a schema definition node on whether it says what it is and its references resolve. i i i i
